Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
A.q: A 64-year-old man is admitted with an inferior myocardial infarction. His heart rate falls to 46 with narrow QRS complexes and P waves that are either inverted (retrograde P waves) or buried in the QRS. Which rhythm is most likely?
opts: Atrial flutter fills the baseline with sawtooth flutter waves at an atrial rate of 250 or more, outnumbering the QRS complexes. This man has a slow rate of 46 and only one P wave per beat, inverted or buried in the QRS. Tell: sawtooth waves mean flutter; a single retrograde or hidden P wave means a junctional origin.

Focal atrial tachycardia is a fast rhythm, over 100 and usually 150 to 250, from one ectopic atrial focus, with one consistently abnormal P wave before each QRS and a normal PR of 0.12 to 0.20 seconds. His rate is 46 and his P waves are inverted or buried. Tell: fast with a P before every QRS is atrial; slow with retrograde P waves is junctional.
ruled out by a stated finding

Sinus bradycardia fits the slow rate, but the impulse starts in the sinus node, so every QRS has a uniform P wave before it with a PR of 0.12 to 0.20 seconds. P waves that are inverted after the QRS or buried in it do not fit. Tell: same slow rate, but a junctional rhythm loses the normal P wave and PR interval.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. A regular, narrow-complex rhythm at 46 with P waves inverted or buried in the QRS means the impulse starts in the atrioventricular (AV) node: a junctional rhythm, usually 40 to 60. When the low node fires first the P wave is retrograde, after the QRS; mid-node firing buries it. Inferior myocardial infarction is a listed cause.

A.io: Identify medical care strategies for ventricular dysrhythmias for the following populations. 3. adult 4. elderly
A.q: An 84-year-old woman with long-standing hypertension has fatigue and dizziness. Her electrocardiogram shows P waves and wide QRS complexes at two separate rates with no relationship, the ventricular rate 36. She has had no tick bites, infections or recent procedures. Which cause of this rhythm is most likely?
opts: Correct. P waves and wide QRS complexes at two unrelated rates, with a ventricular rate of 36, are complete block. Its most common cause is acquired disease of the conduction system, especially degenerative change from old age, chronic hypertension and diabetes, and she is 84 with long-standing hypertension and no infection or procedure.

Lyme carditis is a listed cause of complete block, but she has had no tick bites. In an 84-year-old with long-standing hypertension, the most common cause is degenerative conduction disease. Tell: the stem rules out the infectious causes on purpose.
ruled out by a stated finding

Increased vagal tone is a cause of first-degree and Mobitz type I block, not complete block, and it does not fit an 84-year-old. Degenerative conduction disease, driven by age and hypertension, is the most common cause. Tell: vagal tone belongs to the milder blocks.

Bacterial endocarditis with an associated abscess is a listed cause of complete block, but she has had no infection. Degenerative conduction disease of old age and hypertension is the most common cause. Tell: without an infection, an abscess cannot explain the block.
ruled out by a stated finding

A.io: Identify medical care strategies for atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias for the following populations. 3. adult 4. elderly
A.q: A 70-year-old man with heart failure is admitted with pneumonia and a low oxygen level. His pulse is irregular at 120. His electrocardiogram shows a P wave before every narrow QRS, but the P waves take at least three different shapes in the same lead and the intervals between beats vary. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Atrial fibrillation is also irregular, but it is irregularly irregular with absent P waves and no PR interval. This patient has a P wave before every QRS, so organized atrial activity is present. Tell: irregular with no P waves is atrial fibrillation; irregular with three or more P-wave shapes is multifocal atrial tachycardia.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. An irregular, narrow-complex rhythm at 120 with a P wave before every QRS in at least three distinct shapes in the same lead is multifocal atrial tachycardia, driven by multiple atrial foci. It typically appears when patients with heart failure or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease are acutely ill, as he is with pneumonia and a low oxygen level.

Focal atrial tachycardia arises from a single ectopic focus outside the sinus node, so it is regular with one consistent abnormal P-wave shape. His intervals vary and his P waves take three shapes, which takes several foci. Tell: one abnormal P shape in a regular rhythm means focal; three or more shapes in an irregular rhythm means multifocal.

Sinus arrhythmia is a normal, physiologic irregularity at 60 to 100 that speeds with inspiration and slows with expiration, with uniform P waves. His rate is 120 in an acutely ill man, and his P waves change shape from beat to beat. Tell: sinus arrhythmia keeps one P-wave shape; multifocal atrial tachycardia shows at least three.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following arterial occlusive disease and aortic aneurysm: 2. Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
A.q: A 65-year-old man has a painful, swollen right groin two days after a cardiac catheterization through the femoral artery. Ultrasound shows a blood-filled cavity outside the arterial wall, communicating with the lumen. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Atheroembolism causes painful blue toes from small-vessel debris, usually with palpable pulses. A swollen, painful groin with a cavity outside the arterial wall after catheterization is a pseudoaneurysm. The finding is at the puncture site, not in the toes.

Correct. A pseudoaneurysm is a communication between the arterial lumen and overlying connective tissue after arterial rupture, forming a blood-filled cavity outside the vessel wall. The common site is the femoral artery after cardiac catheterization, from laceration by the access needle, and pain comes from swelling or nerve compression.

Acute limb ischemia is sudden occlusion of a previously patent artery, with a cold, pale, pulseless limb. He has a painful, swollen groin and a blood-filled cavity outside the arterial wall after catheterization, which is a pseudoaneurysm. Local swelling, not distal pulselessness, is his problem.

A true aneurysm involves all three layers of the vessel wall, as a saccular outpouching or a fusiform dilation. His ultrasound shows a blood-filled cavity outside the arterial wall after a femoral puncture, which is a false aneurysm, a pseudoaneurysm. Outside the wall means false.

A.q: A 72-year-old man is diagnosed with an acute aortic dissection. His family asks what happens if it is not treated. Which statement is accurate?
opts: Correct. Acute untreated aortic dissection has a high mortality rate. That is why management moves quickly: systolic pressure is reduced to 100 to 120 mmHg with esmolol or nitroprusside, pain is managed, and surgery grafts and replaces the diseased portion of the aorta.
Only the legs are at risk

Aortic dissection is a tear in the aorta itself, not a leg problem, and the stakes are much higher. Acute untreated aortic dissection carries a high mortality rate. That is why blood pressure is lowered at once and the diseased aorta is grafted and replaced.

Nothing supports spontaneous healing as the expected course; acute untreated dissection has a high mortality rate. Treatment aims to stop progression by lowering blood pressure, then replace the diseased aorta surgically. A reassuring answer here would mislead the family.

A pseudoaneurysm is a separate lesion, a blood-filled cavity outside the vessel wall, typically after femoral catheterization. The danger of untreated acute dissection is a high mortality rate. The family's question has a blunter answer than a change of lesion type.

Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
A.q: A 68-year-old woman with right-sided heart failure is told her palpitations come from atrial flutter. She is stable. Which description best fits her electrocardiogram?
opts: Sawtooth waves outnumbering the QRS complexes

Correct. In atrial flutter the atria fire at 250 or more and the atrioventricular (AV) node blocks some impulses, so sawtooth flutter waves outnumber the narrow QRS complexes; 2:1 block is the most common pattern. Right-sided heart failure is one of the settings in which flutter is commonly seen, as in this woman.
One abnormal P wave before every QRS

One abnormal P wave before every QRS describes focal atrial tachycardia, a single ectopic atrial focus usually firing at 150 to 250 with one P wave per QRS. Flutter has more atrial waves than QRS complexes because the node blocks some of them. Tell: count atrial waves per QRS; more than one in a sawtooth line is flutter.
No P waves and an irregularly irregular rhythm

Absent P waves with an irregularly irregular rhythm is atrial fibrillation. Flutter instead shows organized sawtooth waves, and with a fixed block such as 2:1 the ventricular rhythm is regular. Tell: a chaotic baseline without discrete atrial waves is fibrillation; a repeating sawtooth is flutter.
Three or more P-wave shapes in one lead

At least three different P-wave shapes in one lead is multifocal atrial tachycardia, usually in acutely ill patients with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or heart failure, with one P wave per QRS. Flutter shows a repeating sawtooth pattern with more atrial waves than QRS complexes. Tell: changing P shapes mean multiple foci; a repeating sawtooth means flutter.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
A.q: A 41-year-old woman has had palpitations for a month. The monitor reads a regular rate of 130, and her rhythm strip is shown. Which of the following would most likely account for this rhythm?
opts: Hypothyroidism is a listed cause of sinus bradycardia and of sick sinus syndrome, slowing the sinus rate below 60. Her sinus rhythm is fast at 130. Tell: the thyroid pair splits by direction; hyperthyroidism is on the list of pathologic causes of sinus tachycardia, hypothyroidism on the slow list.

Increased intracranial pressure is listed among the causes of sinus bradycardia, so it would slow this rhythm below 60, not raise it to 130. A fast sinus rate instead points to causes such as pain, anxiety, hypovolemia, anemia, hypoxia or hyperthyroidism. Tell: raised intracranial pressure goes with a slow sinus rate.

Digoxin is listed with beta blockers and nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers as a drug cause of sinus bradycardia; it slows the sinus rate. The drug causes of sinus tachycardia are stimulants, anticholinergics, or abrupt withdrawal of a beta blocker or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker. Tell: digoxin belongs on the slow list.

Correct. A regular rhythm at 130 with a P wave before every narrow QRS is sinus tachycardia, which is usually the result of a physiologic or pathologic process. Hyperthyroidism is one of the listed pathologic causes, alongside hypovolemia, anemia, hypoxia, pulmonary embolism and myocardial infarction, and it fits a month of palpitations.
A.alt: Rhythm strip with closely spaced, regular narrow complexes, each preceded by an upright P wave

A.q: An 80-year-old man is found unresponsive and pulseless. The monitor shows a flat line in two leads with no P waves or QRS complexes. Compressions are underway. Which drug is a mainstay of treatment?
opts: Lidocaine may be considered in shock-refractory ventricular fibrillation, not in asystole. Asystole is treated with high-quality compressions and epinephrine every 3 to 5 minutes. Tell: a flat line gets epinephrine, not an antiarrhythmic.

Correct. A flat line in two leads with no P waves or QRS complexes is asystole, which is unshockable. High-quality chest compressions and epinephrine 1 mg (1:10,000) by intravenous or intraosseous push every 3 to 5 minutes are the mainstays of treatment, and early intubation is considered.

Amiodarone is for ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia that persists after shocks. Asystole is unshockable, and its mainstays are high-quality compressions and epinephrine. Tell: antiarrhythmics follow shocks, and asystole is never shocked.

Magnesium is the treatment that breaks torsades de pointes. Asystole is treated with high-quality compressions and epinephrine every 3 to 5 minutes, with early intubation considered. Tell: a flat line with no QRS has no rhythm for magnesium to fix.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
A.q: A 56-year-old woman has fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, dry skin and a heart rate of 54. Echocardiogram shows a large pericardial effusion without chamber collapse. Which test best addresses the cause her features suggest?
opts: Nothing in her history points to tuberculosis; her fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, dry skin and slow heart rate point to myxedema. A tuberculin skin test belongs in the effusion workup when tuberculous pericarditis is a concern, which would also prompt acid-fast stain and mycobacterial culture of pericardial fluid. Tell: exposure history points to tuberculosis; cold intolerance points to the thyroid.

Correct. Fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, dry skin and a heart rate of 54 suggest myxedema (hypothyroidism), a metabolic cause of effusion. Thyroid function tests sit in the effusion lab workup specifically for myxedema, and the underlying cause is usually found through a careful history and physical examination, exactly as her features show.

An antinuclear antibody belongs to the rheumatologic workup, which fits an effusion when the history suggests an autoimmune disease. Her clues are not rheumatologic: weight gain, cold intolerance, dry skin and bradycardia match myxedema, which thyroid function tests address. Tell: joint or systemic autoimmune clues send you to rheumatologic testing; hypothyroid features send you to the thyroid.

Blood cultures look for infection, and she has no fever or other sign of a purulent process. When purulent pericarditis is suspected, pericardial fluid is sent for Gram stain and bacterial and fungal culture. Her weight gain, cold intolerance and slow heart rate instead point to myxedema and thyroid function tests. Tell: infection needs signs of infection.

Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
A.q: A 63-year-old man has an incidental 4.0 cm ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm on a chest radiograph and follow-up imaging. He has no symptoms. Which surveillance plan is appropriate?
opts: Computed tomography or magnetic resonance every 3 to 5 years

Correct. A root, ascending or descending thoracic aneurysm under 4.5 cm is followed with computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging every 3 to 5 years. His 4.0 cm ascending aneurysm is asymptomatic and below every repair trigger, so this interval applies.
Abdominal ultrasound every three years with no other imaging

Three-yearly ultrasound is the plan for small abdominal aortic aneurysms of 3.0 to 3.9 cm, not the thoracic aorta. His ascending thoracic aneurysm is followed with computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging. Abdominal surveillance does not image the chest.
Open repair with aortic root replacement within the month

Asymptomatic ascending repair is generally indicated above 5.5 cm or with growth over 0.5 cm per year. At 4.0 cm with no symptoms he needs surveillance, not surgery. Open repair with root replacement is the method once repair is indicated, not the plan now.
Computed tomography or magnetic resonance every 6 to 12 months

Imaging every 6 to 12 months applies to thoracic aneurysms of 4.5 to 5.4 cm. At 4.0 cm, his aneurysm is below 4.5 cm, so the interval is every 3 to 5 years. Check which side of 4.5 cm the measurement falls.

A.q: A 52-year-old man with uncomplicated superficial thrombophlebitis of the forearm after an intravenous catheter is discharged on warm compresses, elevation and an anti-inflammatory drug. He is anxious that the clot could travel to his lungs. Which follow-up instruction is most appropriate?
opts: A recheck at 24 to 48 hours is too early to tell whether an uncomplicated superficial clot is resolving or progressing, and nothing in his course calls for urgent review. The scheduled repeat examination falls within 7 to 10 days, and only persistent or worsening signs at that visit lead to a repeat duplex ultrasound.

Six to 8 weeks leaves a possibly progressing clot unchecked far too long for a man just started on compresses, elevation and an anti-inflammatory drug. The repeat examination belongs within 7 to 10 days, when resolution versus progression can be judged and a repeat duplex ultrasound ordered if signs persist or worsen.

Waiting for fever would miss a clot that persists or extends without infection, because progression is judged by examination, not by temperature. Management schedules a repeat examination within 7 to 10 days for everyone, with a repeat duplex ultrasound if the signs persist or worsen.

Correct. His superficial thrombophlebitis is uncomplicated and already on the standard regimen of warm compresses, elevation and a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID). The next step is a repeat physical examination within 7 to 10 days to judge resolution versus progression; persistent or worsening signs then prompt a repeat duplex ultrasound.

A.q: A 54-year-old man has a regular narrow complex tachycardia at 210. His blood pressure is 72/40, and he is confused and sweating. Which is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
opts: Adenosine, repeated once if needed, follows a vagal maneuver in stable supraventricular tachycardia; it may convert the rhythm or slow it enough to show P waves. His blood pressure of 72/40 and confusion make him unstable, so a drug trial would delay the shock he needs. Tell: stable gets vagal maneuver then adenosine; unstable gets cardioversion.

A vagal maneuver is the first-line step only for stable supraventricular tachycardia. With a blood pressure of 72/40, sweating and new confusion he is hemodynamically unstable, and immediate synchronized cardioversion comes first. Tell: check blood pressure and mental status before choosing a maneuver over a shock.

Correct. A regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 210 with a blood pressure of 72/40, confusion and sweating is hemodynamically unstable supraventricular tachycardia, which gets immediate synchronized cardioversion: a timed shock at decreased voltage. Collapse like this is expected once the rate goes above 200, as his has.

An unsynchronized shock is not the treatment for unstable supraventricular tachycardia; the shock used is synchronized, meaning timed, and given at decreased voltage. He has a pulse and a regular narrow rhythm, the setting for synchronized cardioversion. Tell: an organized narrow-complex rhythm in an unstable patient means a timed, synchronized shock.

A.q: A 77-year-old woman has no symptoms, but her routine electrocardiogram shows P waves at a steady rate with a constant PR interval and an occasional P wave not followed by a QRS. Which is the most appropriate management?
opts: Observation suits asymptomatic first-degree or Mobitz type I block, not this pattern. A constant PR with an occasional dropped QRS is Mobitz type II, considered dangerous even without symptoms. Tell: in type II, the lack of symptoms does not buy time.

Catheter ablation is itself a listed cause of Mobitz type II block, so it cannot treat it. Her constant PR with an occasional dropped QRS is Mobitz type II, treated definitively with a permanent pacemaker. Tell: a procedure that causes a block cannot fix it.

Correct. Steady P waves, a constant PR and an occasional P wave without a QRS are Mobitz type II block. It is considered dangerous even without symptoms because of its unpredictable progression to complete block and sudden cardiac death, and its escape rhythm is weak and unreliable; the definitive treatment is a permanent pacemaker.

Beta blockers are listed causes of first-degree and Mobitz type I block, not a treatment for block. Mobitz type II, even without symptoms, needs a permanent pacemaker. Tell: rate-slowing drugs belong on the cause list, not the treatment list.

A.q: A 34-year-old woman is brought in after a car crash with a heart rate of 128 and a blood pressure of 88/56. The rhythm is regular with a normal P wave before every narrow QRS. Bedside ultrasound shows free fluid in the abdomen. Which is the most appropriate approach to her heart rate?
opts: Correct. A regular rhythm at 128 with a normal P wave before every narrow QRS is sinus tachycardia, and with a blood pressure of 88/56 and free abdominal fluid after a crash it is an appropriate response to hypovolemia. Appropriate sinus tachycardia is managed by treating the underlying cause, here the bleeding.

Adenosine is used in stable supraventricular tachycardia after a vagal maneuver, to convert the rhythm or slow it enough to see P waves. Her P waves are already visible before every QRS, and her sinus rate is a response to blood loss. Tell: a normal P wave before each QRS plus an obvious cause means sinus tachycardia, so treat the cause.

Within sinus tachycardia, beta blockers come up only for the inappropriate form, a diagnosis of exclusion with no secondary cause, and even there they are not well tolerated. Her tachycardia has an obvious cause, hypovolemia from bleeding, which makes it appropriate. Tell: an identified cause means treat the cause, not the rate.

Synchronized cardioversion is for hemodynamically unstable tachyarrhythmias such as supraventricular tachycardia, atrial flutter or atrial fibrillation. Her rhythm is sinus, driven by bleeding, so a shock would leave the cause untouched. Tell: a sinus P wave before every QRS rules out cardioversion; appropriate sinus tachycardia is managed by treating the cause.

Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
A.q: A 57-year-old man with knee osteoarthritis felt a sudden sharp pain behind the right knee while climbing stairs, followed by severe calf discomfort and swelling. Venous duplex ultrasound shows no thrombus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Superficial thrombophlebitis is a clot in a superficial vein, not a sudden event that starts behind the knee during exertion. The tell is the abrupt pain behind the knee followed by severe calf discomfort with a clot-free ultrasound, which on the differential of deep vein thrombosis belongs to a ruptured popliteal (Baker) cyst.

A calf muscle pull or tear usually has an inciting injury in the history and may leave bruising at the ankle. Climbing stairs is ordinary activity and he has no bruising; pain that began behind the knee and then became severe calf discomfort favors a ruptured popliteal (Baker) cyst.

Post-thrombotic (postphlebitic) syndrome is symptomatic chronic venous insufficiency that follows a deep vein thrombosis by 6 to 24 months. He has no prior clot and his symptoms began suddenly, so a chronic after-clot process does not fit; abrupt onset behind the knee is the tell for a ruptured cyst.

Correct. Sudden pain behind the knee followed by severe, sudden calf discomfort and swelling, with a duplex ultrasound that shows no thrombus, fits a ruptured popliteal (Baker) cyst. It sits on the differential of deep vein thrombosis (DVT) because it mimics the swollen, painful calf of a clot.

Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
A.q: A 36-year-old woman has bothersome palpitations from premature ventricular contractions. Her heart is structurally normal, she has never fainted, and her monitor shows a low burden of early beats. Which is the first-line treatment?
opts: Reassurance and removing triggers suit low-risk patients with a low burden and no symptoms. Her palpitations are bothersome, so she needs treatment, and a beta blocker is first-line. Tell: in a low-risk patient, symptoms are what earn a beta blocker.
ruled out by a stated finding

An implantable defibrillator is meant to prevent sudden cardiac death from fatal rhythms; low-risk premature beats in a structurally normal heart do not need one. Tell: a low burden, a normal heart and no syncope mean low risk, which never calls for a defibrillator.

Catheter ablation is for low-risk patients whose symptoms are refractory to a beta blocker or who cannot tolerate drug therapy. She has not tried a beta blocker yet. Tell: the drug comes before the procedure in low-risk patients.

Correct. A structurally normal heart, no syncope and a low burden make her low risk, but her palpitations are bothersome. In a low-risk patient with symptoms, a beta blocker is first-line, and catheter ablation is kept for symptoms that are refractory or a drug that cannot be tolerated.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
A.q: Constrictive pericarditis results from which change in the pericardium?
opts: Stiffening of the myocardium by infiltration

Infiltration that stiffens the myocardium places the problem in the heart muscle, while constriction is a disease of the pericardium itself. Constrictive pericarditis is fibrous scarring of the pericardium with loss of elasticity of the sac. Tell: read whether the option names the myocardium or the pericardium; only the pericardial change defines constriction.
Acute inflammation lasting under six weeks

Inflammation of the pericardial sac lasting under 4 to 6 weeks defines acute pericarditis, not constriction. Duration defines the pericarditis categories (acute, incessant up to 3 months, chronic beyond 3 months), whereas constriction is a structural change: fibrous scarring with loss of elasticity. Tell: a time window describes pericarditis; a stiff, scarred sac describes constriction.
Rapid accumulation of fluid under pressure

Fluid accumulating under pressure and compressing the heart is the definition of cardiac tamponade. In constrictive pericarditis the sac itself is scarred and noncompliant, so no fluid is needed. Tell: fluid under pressure means tamponade; a stiff, scarred sac means constriction; both together, with constriction that persists after drainage, is effusive-constrictive pericarditis.
Fibrous scarring with loss of elasticity

Correct. Constrictive pericarditis is defined by fibrous scarring of the pericardium with loss of elasticity of the pericardial sac, which leaves the pericardium noncompliant. The problem is the stiff sac itself, not fluid inside it and not inflammation of a set duration.

A.io: Identify medical care strategies for cardiomyopathies for the following populations. 8. adolescent 9. adult 10. elderly
A.q: Which device therapies are part of adult cardiomyopathy care?
opts: Correct. Device therapy for adults with cardiomyopathy is an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) or a biventricular pacemaker, alongside guideline-directed drugs and lifestyle changes. A left ventricular assist device (LVAD) or transplant is considered in advanced cases.
Carotid stent or vena cava filter devices

Neither a carotid stent nor a vena cava filter is listed for cardiomyopathy. Adult device therapy is an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator or a biventricular pacemaker, with an assist device or transplant in advanced cases. Tell: the adult devices are cardiac, a defibrillator or a pacemaker.

Temporary external pacing is not the listed strategy. Adults receive an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator or a biventricular pacemaker, and select adolescents may also receive a defibrillator. Tell: the listed devices are implanted, not external.
Intra-aortic balloon pump for all patients

An intra-aortic balloon pump is not listed, and no device is given to all patients. Adult device therapy is a defibrillator or biventricular pacemaker, while a left ventricular assist device is considered only in advanced cases. Tell: for all patients is the giveaway, since devices are chosen by need.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
A.q: A 31-year-old woman has sudden palpitations with visible pounding in her neck (frog sign). She is alert, with a blood pressure of 120/74. Her electrocardiogram shows a regular, narrow-complex tachycardia at 170 with no visible P waves. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Focal atrial tachycardia comes from one ectopic atrial focus and shows a consistent abnormal P wave before every QRS. Her P waves are not visible at all, and neck pulsations (frog sign) are a typical complaint in nodal reentry. Tell: a visible abnormal P wave before each QRS points focal; hidden P waves with neck pulsations point nodal reentry.
ruled out by a stated finding

Multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular, with at least three P-wave shapes in one lead, and arises in acutely ill patients with severe lung disease or heart failure. Her rhythm is regular with no visible P waves, and she is a well young woman. Tell: irregular with changing P waves is multifocal; regular with hidden P waves is nodal reentry.

Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular with absent P waves. Her tachycardia is regular, starts suddenly and comes with neck pulsations, which fits nodal reentry. Tell: both may lack visible P waves, so judge the regularity; regular means reentry, irregularly irregular means fibrillation.

Correct. A sudden, regular, narrow-complex tachycardia at 170 with no visible P waves in a young woman, plus visible neck pulsations (frog sign), is atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia. It is a reentry circuit within the atrioventricular node, usually at 140 to 180 with hidden P waves, and is far more common in women than men.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
A.q: A 79-year-old woman has a week of fatigue and dizziness. Her heart rate is 36. The electrocardiogram shows regular P waves at 80 per minute and regular wide QRS complexes at 36 per minute, with no consistent relationship between them; some P waves sit inside T waves. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Mobitz type II conducts some P waves with a constant PR and drops others at random. Here no P wave relates to any QRS, with atria at 80 and ventricles at 36. Tell: if there is never a consistent PR, it is not second-degree block.

Correct. Regular P waves at 80 and regular wide QRS complexes at 36 with no relationship, and P waves buried in T waves, are two separate rhythms: third-degree (complete) block, in which no P waves conduct. The ventricular rate is usually under 40, and her dizziness and fatigue fit; she needs pacing, then a permanent pacemaker.

Mobitz type I shows a PR that progressively lengthens until a QRS drops. Here there is no consistent PR at all, because atria and ventricles beat independently. Tell: lengthening PRs mean type I; no relationship at all means complete block.

Ventricular tachycardia is a fast wide rhythm of 100 to 250 per minute. A wide rhythm at 36 with independent P waves at 80 is complete block with a ventricular escape rhythm. Tell: wide plus slow plus dissociated P waves means third degree.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following venous disorders: 2. Deep vein thrombosis 3. Phlebitis a. Thrombophlebitis Septic thrombophlebitis 4. Arteriovenous fistula of the extremity a. Acquired (e.g. trauma, iatrogenic) b. Created (i.e. for hemodialysis) 5. Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
A.q: A 63-year-old man with chronic venous insufficiency has two days of warmth, tenderness and spreading blanching redness of the lower leg, with a low-grade fever. Which treatment is most appropriate?
opts: Cellulitis complicating chronic venous insufficiency calls for oral antibiotics, cephalexin or clindamycin, not a topical product. Topical care in this setting means cleansers, emollients and barrier creams for stasis dermatitis; his fever and spreading warmth mark an infection that needs an oral drug.

Flavonoids are used to increase venous tone, and no oral medication has yet been proven useful for venous disease itself. They do nothing for infection: his fever with spreading warm, tender redness is cellulitis, which is treated with oral cephalexin or clindamycin.

Correct. Two days of warmth, tenderness and spreading blanching redness with a low-grade fever in a leg with chronic venous insufficiency describe cellulitis. Oral antibiotics are recommended for this cellulitis, and cephalexin or clindamycin are the named choices.

Mid-potency topical corticosteroids such as triamcinolone treat the erythema, inflammation, itching and vesicles of stasis dermatitis. Here the fever and the spreading warm, tender redness point to cellulitis, an infection, which needs oral cephalexin or clindamycin rather than an anti-inflammatory cream.

A.q: Which electrolyte is given as an intravenous push and then as an infusion to break torsades de pointes?
opts: Potassium is not the drug that breaks torsades de pointes. Hypokalemia is a cause of acquired long QT and should be corrected, but the push-then-infusion treatment is magnesium. Tell: torsades is 'mag, mag, mag'; an unstable patient is defibrillated instead.

Phosphate has no role in torsades de pointes. The conscious patient gets intravenous magnesium to break the rhythm, then a magnesium infusion, while an unstable patient is defibrillated. Tell: magnesium is the only electrolyte repeated as push and infusion.

Correct. In a conscious patient, intravenous magnesium is given to break torsades de pointes, followed by more magnesium as an infusion. Amiodarone, procainamide and beta blockers are avoided because they prolong the QT, and lidocaine is the only antiarrhythmic that can be used.

Calcium is not the treatment that breaks torsades de pointes; hypocalcemia is a cause of acquired long QT. Calcium gluconate is only considered in refractory ventricular fibrillation arrest. Tell: the electrolyte given as a push and then an infusion for torsades is magnesium.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
A.q: A 66-year-old woman with chronic obstructive lung disease is admitted with an exacerbation. She is confused, and the monitor shows runs of skipped beats from frequent early, wide QRS complexes without P waves. Her arterial oxygen tension is low. Which underlying problem should be corrected first?
opts: Blood glucose is not a named cause of premature ventricular contractions. Her low arterial oxygen tension is: hypoxemia heads the list with electrolyte imbalance. Tell: correct the abnormal value the stem gives you.

Body temperature is not a named cause of premature ventricular contractions. Hypoxemia, along with electrolyte imbalance, is, and her low arterial oxygen tension during a lung disease exacerbation is the cause to correct first. Tell: her lung disease and low oxygen tension point straight to hypoxemia.

Correct. Early, wide QRS complexes without P waves are premature ventricular contractions, and hypoxemia is a named cause, along with electrolyte imbalance. Her chronic obstructive lung disease exacerbation, confusion and low arterial oxygen tension make hypoxemia the problem to correct first.

Blood pressure is not a named cause of premature ventricular contractions. The named causes are hypoxemia and electrolyte imbalance, and her low arterial oxygen tension during a lung disease flare is the clear one. Tell: the stem hands you a low oxygen value.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
A.q: A 70-year-old woman with restrictive cardiomyopathy has pulmonary and systemic congestion, with crackles and leg edema. A diuretic is being started. Which statement about diuretic use in her is most accurate?
opts: Use with caution; stiff ventricles need preload

Correct. Diuretics are used for her pulmonary and systemic congestion, but with caution, because they lower preload and noncompliant ventricles depend on preload to maintain cardiac output. Beta blockers or verapamil and diltiazem may also help by lengthening left ventricular filling time.
Only useful once the ejection fraction falls

Diuretics are given for pulmonary and systemic congestion, which she has now; the indication is congestion, not a falling ejection fraction. The caution is about lowering preload in noncompliant ventricles. Tell: treat the congestion that is present, carefully.
Give aggressively to fully dry the lungs

Aggressive diuresis drops the preload that noncompliant ventricles rely on to maintain cardiac output. Diuretics are used for congestion, but cautiously. Tell: in restrictive disease the goal is relief of congestion without stripping the preload the heart needs.

Diuretics are not contraindicated; they are the listed treatment for pulmonary and systemic congestion in restrictive cardiomyopathy. They are simply used with caution because noncompliant ventricles depend on preload. Tell: caution is not a contraindication.

Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
A.q: A 68-year-old woman has atrial fibrillation found at a routine visit. Her heart rate is 84, she has no symptoms of instability, and her blood pressure is 128/76. Which is the most appropriate rate management?
opts: Atropine is not part of atrial fibrillation management, which is synchronized cardioversion if unstable, intravenous rate control if stable in rapid ventricular response, and rate control if stable without it. Her rate of 84 needs no speeding up.

Intravenous rate control is for a hemodynamically stable patient in rapid ventricular response (RVR). Her rate of 84 is not rapid, so she gets rate control without the intravenous route; the tell is the heart rate, not her stability.

Correct. She is hemodynamically stable (blood pressure 128/76, no instability) and a rate of 84 is not a rapid ventricular response, so she gets rate control; the intravenous route is kept for stable patients in rapid ventricular response. Anticoagulation is then weighed for her, guided by her CHA2DS2-VASc stroke-risk score.

Synchronized cardioversion is for hemodynamically unstable atrial fibrillation, and elective outpatient cardioversion comes only after 21 days of anticoagulation. She is stable with a blood pressure of 128/76, so rate control comes first.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
A.q: A 24-year-old man is brought in after a stab wound to the left chest. He is hypotensive with distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds, and a bedside scan shows blood in the pericardial space. Which treatment is most appropriate?
opts: Needle pericardiocentesis is the treatment for nonhemorrhagic tamponade. His pericardial blood comes from a penetrating stab wound, and hemorrhagic tamponade secondary to trauma calls for emergent surgery to repair the injury. Tell: blood in the pericardium after penetrating trauma means the operating room; nontraumatic fluid means a needle.

Diuretics remove volume, but tamponade is treated with aggressive volume expansion using intravenous fluids while the compression is relieved. This hypotensive patient with the Beck triad needs that support plus emergent surgical repair of his cardiac wound. Tell: in tamponade you add volume and relieve the pressure; you never pull fluid off.

Correct. Hypotension, distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds are the Beck triad of tamponade, and the scan shows blood from a stab wound, so this is hemorrhagic tamponade secondary to penetrating trauma. That calls for emergent surgery to repair the injury, with aggressive intravenous fluid volume expansion as support in the meantime.

Aspirin and colchicine are anti-inflammatory therapy for pericarditis; they do nothing for a bleeding penetrating injury compressing the heart. Tamponade is a medical emergency requiring immediate drainage, and when it is hemorrhagic from trauma, emergent surgical repair. Tell: hypotension with the Beck triad calls for relieving the compression, not anti-inflammatory drugs.

Deep vein thrombosis 3. Phlebitis a. Thrombophlebitis Septic thrombophlebitis 4. Arteriovenous fistula of the extremity a. Acquired (e.g. trauma, iatrogenic) b. Created (i.e. for hemodialysis) 5. Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
A.q: A 50-year-old man developed a single large arteriovenous fistula of the forearm after a penetrating injury. It causes swelling and a bruit over the arm. Which is the management for this acquired fistula?
opts: Anticoagulation does not close or shrink an abnormal artery-to-vein connection, and nothing here describes a clot. A fistula acquired from a penetrating injury, like his, is managed surgically by removing the fistula or decreasing its size.

Elastic support hose is the conservative treatment for congenital fistulas, which are hard to treat because their communications can be numerous. His is a single large fistula acquired from a penetrating injury, so it is managed surgically by removal or size reduction.

Correct. His fistula is acquired, from a penetrating injury, and is a single large connection. Acquired arteriovenous (AV) fistulas are managed surgically, by removing the fistula or decreasing its size; elastic support hose and embolization are the approaches described for congenital fistulas.

Warm compresses and elevation do not treat an artery-to-vein connection. The tell is the cause: a fistula acquired from injury is corrected surgically, by removing it or decreasing its size, while a congenital one with numerous communications is managed conservatively with elastic support hose.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
A.q: Without treatment, how quickly does acute infective endocarditis progress to death?
opts: Within hours is far too fast. Acute infective endocarditis is a hectically febrile illness whose symptoms typically build over 3-10 days, and if untreated it progresses to death within weeks. Tell: even the onset of acute disease takes days, so hours fits neither form.

Correct. If untreated, acute infective endocarditis progresses to death within weeks. A virulent, invasive organism causes a hectically febrile illness that rapidly damages cardiac structures and seeds extracardiac sites, with rapid onset of high fevers and systemic toxicity typically over 3-10 days.

Several months is the time scale of subacute endocarditis, whose lower fevers, malaise and weight loss occur over weeks or months. The question asks about the acute form, which progresses to death within weeks if untreated. Tell: months pairs with the indolent subacute form; acute pairs with weeks.

A years-long course fits neither form. Even subacute endocarditis evolves over weeks or months and is gradually progressive unless a major embolic event or ruptured mycotic aneurysm intervenes, while untreated acute disease kills within weeks. Tell: acute means rapid, toxic and fatal in weeks.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
A.q: A 29-year-old man with acute myocarditis after a viral illness has fluid retention with bilateral leg edema and crackles, but his blood pressure is stable. He is receiving supportive care. Which medication may be added as needed for his fluid retention?
opts: Correct. Supportive care is the mainstay of myocarditis treatment, and medications are added as needed for the clinical scenario. For his fluid retention, with leg edema and crackles, that means a diuretic; vasodilators, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, antiarrhythmics and anticoagulation are the other as-needed options.

Alcohol septal ablation is a procedure, not a medication, and it is not part of myocarditis care. Fluid retention in myocarditis is managed with a diuretic as part of supportive care. Tell: the question asks for a drug for fluid, which is a diuretic.

A positive inotrope is not on the myocarditis medication list, and with a stable blood pressure he needs no hemodynamic rescue. The as-needed medication for fluid retention is a diuretic. Tell: match the drug to the problem, and fluid means diuretic.

A thrombolytic is not on the myocarditis medication list, and nothing in his case involves a clot. The as-needed medications are vasodilators, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, diuretics, antiarrhythmics and anticoagulation. Tell: fluid retention points to the diuretic.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
A.q: A slow sinus rhythm that is causing hypotension and confusion is treated first with which drug?
opts: Adenosine is used in stable supraventricular tachycardia, after a vagal maneuver, to convert the rhythm or slow it enough to reveal P waves. Slowing is the opposite of what an unstable bradycardia needs. Tell: adenosine is for a fast narrow rhythm; atropine is for a slow, unstable one.

Digoxin is listed with beta blockers and nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers as a drug cause of sinus bradycardia, so it would worsen this rhythm. Look for it as the culprit in a slow patient, not the rescue. Tell: drugs that cause bradycardia never treat it; atropine does.

Metoprolol is a beta blocker, and beta blockers are a listed cause of sinus bradycardia, so giving one would slow this patient further. Beta blockers belong in fast rhythms, such as rate control for stable atrial flutter. Tell: a hypotensive, confused patient with a slow sinus rhythm needs atropine first, then a temporary pacemaker.

Correct. A slow sinus rhythm causing hypotension and confusion is acute, symptomatic, hemodynamically unstable bradycardia, and atropine is first line. If it fails, a temporary pacemaker follows; chronic symptomatic bradycardia is treated with a permanent pacemaker instead.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following arterial occlusive disease and aortic aneurysm: 2. Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
A.q: A 66-year-old woman with a 4.8 cm abdominal aortic aneurysm has a history of severe reaction to contrast dye. She is stable, and the extent of the aneurysm must be defined. Which imaging is most appropriate?
opts: A plain film shows only a calcified outline, in about 75% of aneurysms, and misses the 25% that are not calcified. It cannot define extent. Magnetic resonance imaging can, without dye, which suits her allergy.

Correct. Magnetic resonance imaging is comparable to computed tomography without exposure to dye or ionizing radiation, which makes it useful in stable patients with a dye allergy. She is stable, her severe contrast reaction rules out dye-based studies, and the extent of her 4.8 cm aneurysm can still be defined.

Computed tomography angiography is the best diagnostic and pre-intervention planning study, but it relies on contrast dye, and she has had a severe reaction. Magnetic resonance imaging gives comparable information without dye. Her allergy is the clue that moves the choice.

Conventional angiography requires contrast injected through a catheter, which her severe dye reaction rules against. For a stable patient with a dye allergy, magnetic resonance imaging defines the aneurysm without dye or ionizing radiation. Any contrast-based study is the wrong choice for her.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
A.q: A 71-year-old man had his aortic valve replaced 6 weeks ago. He now has a fever of 38.9 °C (102.0 °F) and a new regurgitant murmur, and transesophageal imaging shows a vegetation on the prosthesis. Which organisms are most likely?
opts: Correct. A vegetation on an aortic prosthesis placed only 6 weeks ago is early prosthetic valve endocarditis, which is caused by coagulase-negative staphylococci (Staphylococcus epidermidis) and Staphylococcus aureus, both skin organisms. The recent surgery is the decisive clue.

The HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) group from the upper respiratory tract is a subacute, native valve cause, not an early prosthetic valve organism. Tell: a prosthesis infected within weeks of surgery points to skin staphylococci, not to airway gram-negatives.

Viridans streptococci from the oral cavity cause LATE prosthetic valve endocarditis. At only 6 weeks after valve replacement this is early disease, which is staphylococcal. Tell: early after surgery means skin staphylococci; late after surgery shifts to Streptococcus viridans.

Enterococci come from the genitourinary tract and are a native valve and subacute cause. Nothing in this stem points to a urinary source, and infection 6 weeks after valve surgery is early prosthetic disease from skin staphylococci. Tell: recent valve surgery, not a urinary procedure, is the clue.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following arterial occlusive disease and aortic aneurysm: 2. Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
A.q: A 68-year-old man had a transient ischemic attack last month. Duplex shows 85% stenosis of the ipsilateral internal carotid artery, and he is a good surgical candidate. Which treatment is most appropriate?
opts: Duplex is used for serial monitoring, but his symptomatic 85% stenosis already meets the over-70% threshold for surgery. Waiting a year after a transient ischemic attack delays indicated treatment. Monitoring fits disease below the threshold, not above it.

Correct. A transient ischemic attack last month makes his disease symptomatic, and surgery is advised for symptomatic stenosis over 70%; his is 85%. Because he is a good surgical candidate, carotid endarterectomy, removal of plaque through a surgical incision, is the gold standard for high-grade stenosis.

Medical management alone is advised for low-grade stenosis under 50%. His transient ischemic attack last month makes him symptomatic, and his 85% stenosis exceeds the over-70% threshold for surgery. Antiplatelets continue, but they are not enough alone.

Carotid angioplasty with stenting, usually through the common femoral artery, is less invasive and is chosen for poor surgical candidates. He is a good surgical candidate, so the gold standard, carotid endarterectomy, is preferred. Stenting is the fallback when surgery is risky.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
A.q: At a second recurrence, low-to-moderate dose prednisone is reserved for which patients?
opts: Those with a typical viral prodrome

A viral prodrome does not point to systemic autoimmune disease, the only group for which prednisone is reserved at a second recurrence. Idiopathic pericarditis instead gets an added interleukin-1 blocker if it is colchicine-resistant with a history of prior C-reactive protein elevation. Tell: an autoimmune background means prednisone; otherwise think interleukin-1 blocker.

Pericarditis after surgery falls under post-cardiac injury syndrome, which at a second recurrence is grouped with idiopathic disease for an added interleukin-1 blocker if colchicine-resistant with prior C-reactive protein elevation. Prednisone at this step is kept for underlying systemic autoimmune disease. Tell: injury or surgery points to the interleukin-1 blocker, not the steroid.

Correct. At a second recurrence, low to moderate dose prednisone is reserved for patients with an underlying systemic autoimmune disease. Idiopathic pericarditis and post-cardiac injury syndrome instead get an added interleukin-1 blocker if they are colchicine-resistant with a history of prior C-reactive protein elevation.

Idiopathic recurrent pericarditis that is colchicine-resistant with a history of C-reactive protein elevation gets an added interleukin-1 blocker at a second recurrence, not prednisone. Low to moderate dose prednisone is for patients whose pericarditis sits on an underlying systemic autoimmune disease. Tell: no systemic autoimmune disease, no prednisone at this step.

A.io: Identify medical care strategies for infective endocarditis for the following populations. 8. infant 9. child 10. adolescent 11. adult 12. elderly
A.q: What drives most pediatric infective endocarditis?
opts: Congenital heart disease and central lines

Correct. Pediatric infective endocarditis is driven overwhelmingly by congenital heart disease, present in about 53-68% of pediatric cases in developed countries, and by indwelling central venous catheters, which explain the catheter-related staphylococcal and Candida disease of neonates and infants.
Injection drug use in early childhood

Injection drug use matters only in adolescents, whose profile converges toward adults with injection-associated Staphylococcus aureus disease. It does not drive disease in younger children, where congenital heart disease and central venous catheters dominate. Tell: injection drug use is an adolescent clue.

Degenerative valve disease is an adult substrate. Pediatric disease is driven by congenital heart disease and central venous catheters rather than degenerative valve disease, which becomes relevant only as adolescents converge toward the adult profile. Tell: aging valves belong to adults, not children.

Rheumatic heart disease is no longer the main pediatric substrate in developed countries: congenital heart disease has replaced it and is present in about 53-68% of pediatric cases. Tell: in high-income settings, think congenital lesions and central lines, not rheumatic valves.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
A.q: A 59-year-old woman with crushing chest pain becomes lightheaded but stays awake, with a pulse and a blood pressure of 104/66. Her QT interval was normal on a tracing an hour ago, and her rhythm strip is shown. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Correct. Wide complexes that keep changing shape are polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, and with a normal QT and crushing chest pain, acute ischemia is the most common cause. Even though she is awake with a pulse, polymorphic tachycardia is never truly stable, so she is defibrillated, then sent for urgent coronary angiography.

Intravenous magnesium breaks torsades de pointes, the polymorphic tachycardia of a prolonged QT. Her QT was normal an hour ago, and polymorphic tachycardia without a long QT is most often from acute ischemia, so she is defibrillated. Tell: magnesium needs a long QT.
ruled out by a stated finding

Synchronized cardioversion is for unstable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia with a pulse. Her strip shows complexes that keep changing shape, so the rhythm is polymorphic and is defibrillated. Tell: a changing QRS shape means an unsynchronized shock.

Intravenous amiodarone may be added after the shock, but drug therapy alone is for stable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia. Polymorphic tachycardia is never truly stable, even in a patient who is awake. Tell: a polymorphic strip means defibrillation first.
A.alt: Rhythm strip of a rapid, wide-complex rhythm whose complexes vary in height, width and shape from beat to beat

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
A.q: A 52-year-old woman on long-term immunosuppression has endocarditis, and her blood cultures grow Candida. Which complication is most likely?
opts: Correct. Her blood cultures grow Candida, which makes this fungal endocarditis, and the most likely complication of fungal endocarditis is embolism with occlusion of larger peripheral arteries. Her immunosuppression is the setting, but the organism is what predicts the complication.

Rheumatic carditis is not listed as a complication of endocarditis, fungal or otherwise. With Candida on culture, the complication to expect is embolism and occlusion of larger peripheral arteries. Tell: a fungal organism points to large-vessel emboli, not to a separate inflammatory carditis.

A pericardial knock is not among the complications of fungal endocarditis. The fungal complication to anticipate is embolization that occludes larger peripheral arteries. Tell: the danger with Candida is a large-vessel arterial occlusion, a vascular event, not an added heart sound.

Nothing about fungal endocarditis suggests a quick cure; its expected course is complicated by embolism and occlusion of larger peripheral arteries. Tell: Candida on culture signals an embolizing, hard-to-treat infection, unlike viridans streptococci, which carry a relatively good prognosis when treated early.

A.io: Identify medical care strategies for atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias for the following populations. 3. adult 4. elderly
A.q: A 66-year-old woman has had stable atrial fibrillation for 2 months. Her rate is now controlled, but she would like her normal rhythm restored. Which must come before an outpatient cardioversion?
opts: A permanent pacemaker treats chronic symptomatic bradycardia, such as sick sinus syndrome with symptomatic slow rates. She has a controlled atrial fibrillation and wants her rhythm restored, which calls for 21 days of anticoagulation before an outpatient cardioversion. Tell: pacemakers answer slow rhythms, not elective conversion of a fast one.

Correct. Her atrial fibrillation is stable and rate controlled, and she wants sinus rhythm restored electively. Outpatient cardioversion is done after 21 days of anticoagulation, and anticoagulation is part of the plan for all patients with atrial fibrillation unless bleeding risk is high.

Adenosine is a step in stable supraventricular tachycardia, given after a vagal maneuver to convert a regular narrow rhythm or slow it enough to reveal P waves. Her atrial fibrillation is already diagnosed and controlled, so there is nothing to unmask. Tell: preparing for elective cardioversion of atrial fibrillation means 21 days of anticoagulation.

Rate control is the listed management for stable atrial fibrillation without rapid ventricular response, and stopping it is not the prerequisite for cardioversion. What must come first for an outpatient cardioversion is 21 days of anticoagulation. Tell: the prerequisite is about clot and stroke risk, not about the rate.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
A.q: A 45-year-old woman developed early signs of constriction 6 weeks after an episode of acute pericarditis. She is hemodynamically stable, and cardiac magnetic resonance shows pericardial edema with late gadolinium enhancement. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Observation is not an option for constriction, since survival without treatment is low. Her disease is early and stable and imaging shows active inflammation, the situation in which a 2 to 3 month trial of anti-inflammatory therapy is offered. Tell: edema and late gadolinium enhancement on cardiac magnetic resonance are reasons to treat medically, not to watch.

Pericardiectomy treats established constriction, but edema and late gadolinium enhancement on cardiac magnetic resonance identify inflammatory, potentially reversible constriction before committing to surgery. In a hemodynamically stable patient with early disease, a medical trial comes first. Tell: active inflammation on imaging argues for medicines before an operation.

Pericardiocentesis drains a moderate to large effusion, particularly one causing tamponade. She is hemodynamically stable and her problem is an inflamed, stiffening pericardium rather than fluid under pressure, so drainage has nothing to fix. Tell: a needle treats fluid; early, inflamed constriction is treated with a longer course of anti-inflammatory drugs.
A longer course of pericarditis drugs

Correct. Her constriction is early and she is hemodynamically stable, and pericardial edema with late gadolinium enhancement on cardiac magnetic resonance marks inflammatory, potentially reversible constriction. Such patients may get a trial of the acute pericarditis medicines, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and colchicine, for a longer 2 to 3 months, with diuretics for fluid overload.

A.q: A 71-year-old woman is brought in after fainting at home. She is confused, her heart rate is 34 and her blood pressure is 78/40. The electrocardiogram shows regular P waves, a constant PR interval in the conducted beats and many P waves with no QRS after them. Medications given so far have not raised her rate. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Observation is unsafe: she fainted, is confused and has a blood pressure of 78/40 at a rate of 34. Mobitz type II is dangerous even without symptoms, and with instability and failed medications she needs transcutaneous pacing now. Tell: a symptomatic, hypotensive block is never watched.

Correct. Regular P waves, a constant PR in conducted beats and dropped QRS complexes are Mobitz type II, and her confusion, hypotension and rate of 34 make her unstable. Emergent options are atropine, epinephrine and transcutaneous pacing; with drugs failing, transcutaneous pacing bridges her to a permanent pacemaker.

Defibrillation is for ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia. She has a pulse, a rate of 34 and a Mobitz type II pattern, so the problem is too few conducted beats. Tell: shocks treat fast lethal rhythms; transcutaneous pacing treats slow unstable ones.

Synchronized cardioversion terminates unstable tachycardias with a pulse. Her rate is 34 from a block that usually sits at the bundle of His, so there is no fast rhythm to convert. Tell: a slow, blocked rhythm needs pacing, and the emergent form is transcutaneous pacing.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
A.q: A 68-year-old woman has crushing chest pain and breathlessness the day after her husband's funeral. She has no hypertension, diabetes or smoking history. The electrocardiogram shows ST elevation with T-wave inversion, troponin is elevated, and echocardiogram shows hypokinesis of the mid and apical segments of the left ventricle. Catheterization shows normal coronary arteries. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy does not explain chest pain triggered by grief with regional hypokinesis and normal coronaries. Takotsubo is triggered by a significant emotional or physical stressor, and 90% of cases are postmenopausal women. Tell: death of a loved one is a listed trigger for Takotsubo.

Dilated cardiomyopathy does not fit a sudden presentation the day after a funeral with regional mid and apical hypokinesis. Transient regional left ventricular dysfunction after an emotional stressor, with normal coronaries, is Takotsubo. Tell: a stressor, a regional wall-motion defect and clean coronaries make Takotsubo.

Correct. A postmenopausal woman with chest pain the day after her husband's funeral, no cardiac risk factors, mid and apical hypokinesis and normal coronary arteries has Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy: transient regional systolic dysfunction that mimics acute coronary syndrome without angiographic coronary disease.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy does not present as sudden chest pain after a bereavement. Takotsubo mimics acute coronary syndrome after a stressor, in patients with low or no cardiac risk factors, as in this woman. Tell: no hypertension, diabetes or smoking plus a recent loss points to Takotsubo.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following arterial occlusive disease and aortic aneurysm: 2. A.q: Which syndrome results when atheroemboli occlude the digital arteries?
opts: Compartment syndrome is not the result described for atheroemboli. Digital vascular occlusion from atheroemboli causes ischemia and blue toe syndrome, and digital necrosis and gangrene may develop. Discolored, tender toes are the hallmark.

Correct. Atheroemboli of fibrin, platelets and cholesterol debris lodge in small vessels, and digital vascular occlusion causes ischemia and blue toe syndrome. Localized tenderness, pallor and livedo reticularis occur at the sites of emboli, digital necrosis and gangrene may develop, and distal pulses usually remain palpable.

Leriche syndrome is the triad of claudication, absent or diminished femoral pulses and erectile dysfunction from aortoiliac disease. Atheroemboli occluding digital arteries cause blue toe syndrome, usually with palpable distal pulses. Leriche weakens the femoral pulses; blue toe spares the pulses.

Carotid steal syndrome is not part of the atheroembolism picture. When atheroemboli occlude digital vessels, the result is ischemia and blue toe syndrome, with localized tenderness, pallor and livedo reticularis. The toes, not the neck, name the syndrome.

A.q: A 38-year-old man who injects drugs has finished a course of intravenous antibiotics for tricuspid valve endocarditis and is preparing for discharge. He says he wants help to stay safe. Which consultation should be arranged?
opts: Ophthalmology is not among the consultations listed for endocarditis care, which are infectious disease, cardiothoracic surgery and addiction medicine. His request to stay safe while injecting drugs is a harm-reduction need. Tell: the patient's ask is about drug use, not the eyes.

Nephrology is not among the listed consultations (infectious disease, cardiothoracic surgery, addiction medicine), and his antibiotic course is already finished. His request for help staying safe as a person who injects drugs is harm reduction. Tell: no kidney problem is described in the stem.

Correct. He injects drugs, has just finished treatment for tricuspid valve endocarditis and asks for help to stay safe, which is harm reduction. Addiction medicine provides harm reduction for people who inject drugs, working alongside infectious disease and cardiothoracic surgery in the multidisciplinary team.

Dermatology is not among the consultations listed for endocarditis (infectious disease, cardiothoracic surgery, addiction medicine), and the stem describes no skin problem. His need is harm reduction for injection drug use. Tell: his own request, staying safe while using, points to addiction medicine.

A.io: Identify medical care strategies for infective endocarditis for the following populations. 8. infant 9. child 10. adolescent 11. adult 12. elderly
A.q: A 7-year-old with congenital heart disease is admitted with viridans streptococcal endocarditis. Which approach to antibiotic therapy is most appropriate?
opts: Correct. Management in children is essentially the same as in adults: antibiotics that are prolonged, bactericidal, parenteral (intravenous, not intramuscular), pathogen-directed and weight-based. This 7-year-old's dose is calculated by weight, given intravenously and continued for a prolonged course.

Observation leaves a confirmed viridans streptococcal infection untreated. Pediatric management is essentially the same as adult management: prolonged, bactericidal, parenteral, pathogen-directed and weight-based antibiotics. Tell: every listed pediatric strategy starts with antibiotics; none is watchful waiting.

This gets two details wrong for a child. Parenteral therapy in pediatric endocarditis means intravenous, not intramuscular, and the dose is weight-based rather than a fixed adult dose. Tell: a 7-year-old receives intravenous drug dosed by weight, so both intramuscular and fixed adult dosing are traps.

A short oral course does not meet the standard. Pediatric antibiotics for endocarditis must be prolonged, bactericidal and parenteral, given intravenously and dosed by weight, the same as in adults. Tell: both oral and one week contradict the prolonged intravenous rule.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following venous disorders: 2. Deep vein thrombosis 3. Phlebitis a. Thrombophlebitis Septic thrombophlebitis 4. Arteriovenous fistula of the extremity a. Acquired (e.g. trauma, iatrogenic) b. Created (i.e. for hemodialysis) 5. Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
A.q: An elevated D-dimer implies increased activity of which process?
opts: Correct. D-dimer elevation implies increased fibrinolysis, the breakdown of fibrin clot. Because it is sensitive but not specific, it serves as a rule-out test for deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism: a negative result in a low-risk patient ends the work-up, while a positive one leads to ultrasound.

Red cell destruction is not what a D-dimer reports; the test reflects fibrinolysis, the breakdown of fibrin. That is why it is used in suspected deep vein thrombosis as a sensitive marker that rules a clot out when negative but cannot confirm one when positive.

Vitamin K depletion is not what a D-dimer measures. An elevated D-dimer implies increased fibrinolysis, so it rises when fibrin clot is being broken down, and that sensitivity is what makes a negative result useful for ruling out deep vein thrombosis.

Platelet production is not reflected by a D-dimer. The test rises with increased fibrinolysis, the breakdown of fibrin, which is why it is sensitive but not specific for a venous clot and is followed by ultrasound when positive.
