Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
A.q: A 36-year-old man has a regular tachycardia at 170 with an identical, abnormally shaped P wave before every QRS. Adenosine briefly slows the ventricular response, but the abnormal atrial rhythm continues unchanged afterward. Which rhythm does this response point to?
opts: Orthodromic atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia runs through the atrioventricular node, and adenosine is first line for it; its P waves are hidden or retrograde, after the QRS. This rhythm shows an abnormal P wave before each QRS that persists after adenosine. Tell: a rhythm that keeps going despite nodal block is atrial, not node-dependent reentry.
ruled out by a stated finding

Nodal reentrant tachycardia is a circuit within the atrioventricular node and almost always terminates with vagal maneuvers or adenosine; its P waves are hidden. Here a visible abnormal P wave precedes every QRS and the atrial rhythm survives adenosine. Tell: termination with adenosine suggests nodal reentry; persistence suggests focal atrial tachycardia.
ruled out by a stated finding

Multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular, with at least three different P-wave shapes in one lead from multiple foci. This rhythm is regular with one identical abnormal P wave before every QRS, which takes a single focus. Tell: one abnormal P shape is focal; three or more shapes is multifocal.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. A regular tachycardia at 170 with one identical abnormal P wave before every QRS comes from a single ectopic atrial focus. Adenosine is a diagnostic tool here because it is usually less effective at terminating focal atrial tachycardia than the node-dependent reentry rhythms, so brief slowing with the atrial rhythm carrying on fits.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
A.q: A 62-year-old woman taking metoprolol and diltiazem for palpitations has a new rhythm in which the PR interval lengthens until a QRS is dropped. She has mild fatigue. Which part of her history is a named cause of this rhythm?
opts: Sex is not a named cause of Mobitz type I. Beta blockers, nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers and digoxin are, and she takes metoprolol and diltiazem. Tell: look at her medication list before anything else.

Palpitations are the reason she takes her drugs, not a cause of block. The named causes in her history are metoprolol and diltiazem, a beta blocker and a nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker. Tell: the treatment, not the complaint, produced the block.

Correct. A PR that lengthens until a QRS drops is Mobitz type I (Wenckebach), and beta blockers and nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, with digoxin, are named causes. She takes metoprolol, a beta blocker, and diltiazem, a nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker, so her drugs are the first place to look.

Fatigue is a possible symptom of Mobitz type I, not its cause. The named causes in her history are her rate-slowing drugs: metoprolol, a beta blocker, and diltiazem, a nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker. Tell: a symptom cannot be the cause of the rhythm.

Deep vein thrombosis 3. Phlebitis a. Thrombophlebitis Septic thrombophlebitis 4. Arteriovenous fistula of the extremity a. Acquired (e.g. trauma, iatrogenic) b. Created (i.e. for hemodialysis) 5. Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
A.q: A 45-year-old man has dilated superficial leg veins with dull aching after standing. He has no edema, skin changes or ulceration, and his pedal pulses are normal. Which is the most appropriate initial management?
opts: Sclerotherapy is a venous intervention, and intervention is offered only after a trial of conservative therapy with stockings, generally for weeks to months. His varicose veins are isolated, with no edema, skin changes or ulceration, so elevation, exercise and compression come first.

Correct. His varicose veins are isolated, with no edema, skin changes or ulceration, so management starts conservatively with leg elevation, exercise and compression stockings. His normal pedal pulses matter because arterial disease must be ruled out before compression, and stockings are tried for weeks to months before ablation is offered.

Vein stripping is a surgical intervention, and he has not yet had the trial of compression stockings that comes first, generally for weeks to months. With no edema, skin changes or ulceration, his isolated varicose veins are managed conservatively before any procedure is considered.

Venous ablation therapy is offered only after a trial of conservative therapy with stockings, generally for weeks to months. He has not had that trial, and isolated varicose veins without edema, skin changes or ulceration call for elevation, exercise and compression first.

Deep vein thrombosis 3. Phlebitis a. Thrombophlebitis Septic thrombophlebitis 4. Arteriovenous fistula of the extremity a. Acquired (e.g. trauma, iatrogenic) b. Created (i.e. for hemodialysis) 5. Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
A.q: Which Virchow triad component can be inherited or acquired?
opts: Endothelial injury comes from trauma, surgery (especially knee or hip replacement or hip fracture), intravenous drug use and burns, all acquired events. The component with both inherited and acquired forms is the hypercoagulable state, as with factor V Leiden or protein C deficiency.

Correct. The hypercoagulable state is the Virchow triad component described as inherited or acquired. Inherited examples are factor V Leiden, prothrombin gene mutation, protein C or S deficiency and antithrombin deficiency; acquired examples include cancer, oral contraceptives or postmenopausal estrogen, and pregnancy.

The three components are not alike here: only the hypercoagulable state is described as inherited or acquired. Venous stasis comes from immobilization, venous insufficiency or heart failure, and endothelial injury from trauma, surgery or intravenous drug use, which are acquired circumstances rather than inherited traits.

Venous stasis is altered blood flow from immobilization (long flights, prolonged sitting, postoperative inactivity), venous insufficiency or heart failure, which are acquired situations. Inherited forms such as factor V Leiden belong to the hypercoagulable state, the component that can be inherited or acquired.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
A.q: A 59-year-old woman develops fever and positional chest pain with a friction rub (a scratchy, squeaking sound) 2 weeks after a myocardial infarction treated with a coronary stent. Echocardiography shows a small effusion and her vital signs are stable. Which anti-inflammatory regimen is most appropriate?
opts: Glucocorticoids are avoided in peri-infarction pericarditis, and elsewhere prednisone is second-line, kept for refractory cases or a contraindication to nonsteroidal drugs. Two weeks after a stented infarction, aspirin plus colchicine is used instead. Tell: after an infarction, the only anti-inflammatory partner for colchicine is aspirin.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Fever, positional pain and a rub 2 weeks after a stented myocardial infarction make this post-infarction pericarditis. Nonsteroidal drugs other than aspirin, such as ibuprofen and indomethacin, are not given for post-infarction pericarditis, and glucocorticoids are also avoided, so aspirin, itself a first-line option, is paired with colchicine.

Ibuprofen plus colchicine is first-line for most acute pericarditis, but nonsteroidal drugs other than aspirin are not given for post-infarction pericarditis. Two weeks after her stented infarction, aspirin takes ibuprofen's place alongside colchicine. Tell: the colchicine stays the same; the recent infarction swaps ibuprofen for aspirin.
ruled out by a stated finding

Indomethacin is another first-line option for typical pericarditis, but like ibuprofen it is avoided in patients on aspirin as an antiplatelet agent, including peri-infarction pericarditis. Her infarction 2 weeks ago rules it out, and aspirin plus colchicine is used. Tell: any non-aspirin anti-inflammatory is the trap after a myocardial infarction.
ruled out by a stated finding

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following arterial occlusive disease and aortic aneurysm: 2. Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
A.q: A 68-year-old man has had a cold, pulseless right leg for three hours, with pallor, tingling and mild weakness of the toes. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Cilostazol is an oral antiplatelet and vasodilator for chronic claudication. An acute occlusion with pallor, tingling and weakness needs an immediate vascular surgery consult and intravenous heparin, not an oral drug with follow-up. Delay risks the limb.

Correct. A cold, pulseless leg for three hours with pallor, tingling and toe weakness is acute limb ischemia, a vascular emergency, and weakness places it at least in the immediately threatened category. Management begins with an immediate vascular surgery consult and intravenous heparin, with testing guided by the category of ischemia.

The ankle-brachial index is the initial test for chronic peripheral artery disease in a stable patient. A sudden cold, pulseless leg with sensory and motor changes is a vascular emergency needing an immediate vascular surgery consult. Clinic testing would waste critical time.

Supervised exercise improves walking distance in stable claudication. His cold, pale, pulseless leg with tingling and weakness for three hours is acute limb ischemia, which needs an immediate vascular surgery consult. Exercise has no role in an acute occlusion.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following arterial occlusive disease and aortic aneurysm: 2. Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
A.q: What is peripheral bypass grafting principally used to treat?
opts: Correct. Bypass grafting is invasive surgery principally used to treat severe critical leg ischemia, bypassing diseased segments with a saphenous vein or synthetic graft. It is highly effective, but its complications include myocardial infarction, stroke, graft infection and peripheral embolization.

Carotid narrowing is not the target of a peripheral bypass; carotid disease is treated with endarterectomy or stenting when surgical thresholds are met. Peripheral bypass grafting reroutes flow around diseased leg segments in severe critical leg ischemia. Peripheral here means the limb, not the neck.

Mild claudication is managed with risk-factor reduction, exercise therapy and drugs, not open surgery. Bypass grafting is principally reserved for severe critical leg ischemia, given its invasiveness and its risks of myocardial infarction, stroke and graft infection. Severity, not the mere presence of symptoms, drives bypass.

Small abdominal aneurysms are followed with surveillance imaging, and larger ones are repaired by endovascular or open grafting of the aorta. Peripheral bypass grafting with a saphenous vein or synthetic graft is principally used for severe critical leg ischemia. Aneurysm repair lines or replaces the aorta rather than bypassing a leg segment.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
A.q: A 33-year-old man with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy confirmed by echocardiography has typical findings and no plans for surgery or a device. A colleague suggests cardiac catheterization to complete the work-up. When is cardiac catheterization indicated in this condition?
opts: Always, to rule out coronary disease

Catheterization is not routine in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; it is obtained only when a pacemaker or surgery is planned. Exercise echocardiography can assess exercise-induced ischemia without it. Tell: always is the wrong word for a test reserved for planned procedures.
Only if the murmur is very loud

Murmur loudness is not an indication for catheterization. It is obtained only when invasive therapy, a pacemaker or surgery, is planned. Tell: the trigger is a planned procedure, not an examination finding, and he has no procedure planned.
Only if surgery or a pacemaker is planned

Correct. Cardiac catheterization is not required for diagnosis of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; it is obtained when invasive modalities of therapy, a pacemaker or surgery, are planned. With his diagnosis already confirmed and no such plans, it adds nothing now.

Catheterization is not required for diagnosis; his was already confirmed by echocardiography, and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging helps when echo is questionable. Tell: catheterization waits for a plan for a pacemaker or surgery.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
A.q: A 78-year-old woman has a harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border radiating to the carotids, and her electrocardiogram shows a left bundle branch block. Which of her conditions is singled out as a cause of this block?
opts: Tricuspid regurgitation is a right-sided valve lesion and is not singled out as a cause of left bundle branch block. Aortic stenosis is, and her murmur radiating to the carotids fits it. Tell: 'valvular disease, especially aortic stenosis' is the phrase to remember.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Valvular heart disease, especially aortic stenosis, is singled out as a cause of left bundle branch block, and her harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border radiating to the carotids is the aortic stenosis murmur. Other listed causes are chronic hypertension, ischemic heart disease and dilated cardiomyopathy.

Mitral stenosis is not the valve lesion singled out for left bundle branch block, and her murmur is systolic at the right upper sternal border, not a mitral murmur. Aortic stenosis is named. Tell: a murmur radiating to the carotids points to the aortic valve.
ruled out by a stated finding

Pulmonic stenosis is a right-sided lesion and is not the valve disease singled out for left bundle branch block. Valvular disease, especially aortic stenosis, is named. Tell: a left-sided block goes with the left-sided outflow valve that her murmur points to.
ruled out by a stated finding

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
A.q: A 77-year-old man had cardiac surgery last year. A rhythm strip shows normal sinus beats, then a sudden pause with no P wave, after which narrow beats at 45 appear with no visible P waves. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Sinus bradycardia is a regular rhythm under 60 with a uniform P wave before every QRS. This strip shows a sudden pause and then narrow beats with no P waves, so the sinus node is not driving the slow beats at all. Tell: in sinus bradycardia every beat still has its P wave.

Atrial flutter shows sawtooth waves at an atrial rate of 250 or more, outnumbering the QRS complexes. This strip shows a flat pause followed by slow narrow beats with no atrial waves at all. Tell: flutter fills the baseline with waves; sinus arrest leaves it empty and then hands over to a junctional rhythm.

Sinus arrhythmia is a normal, physiologic rhythm at 60 to 100 that varies with breathing, with a uniform P wave before every QRS. A sudden pause followed by slow beats with no P waves in a man after cardiac surgery is pathologic. Tell: sinus arrhythmia never loses its P waves or stops abruptly.

Correct. Normal sinus beats followed by a sudden pause with no P wave mean the sinus node stopped generating impulses: sinus arrest, a form of sick sinus syndrome. The escape rhythm is junctional, narrow beats at 45 with no visible P waves. Injury to the sinus node from cardiac surgery is a listed cause, matching his history.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
A.q: Which electrical treatment is delivered for polymorphic ventricular tachycardia?
opts: Synchronized cardioversion is used for unstable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia with a pulse. Polymorphic tachycardia is defibrillated (unsynchronized) instead, because it is never truly stable. Tell: monomorphic with a pulse gets synchronized; polymorphic gets unsynchronized.

Transcutaneous pacing treats slow, blocked rhythms such as Mobitz type II or complete block, not a fast ventricular rhythm. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is treated with defibrillation (unsynchronized cardioversion). Tell: pace the slow, shock the fast.

Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is never truly stable, even if the patient looks well; it is a short-lived transitional state. So there is no drug trial first: the patient is defibrillated, and intravenous metoprolol or amiodarone may be added. Tell: drugs-first fits stable monomorphic tachycardia only.

Correct. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is never truly stable, even when the patient looks fine, because it is a short-lived transitional state. It is treated with defibrillation (unsynchronized cardioversion), followed by urgent coronary angiography with possible revascularization.

A.io: Discuss prophylaxis for bacterial endocarditis.
A.q: A 52-year-old man with a prosthetic mitral valve is booked for a diagnostic bronchoscopy. No biopsy or mucosal incision is planned. Which advice about endocarditis prophylaxis is most accurate?
opts: Not every bronchoscopy qualifies. Bronchoscopy is on the list of procedures that do not require endocarditis prophylaxis unless it involves incision of the mucosa, such as a biopsy, and none is planned here. Tell: his prosthetic valve does not change this, because the procedure itself does not qualify.

Intravenous vancomycin is not one of the prophylaxis regimens, which use amoxicillin, ampicillin, cephalosporins, macrolides or doxycycline, and this procedure needs no prophylaxis at all. Diagnostic bronchoscopy without biopsy or mucosal incision is on the no-prophylaxis list. Tell: no incision means no drug.

Prophylaxis is a single dose given 30-60 minutes before a qualifying procedure, never a week-long course. And this bronchoscopy does not qualify, because no biopsy or mucosal incision is planned. Tell: a week of antibiotics is a treatment pattern, not prophylaxis.
None is needed for this procedure

Correct. Bronchoscopy does not require endocarditis prophylaxis unless it involves incision of the respiratory mucosa, such as a biopsy. His is diagnostic with no biopsy or incision planned, so no antibiotic is given despite the prosthetic mitral valve; respiratory prophylaxis is reserved for procedures that incise or biopsy mucosa.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
A.q: A 48-year-old woman started a medication known to prolong the QT interval last week. She now has palpitations but is awake and talking, and her rhythm strip is shown. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Beta blockers are avoided in torsades de pointes: the bradycardia they cause lengthens the R-to-R interval and indirectly the QT.

Correct. A polymorphic ventricular tachycardia whose complexes twist around the baseline in a patient with a long QT is torsades de pointes; in a conscious patient intravenous magnesium breaks it, then more magnesium as an infusion.
Amiodarone (like procainamide) is avoided in torsades de pointes because it prolongs the QT further; magnesium is the treatment.

Adenosine is not among the torsades de pointes treatments: intravenous magnesium for a conscious patient, defibrillation if unstable, and lidocaine as the one antiarrhythmic that can be used. Her twisting polymorphic rhythm on a QT-prolonging drug calls for magnesium.
A.alt: Rhythm strip of a rapid, wide-complex rhythm whose complexes grow taller, shrink, then grow again, as if turning around the baseline

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
A.q: How often is heart muscle biopsy useful in dilated cardiomyopathy?
opts: There is no surveillance biopsy; biopsy is rarely useful in dilated cardiomyopathy and is kept for two indications, recent rapidly deteriorating cardiac function or systemic disease with possible cardiac involvement. Tell: rarely useful rules out a yearly schedule.

Treatment does not wait for tissue: the drug list of angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, beta blockers and others is used without biopsy, which is not used routinely. Tell: biopsy is reserved for recent rapid deterioration or a systemic disease such as sarcoidosis or amyloidosis.

Correct. Endocardial biopsy is not used routinely in dilated cardiomyopathy and is rarely useful. It is reserved for recent onset of rapidly deteriorating cardiac function or a history of systemic disease with possible cardiac involvement, such as hemochromatosis, sarcoidosis or amyloidosis.

Biopsy is not needed to confirm dilated cardiomyopathy; it is not used routinely and is rarely useful. Gadolinium-enhanced cardiac magnetic resonance imaging helps identify inflammatory, ischemic or infiltrative processes instead. Tell: biopsy is kept for rapid deterioration or systemic disease.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
A.q: Adenosine slows a tachycardia and reveals atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White. Which drug is used?
opts: A repeat dose of adenosine is allowed for ordinary stable supraventricular tachycardia, but once atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White is revealed, adenosine must never be used. Intravenous procainamide takes its place. Tell: the moment a pre-excited atrial fibrillation appears, adenosine is off the table.

Correct. Slowing from adenosine has unmasked atrial fibrillation conducting with Wolff-Parkinson-White, and in that setting intravenous procainamide is used, never adenosine. The same rule applies whenever Wolff-Parkinson-White is already known; adenosine stays first line only for ordinary orthodromic reentry.

Intravenous magnesium is not the listed drug for atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White. When adenosine slows a tachycardia and reveals this combination, intravenous procainamide is used and adenosine is not repeated. Tell: pre-excited atrial fibrillation has one named drug answer, procainamide.

Atropine is first line for acute, symptomatic, hemodynamically unstable bradycardia, a slow rhythm. This patient has a fast atrial fibrillation conducting with Wolff-Parkinson-White, the opposite problem, which is treated with intravenous procainamide. Tell: atropine is for a slow rate; procainamide is for pre-excited atrial fibrillation.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
A.q: A 38-year-old woman has three months of worsening breathlessness on exertion and ankle swelling. Dilated cardiomyopathy is suspected, but her 12-lead electrocardiogram is completely normal. Which interpretation of the normal tracing is most accurate?
opts: It is what most dilated cardiomyopathy shows

The opposite holds: the electrocardiogram is usually abnormal in dilated cardiomyopathy, with left ventricular hypertrophy, atrial fibrillation, premature ventricular contractions or conduction delays. Tell: usually abnormal means a normal tracing argues against the disease.
It excludes every cause of heart failure

A normal electrocardiogram speaks only to dilated cardiomyopathy, which it almost rules out; it cannot exclude every cause of heart failure. Her symptoms still need explaining with tests such as a blood count for anemia and thyroid function. Tell: one normal test narrows one diagnosis, not all of them.
It points to restrictive disease instead

A normal tracing does not point to any particular alternative; it only makes dilated cardiomyopathy unlikely, because that disease usually produces an abnormal electrocardiogram. Tell: a normal result lowers the probability of one diagnosis without naming another.
It makes dilated cardiomyopathy very unlikely

Correct. The electrocardiogram is usually abnormal in dilated cardiomyopathy, with findings such as left ventricular hypertrophy, atrial fibrillation, premature ventricular contractions or left bundle branch block, so her completely normal tracing will almost rule it out. An echo with dilated, thin walls would be needed to support it.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following arterial occlusive disease and aortic aneurysm: 2. Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
A.q: A 64-year-old woman who smokes has cramping in her right calf after walking one block that eases after she stands still for several minutes. Her pedal pulses are diminished on the right. Which is the best initial test?
opts: Conventional angiography is the invasive gold standard, requiring vascular puncture and contrast, and is used mainly to guide a planned intervention. It is not where the evaluation of new claudication begins; the bedside ankle-brachial index is. Gold standard does not mean first test.

Magnetic resonance angiography is an alternative to computed tomography angiography in contrast allergy and, like it, is used mainly to guide a planned intervention. Her suspected peripheral artery disease starts with the bedside ankle-brachial index. Anatomy studies come after the diagnosis is established.

Computed tomography angiography uses contrast to delineate arterial anatomy and is used mainly to plan an intervention. For a first evaluation of suspected peripheral artery disease, the simple bedside ankle-brachial index comes first. Contrast studies are for planning, not for initial testing.

Correct. Calf cramping after one block that eases with standing still, plus diminished right pedal pulses in a smoker, is classic claudication. The ankle-brachial index is a simple bedside test and the important initial test, with 0.4 to 0.9 the claudication band; it divides the higher ankle pressure by the higher arm pressure.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
A.q: A 17-year-old boy with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy asks his clinician what the most serious risk of his disease is. He has occasional palpitations and plays recreational basketball. Which complication is the leading cause of death in this condition?
opts: Heart failure symptoms do gradually progress in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and transplantation is an option if the disease stops responding to therapy, but sudden cardiac death is the leading cause of mortality. Tell: progressive failure is the slow course; sudden death is the leading cause.

Aortic dissection is not part of the hypertrophic cardiomyopathy course. The leading cause of mortality is sudden cardiac death, with heart failure symptoms progressing more slowly. Tell: the leading killer in this disease is sudden and cardiac, not vascular.

Correct. For this teenager with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and palpitations, the most serious risk is sudden cardiac death, the leading cause of mortality in the disease. Patients are classically advised to keep to mild to moderate, noncompetitive activity, stay hydrated and avoid excess alcohol.

Embolic stroke is not the leading cause of death in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Sudden cardiac death is, while heart failure symptoms progress gradually in others. Tell: for a young athlete with this disease, the danger to name is sudden death.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
A.q: A 30-year-old woman with known atrioventricular nodal reentry has a regular narrow complex tachycardia at 178. She is stable. Which treatment almost always terminates it?
opts: Catheter ablation offers a definitive cure, over 95 percent, for a select subset of patients with nodal reentry, but it is a planned procedure, not how an acute episode is stopped. Her stable episode now responds to vagal maneuvers or adenosine. Tell: the question asks what terminates the episode, not what prevents the next one.

Synchronized cardioversion is rarely required in atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia and is held for hemodynamic instability. She is stable, so she gets vagal maneuvers or adenosine first. Tell: a stable patient with nodal reentry almost never needs a shock.

Intravenous procainamide is used when Wolff-Parkinson-White is known or when adenosine reveals atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White. She has known nodal reentry, a circuit within the node with no accessory pathway. Tell: procainamide answers an accessory pathway; nodal reentry answers to vagal maneuvers or adenosine.

Correct. She is stable with a regular narrow tachycardia at 178 and known nodal reentry, and atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia almost always terminates with vagal maneuvers or adenosine. An educated patient whose vagal maneuver works at home usually does not need urgent medical attention.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
A.q: A 19-year-old man had a brief episode of racing heartbeat that stopped on its own. His resting electrocardiogram in sinus rhythm shows a short PR interval and a slurred upstroke at the start of each QRS (delta wave). Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. A short PR interval with a slurred upstroke of the QRS (delta wave) on a resting tracing in sinus rhythm is pre-excitation, which signals an accessory pathway (bundle of Kent): Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome. His self-limited burst of racing heartbeat fits the potential for atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia that this pathway carries.

Left bundle branch block does not explain a short PR interval with a slurred QRS upstroke; that pair is pre-excitation, the signature of an accessory pathway. With his brief racing episode it points to Wolff-Parkinson-White. Tell: check the PR interval and the start of the QRS; short and slurred means pre-excitation.

First-degree atrioventricular block is a conduction delay, which would not produce a short PR interval or a slurred QRS upstroke. A short PR with a delta wave means the impulse is reaching the ventricles early through an accessory pathway. Tell: a short PR plus a delta wave on a resting tracing is Wolff-Parkinson-White.

Nodal reentrant tachycardia is a reentry circuit within the atrioventricular node, a regular narrow tachycardia with hidden P waves during an episode. It needs no accessory pathway, so it does not explain a short PR and delta wave on his resting tracing. Tell: pre-excitation in sinus rhythm points to the bundle of Kent.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
A.q: A 33-year-old man with typical acute pericarditis after a viral illness has a troponin that is above the reference range. Coronary angiography shows normal arteries. Which process does the troponin elevation most likely reflect?
opts: Correct. Typical acute pericarditis after a viral illness with a troponin above the reference range and normal coronary arteries means the inflammation has reached the myocardium, myopericarditis. Troponin may rise when the myocardium is also affected, and an elevated troponin is a higher-risk feature that can call for hospitalization.

Nothing suggests a laboratory error, and an elevated troponin has a defined meaning in acute pericarditis: the myocardium is also inflamed. Dismissing it would miss a higher-risk feature that can warrant hospitalization. Tell: a raised troponin in typical pericarditis with normal coronary arteries points to myopericarditis, not to a faulty assay.

Coronary angiography showed normal arteries, which removes an occlusion as the source of his troponin. In acute pericarditis, troponin rises when inflammation also involves the myocardium (myopericarditis). Tell: a pericarditis picture, a raised troponin and clean coronary arteries together mean myopericarditis.
ruled out by a stated finding

Troponin rises when the myocardium is also affected; it is not a marker of constrictive physiology, and his illness is a fresh, typical episode after a viral infection. The elevated value signals myopericarditis, a higher-risk feature for hospitalization. Tell: in acute pericarditis, troponin tracks myocardial involvement and nothing else.

A.io: Demonstrate understanding of modified Duke diagnostic criteria.
A.q: A 61-year-old woman with a prosthetic mitral valve has a fever of 38.7 °C (101.7 °F) and Osler nodes (painful red nodules on the pads of her fingers). Under the modified Duke criteria, which category do the Osler nodes fall into?
opts: Predisposition is a separate minor criterion covering predisposing heart conditions or injection drug use. In her case the prosthetic mitral valve fills that slot, not the Osler nodes. Tell: predisposition describes the patient's background; Osler nodes are a finding on exam.

Vascular phenomena are embolic findings: major arterial emboli, septic pulmonary infarcts, mycotic aneurysm, intracranial hemorrhage, conjunctival hemorrhages and Janeway lesions. Osler nodes are not on that list. Tell: painful Osler nodes are immunologic; painless Janeway lesions are vascular.

Correct. Osler nodes are an immunologic phenomenon in the modified Duke criteria, a minor criterion shared with glomerulonephritis, Roth spots and rheumatoid factor. Her other findings count separately: the prosthetic valve is predisposition, and 38.7 °C (101.7 °F) meets the fever criterion of 38.0 °C or higher.

The major blood culture criterion requires a typical organism in two separate blood cultures or persistently positive cultures, so a skin finding cannot fill it, and no cultures are reported here. Tell: Osler nodes are seen at the bedside and count only as a minor immunologic criterion.

Deep vein thrombosis 3. Phlebitis a. Thrombophlebitis Septic thrombophlebitis 4. Arteriovenous fistula of the extremity a. Acquired (e.g. trauma, iatrogenic) b. Created (i.e. for hemodialysis) 5. Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
A.q: A 33-year-old man had a plaster cast removed from his right lower leg two days ago after a tibial fracture. He now has right calf swelling that measures 4 cm more than the left, and tenderness along the deep veins of the calf. Nothing else on the Wells criteria is present and no alternative diagnosis is as likely. What is his Wells score?
opts: One point counts only one of his three positive items. The recent plaster cast, the calf swelling over 3 cm and the tenderness along the deep veins each score 1, and the 2-point subtraction applies only when an alternative diagnosis is at least as likely, which the stem excludes.

Two points misses one of his three findings, most often the recent plaster immobilization, which counts even though the cast is already off. Cast 1 + calf swelling over 3 cm 1 + deep venous tenderness 1 = 3, a high likelihood rather than the moderate range of 1 to 2.

Correct. Recent plaster immobilization of the lower extremity 1 + calf swelling 4 cm more than the other leg (over 3 cm) 1 + localized tenderness along the deep venous system 1 = 3. No alternative diagnosis is as likely, so nothing is subtracted; a score of 3 or greater means a high clinical likelihood of deep vein thrombosis (DVT).

Four points adds an item he lacks, such as pitting edema, swelling of the entire leg, active cancer or a previously documented deep vein thrombosis. His three positives, the recent cast, calf swelling over 3 cm and deep venous tenderness, total 3.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
A.q: A 71-year-old man with a new inferior myocardial infarction involving the right ventricle is hypotensive with distended jugular veins and clear lungs. Tamponade is considered. Why must his infarction stay on the differential?
opts: His picture is abrupt and arrives with a new infarction, the acute setting. Myocardial infarction belongs in the differential of acute tamponade, while subacute tamponade is mimicked by constrictive pericarditis, congestive heart failure and cirrhosis. Tell: sudden events (infarction, dissection, massive embolism) mimic acute tamponade; slow congestive states mimic subacute.

Infarction appears in the differential because it mimics acute tamponade, not because it is the leading cause. Among causes of effusion, post-infarction disease is one cardiac cause on a long list that also includes idiopathic disease, malignancy, infection, metabolic disease and trauma. Tell: the question asks why it stays on the differential, which is because it looks like tamponade.

An infarction does not rule tamponade out; post-infarction disease and Dressler syndrome are listed cardiac causes of pericardial effusion. Because the two can coexist and look alike, tamponade remains a clinical diagnosis, confirmed only by the response to pericardiocentesis. Tell: a mimic stays on the list; it does not erase the other diagnosis.

Correct. Hypotension with distended jugular veins and clear lungs fits tamponade, but a right ventricular infarction can look the same. Myocardial infarction, especially with right ventricular involvement, heads the differential of acute tamponade along with aortic dissection and massive pulmonary embolism, so his infarction must stay on the list.

Deep vein thrombosis 3. Phlebitis a. Thrombophlebitis Septic thrombophlebitis 4. Arteriovenous fistula of the extremity a. Acquired (e.g. trauma, iatrogenic) b. Created (i.e. for hemodialysis) 5. Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
A.q: A 76-year-old man has had symmetric pitting swelling of both ankles for three weeks. He started amlodipine for hypertension one month ago. There is no warmth, redness, tenderness or skin discoloration, and he has no history of heart, kidney or liver disease. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. Symmetric pitting swelling of both ankles that began after starting amlodipine, with no warmth, redness or tenderness, fits drug-induced edema. Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers such as amlodipine commonly cause it; the swelling is often bilateral and usually shows no signs of inflammation.

Lymphedema is chronic edema of the extremities, usually with a history of pelvic surgery, malignancy or radiation therapy, none of which he has. The timing is the tell: his swelling started weeks after amlodipine was begun and is bilateral without inflammation, the pattern of drug-induced edema.

Drug-induced edema sits on the differential of deep vein thrombosis (DVT) because it swells the legs, but it is often bilateral and usually lacks signs of inflammation. His symmetric swelling without warmth, redness or tenderness began a month after amlodipine, which points to the drug rather than clots in both legs.

Chronic venous insufficiency in its post-thrombotic form follows a deep vein thrombosis by 6 to 24 months, and he has no history of a clot. His swelling is only three weeks old, bilateral, without skin discoloration, and began after amlodipine, which fits drug-induced edema.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
B.q: A 65-year-old woman developed chest pain and dyspnea during a hurricane evacuation. She has ST elevation, an elevated troponin and B-type natriuretic peptide, and an echocardiogram showing akinesis of the left ventricular apex. Which test confirms stress cardiomyopathy?
opts: Troponin I and T are usually elevated in Takotsubo, as they are in acute coronary syndrome, so repeating them cannot separate the two. Cardiac catheterization showing normal coronary arteries confirms the diagnosis. Tell: shared markers cannot confirm; the coronary arteries decide.

An exercise stress test does not confirm Takotsubo and is not part of its work-up, which follows acute coronary syndrome protocols. Cardiac catheterization confirms the diagnosis by showing normal coronary arteries. Tell: with ST elevation and raised troponin, the next look is at the coronaries, not a treadmill.

Correct. Her stressor (a hurricane evacuation), chest pain, ST elevation, raised troponin and B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP), and apical akinesis all fit stress cardiomyopathy but also mimic acute coronary syndrome. The diagnosis is confirmed with cardiac catheterization, which most often shows normal coronary arteries.

Endomyocardial biopsy is not part of the stress cardiomyopathy work-up. Confirmation comes from cardiac catheterization, which most often shows normal coronary arteries. Tell: the question that matters is whether the coronaries are blocked, which only catheterization answers.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
B.q: A 24-year-old man whose Wolff-Parkinson-White was found on a school electrocardiogram presents with palpitations. The rhythm is irregular and wide-complex, at rates up to 260, with varying delta waves (slurred upstrokes). He is alert with a blood pressure of 118/74. Which drug is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Atropine is the first-line drug for acute, symptomatic, unstable bradycardia. This man has a very fast, irregular rhythm conducting with Wolff-Parkinson-White, the opposite problem, so atropine has no role. Tell: atropine is for slow rates; known Wolff-Parkinson-White with a fast rhythm calls for procainamide.

Correct. An irregular, wide-complex tachycardia up to 260 with varying delta waves in a man with known Wolff-Parkinson-White is atrial fibrillation conducting over the accessory pathway. When Wolff-Parkinson-White is known, intravenous procainamide is used, never adenosine; he is alert with a normal blood pressure, so a drug is appropriate.

Intravenous magnesium is not the listed treatment for atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White. Irregular, wide complexes with varying delta waves in a patient with a known accessory pathway call for intravenous procainamide. Tell: known Wolff-Parkinson-White plus a fast irregular rhythm means procainamide.

Adenosine must never be used when Wolff-Parkinson-White is known or atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White is present; it is first line only for ordinary orthodromic reentry. His irregular, wide, delta-wave complexes in known Wolff-Parkinson-White are exactly that exception. Tell: an irregular wide rhythm with delta waves rules adenosine out.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
B.q: A 77-year-old woman is found unresponsive and pulseless, and chest compressions are started. Her monitor strip is shown, and the same flat tracing appears in every lead. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Defibrillation treats ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia. A flat tracing in every lead is asystole, which is unshockable. Tell: a flat line is never shocked; compressions and epinephrine are the treatment.

Synchronized cardioversion needs a QRS complex to time the shock to and is for a patient with a pulse. Asystole has neither and is unshockable. Tell: with no QRS and no pulse, the answer is compressions and epinephrine.

Correct. A flat tracing in every lead, with no P waves or QRS complexes, is asystole, which is unshockable. High-quality chest compressions and epinephrine 1 mg (1:10,000) by intravenous or intraosseous push every 3 to 5 minutes are the mainstays, early intubation is considered, and the prognosis is poor.

Amiodarone is for ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia that persists after shocks. Asystole is treated with high-quality compressions and epinephrine. Tell: antiarrhythmics belong to the shockable side of the arrest algorithm.
B.alt: Rhythm strip with a nearly flat line across the whole page and no complexes

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following venous disorders: 2. Deep vein thrombosis 3. Phlebitis a. Thrombophlebitis Septic thrombophlebitis 4. Arteriovenous fistula of the extremity a. Acquired (e.g. trauma, iatrogenic) b. Created (i.e. for hemodialysis) 5. Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
B.q: A 55-year-old man has a positive D-dimer during evaluation of calf pain two weeks after a bicycle crash with extensive bruising. He asks why his clinician says the result cannot confirm a clot. Which explanation is accurate?
opts: It reflects fibrinolysis from many causes

Correct. An elevated D-dimer implies increased fibrinolysis, and the test is sensitive but not specific, so a positive result does not prove a deep vein thrombosis (DVT). Poor specificity means causes other than a clot, such as his recent crash with extensive bruising, can raise it; imaging is needed to confirm or exclude a clot.
It rises only with pulmonary embolism

D-dimer is used as a rule-out test for both deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, so it is not tied to one disease. It reflects fibrinolysis, which is why a positive result in a man with recent extensive bruising cannot confirm a clot of any kind.
It is specific but not sensitive

This reverses the test's profile: D-dimer is sensitive but not specific. Sensitivity is what lets a negative result help rule out a clot, and poor specificity is why his positive result needs venous duplex ultrasound before anyone calls it a deep vein thrombosis.
It rises only with thigh clots

D-dimer is a blood test that reflects fibrinolysis; it gives no location for a clot, in the thigh or anywhere else. Locating a thrombus takes imaging, which is why venous duplex ultrasound, which has replaced venography, follows a positive result.

Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
B.q: Which is a risk factor for multiple recurrences of pericarditis?
opts: Risk rises with the severity of pericardial late gadolinium enhancement, so mild uptake sits at the low-risk end, not the risk-factor end. Severe enhancement, a large C-reactive protein rise and an autoimmune etiology are the listed predictors of multiple recurrences. Tell: the option flips the severity; the risk factor is severe enhancement.

It is the magnitude of C-reactive protein elevation that predicts multiple recurrences, so a low value points the other way. A high C-reactive protein (above 10 mg/L) is also part of the inflammatory phenotype that supports earlier anti-interleukin-1 therapy. Tell: the option reverses the direction of the marker; risk travels with a high level.

A prompt recovery is not a listed risk factor and suggests a self-limited episode. The predictors of multiple recurrences are the magnitude of C-reactive protein elevation, the severity of pericardial late gadolinium enhancement and an autoimmune etiology. Tell: risk factors describe more inflammation or systemic disease, never a quick recovery.

Correct. An autoimmune etiology is one of the three listed risk factors for multiple recurrences of pericarditis, alongside the magnitude of C-reactive protein elevation and the severity of pericardial late gadolinium enhancement. Autoimmune disease also shapes treatment, since prednisone at a second recurrence is reserved for underlying systemic autoimmune disease.

Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
B.q: What causes the pain of a pseudoaneurysm?
opts: Correct. A pseudoaneurysm presents with pain due to increased pressure from swelling or from nerve compression. It forms when arterial rupture, commonly laceration of the femoral artery by the access needle of a cardiac catheterization, lets blood fill a cavity outside the vessel wall.

An intimal tear is how an aortic dissection begins, creating a false lumen within the media. A pseudoaneurysm forms outside the vessel wall after arterial rupture, and its pain comes from swelling pressure or nerve compression. Within the wall means dissection; outside the wall means pseudoaneurysm.

Muscle ischemia on walking is claudication, a symptom of arterial narrowing. A pseudoaneurysm is a blood-filled cavity outside the vessel wall, and its pain comes from increased pressure due to swelling or from nerve compression. Exertional muscle pain points to stenosis, not to a leak.

Retroperitoneal bleeding is the event of a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm. A pseudoaneurysm is a contained blood-filled cavity, commonly at the femoral artery after catheterization, painful from swelling pressure or nerve compression. Local pain at the puncture site fits the pseudoaneurysm; shock with back pain fits rupture.

B.io: Identify medical care strategies for cardiomyopathies for the following populations. 8. adolescent 9. adult 10. elderly
B.q: Why is a patient with cardiomyopathy referred to cardiology?
opts: Only once symptoms occur at rest

Waiting for symptoms at rest, New York Heart Association (NYHA) class IV, is not the referral rule. Referral is made to establish care, consider genetic testing and review high-risk features. Tell: these are planning and risk-review reasons, which apply well before symptoms become severe.
Only when a device must be implanted

A device is only one possible intervention. Referral is made to establish care, consider genetic testing, review high-risk features and discuss medications or the need for any intervention. Tell: the word only is wrong, because referral serves several purposes.
To establish care and review risk features

Correct. A patient with cardiomyopathy is referred to cardiology to establish care, consider genetic testing, review any high-risk features, and discuss medications or the need for an intervention. This applies across the three types: dilated, hypertrophic and restrictive cardiomyopathy.
Only after an admission for edema

No admission for edema is required first. Cardiology referral is made to establish care, consider genetic testing, review high-risk features and discuss medications or interventions. Tell: referral is part of setting up care, not a step that waits for a complication.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
B.q: A 55-year-old woman with metastatic lung cancer has 2 days of worsening dyspnea and chest discomfort. Blood pressure is 84/56, heart rate 122, jugular veins are distended, and heart sounds are muffled. Her blood pressure drops by 18 mmHg on inspiration (pulsus paradoxus, an inspiratory drop in blood pressure). Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Constrictive pericarditis does not explain the full Beck triad she shows: muffled heart sounds, distended jugular veins and hypotension, the signature of fluid under pressure compressing the heart. Her 2-day decline with cancer, a listed cause of effusion, fits an acute effusion causing tamponade. Tell: the Beck triad plus pulsus paradoxus points to fluid, not a scarred sac.

Her findings are cardiac, not pulmonary: distant heart sounds, distended jugular veins and hypotension make up the Beck triad, and an 18 mmHg inspiratory drop is pulsus paradoxus. With malignancy as a known cause of effusion, these signs point to tamponade. Tell: muffled heart sounds with pulsus paradoxus localize the problem to the pericardium.

Correct. Blood pressure 84/56 with distended jugular veins and muffled heart sounds is the Beck triad, and an 18 mmHg inspiratory drop is pulsus paradoxus. Malignancy is a listed cause of pericardial effusion, and over 2 days even a small effusion can compress the heart, since acute effusions can cause tamponade with under 200 mL of fluid.

Acute pericarditis alone does not produce hypotension, distended jugular veins and muffled heart sounds; that Beck triad signals fluid under pressure compressing the heart. Her malignancy and rapid 2-day decline fit an acute effusion causing tamponade, which can occur with under 200 mL of fluid. Tell: once the Beck triad appears, think tamponade.

B.io: Demonstrate understanding of modified Duke diagnostic criteria.
B.q: A 47-year-old man who injects drugs has a fever of 39.4 °C (102.9 °F) and Janeway lesions (painless hemorrhagic macules) on the soles of both feet. Blood cultures are pending. Under the modified Duke criteria, which category do the Janeway lesions fall into?
opts: Immunologic phenomena are glomerulonephritis, Osler nodes, Roth spots and rheumatoid factor, and Janeway lesions are not on that list. Tell: the painful lesion (Osler node) is immunologic, while the painless hemorrhagic macule described here (Janeway lesion) is vascular.

Correct. Janeway lesions, the painless hemorrhagic macules on his soles, are a vascular phenomenon, a minor criterion grouped with major arterial emboli, septic pulmonary infarcts, mycotic aneurysm, intracranial hemorrhage and conjunctival hemorrhages. His injection drug use and fever of 39.4 °C (102.9 °F) are separate minor criteria.

Microbiologic evidence is a positive blood culture that does not meet the major criterion, or serologic evidence of active infection. His cultures are still pending, so nothing microbiologic can be counted yet. Tell: microbiologic criteria come from the laboratory, not from the skin.
ruled out by a stated finding

The major endocardial criterion requires a positive echocardiogram (oscillating intracardiac mass, abscess or new partial dehiscence of a prosthetic valve) or new valvular regurgitation. A skin lesion does not show endocardial involvement. Tell: endocardial evidence is seen in the heart; Janeway lesions are seen on the skin.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
B.q: A 67-year-old woman has had 2 months of low-grade fevers to 38.4 °C (101.1 °F), fatigue and a 4-kilogram weight loss. She had a tooth extracted 10 weeks ago. A new apical systolic murmur is heard, and splinter hemorrhages (thin dark lines under the nail plates) are seen on two fingers. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Tuberculosis would not explain a new apical systolic murmur or splinter hemorrhages. Her 2 months of lower fevers, fatigue and weight loss after a tooth extraction, plus the new murmur, fit the indolent course of subacute infective endocarditis. Tell: a new murmur with nail hemorrhages points to the valves, not the lungs.

Acute endocarditis is a hectically febrile illness with rapid onset over typically 3-10 days, high fevers and systemic toxicity. She has had 2 months of low-grade fever, fatigue and weight loss, which is the indolent subacute pattern. Tell: a duration of months and modest fevers separate subacute from acute.

Correct. Two months of lower fevers (38.4 °C), fatigue and a 4-kilogram weight loss is the indolent course of subacute infective endocarditis, in which fever, malaise and weight loss occur over weeks or months. The new murmur and splinter hemorrhages place the problem on a valve, and the recent extraction is a plausible dental source.

Polymyalgia rheumatica would not produce a new apical systolic murmur or splinter hemorrhages. Low-grade fever, malaise and weight loss over weeks to months with a new murmur after dental work fits subacute infective endocarditis. Tell: look for a new murmur and embolic nail findings before blaming a rheumatologic cause.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
B.q: A 52-year-old man has a cardiac arrest after choking on food at a restaurant. The obstruction is removed, but he remains pulseless with an organized rhythm on the monitor. Compressions are underway. Which airway step should be considered early?
opts: Correct. A pulseless patient with an organized rhythm has pulseless electrical activity, which is unshockable. Compressions start immediately and intubation is considered early; hypoxia, as from choking, is one of its two leading causes in adults, with hypovolemia, and epinephrine every 3 to 5 minutes is a mainstay.

Defibrillation is not an airway step, and an organized pulseless rhythm is pulseless electrical activity, which is unshockable. Compressions continue and early intubation addresses the hypoxia from choking. Tell: only ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia are shocked.
ruled out by a stated finding

A nebulized bronchodilator does not secure an airway in a pulseless patient. Pulseless electrical activity is treated with immediate compressions, epinephrine and early intubation. Tell: the airway step in this arrest is intubation.

Airway support is not delayed until a pulse returns. In pulseless electrical activity, compressions start immediately and intubation is considered early, especially here, where choking caused hypoxia. Tell: early intubation is part of treating this unshockable rhythm.

B.io: Demonstrate understanding of modified Duke diagnostic criteria.
B.q: A 62-year-old man with fever has four sets of blood cultures drawn. One set grows coagulase-negative staphylococci, and the other three are negative. How should this single positive culture be counted under the modified Duke criteria?
opts: As the major blood culture criterion

The major blood culture criterion needs a typical organism, such as viridans streptococci or Staphylococcus aureus, in two separate cultures, or persistently positive cultures. One of four sets growing coagulase-negative staphylococci meets neither. Tell: one positive set out of four is not persistent bacteremia.

Correct. A single positive culture for coagulase-negative staphylococci, with the other three sets negative, is excluded from the criteria because coagulase-negative staphylococci (like diphtheroids) are common culture contaminants. It counts as neither a major criterion nor the minor microbiologic criterion.

Vascular phenomena are embolic findings such as major arterial emboli, septic pulmonary infarcts, mycotic aneurysm, conjunctival hemorrhages and Janeway lesions. A culture result is never counted there. Tell: vascular criteria are found on exam or imaging; cultures fall under the blood culture or microbiologic criteria.

One positive culture is not definite proof: a single coagulase-negative staphylococcal set is excluded as a common contaminant, and even one major criterion alone does not make endocarditis definite. Definite endocarditis requires two major criteria, one major plus three minor, or five minor. Tell: a lone contaminant set counts toward no criterion.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following arterial occlusive disease and aortic aneurysm: 2. Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
B.q: A 60-year-old man who smokes has a 4.3 cm asymptomatic thoracic aortic aneurysm and a blood pressure of 158/94. He asks what he can do to help himself. Which counseling point is most appropriate?
opts: Correct. Management of a thoracic aortic aneurysm includes smoking cessation, beta-adrenergic blockers and aggressive blood pressure control, which target his smoking and his pressure of 158/94. At 4.3 cm, under 4.5 cm, he also needs surveillance with computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging every 3 to 5 years.
Smoking matters only for leg disease

Smoking cessation is listed first in thoracic aortic aneurysm management, so it matters for his aorta, not just his leg arteries. Quitting, along with beta-adrenergic blockers and aggressive blood pressure control, is what he can do himself. Smoking is not a leg-only risk.
Blood pressure matters only after surgery

Aggressive blood pressure control is part of thoracic aneurysm management now, not just after repair, and his 158/94 needs treatment. At 4.3 cm he is on surveillance, not heading to surgery. Risk-factor control starts at diagnosis.

Management starts at diagnosis, not at repair: smoking cessation, beta-adrenergic blockers and aggressive blood pressure control. At 4.3 cm he is below the repair thresholds and is followed with imaging every 3 to 5 years, while those measures apply throughout.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following arterial occlusive disease and aortic aneurysm: 2. B.q: A 74-year-old man with sudden leg ischemia has sensory loss extending beyond the toes with rest pain, mild-to-moderate weakness, an inaudible arterial Doppler signal and an audible venous signal. Where should his evaluation and treatment take place?
opts: Sufficient time for vascular imaging such as computed tomography angiography belongs to viable and marginally threatened limbs, which have no sensory loss or weakness. His deficits make the limb immediately threatened, so evaluation and treatment belong in the surgical suite. His weakness removes the time for imaging.

Major amputation is for irreversibly ischemic limbs with profound sensory loss, paralysis and inaudible arterial and venous Doppler signals. His venous signal is audible and his weakness only mild to moderate, so the limb is immediately threatened and still salvageable with immediate revascularization.
In the surgical suite, without delay

Correct. Sensory loss beyond the toes with rest pain, mild-to-moderate weakness, an inaudible arterial Doppler signal and an audible venous signal define an immediately threatened limb. It is salvageable with immediate revascularization, so it should preferentially undergo further evaluation and treatment in a surgical suite.

Outpatient testing wastes time this limb does not have. Sensory loss beyond the toes with mild-to-moderate weakness means an immediately threatened limb, salvageable only with immediate revascularization in a surgical suite. Outpatient pathways belong to chronic disease.

Deep vein thrombosis 3. Phlebitis a. Thrombophlebitis Septic thrombophlebitis 4. Arteriovenous fistula of the extremity a. Acquired (e.g. trauma, iatrogenic) b. Created (i.e. for hemodialysis) 5. Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
B.q: Which history typically accompanies lymphedema when it mimics deep vein thrombosis?
opts: A recent long flight is not the history linked to lymphedema. Lymphedema is chronic edema of the extremities, usually accompanied by pelvic surgery, malignancy or radiation therapy, so the tell is a long-standing swelling with a pelvic or cancer history, not a recent trip.
Starting a new blood pressure drug

Starting a new drug fits drug-induced edema, a common adverse effect of some drugs such as dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (amlodipine), with swelling that is often bilateral and lacks inflammation. Lymphedema instead follows pelvic surgery, malignancy or radiation therapy.

Correct. Lymphedema is chronic edema of the extremities that is usually accompanied by a history of pelvic surgery, malignancy or radiation therapy. That history is the clue that separates it from deep vein thrombosis (DVT) on the differential of a swollen leg.

A sudden injury fits a calf muscle pull or tear, where the inciting injury is usually part of the history and bruising may appear at the ankle. Lymphedema is chronic edema linked to pelvic surgery, malignancy or radiation therapy, not to an acute event.
