B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
B.q: A 52-year-old woman with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has a rhythm strip in which a normal beat is followed by an early beat with an abnormal P wave and a narrow QRS, repeating so that every other beat is early (bigeminy). Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: A junctional rhythm is a regular, steady rhythm usually at 40 to 60 with P waves that are inverted, buried in the QRS or after it. This strip alternates normal beats with early beats that carry their own abnormal P wave. Tell: early beats point to ectopics; a steady slow rhythm with inverted or hidden P waves is junctional.

Atrial flutter with 2:1 block shows a continuous sawtooth line at an atrial rate of 250 or more, with two flutter waves per QRS and a regular rhythm. Her strip alternates a normal beat with an early beat, each with a single P wave. Tell: flutter has no normal beats in between; bigeminy alternates normal and early beats.

Premature ventricular contractions begin in the ventricles and are early, wide and bizarre with no P wave. Her early beats are narrow and each has an abnormal P wave, which places them in the atria. Tell: a narrow early beat with a P wave is atrial; a wide, bizarre early beat without one is ventricular.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Each early beat has an abnormal P wave and a narrow QRS, which marks a premature atrial contraction beginning in the atria, and an ectopic beat every other beat is bigeminy. Premature atrial contractions are common in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, which fits this patient.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
B.q: Which history precedes viral myocarditis?
opts: Chest trauma is not the history of viral myocarditis; the prodrome is an infection, not an injury. The patient describes a flulike syndrome with fever and myalgia in the 1 to 2 weeks before heart failure symptoms. Tell: a viral cause needs a viral illness, and the gap is weeks, not days.
A flulike illness 1 to 2 weeks before

Correct. Viral myocarditis follows a recent flulike syndrome 1 to 2 weeks earlier, with fever, myalgia, fatigue, respiratory symptoms or gastroenteritis. Only then do heart failure symptoms appear, such as exercise intolerance, shortness of breath and chest pain, in a person with no underlying cardiac dysfunction.

An emotional shock hours earlier is not the viral prodrome. Viral myocarditis follows a flulike syndrome, with fever, myalgia, fatigue or gastroenteritis, 1 to 2 weeks before the heart failure symptoms. Tell: look for infectious symptoms and a gap of 1 to 2 weeks, not a stressor and a gap of hours.

Years of heavy drinking is a long, chronic exposure, while myocarditis presents as an acute decompensation of heart failure in a person with no underlying cardiac dysfunction or low cardiac risk. The viral form follows a flulike illness 1 to 2 weeks earlier. Tell: myocarditis is recent and acute.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
B.q: A 39-year-old woman who injects drugs has native valve endocarditis, and her blood cultures grow methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. Which antibiotic is most appropriate?
opts: Correct. Her cultures grow methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus on a native valve, which is treated with vancomycin or daptomycin. Methicillin resistance is the decisive clue: it rules out nafcillin, oxacillin and cefazolin, which are used for susceptible strains. Therapy is bactericidal, parenteral and prolonged.

Nafcillin or oxacillin treats methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus. Her isolate is methicillin-resistant, so these drugs will not work. Tell: the word resistant on the culture report moves you from nafcillin or oxacillin to vancomycin or daptomycin.
ruled out by a stated finding

Ampicillin with gentamicin is not among the staphylococcal regimens. Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus is treated with vancomycin or daptomycin; gentamicin is an add-on in prosthetic valve staphylococcal infection or for viridans streptococci. Tell: a resistant staphylococcus on a native valve means vancomycin or daptomycin.

Cefazolin is an option for methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus, alongside nafcillin or oxacillin. Her organism is methicillin-resistant, so cefazolin alone is inadequate. Tell: cefazolin pairs with susceptible strains; resistant strains need vancomycin or daptomycin.
ruled out by a stated finding

Deep vein thrombosis 3. Phlebitis a. Thrombophlebitis Septic thrombophlebitis 4. Arteriovenous fistula of the extremity a. Acquired (e.g. trauma, iatrogenic) b. Created (i.e. for hemodialysis) 5. Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
B.q: A 71-year-old man has been on strict bed rest for six days during an admission for pneumonia and now has swelling and aching of the entire left leg. Which component of the Virchow triad does his prolonged bed rest represent?
opts: Endothelial injury comes from trauma, surgery such as knee or hip replacement, intravenous drug use or burns. Bed rest during pneumonia does not injure the vein wall; it alters blood flow, which places it under venous stasis.

A hypercoagulable state is a clotting tendency, inherited (factor V Leiden, protein C or S deficiency) or acquired (cancer, estrogen, pregnancy). Lying still changes blood flow rather than the blood's clotting tendency, so his bed rest belongs to venous stasis.

Arterial vasospasm is not one of the three Virchow components, which are venous stasis, a hypercoagulable state and vascular endothelial injury. His risk comes from immobilization, which the triad lists under venous stasis along with long flights and postoperative inactivity.

Correct. Six days of strict bed rest is immobilization, which alters blood flow: the venous stasis arm of the Virchow triad. Immobilization carries about a 20-fold increased risk for deep vein thrombosis (DVT), which fits his new swelling and aching of the entire leg.

Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
B.q: A 26-year-old woman with asthma used her inhaler repeatedly during an attack and then felt a sudden, rapid pounding in her chest. Her electrocardiogram shows a regular, narrow-complex tachycardia at 170 with no visible P waves. Which factor most likely triggered this rhythm?
opts: Hypothyroidism is listed among causes of sinus bradycardia and sick sinus syndrome, conditions that slow the heart. It is not among the triggers of nodal reentry, and her rhythm is fast and sudden. Tell: thyroid underactivity belongs on the slow list; her trigger is the inhaler she just used.

Increased vagal tone causes slow rhythms, such as a junctional rhythm in well-conditioned athletes, and vagal maneuvers are what terminate nodal reentry. Raising vagal tone would stop this tachycardia, not start it. Tell: vagal stimulation is the treatment for nodal reentry, not the trigger.

Low potassium is not among the listed triggers of nodal reentrant tachycardia, which are exertion, caffeine, alcohol, beta-agonists and sympathomimetics. Electrolyte abnormalities instead appear among the causes of sick sinus syndrome. Tell: the clue in the stem is the repeated inhaler use just before the onset.

Correct. A sudden, regular, narrow-complex tachycardia at 170 with no visible P waves in a young woman is nodal reentrant tachycardia, which may start spontaneously or with exertion, caffeine, alcohol, beta-agonists or sympathomimetics. Repeated puffs of her rescue inhaler delivered a beta-agonist just before the onset.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following arterial occlusive disease and aortic aneurysm: 2. Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
B.q: What makes up atheroemboli?
opts: Bone marrow fat is not the material described. Atheroemboli come from proximal atherosclerotic plaques and consist of fibrin, platelets and cholesterol debris. The source is an arterial plaque, not bone, and the debris lodges in small vessels of skin and muscle.

Air is not part of atheroembolism, and atheroemboli travel in arteries, not veins. They are multiple small deposits of fibrin, platelets and cholesterol debris that embolize from proximal atherosclerotic lesions. The prefix athero points to plaque material.
Clot formed in the left atrium

Clot formed in a heart chamber is a thromboembolus, the most common cause of acute embolic limb ischemia, with absent pulses distal to the occlusion. Atheroemboli are different: multiple small deposits of fibrin, platelets and cholesterol debris from proximal atherosclerotic lesions. Cholesterol debris is their marker.

Correct. Atheroembolism is multiple small deposits of fibrin, platelets and cholesterol debris embolizing from proximal atherosclerotic lesions. The debris lodges in small vessels of muscle and skin and may not occlude large vessels, so distal pulses usually remain palpable.
B.cite: Arterial Occlusive Diseaase and Aneurysms - Carter.pptx, Slide 68

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
B.q: A 70-year-old woman on telemetry has torsades de pointes (QRS complexes that twist around the baseline). The first-line intravenous push broke the first run, but short runs keep recurring. She is alert with a pulse and a normal blood pressure. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Shocks are for the hemodynamically unstable patient, and torsades in that setting is defibrillated (unsynchronized), not given a synchronized shock. She is alert with a normal blood pressure, so she gets a magnesium infusion. Tell: a stable, conscious patient with torsades gets magnesium, not a shock.

Correct. In a conscious patient, intravenous magnesium breaks torsades de pointes, and more magnesium is then given as an infusion. The push broke her first run, so with short runs recurring in an alert, normotensive patient, the next step is a magnesium infusion; amiodarone, procainamide and beta blockers are avoided.

Procainamide prolongs the QT and is avoided in torsades de pointes, like amiodarone. A conscious patient with recurring runs after the first push gets magnesium as an infusion. Tell: drugs that prolong the QT feed torsades rather than stopping it.

Amiodarone prolongs the QT and is avoided in torsades de pointes. Her recurring runs after the first magnesium push are treated with a magnesium infusion. Tell: in torsades, the follow-up to magnesium is more magnesium.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
B.q: A 69-year-old woman with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is admitted in an acute exacerbation. She is tachycardic and irregular, and her electrocardiogram shows three or more different P-wave shapes in one lead with a P wave before each QRS. Which is the most important treatment for this rhythm?
opts: Correct. An irregular tachycardia with three or more P-wave shapes and a P wave before each QRS is multifocal atrial tachycardia, and in an acute chronic obstructive pulmonary disease exacerbation it reflects right heart stress from acute illness. Management is treating the underlying condition; a beta blocker or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker may be added in hospital.

Adenosine terminates node-dependent reentry and is usually less effective even for focal atrial tachycardia, where it serves mainly as a diagnostic tool. Her irregular rhythm with several P-wave shapes is driven by acute lung disease, which adenosine does not touch. Tell: in multifocal atrial tachycardia the target is the lung disease, not the node.

Catheter ablation is usually curative, about 90 percent, for focal atrial tachycardia, which has a single ectopic focus to target. Her rhythm comes from multiple foci provoked by an acute exacerbation, so the fix is treating the lung disease. Tell: one focus can be ablated; multiple foci from acute illness are treated at the cause.

Synchronized cardioversion is used for hemodynamically unstable tachycardias, such as unstable focal atrial tachycardia. Multifocal atrial tachycardia is managed by treating the underlying condition, here her chronic obstructive pulmonary disease exacerbation. Tell: multifocal atrial tachycardia is a marker of acute illness and a poor prognostic sign, so treat the cause.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
B.q: In sick sinus syndrome, a fast run that is irregularly irregular with no P waves alternates with pauses. Which rhythm is the fast run?
opts: Correct. A fast run that is irregularly irregular with no P waves is atrial fibrillation. In tachy-brady syndrome, the form of sick sinus syndrome in which a tachyarrhythmia alternates with symptomatic bradycardia or pauses, atrial fibrillation is the most common cause of the fast rhythm.

Multifocal atrial tachycardia is also irregular, but each QRS has a P wave, in at least three different shapes in the same lead. A fast run with no P waves at all is atrial fibrillation, the most common fast rhythm of tachy-brady syndrome. Tell: P waves present in several shapes means multifocal; absent P waves means fibrillation.
ruled out by a stated finding

Sinus tachycardia is regular, at over 100 to 160, with a uniform P wave before every QRS. This fast run is irregularly irregular with no P waves, so it is not coming from the sinus node. Tell: a P wave before every beat keeps the rhythm sinus; irregularity without P waves means atrial fibrillation.
ruled out by a stated finding

Ventricular tachycardia can be the fast rhythm of tachy-brady syndrome, and then the patient needs a permanent pacemaker with an implantable defibrillator. But ventricular tachycardia is regular, at about 150 to 200, while this run is irregularly irregular with no P waves. Tell: an irregularly irregular run without P waves is atrial fibrillation.
ruled out by a stated finding

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following venous disorders: 2. Deep vein thrombosis 3. Phlebitis a. Thrombophlebitis Septic thrombophlebitis 4. Arteriovenous fistula of the extremity a. Acquired (e.g. trauma, iatrogenic) b. Created (i.e. for hemodialysis) 5. Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
B.q: A 62-year-old woman receiving chemotherapy through a central venous catheter has two days of right arm swelling and aching. The catheter injuring the vein wall is the endothelial trauma component of the Virchow triad. Which is the best diagnostic test?
opts: The ankle-brachial index is not a venous imaging test and plays no part in diagnosing deep vein thrombosis, which rests on venous duplex ultrasound of the involved extremity. Her swollen arm with an indwelling catheter needs that ultrasound to show the clot.

Contrast ascending venography is the definitive gold standard for deep vein thrombosis, but it has been replaced by venous duplex ultrasound of the involved extremity. It is not where her work-up starts; the noninvasive ultrasound is.

D-dimer is sensitive but not specific: elevation implies fibrinolysis, so a positive result cannot confirm a clot, and the test is used to rule out rather than diagnose. With arm swelling around a catheter she needs venous duplex ultrasound of the arm to show the thrombus.

Correct. Two days of arm swelling and aching with a central venous catheter call for imaging of that limb, and venous duplex ultrasound of the involved extremity is the test that has replaced contrast venography for deep vein thrombosis (DVT). A D-dimer could not confirm the clot, because it is sensitive but not specific.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
B.q: A 52-year-old man is discharged after a large viral pericardial effusion was found without tamponade. He asks how the effusion will be monitored. Which follow-up plan is most appropriate?
opts: A chest radiograph shows only an enlarged cardiac silhouette, an indirect sign, while echocardiography is the gold standard that shows the effusion itself and any right ventricular diastolic collapse. Large effusions are followed with serial transthoracic echocardiograms. Tell: follow fluid with the test that images fluid.

Symptom relief is not the end point for a large effusion. All large pericardial effusions should be followed with serial transthoracic echocardiograms, together with close clinical follow-up for the underlying cause. Tell: the word large triggers routine imaging follow-up whatever the symptoms do.

Correct. His effusion is large, and all large pericardial effusions should be followed with serial transthoracic echocardiograms, the gold-standard test that shows the effusion and any right ventricular diastolic collapse. Close clinical follow-up with the specialty matching the cause rounds out the plan.

An electrocardiogram can show electrical alternans in tamponade, but it does not measure the effusion. Large effusions are followed with serial transthoracic echocardiograms, which show the fluid and any right ventricular collapse. Tell: tracings capture electrical signs; echocardiography tracks the fluid.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
B.q: A 19-year-old woman has had three episodes of a regular, narrow-complex tachycardia at 230 that converted with adenosine. Her tracing in sinus rhythm shows a short PR interval and a slurred QRS upstroke (delta wave). Which is the first-line long-term treatment?
opts: A permanent pacemaker treats chronic symptomatic bradycardia, as in sick sinus syndrome. Her problem is a fast reentry circuit through an accessory pathway, not a slow rate. Tell: a delta wave points to a pathway to remove, and catheter ablation removes it.

Oral beta blockers or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are the initial chronic therapy for focal atrial tachycardia. In Wolff-Parkinson-White, catheter ablation of the accessory pathway is the first-line long-term treatment. Tell: a delta wave in sinus rhythm means the long-term answer is ablation, not daily drugs.

A pill-in-the-pocket beta blocker or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker is an option for nodal reentrant tachycardia, a circuit within the node. Her short PR and delta wave reveal an accessory pathway, and Wolff-Parkinson-White is managed long term by ablating it. Tell: pill in pocket goes with nodal reentry; ablation goes with a delta wave.

Correct. Recurrent regular narrow tachycardia at 230 that converts with adenosine, plus a short PR and slurred QRS upstroke (delta wave) in sinus rhythm, is reentry through an accessory pathway: Wolff-Parkinson-White. For chronic management, catheter ablation of the accessory pathway is the first-line treatment.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
B.q: A 58-year-old man collapses in a gym. He is unresponsive, not breathing and has no pulse. The monitor shows chaotic, irregular waves of varying size with no identifiable QRS complexes. Which rhythm is present?
opts: Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia still has QRS complexes whose shape varies, as in torsades de pointes, where they twist around the baseline. This monitor shows no identifiable QRS complexes, only chaotic waves. Tell: varying QRS complexes mean polymorphic tachycardia; no QRS at all means fibrillation.

Correct. Ventricular fibrillation has no pulse and no perfusion, a rate of 0, no rhythm, no P waves and no PR interval, only uncoordinated activity in place of QRS complexes. Chaotic waves of varying size in an unresponsive, pulseless man fit exactly, and he needs defibrillation.
Asystole is a flat line with no rate, rhythm or QRS complexes. Chaotic, irregular waves of varying size are ventricular fibrillation. Tell: a flat line is asystole; chaotic waves are fibrillation.

Pulseless electrical activity shows an organized rhythm, often one that would be expected to produce a pulse, yet no pulse is felt. This monitor shows chaotic waves without any identifiable QRS. Tell: organized without a pulse is pulseless electrical activity; chaos is fibrillation.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
B.q: A 65-year-old woman with lung cancer has a moderate effusion, dyspnea and a blood pressure of 100/68. Her clinician measures her blood pressure through the respiratory cycle. Which result most supports tamponade?
opts: In tamponade arterial blood pressure falls, not rises, with inspiration; pulsus paradoxus is a drop of 10 mmHg with inspiration. A rise does not support tamponade. Tell: in tamponade the jugular venous pressure may climb with inspiration (Kussmaul sign), but the arterial pressure falls, so do not mix up the two directions.

Correct. A 15 mmHg fall in blood pressure on inspiration exceeds the 10 mmHg inspiratory drop that defines pulsus paradoxus, a sign of tamponade. In this woman with lung cancer, a moderate effusion, dyspnea and a borderline pressure of 100/68, it supports fluid compressing the heart and limiting filling.

A pressure that holds steady through the respiratory cycle lacks pulsus paradoxus, the drop of 10 mmHg with inspiration expected in tamponade. It does not support tamponade from her effusion. Tell: tamponade shows itself on inspiration, when the blood pressure falls.

A 4 mmHg dip is well short of the 10 mmHg inspiratory drop in blood pressure that defines pulsus paradoxus, so it does not support tamponade. Tell: measure the size of the fall against 10 mmHg; a small physiologic dip is not pulsus paradoxus, while a fall of 10 mmHg or more alongside the Beck triad is.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
B.q: A 63-year-old woman with dilated cardiomyopathy comes to clinic with mild breathlessness on exertion. Her examination shows trace ankle edema and clear lungs. Her B-type natriuretic peptide is 60 pg/mL. What does this natriuretic peptide result indicate?
opts: A natriuretic peptide cannot confirm myocarditis; inflammatory processes are identified with gadolinium-enhanced cardiac magnetic resonance imaging. Her level of 60 pg/mL is below 100, which excludes heart failure. Tell: this test speaks to filling pressure, not to the cause.

An elevated B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) indicates raised left ventricular filling pressure and dysfunction, but her level of 60 pg/mL is below the 100 pg/mL threshold that excludes heart failure. Tell: the number points away from heart failure, not toward it.

Correct. B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) is released when ventricular filling pressures are high, and a level below 100 pg/mL excludes heart failure. Her value of 60 pg/mL, with clear lungs and only trace edema, makes heart failure an unlikely cause of her mild exertional breathlessness.

Raised filling pressure releases B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) and pushes the level up; an elevated level indicates increased left ventricular filling pressure and dysfunction. Her 60 pg/mL is low. Tell: a level below 100 pg/mL excludes heart failure, so raised pressure is not shown.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following arterial occlusive disease and aortic aneurysm: 2. Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
B.q: A 66-year-old man with hypertension has sudden, severe, ripping chest pain. His electrocardiogram is normal. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: The ankle-brachial index grades lower extremity arterial disease and says nothing about chest pain. Suspected dissection is imaged with computed tomography of the chest and abdomen, or with magnetic resonance imaging or transesophageal echocardiography. Match the test to the vessel at risk.
Reassure him; the tracing is normal

A normal electrocardiogram does not rule out aortic dissection, in which the tracing may be normal. Sudden ripping chest pain in a man with hypertension needs computed tomography of the chest and abdomen. Reassurance on a normal tracing is the classic error here.

Correct. Sudden, severe, ripping chest pain in a man with hypertension is the presentation of aortic dissection, and the electrocardiogram may be normal in dissection, so his normal tracing does not exclude it. Computed tomography of the chest and abdomen delineates the extent of the dissection.

A plain abdominal film is not among the studies for aortic dissection and cannot show its extent. Computed tomography of the chest and abdomen delineates the extent; magnetic resonance imaging and transesophageal echocardiography are alternatives. His ripping chest pain needs cross-sectional imaging.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
B.q: What is the prognosis of viridans streptococcal infective endocarditis?
opts: Staphylococcus aureus, not viridans streptococci, is the most lethal endocarditis organism, with mortality of about 30% in people who do not inject drugs and 50% in prosthetic valve endocarditis. Viridans streptococci carry a relatively good prognosis. Tell: most lethal always belongs to Staphylococcus aureus.

Correct. Viridans streptococcal endocarditis has a relatively good prognosis if antibiotic treatment is started before complications occur. Timing is the key qualifier: the good outlook depends on treating early, before complications develop.

Valve replacement in a large share of cases describes enterococcal endocarditis, where major complications and need for valve replacement reach about 30-40% and antibiotic resistance makes treatment difficult. Viridans streptococcal disease does relatively well. Tell: high surgery rates go with enterococci.

A poor outcome despite prompt treatment contradicts the viridans streptococcal pattern: the prognosis is relatively good when antibiotics start before complications. Poor outcomes are tied to Staphylococcus aureus, the most lethal organism. Tell: for viridans streptococci, early treatment is what makes the outlook good.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
B.q: A 26-year-old marathon runner has a resting heart rate of 48 at a preparticipation physical. He denies dizziness, fainting or chest pain. The electrocardiogram shows a regular rhythm with a normal P wave before every narrow QRS and a PR interval of 0.16 seconds. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: A permanent pacemaker is for chronic, symptomatic bradycardia. This runner denies dizziness, fainting and chest pain, and his slow rate is an adaptive response to conditioning. Tell: a pacemaker needs symptoms that track the slow rate, and none are present here.

Sinus bradycardia is seen in healthy people as an adaptive response, particularly in well-conditioned athletes. His training is the reason for the slow rate, and with no symptoms nothing needs treating or stopping. Tell: an athlete's asymptomatic sinus bradycardia gets reassurance only, not activity limits.

Correct. A regular rhythm at 48 with a normal P wave before every narrow QRS and a PR of 0.16 seconds is sinus bradycardia. In a well-conditioned marathon runner with no dizziness, fainting or chest pain it is an adaptive response, and asymptomatic sinus bradycardia is not treated.

Atropine is first line for acute, symptomatic, hemodynamically unstable bradycardia. This runner is well, with no dizziness, fainting or chest pain. Tell: atropine needs symptoms and instability; an asymptomatic athlete with sinus bradycardia needs neither a drug nor a device.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
B.q: A 79-year-old woman is brought in after fainting. Her pulse is 34. Her electrocardiogram shows regular P waves at 80 and regular wide QRS complexes at 34, with no fixed relationship between them. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Sinus bradycardia would have one P wave before every QRS at a fixed PR. Her atria beat at 80 while the ventricles beat at 34 with no relationship, which is complete block. Tell: two different rates rule out sinus bradycardia.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Regular P waves at 80 and regular wide QRS complexes at 34 with no fixed relationship are complete dissociation of the atria from the ventricles: third-degree (complete) block, with a ventricular rate usually under 40. Her syncope matters because it is associated with an increased risk of sudden death.

A junctional rhythm does not explain two separate regular rhythms: her regular P waves at 80 run independently of wide QRS complexes at 34. That dissociation defines third-degree (complete) block. Tell: two independent rates mean third degree.

Mobitz type II conducts most P waves with a constant PR and drops an occasional QRS. Here no P wave has a fixed relationship to any QRS, and the ventricular rate is 34. Tell: if no PR is fixed, it is complete block, not second degree.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
B.q: A 30-year-old cyclist with no symptoms has a rhythm in which the PR interval lengthens beat by beat until a QRS complex is dropped, after which the cycle starts again. Echocardiogram is normal. Which is the most appropriate management?
opts: Transcutaneous pacing is an emergency bridge for unstable high-grade block such as Mobitz type II or complete block. This cyclist has stable, silent Mobitz type I. Tell: emergency pacing needs an unstable, slow patient.

Correct. A PR that lengthens beat by beat until a QRS drops, then restarts, is Mobitz type I (Wenckebach) block, which is usually asymptomatic. With no symptoms and a normal echocardiogram, no treatment is needed; a permanent pacemaker is considered only for symptomatic patients, and increased vagal tone is a named cause.

A permanent pacemaker is considered for symptomatic Mobitz type I, and this cyclist has no symptoms. Mobitz type II is the block paced even without symptoms. Tell: in type I, the decision to pace follows symptoms.

Cardiac ablation is itself a named cause of Mobitz type I, so it cannot be the treatment. A silent Wenckebach pattern with a normal echocardiogram needs no treatment. Tell: a procedure that causes a block cannot fix it.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following venous disorders: 2. Deep vein thrombosis 3. Phlebitis a. Thrombophlebitis Septic thrombophlebitis 4. Arteriovenous fistula of the extremity a. Acquired (e.g. trauma, iatrogenic) b. Created (i.e. for hemodialysis) 5. Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
B.q: A 38-year-old woman has long-standing swelling of both legs just above the ankles that is symmetric, with normal skin color and no ulcers or varicose veins. Cardiac, kidney and liver evaluations are normal. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Lymphedema typically causes unilateral swelling with absent varicosities and pitting edema, and brawny discoloration is rare. Her swelling is bilateral and symmetric and sits just above the ankles, the distinguishing pattern of lipedema.

Chronic venous insufficiency is the usual source of the skin changes and leg ulcers that history and examination pick up, and it is confirmed with venous duplex ultrasound. She has normal skin color, no ulcers and no varicose veins, so symmetric swelling just above the ankles fits lipedema instead.

Correct. Bilateral, symmetric swelling just above the ankles in a woman is how lipedema is described. Her normal cardiac, kidney and liver evaluations exclude the systemic causes of bilateral edema, and the absence of varicose veins, ulcers or skin color change argues against venous disease.

Heart failure, chronic kidney disease and decompensated liver disease do cause bilateral leg edema, but her cardiac, kidney and liver evaluations are normal. With those causes excluded, symmetric swelling just above the ankles in a woman points to lipedema.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
B.q: A 48-year-old woman with obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is admitted after surgery with low blood pressure, and a resident proposes a drug to strengthen her heart's contraction. Which drug class should be avoided in her?
opts: Correct. In her obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, a drug to strengthen contraction is exactly what to avoid: positive inotropes such as digoxin, epinephrine and norepinephrine increase contractility, which increases the risk of myocardial ischemia and may induce arrhythmias. Beta blockers do the reverse, decreasing contractility.

Amiodarone is used, not avoided: it reduces the incidence and risk of sudden cardiac death with or without outflow obstruction and converts atrial fibrillation and flutter. Positive inotropes are the class to avoid. Tell: the proposal in the stem is a drug to strengthen contraction, and that is the danger.

Beta blockers such as metoprolol are the initial medication for outflow tract obstruction, not a class to avoid. They are negative chronotropes and inotropes that enhance diastolic filling. Tell: the class to avoid is the one that increases contractility, which is what the resident proposed.

Verapamil and diltiazem, nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, are used for outflow tract obstruction as negative chronotropes and inotropes. They are not the class to avoid. Tell: the helpful drugs reduce contractility; the drugs to avoid increase it.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
B.q: A 48-year-old woman with known pulmonary sarcoidosis faints at work. She takes no medications. Her heart rate is 35, and the electrocardiogram shows P waves at a regular rate with no relationship to slow QRS complexes. Which named cause of her block fits her best?
opts: Increased vagal tone is a cause of first-degree and Mobitz type I block; it is not on the complete block list. Her known sarcoidosis is, since inflammatory and infiltrative disease is a named cause of third-degree block. Tell: her history hands you the cause.

Correct. Her rate of 35 with P waves unrelated to the QRS complexes is complete block, and her syncope matters because it carries an increased risk of sudden death. Inflammatory and infiltrative disease (myocarditis, amyloidosis, sarcoidosis) is a named cause, and her known sarcoidosis, a granulomatous disease, is the fit at 48.

Degenerative disease of the conduction system is the most common cause of complete block overall, especially with old age, hypertension and diabetes. At 48, with known sarcoidosis and none of those, her infiltrative disease is the better fit. Tell: a named disease in the history beats the base rate.

She takes no medications, so a drug effect is ruled out by the stem. Sarcoidosis, an infiltrative disease, is a named cause of complete heart block and is already in her history. Tell: the stem removes drugs on purpose to point at her known disease.
ruled out by a stated finding

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
B.q: A 55-year-old man has progressive breathlessness on exertion, fatigue and swelling of both legs. The apical impulse is displaced laterally, a third heart sound (an early diastolic sound just after the second heart sound) is present, and there is a soft murmur at the apex. Which echocardiogram finding would support dilated cardiomyopathy?
opts: Normal cavity size with large atria and stiff walls

Normal cavity size with large atria does not support dilated cardiomyopathy, whose echo shows dilated, thin walls, possibly all four chambers dilated and an ejection fraction below 40%. Tell: in dilated disease the ventricles themselves are enlarged and weak.
Dilated thin walls with a reduced ejection fraction

Correct. His displaced apical impulse, third heart sound and apical murmur fit dilated cardiomyopathy, and the supporting echocardiogram shows dilated, thin walls (the prominent feature) with an ejection fraction below 40%. Hypokinetic chambers, dilation of up to all four chambers, mitral or tricuspid regurgitation and sometimes thrombus may also appear.

Hypokinesis confined to the mid and apical segments is a limited regional pattern; dilated cardiomyopathy shows dilated, thin walls with an ejection fraction below 40% and hypokinetic chambers. Segmental wall-motion abnormalities can occur, but dilation is the prominent feature. Tell: look for dilation, not a regional defect alone.
A thick septum and a small left ventricular cavity

A thick septum with a small cavity is the opposite of the dilated picture. Dilated cardiomyopathy shows dilated, thin walls, an ejection fraction below 40% and hypokinetic chambers. Tell: dilated means big chambers with thin walls, not a small, thick-walled one.

B.io: Identify medical care strategies for cardiomyopathies for the following populations. 8. adolescent 9. adult 10. elderly
B.q: An 86-year-old woman with end-stage cardiomyopathy has breathlessness at rest, edema and fatigue despite maximal tolerated therapy. She is not a transplant or device candidate and says she wants comfort at home. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: She is not a transplant candidate and has asked for comfort at home. In end-stage cardiomyopathy the step is advance care planning, goals-of-care discussion and hospice referral. Tell: when advanced therapies are off the table, palliative care leads.

She is not a device candidate, and her goal is comfort at home. Elderly care focuses on symptom control and quality of life, with palliative care discussions in advanced stages and hospice referral in end-stage disease. Tell: her stated wish and end-stage disease point to palliative care.
Stop all of her symptom medicines

Palliative care actively manages dyspnea, fatigue and edema; it does not withdraw symptom relief. The next step is a goals-of-care discussion and hospice referral. Tell: comfort care still treats symptoms, especially in a frail elderly patient.
Discuss goals of care and hospice

Correct. She has end-stage cardiomyopathy, is not a transplant or device candidate and wants comfort at home. Palliative care covers symptom management of dyspnea, fatigue and edema, advance care planning and goals-of-care discussions, caregiver support and hospice referral in end-stage disease.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
B.q: How is polymorphic ventricular tachycardia treated, even when the patient has a pulse?
opts: Intravenous lidocaine alone is not enough: drug cardioversion is for stable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia, and lidocaine is otherwise the one antiarrhythmic allowed in torsades. Polymorphic tachycardia is never truly stable and is defibrillated. Tell: a pulse does not make polymorphic tachycardia safe.

Correct. Even when the patient has a pulse and looks well, polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is never truly stable; it is a short-lived transitional state. It is defibrillated, followed by urgent coronary angiography with possible revascularization, and intravenous metoprolol or amiodarone may be added.

Synchronized cardioversion is for unstable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia with a pulse. Polymorphic tachycardia is defibrillated (unsynchronized) even when a pulse is present, because it is never truly stable. Tell: a QRS that keeps changing shape gets an unsynchronized shock.

Observation is unsafe: even if the patient looks fine, polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is only a short-lived transitional state that will need defibrillation. Tell: 'never truly stable' means it is shocked as soon as it is seen, then followed by urgent coronary angiography.

B.io: Discuss indications and antibiotic regimens for subacute bacterial endocarditis prophylaxis.
B.q: A 71-year-old woman with a prosthetic mitral valve is having a gum biopsy. She is not allergic to penicillin, but she cannot swallow pills after a recent stroke. Which prophylaxis is most appropriate?
opts: Clindamycin is no longer recommended for endocarditis prophylaxis because of the risk of Clostridioides difficile infection, whatever the route. A non-allergic patient who cannot take oral medication receives ampicillin by injection instead. Tell: clindamycin has been removed from the list entirely.

Prophylaxis is indicated here. A gum biopsy manipulates gingival tissue and perforates the oral mucosa, and prosthetic cardiac valves are on the list of conditions that qualify. Tell: unlike dental radiographs or anesthetic injections through noninfected tissue, a biopsy cuts the mucosa.
ruled out by a stated finding

Oral amoxicillin 2 g is the standard regimen only for a patient who can take oral medication. After her stroke she cannot swallow pills, so the oral route is out. Tell: same non-allergic patient, but the inability to take oral medication shifts amoxicillin to injectable ampicillin.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. She has a prosthetic mitral valve and a gum biopsy that manipulates gingival tissue, so prophylaxis is indicated. With no penicillin allergy but no ability to take oral medication, the regimen is ampicillin 2 g intramuscularly or intravenously within 30-60 minutes before the procedure.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
B.q: A 66-year-old woman with ovarian cancer has had three drainages for a recurrent pericardial effusion, and the latest echocardiogram shows a loculated collection behind the heart. Which procedure is most appropriate?
opts: Correct. She has had three drainages for a recurrent effusion and now has a loculated collection behind the heart, two separate indications for a pericardial window or pericardiectomy. A posterior loculated effusion cannot be approached percutaneously, and the window also addresses the recurrence.

Pericardiocentesis is a percutaneous needle approach, and a loculated collection located posteriorly cannot be reached that way. Her effusion has also recurred after three drainages, and recurrent effusions are themselves an indication for a window. Tell: recurrent or posterior loculated effusions move from the needle to the window.

Her fluid sits in the pericardium, so a procedure aimed at the pleural space around the lung does not reach it. The pericardial options are needle pericardiocentesis or a pericardial window, and recurrence with posterior loculation selects the window. Tell: match the procedure to the space that holds the fluid.

Diuretics do not drain a pericardial collection; after drainage, further management is therapy aimed at the underlying cause, here the cancer. Her recurrent, posterior loculated effusion needs a pericardial window. Tell: recurrence plus loculation is a surgical indication, not a medication problem.

B.q: A 64-year-old woman with heart failure has had a regular, wide-complex tachycardia at 150 for 40 minutes, every QRS the same shape. She is alert, with no chest pain or shortness of breath and a blood pressure of 126/78. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Defibrillation (unsynchronized cardioversion) is for pulseless ventricular tachycardia or ventricular fibrillation. She is alert with a pulse and a blood pressure of 126/78, so she gets pharmacologic cardioversion. Tell: no pulse means defibrillation; a stable patient with a pulse gets drugs.

Correct. A regular wide tachycardia of one shape for 40 minutes is sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia, often seen with heart failure. She is hemodynamically stable, so it is pharmacologically cardioverted with an intravenous antiarrhythmic; amiodarone suits her, since procainamide is avoided in congestive heart failure.

Intravenous magnesium breaks torsades de pointes, a polymorphic tachycardia of a long QT. Her complexes are all one shape, so this is monomorphic ventricular tachycardia, treated with an intravenous antiarrhythmic. Tell: magnesium is for twisting complexes, not identical ones.

Synchronized cardioversion is for unstable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia with a pulse, marked by chest pain, altered mental status, shortness of breath or hypotension. She has none of these, so she gets pharmacologic cardioversion. Tell: a stable patient gets a drug first.

Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
B.q: A 28-year-old woman has sudden palpitations after three energy drinks. She notices her neck throbbing, and examination shows a frog sign (rapid visible pulsations in the neck). Her heart rate is 172 and regular, with a narrow QRS and no visible P waves. She has no heart disease. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. A sudden, regular narrow tachycardia at 172 with hidden P waves, neck pulsations (frog sign) and a caffeine trigger in a young woman without heart disease is atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia. It is a reentry circuit within the node, far more common in women, and usually runs at 140 to 180.

Multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular, with at least three P-wave shapes, and occurs in acutely ill patients with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or heart failure. She is healthy and her rhythm is regular with no visible P waves. Tell: changing P waves in a sick lung patient is multifocal; hidden P waves after a stimulant is nodal reentry.

Sinus tachycardia runs at over 100 to 160 with a uniform P wave before every QRS. Her rate is 172 with no visible P waves, a sudden onset and neck pulsations. Tell: a normal P wave before each QRS means sinus; hidden P waves with the frog sign point to nodal reentry.
ruled out by a stated finding

Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular with absent P waves, often in older patients with hypertension, diabetes or heart disease. Her rhythm is regular, which points to a reentry circuit. Tell: both may show no P waves, but only atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular.
ruled out by a stated finding

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
B.q: A 35-year-old woman with obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy developed severe asthma symptoms when a beta blocker was started, and it was stopped. She still has exertional breathlessness from outflow obstruction. Which medication is the appropriate alternative?
opts: Norepinephrine is a positive inotrope, avoided because increased contractility raises the risk of myocardial ischemia and may induce arrhythmias. Verapamil or diltiazem, which reduce contractility, is the alternative. Tell: she needs a negative inotrope, not a positive one.

Nifedipine is not one of the calcium channel blockers named for outflow tract obstruction; only the nondihydropyridine agents verapamil and diltiazem are, and drugs that reduce afterload may aggravate obstruction. Tell: in this disease the calcium channel blocker must slow the heart and reduce contractility.

Nitrates reduce preload or afterload and may increase symptoms by aggravating outflow tract obstruction, so they are avoided if possible. The alternative to a beta blocker is verapamil or diltiazem. Tell: in obstruction, anything that unloads the heart is avoided.

Correct. With the beta blocker stopped because of her asthma, the other listed medication for outflow tract obstruction is a nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker, verapamil or diltiazem. Like a beta blocker, it is a negative chronotrope and negative inotrope.

B.q: A 19-year-old swimmer has an electrocardiogram before a sports physical. She has no symptoms. The rate is 72, with a normal P wave before every narrow QRS, but the beats come closer together as she breathes in and spread apart as she breathes out. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. A rate of 72 with a normal P wave before every narrow QRS, beats closer together on inspiration and farther apart on expiration, is sinus arrhythmia. It is a normal, physiologic rhythm at 60 to 100 that is irregular with a pattern, which fits a healthy swimmer with no symptoms.

Sick sinus syndrome is an irregular rhythm with variable P waves, from sinus exit block, sinus arrest or tachy-brady swings with pauses. She has a uniform P wave before every beat and a variation tied to breathing, with no pauses. Tell: a breathing-linked pattern is physiologic; pauses and fast-slow swings suggest a diseased node.

Multifocal atrial tachycardia is a fast rhythm, over 100, with at least three different P-wave shapes in one lead, usually in acutely ill patients. She has one normal P-wave shape at 72. Tell: multifocal needs both tachycardia and changing P waves, and she has neither.

Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular with absent P waves. She has a normal P wave before every QRS, and her irregularity follows her breathing. Tell: patterned irregularity with P waves is sinus arrhythmia; patternless irregularity without P waves is fibrillation.

B.q: A 71-year-old man with dilated cardiomyopathy and a reduced ejection fraction has worsening dyspnea and fatigue despite medical therapy. His electrocardiogram shows a QRS of 0.16 seconds with a dominant S wave in V1 and monophasic R waves in I, V5 and V6. Which is the most appropriate treatment for this conduction problem?
opts: Catheter ablation cannot restore conduction through a blocked left bundle. His wide QRS with a dominant S in V1 and monophasic lateral R waves is left bundle branch block, and with symptoms and a reduced ejection fraction it is treated with a biventricular pacemaker. Tell: block plus low ejection fraction means biventricular pacing.

Most left bundle branch block is left untreated, but he is the exception: symptomatic block with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, which gets a biventricular pacemaker. Tell: his worsening dyspnea and fatigue despite therapy move him past observation.

Synchronized cardioversion shocks an unstable tachycardia; left bundle branch block is a conduction delay, not a fast rhythm. With symptoms and a reduced ejection fraction, he needs a biventricular pacemaker. Tell: there is no tachycardia here to convert.

Correct. A QRS of 0.16 seconds with a dominant S wave in V1 and monophasic R waves in I, V5 and V6 is left bundle branch block, and dilated cardiomyopathy is a named cause. The block is usually left untreated, except symptomatic block with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, exactly his case, which gets a biventricular pacemaker.

B.q: A 58-year-old man who takes a beta blocker has an irregular pulse at a routine visit. He has no symptoms, and his rhythm strip is shown. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Third-degree block shows no relationship between P waves and QRS complexes. On this strip the conducted beats keep a PR that lengthens in a repeating pattern, so the atria and ventricles are still linked. Tell: a predictable PR pattern rules out complete block.

First-degree block is a long but constant PR with every P wave conducted. This strip has a P wave that is not followed by a QRS, after the PR has lengthened. Tell: any dropped beat moves the rhythm beyond first degree.
ruled out by a stated finding

Mobitz type II keeps a constant PR before randomly dropped QRS complexes. On this strip the PR lengthens progressively before each drop. Tell: a lengthening PR before the drop is type I; a constant PR is type II.

Correct. The PR grows longer beat by beat until a P wave is not followed by a QRS, then the cycle restarts, which explains the irregular pulse: second-degree Mobitz type I (Wenckebach) block. Beta blockers are a named cause, and since he has no symptoms, the block itself needs no treatment.
B.alt: Rhythm strip with small upright P waves and narrow complexes in groups, with a gap where one P wave stands alone

B.q: A 70-year-old man with a recent transient ischemic attack has a high-grade carotid stenosis on duplex and is being prepared for intervention. Which study is considered the gold standard?
opts: Correct. Digital subtraction angiography is an invasive angiographic technique considered the gold standard for carotid artery disease. It is not used for screening but for guiding therapeutic interventions, which fits a man whose high-grade stenosis after a transient ischemic attack is already headed for intervention.

Duplex ultrasonography is the most widely used initial screening tool, and it already found his high-grade stenosis; it is also used for serial monitoring. The gold standard, used to guide intervention, is digital subtraction angiography. Duplex screens and follows; angiography guides treatment.

Magnetic resonance angiography images the cervical and intracranial carotid and vertebral circulation and the brain very effectively, but it is not the gold standard. For this man being prepared for intervention, digital subtraction angiography, the invasive gold standard, guides therapy. Effective imaging is not the reference test.

A bruit is an examination finding, auscultated one side at a time with the breath held, not an imaging study. It cannot define his stenosis for intervention; digital subtraction angiography is the gold standard used to guide therapeutic interventions. An examination sign is not a test standard.

B.q: A 24-year-old soccer player comes to urgent care with left calf pain that began two days ago when he felt a sudden pull while sprinting, and he has bruising around the ankle. He has no leg swelling, tenderness along the deep veins, cancer, cast or history of clots. By the Wells criteria, a calf muscle tear is at least as likely as deep vein thrombosis. Which is the most appropriate first test?
opts: Contrast ascending venography is the definitive gold standard, but it has been replaced by venous duplex ultrasound and is not a first test. For a low-likelihood score like his, the pathway begins with a D-dimer and moves to imaging only if it is positive.

Venous duplex ultrasound comes first only for a high-risk patient, or after a positive D-dimer in a low-risk one. His likelier alternative diagnosis puts his Wells score at zero or below, so a D-dimer comes first and a negative result ends the evaluation.

Computed tomography of the leg is not part of the initial pathway for suspected deep vein thrombosis, which runs from the Wells score to a D-dimer or ultrasound. For his low-likelihood score the first step is a D-dimer, with ultrasound reserved for a positive result.

Correct. He has no positive Wells items, and a calf muscle tear at least as likely as deep vein thrombosis (DVT) subtracts 2, so his score is minus 2, a low likelihood (zero or less). Low-risk patients start with a D-dimer, which is sensitive: a negative result stops the work-up, and only a positive one leads to ultrasound.

B.q: A 67-year-old woman with pulmonary hypertension has palpitations and dyspnea. Her electrocardiogram shows a regular, narrow-complex rhythm at 150, with two sawtooth atrial waves before every QRS. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Focal atrial tachycardia has one consistent abnormal P wave per QRS from a single focus, usually at 150 to 250. Two sawtooth waves for every QRS mean the atrial rate is double the ventricular rate, which is atrial flutter with 2:1 block. Tell: one atrial wave per QRS is focal; two in a sawtooth line is flutter.

Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular with absent P waves and no organized atrial activity. Her rhythm is regular with repeating sawtooth waves. Tell: organized sawtooth waves with a regular ventricular rate mean flutter; a chaotic baseline with an irregular rate means fibrillation.

Sinus tachycardia has one uniform P wave before every QRS, at over 100 to 160. She has two sawtooth waves for each QRS, so the atria are beating twice as fast as the ventricles. Tell: one normal P wave per QRS is sinus; two sawtooth waves per QRS is flutter.

Correct. Two sawtooth atrial waves before every narrow QRS mean the atria fire near 300 while the node passes every other impulse: atrial flutter with 2:1 block, the most common pattern, giving a regular rate of 150. Flutter is commonly seen with pulmonary vascular disease, such as her pulmonary hypertension.

B.q: A 55-year-old woman taking a loop diuretic for heart failure has new palpitations felt in her neck. Telemetry shows frequent premature ventricular contractions. Which laboratory values should be checked first?
opts: Thyroid hormone and cortisol are not among the named causes of premature ventricular contractions. The named causes are hypoxemia and electrolyte imbalance, so a patient on a loop diuretic needs potassium and magnesium checked first. Tell: the drug in the stem points to an electrolyte.

Troponin and lipase do not test for the named causes of premature ventricular contractions. The named causes are hypoxemia and electrolyte imbalance (low potassium, low magnesium, high calcium). Tell: her loop diuretic is the clue that points to potassium and magnesium.

Correct. Electrolyte imbalance (hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypercalcemia) and hypoxemia are the named causes of premature ventricular contractions, and her loop diuretic puts potassium and magnesium at risk. Palpitations felt in the neck are the classic symptom of these beats, which occur with or without structural heart disease.

Glucose and lactate are not among the named causes of premature ventricular contractions. The named causes are hypoxemia and electrolyte imbalance (hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypercalcemia). Tell: a patient on a diuretic with new premature beats needs her electrolytes checked.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
B.q: A 52-year-old man has had 10 days of gradually worsening pleuritic (worse with a deep breath) chest pain without a clear onset. His temperature is 38.7 degrees Celsius (101.7 degrees Fahrenheit), and the echocardiogram shows a moderate pericardial effusion without collapse of any chamber. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Nothing here calls for surgery yet: there is no chamber collapse, and his fever, subacute course and moderate effusion are high-risk features that warrant admission and evaluation first. Tell: fever above 38 degrees Celsius, a subacute course and a moderate effusion point to the hospital ward, not the operating room.
Reassurance and repeat echo in 3 months

Waiting 3 months ignores three high-risk features: a temperature above 38 degrees Celsius, a subacute course over days to weeks and a moderate effusion. Each is associated with higher risk and a potential need for hospitalization now. Tell: any one listed high-risk feature takes pericarditis out of watchful waiting.

Nonsteroidal drugs plus colchicine are the initial therapy for most acute idiopathic or viral pericarditis, but his fever above 38 degrees Celsius, subacute onset and moderate effusion are high-risk features that call for admission. Tell: the drugs may be right, but the setting is wrong when high-risk features are present.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. A temperature of 38.7 degrees Celsius (above 38), a subacute course over 10 days without an acute onset of chest pain, and a moderate effusion are each associated with higher risk and a potential need for hospitalization. He should be admitted for evaluation rather than treated as routine outpatient pericarditis.

B.q: A 38-year-old woman has a congenital arteriovenous fistula of the calf with numerous small communications, causing chronic swelling and aching. She has no signs of ischemia or heart failure. Which is the most appropriate initial management?
opts: Ligating every communication is impractical because congenital fistulas can have numerous connections, which is exactly why they are difficult to treat. The initial approach is conservative, with elastic support hose, and embolization is sometimes used to remove the fistula.

Surgical removal or size reduction is the management for an acquired fistula, such as one from trauma or a procedure. Hers is congenital with numerous communications, which makes it difficult to treat, so elastic support hose comes first.

Correct. A congenital arteriovenous (AV) fistula with numerous small communications is difficult to treat, so it is managed conservatively with elastic support hose. She has none of the complications to watch for, such as ischemia or heart failure, and embolization can sometimes remove a congenital fistula later.

Anticoagulation does not treat an abnormal artery-to-vein connection, and her problem is not a clot. Congenital fistulas with numerous communications are treated conservatively with elastic support hose, with embolization as an occasional option.

B.io: Identify medical care strategies for pericardial disease in the lecture topic list for the following populations. 9. adult 10. elderly
B.q: What adjustment is suggested for colchicine in older adults with pericarditis?
opts: No change of route is suggested; the adjustment for colchicine in older adults is to consider a dose reduction. Other cautions in this age group include the Beers list for anti-inflammatory drugs and the osteoporosis risk of corticosteroids. Tell: the age-related change is about how much is given, not how it is given.

Lengthening the course adds drug exposure in the very group where caution is advised. Older adults are flagged on the Beers list for anti-inflammatory drugs, and colchicine should be considered for dose reduction. Tell: in older adults the adjustment goes down, not up.

Correct. Older adults call for caution with anti-inflammatory drugs, which sit on the Beers list, and colchicine in particular should be considered for dose reduction. The drug stays in the regimen at an adjusted dose, while corticosteroids carry their own caution because they raise osteoporosis risk.

Colchicine is not abandoned in older adults; caution is advised and a dose reduction should be considered, so it stays in the regimen at a lower dose. Tell: the recommendation is adjust, not avoid. Corticosteroids carry a separate caution in this age group because they raise osteoporosis risk.

B.q: After parenteral therapy for 5 days, which agents can anticoagulation be switched to?
opts: Warfarin and heparin form the classical but waning strategy, which starts with heparin and bridges to warfarin rather than switching after 5 days of parenteral therapy. The agents taken up after a 5-day parenteral lead-in are dabigatran and edoxaban.

Aspirin and clopidogrel are not among the anticoagulation options for deep vein thrombosis, which are the heparins, fondaparinux, factor Xa inhibitors and dabigatran. After 5 days of parenteral therapy the switch is to dabigatran or edoxaban.

Rivaroxaban and apixaban are the oral monotherapy strategy, given as a loading dose followed by a maintenance dose with no parenteral lead-in. The anticoagulants that follow 5 days of parenteral therapy are dabigatran and edoxaban.

Correct. In the second of the three anticoagulation strategies, parenteral therapy is switched after 5 days to a novel anticoagulant: dabigatran, a direct thrombin inhibitor, or edoxaban, an anti-Xa agent. Rivaroxaban and apixaban differ because they are given orally from the start with a loading dose.

Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
B.q: A 40-year-old man has a stable, regular, narrow-complex tachycardia at 180. It is unclear whether the rhythm comes from a focus in the atria or a reentry circuit that uses the atrioventricular node. Which agent is most useful as a diagnostic tool?
opts: Amiodarone may be tried for chemical cardioversion of focal atrial tachycardia, a treatment step rather than a test. Its effect does not separate an atrial focus from a circuit through the atrioventricular node. Tell: the diagnostic agent is the one whose success or failure differs between the two rhythms, which is adenosine.

Correct. For a stable, regular narrow tachycardia at 180 of unclear origin, adenosine is an important diagnostic tool because it is usually less effective at terminating focal atrial tachycardia than the node-dependent reentry rhythms. If the rhythm stops, a circuit through the node is likely; if the atrial rhythm carries on, an atrial focus is.

Intravenous procainamide is used when Wolff-Parkinson-White is known or when adenosine reveals atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White. It is a treatment for that setting, not a diagnostic test for a regular narrow tachycardia. Tell: in a stable regular narrow rhythm of unclear origin, adenosine is the agent that sorts an atrial focus from nodal reentry.

Magnesium has no stated role in sorting out a regular narrow-complex tachycardia. The agent used diagnostically is adenosine, because it usually terminates reentry that depends on the atrioventricular node but is less effective at terminating focal atrial tachycardia. Tell: a diagnostic agent must behave differently in the two rhythms, and adenosine does.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following arterial occlusive disease and aortic aneurysm: 2. Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
B.q: A 69-year-old woman with claudication, a known contrast allergy and reduced renal function needs arterial imaging before a planned intervention. Which study is relatively contraindicated for her?
opts: Magnetic resonance angiography is the alternative for patients with a contrast allergy. Its listed contraindications are pacemakers and intracranial aneurysm clips, which she does not have. Her allergy and kidneys point away from the contrast study, not this one.

The ankle-brachial index is a simple bedside test that uses no contrast, so neither her allergy nor her kidneys limit it. It is the important initial test, but it does not image anatomy for intervention. It is not the study with a contraindication for her.

Correct. Computed tomography angiography uses contrast to delineate arterial anatomy, and its listed contraindications are contrast allergy and decreased renal function. She has both, so it is the study to avoid; magnetic resonance angiography is the alternative in contrast allergy.

Duplex ultrasound is noninvasive and uses no contrast media or radiation, so it is safe with her allergy and kidney function. It is the mainstay initial noninvasive imaging when stenosis is suspected. No contrast means no conflict here.
