B.q: A 57-year-old man with constrictive pericarditis is scheduled for pericardiectomy next week. He takes a loop diuretic for leg edema. How should the diuretic be handled before surgery?
opts: Correct. He has constrictive pericarditis with pericardiectomy planned next week, and when surgery is planned, diuretics should be used sparingly in the preoperative period. Diuretics still relieve fluid overload in constriction, which is why the advice is sparing use rather than escalation.

Doubling the loop diuretic is the opposite of the advice for a patient awaiting pericardiectomy, in whom diuretics should be used sparingly before surgery. Fuller diuretic use belongs to the medical trial for early, stable constriction. Tell: an operation on the calendar means less diuretic, not more.

No change of route is suggested; with pericardiectomy planned, the preoperative guidance is simply to use diuretics sparingly. Diuretics otherwise relieve fluid overload in constriction managed medically. Tell: the question is how much diuretic before surgery, and the answer is less.

Adding a second diuretic escalates therapy when the advice before pericardiectomy is to use diuretics sparingly. Diuretics belong to the medical trial for early, hemodynamically stable constriction, alongside nonsteroidal drugs and colchicine for 2 to 3 months. Tell: escalation fits a medical trial, not the week before surgery.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
B.q: A 70-year-old woman with hypertension has had palpitations for a week. She is alert, with a blood pressure of 132/80, and her rhythm strip is shown. Which is the first goal of treatment?
opts: Adenosine is a step for stable, regular supraventricular tachycardia, after a vagal maneuver, to convert the rhythm or slow it enough to reveal P waves. Her rhythm is irregularly irregular with no P waves, already recognizable as atrial fibrillation. Tell: an irregularly irregular rhythm without P waves needs rate control, not a diagnostic drug.

Mapping and ablation is one of the later options in managing atrial fibrillation, not the first goal of treatment. A stable patient like her starts with rate control, and anticoagulation is planned for all. Tell: stable atrial fibrillation begins with rate control; procedures come later.

Immediate synchronized cardioversion is for hemodynamically unstable atrial fibrillation. She is alert with a blood pressure of 132/80, so she is stable, and an elective cardioversion would need 21 days of anticoagulation first. Tell: a shock now needs instability, such as hypotension or pulmonary edema.

Correct. The strip shows narrow complexes at irregularly irregular intervals with no P waves, which is atrial fibrillation, and with a blood pressure of 132/80 and a clear mind she is hemodynamically stable. Stable atrial fibrillation is managed with rate control, with anticoagulation decided by her stroke-risk score, to which her hypertension and age contribute.
B.alt: Rhythm strip of narrow complexes at visibly unequal intervals over a wavy baseline with no clear P waves

B.io: Identify medical care strategies for ventricular dysrhythmias for the following populations. 3. adult 4. elderly
B.q: An 81-year-old man takes no medications and has never had a heart attack. A routine electrocardiogram shows a constant PR interval of 0.25 seconds with every beat conducted, and he asks why his heart is doing this. Which explanation is most accurate?
opts: Lyme disease is a named cause of first-degree block, but nothing here suggests it: no tick bite, rash or exposure is described. In an 81-year-old, the most common cause is age-related degenerative change of the conduction system. Tell: advanced age without other clues points to degeneration.

Correct. His constant PR of 0.25 seconds with every beat conducted is first-degree block. He takes no offending drugs (beta blockers, nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, digoxin) and has had no infarction, so at 81 the explanation is the most common cause: age-related degenerative change of the conduction system.

Increased vagal tone from an overreactive vagus nerve is a named cause of first-degree block, but it is not the most common cause, and nothing in this 81-year-old points to it. Age-related degeneration of the conduction system is. Tell: in an elderly patient with no other clues, choose degeneration.
Hidden damage from a heart attack

Atrioventricular node ischemia usually follows a myocardial infarction, and he has never had one. Age-related degenerative change of the conduction system is the most common cause of first-degree block. Tell: the stem rules out infarction on purpose.
ruled out by a stated finding

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
B.q: A 50-year-old woman with chronic lung disease and a low oxygen saturation feels her heart skipping. Her tracing shows that every other beat (bigeminy) is early, wide and bizarre, with no P wave before it. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. Early, wide and bizarre QRS complexes with no P wave are premature ventricular contractions, here every other beat (bigeminy). Her chronic lung disease and low oxygen saturation point to hypoxemia, a main cause along with electrolyte imbalance, and the beats are often felt as skipping or palpitations.

Premature junctional contractions are early with a narrow QRS (usually 0.10 seconds or less) and an inverted, buried or trailing P wave. Her early beats are wide and bizarre, which places their origin in the ventricles. Tell: a narrow early beat is junctional; a wide one with no P wave is ventricular.
ruled out by a stated finding

Ventricular tachycardia is 3 or more consecutive premature ventricular contractions. She has single wide beats alternating with normal ones, which is bigeminy. Tell: alternation is bigeminy; a run is tachycardia.

Premature atrial contractions are early beats that begin in the atria, with an early, abnormally shaped P wave. Her early beats are wide and bizarre with no P wave. Tell: an abnormal P wave in front means atrial; no P wave and a wide QRS means ventricular.
ruled out by a stated finding

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following arterial occlusive disease and aortic aneurysm: 2. Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
B.q: A 70-year-old man with a 6.1 cm abdominal aortic aneurysm is scheduled for elective repair. He asks how the surgeon will choose between endovascular and open repair. Which factor guides the choice?
opts: Correct. Two repair methods exist: endovascular aneurysm repair, a modular graft placed through the iliac or femoral arteries to line the aorta and exclude the sac, and open replacement with a tube or bifurcated prosthetic graft. The choice considers the patient's age and medical comorbidities.
Whether he has a carotid bruit

A carotid bruit relates to carotid artery disease, not the method of aortic repair. The choice between endovascular aneurysm repair and open surgery rests on his age and medical comorbidities. An unrelated examination finding does not drive the decision.

Skin color plays no part in choosing the repair method. The choice between endovascular and open repair considers his age and medical comorbidities. Race bears on how common aneurysms are, not on how they are repaired.
The result of his ankle index

The ankle-brachial index grades lower extremity arterial disease and does not choose the method of aneurysm repair. Age and medical comorbidities decide between endovascular aneurysm repair and open surgery. A leg test does not settle an aortic decision.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
B.q: The HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) group of endocarditis organisms comes from which source?
opts: The genitourinary tract is the source of enterococci, not of the HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) organisms. Tell: enterococci pair with the urinary tract, while the HACEK group are upper respiratory tract organisms.

The gastrointestinal tract is the source of Streptococcus gallolyticus, not of the HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) group. Tell: a bowel source points to Streptococcus gallolyticus; the HACEK group lives in the upper respiratory tract.

The skin is the source of staphylococci, including the coagulase-negative staphylococci and Staphylococcus aureus of early prosthetic valve infection. The HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) organisms are not skin flora. Tell: skin means staphylococci; HACEK means upper airway.

Correct. The HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) organisms come from the upper respiratory tract: Haemophilus aphrophilus, Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans, Cardiobacterium hominis, Eikenella corrodens and Kingella species. They are a subacute, native valve cause.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
B.q: In a stable narrow complex tachycardia, which step comes before any drug?
opts: An echocardiogram is not part of the acute sequence for stable supraventricular tachycardia, which runs vagal maneuver, then adenosine. The question asks for the step before any drug, and that is the vagal maneuver. Tell: the first move in a stable narrow tachycardia is a bedside, drug-free maneuver.

Intravenous procainamide is used when Wolff-Parkinson-White is known or when adenosine reveals atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White; it is not a first step. Stable narrow complex tachycardia begins with a vagal maneuver. Tell: procainamide answers pre-excited atrial fibrillation; a stable narrow tachycardia starts drug-free.

Correct. In stable supraventricular tachycardia, the narrow complex tachycardias, a vagal maneuver is first line, before any drug. Adenosine follows if needed, may be repeated once, and may convert the rhythm or slow it enough to show P waves; synchronized cardioversion is kept for instability.

Synchronized cardioversion, a timed shock at decreased voltage, is immediate treatment only for hemodynamically unstable supraventricular tachycardia. A stable patient starts with a vagal maneuver, then adenosine. Tell: the word stable in the question takes the shock off the table.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
B.q: Which is the definitive treatment for Mobitz type II block?
opts: Catheter ablation is itself a named cause of Mobitz type II block, so it cannot be the treatment. The definitive treatment is a permanent pacemaker. Tell: a procedure that causes a block cannot fix it.

Transcutaneous pacing is the emergent, temporary measure, alongside atropine and epinephrine, that bridges an unstable patient to definitive therapy. The definitive treatment for Mobitz type II is a permanent pacemaker. Tell: 'definitive' means the permanent device.

Correct. Mobitz type II usually originates at the bundle of His, leaving a weak, unreliable escape rhythm, and carries a higher risk of progression to complete block and sudden cardiac death; it is considered dangerous even without symptoms. Atropine, epinephrine and transcutaneous pacing are emergent; the definitive treatment is a permanent pacemaker.

An implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) detects and shocks fatal fast rhythms; it does not fix a failing conduction system. Mobitz type II needs a permanent pacemaker. Tell: blocks need pacing, not shocking.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
B.q: A 37-year-old man was treated for acute pericarditis 4 weeks ago and now feels well. A repeat electrocardiogram shows widespread T-wave inversions without ST elevation, and troponin is normal. Which best explains the tracing?
opts: Correct. Four weeks after acute pericarditis, in a man who feels well with a normal troponin, widespread T-wave inversion without ST elevation is stage 3 of the classic evolution. ST elevation with PR depression comes first, then ST normalization with T-wave flattening at 1 to 3 weeks, then inversion from 3 weeks on, and finally a normal tracing.

Tamponade from a large effusion shows electrical alternans on the tracing, and he feels well with nothing to suggest compromise. Widespread T-wave inversion 4 weeks after treatment is stage 3 of the expected pericarditis evolution. Tell: inverted T waves in a well patient weeks after pericarditis are evolution, not a new complication.

His troponin is normal, and the tracing fits the timeline of his known pericarditis: T waves flatten at 1 to 3 weeks and invert from about 3 weeks onward before the tracing normalizes. Tell: a normal troponin plus timing that matches stage 3 means expected evolution, not a new infarction.
ruled out by a stated finding

No electrolyte problem is suggested, and the timing alone explains the tracing: in pericarditis, flattened T waves become inverted from about 3 weeks onward, before the electrocardiogram returns to normal. Tell: widespread T-wave inversion 4 weeks after treated pericarditis, in a patient who feels well, is stage 3.

B.io: Identify medical care strategies for infective endocarditis for the following populations. 8. infant 9. child 10. adolescent 11. adult 12. elderly
B.q: A 12-year-old had a ventricular septal defect closed with a prosthetic patch 4 months ago and is now scheduled for a dental extraction. Which is the most appropriate step regarding endocarditis?
opts: Correct. The first 6 months after congenital heart disease repair with prosthetic material or a device is a high-risk pediatric condition, and he is only 4 months out from his patch. A dental extraction manipulates gingival and periapical tissue, so a single prophylactic dose is given 30-60 minutes before the procedure.

He is still inside the high-risk window: the first 6 months after congenital heart disease repair with prosthetic material or a device. A dental extraction with gingival manipulation is exactly the procedure prophylaxis covers. Tell: 4 months after a prosthetic patch is high risk; well past 6 months with no residual defect would not be.
ruled out by a stated finding

Antibiotics given afterward miss the purpose of prophylaxis, which is a single dose given 30-60 minutes before the procedure. This child does qualify, because he is within 6 months of a prosthetic patch repair. Tell: prophylaxis is always timed before the extraction, never after.

Delaying the extraction is not the recommendation. A child within the first 6 months after congenital heart disease repair with prosthetic material is high risk, and the answer is prophylaxis before the dental procedure. Tell: high-risk status changes the antibiotic plan, not the timing of needed dental care.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
B.q: A 73-year-old woman has just been diagnosed with restrictive cardiomyopathy from amyloidosis. She has right-sided heart failure and asks how her condition compares with other kinds of heart muscle disease. Which statement about her prognosis is most accurate?
opts: Complete recovery within weeks is not the restrictive course; this disease carries the poorest prognosis among all heart muscle diseases, with transplantation as the final option. Tell: the restrictive outlook is the worst, not the best.
Poorest of all heart muscle diseases

Correct. Restrictive cardiomyopathy has the poorest prognosis among all types of heart muscle disease. Management treats the underlying disorder, such as her amyloidosis, uses diuretics with caution and anticoagulants or a pacemaker as needed, and ends with cardiac transplantation.

The opposite is true: restrictive cardiomyopathy has the poorest prognosis among all types of heart muscle disease. Tell: remember restrictive as the worst outlook, with cardiac transplantation as the last option.
A normal life span with diuretics

Diuretics are used for pulmonary and systemic congestion, with caution because noncompliant ventricles depend on preload, but they do not change the outlook. Restrictive cardiomyopathy has the poorest prognosis of all heart muscle diseases. Tell: symptom relief is not the same as a normal life span.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
C.q: A 58-year-old man with chest pain develops a wide tachycardia whose QRS shape varies from beat to beat; his QT interval was normal earlier. He is defibrillated and returns to sinus rhythm. Which study is the most urgent next?
opts: Correct. A wide tachycardia whose QRS shape varies is polymorphic ventricular tachycardia; with a normal QT, it is most commonly due to acute myocardial ischemia, and he had chest pain. After defibrillation, the most urgent next step is coronary angiography with possible revascularization.

Ambulatory monitoring captures intermittent rhythms over time; it does not address an acute ischemic event. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with chest pain and a normal QT points to ischemia, which needs urgent coronary angiography. Tell: the most urgent study after this rhythm is done in the catheterization lab.

A stroke-risk score is not part of the workup after polymorphic ventricular tachycardia. With chest pain and a normal QT, acute ischemia is the likely cause, so urgent coronary angiography comes next. Tell: the priority is the coronary arteries.

A serum digoxin level does not address the likely cause. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with a normal QT is most commonly from acute ischemia, and he had chest pain, so urgent coronary angiography with possible revascularization comes next. Tell: chest pain plus a normal QT points to ischemia.

C.io: Identify medical care strategies for ventricular dysrhythmias for the following populations. 3. adult 4. elderly
C.q: An 80-year-old man has an incidental finding on a preoperative electrocardiogram: a constant PR interval in conducted beats with occasional P waves that are not followed by a QRS complex, and no PR lengthening before the dropped beats. He has no symptoms. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Repeat the tracing in a year

Repeating the tracing in a year ignores the unpredictable progression of Mobitz type II to complete heart block and sudden cardiac death. Guidelines treat it as dangerous even without symptoms. Tell: an incidental type II finding is treated, not watched.

Reassurance suits silent first-degree or Mobitz type I block. A constant PR with dropped beats and no PR lengthening is Mobitz type II, which needs a permanent pacemaker even without symptoms. Tell: in type II, being symptom-free does not change the plan.

An oral beta blocker is not among the listed treatments for Mobitz type II, which usually originates at the bundle of His and is considered dangerous even without symptoms because of its higher risk of complete heart block and sudden cardiac death. Tell: the definitive treatment is a permanent pacemaker, not a rate-slowing drug.

Correct. A constant PR in conducted beats with occasional dropped QRS complexes and no PR lengthening is Mobitz type II. It is considered dangerous even without symptoms because of its unpredictable progression and poor prognosis, with a higher risk of complete block and sudden cardiac death, so the definitive treatment is a permanent pacemaker.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
C.q: A 29-year-old woman has had a resting heart rate of 110 to 120 for months, with a normal P wave before every narrow QRS. Thyroid tests, blood count, oxygen saturation and a drug screen are normal, and she takes no medications or stimulants. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Atrial flutter shows sawtooth waves at an atrial rate of 250 or more, outnumbering the QRS complexes. She has one normal P wave before each QRS at 110 to 120. Tell: one normal P wave per QRS keeps the rhythm sinus; extra sawtooth waves mean flutter.

Focal atrial tachycardia comes from a single ectopic focus outside the sinus node, with a consistently abnormal P wave, usually at 150 to 250, and patients report abrupt-onset palpitations. Her P waves are normal and her rate has sat at 110 to 120 for months. Tell: a normal P-wave shape points sinus; an abnormal one points to an ectopic focus.

Correct. A resting rate of 110 to 120 for months with a normal P wave before every narrow QRS is sinus tachycardia, and normal thyroid tests, blood count, oxygen saturation and drug screen with no medications or stimulants exclude the secondary causes. A sinus tachycardia unexplained after that search is inappropriate sinus tachycardia, a diagnosis of exclusion.

Appropriate sinus tachycardia is a response to physiologic stress, an underlying pathologic condition or medication effects, and is managed by treating that cause. Her thyroid tests, blood count, oxygen saturation and drug screen are normal and she takes nothing, so no cause remains. Tell: once every secondary cause is excluded, the sinus tachycardia is inappropriate.
ruled out by a stated finding

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
C.q: A 48-year-old woman is discharged on ibuprofen and colchicine for acute pericarditis. Which new symptom should prompt her to go straight to the emergency department rather than call for an appointment?
opts: Mild fatigue in the late afternoon

Mild afternoon fatigue during recovery does not signal compromise and is not a red-flag symptom. Discharge teaching centers on red flags for recurrence or tamponade, and breathlessness with lightheadedness suggests the falling blood pressure of tamponade. Tell: emergencies involve the circulation, not ordinary tiredness.
Mild indigestion after doses of ibuprofen

Indigestion after ibuprofen is a medication side effect, the subject of side-effect counseling, and it can be raised at a routine visit. It does not point to tamponade or recurrence. Tell: drug side effects are discussed with the clinician; red-flag symptoms of tamponade send her to the emergency department.

Correct. Lightheadedness with shortness of breath suggests the falling blood pressure of tamponade, one of the red-flag symptoms patients are taught to recognize at discharge. A possible tamponade needs emergency evaluation, not a scheduled appointment.
Pain that still eases on leaning forward

Pain that eases on leaning forward is the familiar positional pattern of her pericarditis, which is worse when supine, not a new warning sign; her response to therapy is reported at follow-up. Red flags are symptoms of recurrence or tamponade, such as lightheadedness with breathlessness. Tell: the familiar pain pattern is follow-up material.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
C.q: A 76-year-old woman is brought in after fainting twice today. She is pale, with a blood pressure of 84/50, and her lead II rhythm strip is shown. Which is the most appropriate emergent treatment?
opts: Correct. P waves at a steady rate with a constant PR, then a P wave with no QRS, is Mobitz type II block. Fainting twice today with a blood pressure of 84/50 makes her unstable, so she needs emergent treatment: atropine, epinephrine or transcutaneous pacing, which bridges her to a permanent pacemaker.

Adenosine is not among the treatments for heart block, and it would not raise a slow rate. This slow rhythm with dropped QRS complexes is Mobitz type II, and an unstable patient needs transcutaneous pacing. Tell: a slow, blocked rhythm with hypotension needs pacing.

A permanent pacemaker is the definitive treatment for Mobitz type II, but with two faints today and a blood pressure of 84/50, she first needs emergent transcutaneous pacing to bridge her there. Tell: 'emergent' points to the temporary measure, 'definitive' to the permanent one.
Synchronized cardioversion shocks an unstable tachycardia with a pulse. This is a slow rhythm with dropped QRS complexes from Mobitz type II, which needs pacing. Tell: pace the slow, shock the fast.
C.alt: Lead II rhythm strip with regular small P waves and narrow complexes; at one point a P wave appears with no complex after it, leaving a long gap

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following venous disorders: 2. Deep vein thrombosis 3. Phlebitis a. Thrombophlebitis Septic thrombophlebitis 4. Arteriovenous fistula of the extremity a. Acquired (e.g. trauma, iatrogenic) b. Created (i.e. for hemodialysis) 5. Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
C.q: Why can a positive D-dimer not confirm deep vein thrombosis?
opts: This reverses the test's strength: D-dimer is sensitive, so false negatives are not the problem, and a negative result is useful for ruling out deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism. Its weakness is poor specificity, which is why a positive result cannot confirm a clot.

Correct. An elevated D-dimer implies increased fibrinolysis, and the test is sensitive but not specific, so conditions other than deep vein thrombosis (DVT) can raise it. A positive result therefore leads to venous duplex ultrasound to confirm a clot.

D-dimer is a blood test of fibrinolysis and gives no information about where a clot is. Locating and confirming a clot takes venous duplex ultrasound of the involved extremity, which has replaced contrast venography.

D-dimer is not limited to arterial clots; it is used as a rule-out test for deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, both venous problems. It cannot confirm a clot because it is not specific, so many conditions raise it.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
C.q: How is the diagnosis of Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy confirmed?
opts: Electrocardiogram changes cannot confirm it: ST segment elevation and T wave inversion are part of why the syndrome mimics acute coronary syndrome in the first place. Confirmation comes from cardiac catheterization showing normal coronary arteries. Tell: a finding shared with acute coronary syndrome cannot be the confirming test.

Troponin I and T are usually elevated in stress cardiomyopathy, but a raised level is also what acute coronary syndrome shows, so it supports the picture without confirming it. Cardiac catheterization showing normal coronary arteries confirms the diagnosis. Tell: confirm means the test that separates it from acute coronary syndrome.

Endomyocardial biopsy is not part of the stress cardiomyopathy work-up. The sequence is troponin, B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP), electrocardiogram and transthoracic echo, then cardiac catheterization to confirm. Tell: the key question is whether the coronary arteries are blocked, which needs a look at the coronaries.

Correct. The diagnosis is confirmed with cardiac catheterization, which most often shows normal coronary arteries. Elevated troponin and B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP), ST elevation and mid and apical wall-motion abnormalities all mimic acute coronary syndrome, so normal coronaries are what separate the two.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
C.q: A 61-year-old woman with mitral valve endocarditis develops worsening breathlessness, crackles and a new loud regurgitant murmur on day 3 of appropriate antibiotics. Echocardiography shows a ruptured chord with severe regurgitation. Which referral is most appropriate?
opts: Correct. On day 3 of appropriate antibiotics she has breathlessness, crackles, a new loud regurgitant murmur and a ruptured chord with severe regurgitation: heart failure due to valvular dysfunction, the most common indication for surgery. Cardiothoracic surgery is consulted to evaluate the need for surgery.

Addiction medicine provides harm reduction for people who inject drugs. Nothing in her history mentions drug use, and her problem is acute valve failure. Tell: a ruptured chord with heart failure needs a surgical evaluation, not a harm-reduction service.

Palliative care can be part of a multidisciplinary plan, but palliative care alone would leave a surgical problem unaddressed. Heart failure due to valvular dysfunction is the most common indication for surgery. Tell: a structural valve failure on day 3 calls for cardiothoracic surgery first.

Outpatient follow-up does not fit acute heart failure developing during inpatient antibiotic treatment. Heart failure due to valvular dysfunction is the leading surgical indication, so cardiothoracic surgery evaluates her now. Tell: a ruptured chord with crackles is urgent, which rules out an outpatient referral.

C.io: Identify medical care strategies for infective endocarditis for the following populations. 8. infant 9. child 10. adolescent 11. adult 12. elderly
C.q: An 8-year-old with endocarditis has a sudden fulminant illness with high spiking fevers, unlike the usual slow course in children. Which organisms does this presentation suggest?
opts: Candida is tied to neonates and infants, where fungal disease follows central venous catheters, hyperalimentation, neonatal intensive care or prematurity. An 8-year-old with fulminant spiking fevers fits Streptococcus pneumoniae or Staphylococcus aureus instead. Tell: fungi go with the neonatal catheter picture.

Viridans group streptococci are the most common organisms in children over 1 year with congenital heart disease, but they cause the usual indolent course of prolonged low-grade fever and fatigue. This child's sudden fulminant illness is the exception. Tell: indolent means viridans; fulminant means pneumococcus or Staphylococcus aureus.

Correct. Most children have an indolent course with prolonged low-grade fever, but a fulminant presentation with high spiking fevers suggests Streptococcus pneumoniae or Staphylococcus aureus. The abrupt, high-fever onset in this 8-year-old is the decisive clue.

Coagulase-negative staphylococci are linked to prosthetic material, recent surgery and neonatal catheter-related disease, not to a fulminant spiking presentation. Tell: think coagulase-negative staphylococci when a device or graft is involved; high spiking fevers point to pneumococcus or Staphylococcus aureus.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
C.q: An 81-year-old man reports dizziness and two fainting spells. His pulse is 36, and his rhythm strip is shown, with arrows marking R waves and P waves. Which description best fits this tracing?
opts: Constant PR with an occasional dropped QRS

A constant PR with an occasional dropped QRS is Mobitz type II. On this strip the distance from each P wave to the next QRS changes every beat, and most P waves are not followed by a QRS. Tell: if no PR repeats, it is not second-degree block.
P waves and QRS complexes at unrelated rates

Correct. The P waves march at their own regular rate and the slow, wide QRS complexes at another, with no fixed relationship: complete dissociation of the atria from the ventricles, third-degree (complete) block, with a ventricular rate usually under 40. His syncope carries an increased risk of sudden death.
PR lengthens until a QRS is dropped

Progressive PR lengthening before a dropped QRS is Mobitz type I. Here the P waves keep no consistent relationship to the QRS complexes at all. Tell: an orderly lengthening pattern is type I; no pattern at all is complete block.
Every P wave conducted with a long PR

A long, constant PR with every P wave conducted is first-degree block. Here most P waves are not followed by a QRS, and P waves and QRS complexes run at different rates. Tell: far more P waves than QRS complexes rules out first degree.
C.alt: Rhythm strip with regularly spaced P waves (upward arrows) and slower complexes (downward arrows) that fall at varying distances from the P waves

Deep vein thrombosis 3. Phlebitis a. Thrombophlebitis Septic thrombophlebitis 4. Arteriovenous fistula of the extremity a. Acquired (e.g. trauma, iatrogenic) b. Created (i.e. for hemodialysis) 5. Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
C.q: A 47-year-old woman has a tender, red, firm segment along a forearm vein after a peripheral intravenous catheter was removed. Venous duplex ultrasound shows a superficial vein with a thickened wall. Which additional finding would establish thrombophlebitis rather than phlebitis alone?
opts: Correct. The ultrasound already shows wall thickening, which by itself means phlebitis, inflammation of the vein wall without thrombus. Clot within the vein together with that thickening establishes thrombophlebitis; duplex ultrasound, the gold standard, shows it as a noncompressible superficial vein with clot.
Wall thickening is already present and is the finding both conditions share; on its own it defines phlebitis. Only the addition of clot within the vein converts the diagnosis to thrombophlebitis.

A fluid collection around the vein is not the criterion that separates the two conditions. Infection within the vein is suggested by high fever, fluctuance or purulent drainage, while thrombophlebitis is defined by clot inside a thickened vein.

Reflux through incompetent valves is not part of how phlebitis and thrombophlebitis are told apart. Duplex ultrasound makes that call on two findings: wall thickening alone is phlebitis, and wall thickening with clot in the vein is thrombophlebitis.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
C.q: A 57-year-old woman whose QT interval became prolonged after starting a new medication has palpitations, and the monitor shows polymorphic ventricular tachycardia whose QRS complexes twist around the baseline (torsades de pointes). She is awake, and intravenous magnesium has been given. If an antiarrhythmic is added, which one can be used?
opts: Procainamide prolongs the QT, so it is avoided in torsades de pointes. It is an option for hemodynamically stable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia instead. Tell: in torsades, the only usable antiarrhythmic is lidocaine.

Beta blockers such as metoprolol are avoided in torsades de pointes because the bradycardia they cause lengthens the R-to-R interval and indirectly prolongs the QT. Tell: her QT is already long, so slowing the heart is harmful.

Correct. Her drug-induced long QT and twisting polymorphic rhythm are torsades de pointes; magnesium is the treatment, and intravenous lidocaine is the one antiarrhythmic that can be used, though evidence for it is limited. Amiodarone and procainamide prolong the QT, and beta blockers prolong it indirectly.

Amiodarone prolongs the QT further, so it is avoided in torsades de pointes. It may be added in polymorphic tachycardia without a long QT, but not here. Tell: with a long QT, the one antiarrhythmic allowed is lidocaine.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
C.q: A 64-year-old man with crushing chest pain develops a wide QRS tachycardia whose complexes vary in shape from beat to beat; his QT before the episode was normal. He is still talking and has a pulse. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Correct. A wide tachycardia with complexes that vary in shape is polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, and with a normal QT and crushing chest pain, acute ischemia is the likely driver. It is never truly stable, so he is defibrillated even with a pulse, then sent for urgent coronary angiography with possible revascularization.

Synchronized cardioversion needs a consistent QRS to time against and suits unstable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia with a pulse. His complexes vary in shape, so he is defibrillated. Tell: monomorphic with a pulse gets synchronized; polymorphic gets unsynchronized.

Observation is unsafe: polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is never truly stable, only a short-lived transitional state that will need defibrillation. Tell: looking well does not make a polymorphic rhythm safe.

Intravenous amiodarone may be added after the shock, but drug therapy alone is for stable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia. Complexes that vary in shape mean polymorphic tachycardia, which is never truly stable and is defibrillated. Tell: a talking patient with polymorphic tachycardia still needs a shock.

C.io: Discuss indications and antibiotic regimens for subacute bacterial endocarditis prophylaxis.
C.q: A 75-year-old man with a prosthetic aortic valve needs a dental extraction. He had a mild delayed rash (no hives, swelling or anaphylaxis) with penicillin and cannot take oral medication. Which prophylaxis is most appropriate?
opts: Correct. He is penicillin-allergic and cannot take oral medication, so the regimen is cefazolin or ceftriaxone 1 g intravenously or intramuscularly 30-60 minutes before the extraction. His reaction was a mild delayed rash, not anaphylaxis, angioedema or urticaria, so a cephalosporin is allowed.

Ampicillin is the injectable choice for patients WITHOUT a penicillin allergy who cannot take oral medication. He reacted to penicillin, and the allergy row covers penicillin or ampicillin. Tell: the allergy history moves the non-oral choice from ampicillin to cefazolin or ceftriaxone.
ruled out by a stated finding

Azithromycin 500 mg is an oral option for penicillin-allergic patients who can swallow. He cannot take oral medication, so an oral agent is out. Tell: allergic and able to take oral medication points to azithromycin, clarithromycin, cephalexin or doxycycline; allergic and unable points to cefazolin or ceftriaxone.
ruled out by a stated finding

Clindamycin is no longer recommended for endocarditis prophylaxis because of the risk of Clostridioides difficile infection. For a penicillin-allergic patient who cannot take oral medication, cefazolin or ceftriaxone by injection is used. Tell: clindamycin is the old answer and has been removed.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
C.q: A 21-year-old man collapses while playing basketball and arrives with a very fast regular tachycardia. He is alert with a blood pressure of 112/70. A vagal maneuver fails, and adenosine slows the rate to reveal an irregular rhythm with wide QRS complexes, each with a delta wave (slurred upstroke). Which is the next step?
opts: Adenosine may be repeated in ordinary stable supraventricular tachycardia, but once it reveals atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White it must never be used again. Irregular wide complexes with delta waves are exactly that finding. Tell: delta waves on an irregular rhythm switch the drug to procainamide.

Atropine is first line for acute, symptomatic, unstable bradycardia, a slow rhythm. His problem is a very fast rhythm conducting over an accessory pathway, the opposite of what atropine treats. Tell: atropine answers slow rates; atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White gets procainamide.

Correct. Adenosine has slowed the rate and revealed an irregular rhythm with wide complexes and delta waves, which is atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White. In that situation intravenous procainamide is used and adenosine is never repeated; he is alert with a blood pressure of 112/70, so a drug is appropriate.

Oral beta blockers serve as chronic therapy for focal atrial tachycardia or as a pill-in-the-pocket option for nodal reentry, not as the acute drug here. Atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White revealed by adenosine is treated with intravenous procainamide. Tell: a pre-excited, irregular wide rhythm calls for intravenous procainamide, not an oral rate-control drug.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
C.q: Which is the first treatment for torsades de pointes in a conscious patient?
opts: Amiodarone prolongs the QT, so it is avoided in torsades de pointes, the polymorphic tachycardia of a prolonged QT. It may be added in polymorphic tachycardia without a long QT. Tell: in torsades, the first drug is intravenous magnesium.

Procainamide prolongs the QT and is avoided in torsades de pointes for the same reason as amiodarone. The first treatment in a conscious patient is intravenous magnesium. Tell: any drug that lengthens the QT feeds torsades rather than stopping it.

Metoprolol is avoided in torsades de pointes: beta blockers cause bradycardia and lengthen the R-to-R interval, which indirectly prolongs the QT. The first treatment is intravenous magnesium. Tell: slowing the heart is harmful when the QT is already long.

Correct. In a conscious patient, intravenous magnesium is given to break torsades de pointes, then more magnesium as an infusion. Amiodarone, procainamide and beta blockers are avoided because they prolong the QT; if the patient becomes hemodynamically unstable, defibrillation replaces drug therapy.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
C.q: A 71-year-old man with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is admitted with an exacerbation and respiratory failure. His pulse is 128 and irregular. The electrocardiogram shows a P wave before every QRS, with at least three different P-wave shapes in lead II. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Atrial flutter with variable conduction can be irregular, but it shows sawtooth flutter waves at an atrial rate of 250 or more that outnumber the QRS complexes. He has one discrete P wave before each QRS, in three different shapes. Tell: one P wave per QRS in changing shapes is multifocal; more sawtooth waves than QRS complexes is flutter.

Correct. An irregular rhythm at 128 with a P wave before every QRS and at least three distinct P-wave shapes in lead II is multifocal atrial tachycardia, from multiple atrial foci. It typically occurs in acutely ill patients with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or heart failure, as with his exacerbation and respiratory failure.

Focal atrial tachycardia comes from a single ectopic atrial focus, so it is regular with one consistent abnormal P-wave shape. His rhythm is irregular and his P waves take at least three shapes. Tell: one shape in a regular rhythm is focal; three or more shapes in an irregular rhythm is multifocal.
ruled out by a stated finding

Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular with absent P waves and no PR interval. His rhythm is irregular too, but every QRS has a P wave before it, in three shapes. Tell: in an irregular narrow tachycardia, look for P waves; absent means fibrillation, multiple shapes mean multifocal atrial tachycardia.
ruled out by a stated finding

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following arterial occlusive disease and aortic aneurysm: 2. Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
C.q: A 73-year-old man with ischemic rest pain notices that walking around the room eases his foot pain, although walking used to cause calf pain. Which explanation should he be given?
opts: Rest pain is not relieved by a natural pain-relief response; it is poorly controlled even by narcotics. Walking helps him because standing puts the foot in a dependent position, and gravity then aids arterial perfusion, the same effect as hanging the leg over the bed. Position explains the relief.
Dependency uses gravity to aid flow

Correct. Ischemic rest pain is relieved by hanging the leg over the edge of the bed or by walking around. In contrast to claudication, walking around uses the gravity effect of dependence on extremity perfusion, which is why walking that once caused his calf pain now eases his foot.

Lower blood pressure would not improve flow to an ischemic foot. The relief comes from dependency: on his feet, gravity aids arterial perfusion, just as hanging the leg over the edge of the bed does. Position, not pressure, explains the paradox.

Venous drainage is not the reason. His foot pain eases with walking because standing makes the limb dependent, and gravity helps arterial flow reach the forefoot. Ischemic rest pain is an arterial supply problem, not venous congestion.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
C.q: A 29-year-old man returns from a camping trip in Connecticut with fatigue and an expanding red rash around a tick bite on his thigh. His electrocardiogram shows a constant PR interval of 0.30 seconds with every P wave conducted. Which infection should be suspected as the cause of his conduction delay?
opts: Infective endocarditis is not on the list of causes of first-degree block; it causes complete block when an abscess forms. A tick bite with an expanding rash after camping points to Lyme disease. Tell: the exposure history, not a murmur or fever, is the clue here.

Chagas disease is a named cause of complete heart block, not of this first-degree delay, and nothing about a Connecticut camping trip suggests it. A tick bite with an expanding rash points to Lyme disease. Tell: tick plus rash means Lyme.

Viral pharyngitis is not a named cause of atrioventricular block, and he has no sore throat. The tick bite and expanding rash point to Lyme disease, which is on the list of causes of first-degree block. Tell: match the infection to the exposure in the stem.

Correct. A tick bite with an expanding red rash after camping in Connecticut points to Lyme disease, a named cause of first-degree atrioventricular block. His constant PR of 0.30 seconds with every P wave conducted is first-degree block, which is most often asymptomatic.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following venous disorders: 2. Deep vein thrombosis 3. Phlebitis a. Thrombophlebitis Septic thrombophlebitis 4. Arteriovenous fistula of the extremity a. Acquired (e.g. trauma, iatrogenic) b. Created (i.e. for hemodialysis) 5. Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
C.q: Which finding makes outpatient therapy for deep vein thrombosis inappropriate?
opts: Good support and reliability, meaning the patient is likely to adhere to the treatment plan and follow-up, makes outpatient therapy appropriate. An iliofemoral (proximal) clot is what moves treatment into the hospital.

Correct. An iliofemoral (proximal) deep vein thrombosis (DVT) is one of the findings that makes outpatient therapy inappropriate, along with concurrent symptomatic pulmonary embolism, high bleeding risk and comorbidities that warrant inpatient care. Every other choice here is on the list that supports outpatient treatment.
Hemodynamic stability is on the list that supports outpatient therapy, not against it. Of these choices, only an iliofemoral (proximal) clot makes outpatient treatment inappropriate.

Absence of renal insufficiency favors outpatient therapy; it is a requirement, not a barrier. An iliofemoral (proximal) clot, a concurrent symptomatic pulmonary embolism or a high bleeding risk would make outpatient treatment inappropriate.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
C.q: Which feature belongs to acute rather than subacute infective endocarditis?
opts: Correct. Acute infective endocarditis is caused by a virulent, invasive organism that rapidly damages cardiac structures and seeds extracardiac sites. Subacute disease, by contrast, rarely metastasizes, so seeding of distant sites marks the acute form.

Rarely metastasizing is a feature of subacute endocarditis, which follows an indolent course and is slow to cause structural cardiac damage. The acute form does the opposite and seeds extracardiac sites. Tell: rarely and slow signal subacute; rapidly and seeds signal acute.

Slow structural damage, if any at all, describes subacute endocarditis. Acute endocarditis rapidly damages cardiac structures, with symptoms typically over 3-10 days and high fevers with systemic toxicity. Tell: the speed of valve damage separates the two forms.

An indolent course defines subacute endocarditis, with lower fevers, malaise and weight loss over weeks or months. Acute endocarditis is a hectically febrile illness from a virulent, invasive organism. Tell: indolent equals subacute; hectic fever and toxicity equal acute.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
C.q: A 41-year-old man who injects drugs is being treated for tricuspid valve endocarditis. On day 2 he develops a new cough, and chest imaging shows several new scattered lesions in both lungs. Which complication best explains these findings?
opts: Correct. He has tricuspid valve endocarditis, a right-sided vegetation, and on day 2 develops a new cough with several scattered lesions in both lungs. The lung is a listed embolic complication of infective endocarditis, along with the spleen, kidney and liver, and multiple new lesions fit septic emboli.

Congestive heart failure is a recognized cardiac complication of endocarditis, but it would not produce several discrete new lesions scattered through both lungs. Tell: multiple separate lesions point to emboli from the tricuspid vegetation; heart failure reflects valvular dysfunction, not seeding.

Drug-induced lung injury is not a listed complication of endocarditis, and new scattered lesions on day 2 fit embolization better. The lung is one of the listed embolic sites, with the spleen, kidney and liver. Tell: a tricuspid vegetation plus multiple new lung lesions spells septic emboli.

Nothing in the stem describes vomiting, and aspiration would not explain several scattered lesions in both lungs. The lung is a listed embolic site of endocarditis, and his tricuspid vegetation is the source. Tell: multiple bilateral lesions in someone with a right-sided vegetation point to emboli.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
C.q: A 38-year-old man who drinks several energy drinks a day is told his skipped beats are premature ventricular contractions. Which description best fits these beats?
opts: Early, wide and bizarre, with no P wave

Correct. A premature ventricular contraction begins in the ventricles, so the early beat has a wide (over 0.12 seconds), bizarre QRS and no P wave. His several energy drinks a day supply caffeine and stimulants, named triggers, and these beats are often felt as skipped beats or palpitations in the neck.
Early and narrow, with an inverted P wave

An early, narrow beat with an inverted P wave is a premature junctional contraction, which begins in the atrioventricular junction. A ventricular beat is wide and bizarre with no P wave. Tell: a narrow beat started above the ventricles.
Early and narrow, with an abnormal P wave

An early beat with an abnormally shaped P wave is a premature atrial contraction, which begins in the atria. A premature ventricular contraction is wide and bizarre with no P wave. Tell: an abnormal P wave in front points to the atria.
Wide, with a slurred upstroke and short PR

A wide beat with a slurred upstroke and short PR is not the description of a premature ventricular contraction. That beat is early, wide and bizarre with no P wave at all, so it has no PR interval. Tell: a beat with no P wave cannot have a short PR.

C.io: Identify medical care strategies for pericardial disease in the lecture topic list for the following populations. 9. adult 10. elderly
C.q: A 72-year-old woman with tamponade from a newly found effusion and no known cancer is being evaluated. Which consideration about the cause is most important at her age?
opts: Her age makes the cause irrelevant

Age does the opposite: in older adults an effusion or tamponade raises the index of suspicion for malignancy, so the cause matters more, not less. Older adults also carry higher morbidity and mortality with surgical interventions, which shapes management. Tell: in older adults, age sharpens the search for a cause.

Correct. In older adults, an effusion or tamponade raises the index of suspicion for malignancy. At 72, with a newly found effusion causing tamponade and no known cancer, the evaluation should actively look for an underlying malignancy.

Nothing in her history is offered to suggest Dressler syndrome, and the point specific to an older adult with effusion or tamponade is a higher index of suspicion for malignancy. Tell: when age is the clue in pericardial effusion or tamponade, think of cancer first.

A viral cause is not what her age flags. For an older adult with a newly found effusion and tamponade, the guidance is a higher index of suspicion for malignancy, and the absence of a known cancer makes that search more pressing, not less. Tell: older age plus effusion or tamponade means look for malignancy.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
C.q: A 34-year-old man has occasional premature junctional contractions (early narrow beats with no visible P wave) on a monitor and is anxious about them. He has no symptoms and no heart disease. Which approach is most appropriate?
opts: Catheter ablation is not among the options for premature junctional contractions; even frequent or persistently symptomatic ones are handled with a search for structural heart disease and a beta blocker. His beats are occasional and cause no symptoms. Tell: infrequent, asymptomatic junctional beats need reassurance only.

A permanent pacemaker is for slow rhythms, such as a junctional rhythm caused by complete or high-grade atrioventricular block or by sick sinus syndrome. He has occasional early beats on an otherwise normal rhythm, not a slow escape rhythm. Tell: a pacemaker treats bradycardia, not premature beats.

A beta blocker such as metoprolol is used for premature junctional contractions only when they are frequent, over 10 per minute or multifocal, or when symptoms persist. His are occasional and he has no symptoms, so lifelong treatment is not indicated. Tell: no symptoms plus infrequent beats means reassurance.

Correct. His premature junctional contractions are occasional, he has no symptoms and no heart disease, and no treatment is needed for asymptomatic, infrequent beats. Reassurance about the benign nature of the rhythm is often enough to ease an anxious patient like him.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
C.q: A 66-year-old man who had cardiac surgery last year reports palpitations and fatigue. His blood pressure is normal, and his rhythm strip is shown. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. Repeating sawtooth flutter waves outnumber the narrow QRS complexes because the atrioventricular node blocks some of the impulses, which is atrial flutter. It is commonly seen with atrial scarring or damage from surgery, as after his cardiac operation, and causes palpitations and fatigue without usually causing collapse.

Sinus tachycardia has one uniform P wave before each QRS at over 100 to 160. This strip has several atrial waves for every QRS in a sawtooth pattern. Tell: one P wave per QRS is sinus; more atrial waves than QRS complexes is flutter.

Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular with absent P waves and no organized atrial activity. This strip shows repeating sawtooth waves between the QRS complexes. Tell: an organized sawtooth baseline is flutter; a chaotic baseline with no P waves is fibrillation.

Multifocal atrial tachycardia has one P wave per QRS in at least three different shapes, usually in acutely ill patients with severe lung disease or heart failure. Here several sawtooth waves fall between each pair of QRS complexes. Tell: changing P shapes, one per beat, is multifocal; a repeating sawtooth outnumbering the QRS complexes is flutter.
C.alt: Rhythm strip of narrow complexes with a continuous zigzag baseline of identical small waves between them, two to four per complex

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
C.q: A 46-year-old man who has drunk heavily for 20 years has six months of worsening breathlessness on exertion and orthopnea (breathlessness lying flat). The apical impulse is displaced laterally and a third heart sound (an early diastolic sound just after the second heart sound) is heard. Echocardiogram shows dilated, thin-walled ventricles with an ejection fraction of 25%, and coronary angiography shows no significant narrowing. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Stress cardiomyopathy does not fit six months of steadily worsening symptoms with globally dilated, thin-walled ventricles. Dilation and impaired contraction without severe occlusive coronary disease define dilated cardiomyopathy. Tell: a slow course and dilated chambers point to dilated disease, not a sudden reaction to a stressor.

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy means thick walls, but his ventricles are dilated and thin-walled; dilated cardiomyopathy increases cardiac mass with little or no wall hypertrophy. Tell: thin, dilated walls with an ejection fraction of 25% point to dilated, not hypertrophic, disease.

Correct. Dilated, thin-walled ventricles with an ejection fraction of 25% and no significant coronary narrowing fit dilated cardiomyopathy: myocardial dysfunction with dilation and impaired contraction in the absence of severe occlusive coronary artery disease. The result is systolic dysfunction, here in a man with 20 years of heavy drinking.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy is not the picture of dilated ventricles with impaired contraction; that combination, with systolic dysfunction and an ejection fraction of 25%, defines dilated cardiomyopathy. Tell: his displaced apical impulse and third heart sound fit a big, weak ventricle.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following venous disorders: 2. Deep vein thrombosis 3. Phlebitis a. Thrombophlebitis Septic thrombophlebitis 4. Arteriovenous fistula of the extremity a. Acquired (e.g. trauma, iatrogenic) b. Created (i.e. for hemodialysis) 5. Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
C.q: A 52-year-old man with a pacemaker implanted two weeks ago has three days of swelling and aching of the left arm. The pacemaker lead has injured the wall of the subclavian vein. Which component of the Virchow triad does this injury represent?
opts: A hypercoagulable state is a tendency of the blood itself to clot, not damage done to a vessel. The decisive clue is a lead that injured the vein wall, a mechanical injury to the lining, which is endothelial trauma.

Correct. The lead has physically injured the wall of the subclavian vein, which is damage to the vessel lining: endothelial trauma. Pacemakers, internal cardiac defibrillators and indwelling central venous catheters are the most common causes of upper-extremity deep vein thrombosis (DVT), which makes up only 5% to 10% of all DVTs.

Impaired lymphatic drainage is not a component of the Virchow triad, which is venous stasis, hypercoagulability and endothelial injury. A pacemaker lead injuring the subclavian vein wall is endothelial trauma, and devices like his are the most common cause of upper-extremity deep vein thrombosis.

Venous stasis means altered blood flow, and nothing in the stem describes immobility. The stated problem is a lead that injured the vein wall, which is endothelial trauma; pacemakers and similar devices are the most common cause of upper-extremity deep vein thrombosis.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
C.q: A 67-year-old woman with suspected restrictive cardiomyopathy has right-sided heart failure and big atria on echocardiogram. Her cardiologist wants to measure pressures inside both ventricles to characterize the filling problem. Which invasive test evaluates ventricular pressure tracings?
opts: Correct. To measure pressures inside both ventricles, the cardiologist needs cardiac catheterization, which is useful in restrictive cardiomyopathy to evaluate ventricular pressure tracings. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging adds information when the cause is unclear, and biopsy is reserved for specific situations.

Exercise echocardiography is noninvasive and does not record pressures inside the ventricles; the echo in restrictive cardiomyopathy shows big atria and abnormal diastolic function but is not definitive. Ventricular pressure tracings come from cardiac catheterization. Tell: the stem asks for an invasive pressure test.

A transesophageal echocardiogram is still an echocardiogram, and echo alone is not definitive in restrictive cardiomyopathy. Direct ventricular pressure tracings require cardiac catheterization. Tell: pressure tracings mean a catheter inside the heart.

Endomyocardial biopsy samples tissue to confirm or exclude a diagnosis that would change management, usually after negative imaging and genetic testing; it does not record pressures. Ventricular pressure tracings come from cardiac catheterization. Tell: tissue says what the disease is; a catheter says what the pressures are.

C.q: Which acute limb ischemia categories leave time for vascular imaging?
opts: Imaging time disappears as the category worsens: the immediately threatened limb goes to the surgical suite, and the irreversible limb generally needs no imaging. Only viable and marginally threatened limbs have sufficient time for vascular imaging. Any option including the two worst categories is wrong.

The immediately threatened limb is salvageable only with immediate revascularization, so it should go to the surgical suite for further evaluation and treatment rather than wait for imaging. Imaging time belongs to viable and marginally threatened limbs. Sensory loss beyond the toes or weakness removes the time for imaging.

Vascular imaging is generally not immediately needed for an irreversibly damaged limb, because nonviable extremities need major amputation regardless of therapy. The categories with sufficient time for imaging are viable and marginally threatened. Imaging helps only when the result can change the plan.

Correct. Viable limbs, under no immediate threat of tissue loss, and marginally threatened limbs, salvageable if treated promptly, both have sufficient time for vascular imaging such as computed tomography angiography. Neither has sensory loss or muscle weakness, so a short delay for imaging does not cost the limb.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. C.q: A 66-year-old woman in urgent care has a fever, a new murmur and splinter hemorrhages (dark lines under the nail plates). Before transfer, a colleague proposes giving a dose of ceftriaxone right away. Which action should be avoided?
opts: Drawing cultures is required, not avoided: three sets of blood cultures from separate sites, and if the presentation suggests acute disease, 2 cultures within the first 1-2 hours. They must come before any antibiotic. Tell: cultures first is exactly the rule the proposed ceftriaxone dose would break.

Echocardiography should not be avoided. Transesophageal echocardiography is highly sensitive and specific, defines the extent of disease and detects vegetations on valve leaflets, so it is a core part of her workup. Tell: the step to avoid here is the premature antibiotic, not imaging.

Correct. Her fever, new murmur and splinter hemorrhages raise suspicion for endocarditis, and empiric therapy is started ONLY after blood cultures have been drawn, three sets from separate sites. Giving ceftriaxone first would compromise the cultures needed to identify the organism and direct the prolonged bactericidal course.

Admission is appropriate, not something to avoid. Endocarditis is managed with intravenous antibiotics, hospital admission, close monitoring of labs, renal function and cardiovascular status, and a multidisciplinary team. Tell: transfer and admission are correct; only the pre-culture antibiotic is wrong.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following arterial occlusive disease and aortic aneurysm: 2. Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
C.q: A 70-year-old woman has a 1.4 cm femoral pseudoaneurysm on ultrasound after cardiac catheterization. She is comfortable and the limb is well perfused. Which management is most appropriate?
opts: Open surgery is not among the listed treatments for a small pseudoaneurysm. At 1.4 cm, under 2 cm, hers may thrombose and regress on its own, so watch and wait is appropriate. The listed active treatment is ultrasound-guided thrombin, not an operation.

Heparin anticoagulates and would work against the thrombosis that seals a pseudoaneurysm. Her 1.4 cm cavity is under 2 cm and may thrombose and regress on its own, so the plan is to watch and wait. The goal here is clot formation, not its prevention.

Catheter-directed thrombolysis dissolves clot in acute limb ischemia, the opposite of what a pseudoaneurysm needs, since the cavity seals as it thromboses. Her 1.4 cm pseudoaneurysm is under 2 cm, so watch and wait is appropriate. Lysis would work against the natural sealing.

Correct. A pseudoaneurysm under 2 cm in diameter may undergo spontaneous thrombosis and regression, and hers is 1.4 cm in a comfortable patient with a well-perfused limb. Watchful waiting is appropriate; ultrasound-guided thrombin injection is the treatment when a leak needs sealing.
