Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
C.q: A 59-year-old man is about to start hemodialysis through a newly created forearm arteriovenous fistula. Which self-check should he be taught to confirm that the fistula is working?
opts: Confirm it stays full when raised

A healthy fistula collapses completely when the arm is elevated, so an access that stays full when raised is not behaving normally. Collapse on elevation and a diffuse thrill with a soft bruit are the signs of a working fistula.
Confirm the skin over it is cool

Skin temperature over the access is not one of the signs of a healthy fistula. A working fistula is recognized by a diffuse thrill and a soft bruit with systolic and diastolic components, and by complete collapse when the arm is raised.
Confirm no sound is heard over it
A healthy fistula is expected to make a sound: a soft bruit with systolic and diastolic components, heard along with a diffuse thrill. Silence over the access is the opposite of the normal finding.

Correct. A healthy arteriovenous (AV) fistula has a diffuse thrill and a soft bruit, both with systolic and diastolic components, so feeling the vibrating thrill over his forearm access is a simple check that it is working. Upper-extremity fistulas like his are created for long-term hemodialysis access.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
C.q: Which set lists the four rhythms that produce cardiac arrest?
opts: Ventricular fibrillation, atrial fibrillation, complete heart block and torsades with a pulse

Atrial fibrillation, complete heart block and torsades with a pulse are not on the list of arrest rhythms. Cardiac arrest results from ventricular fibrillation, pulseless ventricular tachycardia, pulseless electrical activity or asystole. Tell: every arrest rhythm on the list is pulseless.
Pulseless electrical activity, bigeminy, first-degree block and sinus tachycardia

Bigeminy, first-degree block and sinus tachycardia are not arrest rhythms; only pulseless electrical activity in this set belongs. Cardiac arrest results from ventricular fibrillation, pulseless ventricular tachycardia, pulseless electrical activity or asystole. Tell: the list has no perfusing rhythms.
Ventricular fibrillation, pulseless ventricular tachycardia, pulseless electrical activity, asystole

Correct. Cardiac arrest results from one of four rhythms: ventricular fibrillation, pulseless ventricular tachycardia, pulseless electrical activity or ventricular standstill (asystole). These cause sudden cardiac death, unexpected cardiac death within 1 hour of collapse, and coronary artery disease is the most common predisposing condition.
Asystole, sinus bradycardia, Mobitz type II block and atrial flutter with rapid response

Sinus bradycardia, Mobitz type II block and atrial flutter are not on the list of arrest rhythms; only asystole in this set belongs. The four are ventricular fibrillation, pulseless ventricular tachycardia, pulseless electrical activity and asystole. Tell: each of the four leaves the patient without a pulse.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following arterial occlusive disease and aortic aneurysm: 2. Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
C.q: A 68-year-old man who smokes and has diabetes reports aching in both buttocks and hips after walking two blocks, relieved by about 10 minutes of rest. He also reports erectile dysfunction. Both femoral pulses are diminished. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. Buttock and hip claudication points to aortoiliac disease, which can diminish one or both femoral pulses and, when severe, causes erectile dysfunction. Claudication, absent or diminished femoral pulses and erectile dysfunction together form the Leriche syndrome triad, and he has all three.

Tibial disease produces foot claudication, at the far end of the leg, and does not explain weak femoral pulses. His buttock and hip pain, erectile dysfunction and diminished femoral pulses all point to the aortoiliac segment. The pain site maps to the level of the lesion.

Spinal stenosis gives claudication-like symptoms with numbness and weakness, relieved by sitting down or leaning forward, and does not explain weak femoral pulses. His pain eases with rest alone, his femoral pulses are diminished and he has erectile dysfunction, the Leriche triad of aortoiliac disease.

Superficial femoral artery stenosis causes claudication in the upper two-thirds of the calf, the most common site. His pain is in the buttocks and hips with diminished femoral pulses and erectile dysfunction, which places the lesion higher, in the aortoiliac segment. Calf pain would point lower.

Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
C.q: A 71-year-old man has palpitations, chest pressure and crackles at both lung bases. His pulse is irregularly irregular at 170 with no P waves on the monitor, and his blood pressure is 76/48. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Adenosine is a step for stable, regular supraventricular tachycardia after a vagal maneuver. His rhythm is irregularly irregular with no P waves, which is atrial fibrillation, and he is hypotensive. Tell: an unstable patient in atrial fibrillation gets a synchronized shock, not a diagnostic drug.

Intravenous rate control is for atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response in a hemodynamically stable patient. With a blood pressure of 76/48 and crackles from pulmonary edema, he is unstable. Tell: rapid rate plus stability means intravenous rate control; rapid rate plus hypotension means synchronized cardioversion.

Outpatient cardioversion after 21 days of anticoagulation is the elective route for stable atrial fibrillation. He is hypotensive with pulmonary edema and cannot wait three weeks. Tell: instability turns an elective cardioversion into an immediate synchronized one.

Correct. An irregularly irregular rhythm at 170 with no P waves is atrial fibrillation, and a blood pressure of 76/48 with crackles at both bases means severe heart failure with hypotension, a medical emergency. Hemodynamically unstable atrial fibrillation is treated with synchronized cardioversion.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
C.q: A 40-year-old woman has a regular narrow complex tachycardia at 182 with palpitations and mild anxiety. Her blood pressure is 128/80, oxygen saturation 98%, and she is alert without chest pain. Which treatment should be tried first?
opts: Synchronized cardioversion, a timed shock at decreased voltage, is immediate treatment for hemodynamically unstable supraventricular tachycardia. She is alert with a normal blood pressure and no chest pain, so she is stable. Tell: stability means a vagal maneuver first, not a shock.

Adenosine is the second step in stable supraventricular tachycardia, given if a vagal maneuver does not work, and it may be repeated once. It may convert the rhythm or slow it enough to reveal P waves. Tell: the question asks what to try first, and the vagal maneuver comes before any drug.

Amiodarone may be tried for chemical cardioversion of focal atrial tachycardia, not as the opening step for a stable narrow complex tachycardia. Her stable presentation starts with a vagal maneuver, then adenosine. Tell: the first step in stable supraventricular tachycardia needs no drug at all.

Correct. A regular narrow complex tachycardia at 182 with a blood pressure of 128/80, normal oxygen saturation and an alert patient without chest pain is stable supraventricular tachycardia. A vagal maneuver is first line, then adenosine (repeated once if needed), with synchronized cardioversion kept for instability.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
C.q: A 24-year-old man collapses during a basketball game and wakes within a minute. In the ambulance his rhythm is irregular, with wide QRS complexes of varying width at rates approaching 300. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Ventricular tachycardia is the other wide-complex tachycardia to consider, but it is regular, with rates between 150 and 200. This rhythm is irregular and approaches 300. Tell: wide and regular at 150 to 200 is ventricular tachycardia; wide and irregular near 300 is atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White.

Atrial flutter with 2:1 block is a regular rhythm with narrow QRS complexes and two sawtooth flutter waves for every QRS. This rhythm is irregular with wide complexes. Tell: regular and narrow with sawtooth waves is flutter; irregular and wide is pre-excited atrial fibrillation.

Multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular but narrow, with at least three P-wave shapes, and occurs in acutely ill patients with severe lung disease or heart failure. This young athlete has wide complexes at rates near 300. Tell: irregular and narrow with changing P waves is multifocal; irregular and wide near 300 is pre-excited fibrillation.

Correct. An irregular rhythm with wide QRS complexes of varying width at rates approaching 300 is atrial fibrillation conducting with Wolff-Parkinson-White, pre-excited atrial fibrillation. Ventricular tachycardia, the look-alike wide rhythm, is regular at 150 to 200, so the irregularity and the rate near 300 settle it.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
C.q: A 44-year-old man had a tuberculous pericardial effusion drained in the hospital and is starting antituberculous therapy. Which specialty should be part of his close follow-up?
opts: Correct. Close follow-up after a pericardial effusion is matched to the underlying etiology, and his is tuberculosis on antituberculous therapy, an infection, so infectious disease belongs in his care. Long-term prognosis also depends on the underlying cause, which makes treating that cause central.

Nephrology is the follow-up specialty when kidney disease drives the effusion, and nothing here involves the kidneys. Follow-up is matched to the underlying etiology, and his tuberculous effusion on antituberculous therapy points to infectious disease. Tell: name the cause, then pick the specialty that treats it.

Oncology follows malignant effusions, where a symptomatic malignant effusion carries a median life expectancy of 2 to 4 months and palliative care consultation is recommended. His effusion is tuberculous, so infectious disease follows him. Tell: the specialist matches the cause, and his cause is an infection.

Rheumatology joins follow-up when a rheumatologic disease causes the effusion. His cause is tuberculosis on antituberculous therapy, so the etiology-matched specialist is infectious disease. Tell: the follow-up specialty tracks the underlying etiology, and tuberculosis is an infection.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
C.q: A 66-year-old man had coronary bypass surgery two months ago. He now has palpitations and fatigue. His heart rate is 150 and regular, and the electrocardiogram shows sawtooth waves, two for every narrow QRS. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Sinus tachycardia has one uniform P wave before each QRS, at over 100 to 160. He has two sawtooth waves for each QRS, so the atria are beating at twice the ventricular rate. Tell: one P wave per QRS is sinus; two sawtooth waves per QRS is flutter with 2:1 block.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. A regular rate of 150 with two sawtooth waves for every narrow QRS is atrial flutter with 2:1 block, the most common ratio, in which the node blocks one of every two atrial impulses. Atrial scarring or damage from surgery, such as his recent bypass operation, is a common setting for flutter.

Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular with absent P waves and no organized atrial waves. His rhythm is regular at 150 with repeating sawtooth waves. Tell: regular with sawtooth waves is flutter; irregularly irregular without P waves is fibrillation.
ruled out by a stated finding

Multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular, with one P wave per QRS in at least three distinct shapes. His rhythm is regular with two matching sawtooth waves per QRS. Tell: changing P shapes, one per beat, mean multiple foci; a regular sawtooth with two waves per beat is flutter.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
C.q: A 35-year-old woman has 3 days of sharp substernal chest pain that improves when she sits forward. Her vital signs are normal, and no rub is heard on careful auscultation. Which additional finding would complete the clinical diagnosis of acute pericarditis?
opts: B-type natriuretic peptide is not one of the four diagnostic criteria, so it cannot complete the diagnosis. Her sharp, positional pain counts as one criterion; the second must be a friction rub, widespread ST elevation or a new or worsening effusion. Tell: only items on the criteria list count toward the two needed.

Pericardial calcification is not one of the four diagnostic criteria for acute pericarditis. With chest pain already present and no rub heard, widespread ST elevation on the electrocardiogram or a new or worsening effusion would supply the second criterion. Tell: count only the four listed criteria.

Correct. Acute pericarditis needs two of four criteria: sharp substernal chest pain, a pericardial friction rub, suggestive electrocardiogram changes (widespread ST elevation) and a new or worsening effusion. She has the pain, sharp and eased by sitting forward, but no rub, so widespread ST elevation would supply the second criterion.
A troponin above the reference range

Troponin is not a diagnostic criterion; it rises when the myocardium is also affected (myopericarditis), and an elevated value is a higher-risk feature favoring hospitalization. It does not count as her second criterion. Tell: troponin grades risk, while the electrocardiogram helps make the diagnosis.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
C.q: A 59-year-old man with a large pericardial effusion from metastatic cancer reports a hoarse voice, hiccups and difficulty swallowing. Which mechanism explains his hoarseness?
opts: Hoarseness from a large pericardial effusion is attributed to recurrent laryngeal nerve impingement, not to the hypoglossal nerve. His hoarseness, hiccups and dysphagia are the compression symptoms listed for large effusions. Tell: a voice change with a big effusion points to the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
Direct invasion of the vocal cords

Nothing suggests the cancer has reached the larynx; his hoarseness arrives with hiccups and dysphagia, the listed symptoms of a large effusion pressing on nearby structures. Large effusions cause hoarseness through recurrent laryngeal nerve impingement. Tell: the effusion acts by pressing, not by invading.

Superior vena cava obstruction is not among the effects listed for a large effusion and does not explain a hoarse voice. Large effusions produce dysphagia, nausea, hiccups, cough and hoarseness, the hoarseness from recurrent laryngeal nerve impingement. Tell: hoarseness plus hiccups plus dysphagia is the large-effusion compression set.

Correct. His effusion is large, and large effusions can cause dysphagia, nausea, hiccups, cough and hoarseness. The hoarseness comes from impingement of the recurrent laryngeal nerve, which is why his voice change travels with the hiccups and difficulty swallowing.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
C.q: A 49-year-old woman has subacute endocarditis, and her blood cultures grow Eikenella corrodens, a member of the HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) group. Which antibiotic is most appropriate?
opts: Vancomycin is not a listed regimen for HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) organisms; it appears in streptococcal, enterococcal and staphylococcal regimens. Eikenella corrodens endocarditis is treated with ceftriaxone or ampicillin-sulbactam. Tell: a HACEK organism on culture means ceftriaxone.

Correct. Her cultures grow Eikenella corrodens, a HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) organism, and HACEK endocarditis is treated with ceftriaxone 2 g intravenously once daily for 4 weeks. The listed alternative is ampicillin-sulbactam for 4 weeks.

Nafcillin is a staphylococcal drug, used for methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus on native or prosthetic valves. It is not a HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) regimen. Tell: nafcillin follows a staphylococcal culture; Eikenella calls for ceftriaxone.

Rifampin is an add-on in staphylococcal prosthetic valve infection, combined with nafcillin or vancomycin plus gentamicin. It is not a treatment for HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) organisms. Tell: there is no prosthetic valve and no staphylococcus here, so rifampin has no role.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following arterial occlusive disease and aortic aneurysm: 2. Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
C.q: A 64-year-old woman with hypertension has a carotid bruit found on routine examination. She has never had neurologic symptoms. Duplex shows 35% stenosis. Which is the most appropriate management?
opts: Carotid stenting is a less invasive revascularization for poor surgical candidates who need intervention. Her 35% asymptomatic stenosis needs no intervention at all, since under 50% is managed medically. Stenting changes the route, not the indication.

Correct. Medical management is advised for symptomatic and asymptomatic patients with low-grade stenosis under 50%, and hers is 35% without symptoms. It includes antiplatelet therapy such as aspirin or clopidogrel, control of hypertension, diabetes and lipids, smoking cessation, healthy diet, exercise and weight reduction.

Endarterectomy is advised for symptomatic stenosis over 70% or asymptomatic stenosis over 80% with a life expectancy over five years. Her 35% asymptomatic stenosis is far below either threshold and is managed medically. A bruit alone does not trigger surgery.

Digital subtraction angiography is the invasive gold standard used to guide therapeutic interventions, and none is indicated for her. Her 35% stenosis is low grade, under 50%, and is managed medically. An invasive study has no role when no intervention is planned.

Deep vein thrombosis 3. Phlebitis a. Thrombophlebitis Septic thrombophlebitis 4. Arteriovenous fistula of the extremity a. Acquired (e.g. trauma, iatrogenic) b. Created (i.e. for hemodialysis) 5. Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
C.q: A 44-year-old man develops a first calf deep vein thrombosis one week after minor knee arthroscopy under a local nerve block, followed by a long car trip. Which duration of anticoagulation is appropriate?
opts: Three months is the course for a clot provoked by a major transient factor, such as surgery under general anesthesia over 30 minutes, bed rest of 3 days or more, or major trauma or fracture. His minor arthroscopy under a nerve block and a long car trip are minor factors, which call for 3 to 6 months.

Correct. Minor surgery and prolonged travel are both minor transient risk factors, and a first venous thromboembolism (VTE) provoked by a minor transient factor is treated for 3 to 6 months. His arthroscopy used a local nerve block, not general anesthesia over 30 minutes, so it is not a major factor.

Indefinite anticoagulation is for an unprovoked first venous thromboembolism, one with no identifiable risk factor. His clot followed minor surgery and a long car trip, identifiable minor transient factors that call for 3 to 6 months.

Six weeks falls below the minimum: every patient with an acute first venous thromboembolism (deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism) is anticoagulated for at least 3 months. His minor-factor clot calls for 3 to 6 months.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
C.q: A 70-year-old man has 3 weeks of low-grade fever and malaise that began a week after a dental extraction. A new murmur of mitral regurgitation is heard. Three sets of blood cultures are drawn. Which organism are they most likely to grow?
opts: Staphylococcus aureus is a skin organism and a leading acute cause, with a rapid, toxic course. Three weeks of low-grade fever and malaise after a dental extraction is subacute disease from an oral source. Tell: dental work plus an indolent course points to viridans streptococci, not a skin organism.

Candida is listed as the fungal cause of endocarditis, separate from the bacterial causes of subacute disease. A smoldering illness that began a week after a tooth extraction points to the oral cavity, the source of viridans streptococci. Tell: a dental source means viridans streptococci, not a fungus.

Enterococci are a subacute cause, but they come from the genitourinary tract. His illness began after a dental extraction, an oral source. Tell: a urinary source means enterococci; a mouth source means viridans streptococci.

Correct. Three weeks of low-grade fever and malaise is a subacute course, and its onset a week after a dental extraction points to the oral cavity, the source of viridans streptococci. Viridans streptococci are a classic subacute organism and a leading cause of native valve endocarditis.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
C.q: A 38-year-old man who injects drugs is being treated for aortic valve endocarditis. On day 4 his heart rate falls to 38, and the electrocardiogram shows P waves with no relationship to wide QRS complexes. Which complication of his infection explains the new rhythm?
opts: Splinter hemorrhages are a peripheral finding of endocarditis and are not on the list of causes of complete block. Bacterial endocarditis with an associated abscess is. Tell: a sign in the nails cannot block conduction in the heart.

Increased vagal tone is a cause of first-degree and Mobitz type I block, not complete block, and nothing here points to it. During aortic valve endocarditis, new complete block points to an associated abscess. Tell: new complete block during endocarditis means an abscess until proved otherwise.

Correct. On day 4 of aortic valve endocarditis his rate fell to 38, with P waves unrelated to wide QRS complexes: complete block. Bacterial endocarditis with an associated abscess is a named cause of complete block, and the rhythm is treated with pacing, then a permanent pacemaker.

Septic emboli to the lungs are not a named cause of complete heart block. His new rate of 38 with P waves unrelated to wide QRS complexes is complete block, and the endocarditis cause on the list is an associated abscess. Tell: the complication must be in the heart to block conduction.

C.q: A 52-year-old man with chronic venous insufficiency and recurrent ulcers is being considered for an invasive venous procedure. Which test is the gold standard for defining his venous anatomy beforehand?
opts: The ankle-brachial index (ABI) is paired with an arterial pulse examination for any patient with a lower extremity wound, especially older patients, to assess the arteries. It does not map venous anatomy, which catheter-based venography defines before an intervention.

Correct. He is about to have an invasive venous procedure, and catheter-based (invasive) venography is the gold standard test, done before an invasive intervention. It is rarely needed to make the diagnosis of chronic venous insufficiency, which duplex ultrasound handles first.

Venous duplex ultrasound is the first test: it confirms the diagnosis, rules out deep vein thrombosis, finds reflux and determines the level and anatomy of disease. It is not the gold standard; catheter-based venography holds that role and is the test done before an invasive procedure.

Cross-sectional venography with computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging helps evaluate deep veins that ultrasound cannot properly detect. It is a supplementary study, not the gold standard, which is catheter-based venography performed before invasive intervention.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
C.q: In tachy-brady syndrome, which tachyarrhythmia is most common?
opts: Sinus tachycardia is a regular rhythm at over 100 to 160 with a P wave before every QRS, usually driven by a physiologic or pathologic process. The fast phase of tachy-brady syndrome is most commonly atrial fibrillation, not a sinus rhythm. Tell: the named most-common tachyarrhythmia is irregularly irregular without P waves.

Ventricular tachycardia can be the tachyarrhythmia in some patients with tachy-brady syndrome, who then need a permanent pacemaker with an implantable defibrillator. It is not the most common one; atrial fibrillation is. Tell: ventricular tachycardia changes the device, not the most-common answer.

Correct. Tachy-brady syndrome is the form of sick sinus syndrome in which a tachyarrhythmia alternates with symptomatic bradycardia or offset pauses. The most common cause of the fast phase is atrial fibrillation, which appears as an irregularly irregular rhythm without P waves.

Atrial flutter is a fast atrial rhythm with sawtooth waves at an atrial rate of 250 or more, but it is not the named most-common tachyarrhythmia of tachy-brady syndrome. That is atrial fibrillation. Tell: the fast phase is classically irregularly irregular without P waves, which is fibrillation, not a regular sawtooth.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. C.q: A 20-year-old man with acute myocarditis after a flulike illness is on the ward with heart failure symptoms. He reports new palpitations, and his nurse notes a brief episode of lightheadedness. Which complication poses the most immediate threat to his life?
opts: Pericardial thickening is not a complication described for myocarditis and would not explain sudden palpitations with lightheadedness. Those symptoms fit ventricular arrhythmias or atrioventricular block, which can lead to syncope or sudden cardiac death. Tell: the clue is palpitations, a rhythm symptom.

Mitral valve prolapse is not part of the myocarditis picture. New palpitations with lightheadedness here signal ventricular arrhythmia or atrioventricular block, which in myocarditis can progress to syncope or sudden cardiac death. Tell: link the symptoms to the arrhythmia, not to a valve.

Aortic dissection is not part of acute myocarditis, and nothing in his story suggests it. His palpitations and lightheadedness fit the arrhythmic risk of myocarditis, ventricular arrhythmias or atrioventricular block, which can cause syncope or sudden cardiac death. Tell: palpitations plus near-fainting means rhythm.

Correct. In this young man with myocarditis after a flulike illness, new palpitations and a brief episode of lightheadedness point to the arrhythmic danger: palpitations, syncope or sudden cardiac death in myocarditis are due to underlying ventricular arrhythmias or atrioventricular block. Sudden death makes this the most immediate threat.

C.q: A 59-year-old man has frequent premature atrial contractions on a monitor (early beats with abnormal P waves), many per minute. He has no known heart disease. Which evaluation is most appropriate?
opts: Testing for an accessory pathway fits a short PR interval with a delta wave on the resting tracing, the pattern of Wolff-Parkinson-White. His finding is frequent early beats with abnormal P waves, which are premature atrial contractions. Tell: frequent premature atrial contractions prompt a structural heart workup, not a pathway search.

Correct. His premature atrial contractions are frequent, many per minute, and when they are frequent the step is to look for underlying structural heart disease. In patients with heart disease these beats may precede paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia, atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter, which makes the search worthwhile.

A digoxin level matters when digoxin toxicity is suspected, which is a listed cause of junctional rhythm, not of premature atrial contractions. He has frequent early beats with abnormal P waves and no stated digoxin use. Tell: frequent premature atrial beats send you looking for structural heart disease.

No treatment is needed when premature atrial contractions are infrequent and asymptomatic. His are frequent, many per minute, and frequent beats call for a search for underlying structural heart disease. Tell: frequency is the switch; infrequent means reassure, frequent means evaluate.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. C.q: A 30-year-old man is diagnosed with dilated cardiomyopathy. His father had a cardiomyopathy and his older brother died suddenly at 35. No alcohol, drug or chemotherapy exposure is found. Which is the most appropriate referral for him and his family?
opts: Heart biopsies are not a family strategy. The step for a patient with a family history of dilated cardiomyopathy is genetic counseling, part of patient education alongside medication follow-up. Tell: relatives are counseled, not biopsied.

Waiting until 60 makes no sense when his brother died suddenly at 35. Genetic counseling for patients with a family history is part of dilated cardiomyopathy care now. Tell: the family history is already present, so counseling starts at diagnosis.
Reassurance that it is not inherited

Reassurance ignores his father's cardiomyopathy and his brother's sudden death at 35. Genetic counseling is recommended for patients with a family history. Tell: with no alcohol, drug or chemotherapy cause, the family history is the lead to follow.

Correct. His father's cardiomyopathy and his brother's sudden death at 35 are a family history, with no alcohol, drug or chemotherapy cause found. Patient education in dilated cardiomyopathy includes genetic counseling for patients with a family history, alongside removing any offending source and sodium restriction.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following arterial occlusive disease and aortic aneurysm: 2. Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
C.q: A 70-year-old man presents with painful blue toes and palpable pedal pulses. On abdominal examination there is a pulsatile mass above the umbilicus. Which lesion is the likely source of his emboli?
opts: A femoral pseudoaneurysm follows catheterization and causes local groin pain from swelling or nerve compression. His mass is pulsatile and abdominal, above the umbilicus, which points to an abdominal aortic aneurysm shedding emboli to the toes. The location of the mass is the clue.

Aortic dissection forms from an intimal tear that creates a false lumen within the media, not an abdominal pulsatile mass with emboli. His pulsatile mass above the umbilicus with painful blue toes is an abdominal aortic aneurysm with embolic phenomena (blue toe syndrome). Tell: the mass is in the abdomen, not the thorax.

Correct. A symptomatic abdominal aortic aneurysm can produce embolic phenomena that lead to blue toe syndrome. His pulsatile mass above the umbilicus is the aneurysm, and painful blue toes with palpable pedal pulses fit small emboli lodging in the digits rather than a large-artery occlusion.

Carotid plaque is linked to atheroembolization and stroke, and a neck lesion would not explain a pulsatile mass above the umbilicus. His painful blue toes, palpable pedal pulses and pulsatile abdominal mass point to an abdominal aortic aneurysm with embolic phenomena. The mass locates the source.

C.q: A 71-year-old man admitted with pneumonia develops frequent early, wide QRS beats with no preceding P wave on telemetry, and he feels his heart skipping. His oxygen saturation on the monitor is drifting down. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Amiodarone is not part of managing premature ventricular contractions. New frequent premature beats in a patient whose oxygen saturation is falling call for finding and correcting their named causes: hypoxemia and electrolyte imbalance. Tell: fix the cause before reaching for a drug.

Catheter ablation is reserved for symptoms refractory to a beta blocker or isolated premature-beat cardiomyopathy. In a man with pneumonia and falling oxygen saturation, the first step is checking oxygenation and electrolytes. Tell: a reversible cause comes before any procedure.

Correct. Early, wide beats with no P wave are premature ventricular contractions, and hypoxemia and electrolyte imbalance (hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypercalcemia) are the main causes. With pneumonia and a drifting oxygen saturation, checking a blood gas and electrolytes, then correcting what is found, comes first.

Defibrillation is for ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia. He has premature beats with a pulse and feels them skipping. Tell: a patient who can describe his palpitations is not in cardiac arrest.

C.q: A 76-year-old woman with long-standing hypertension and diabetes has two spells of lightheadedness this week. Her electrocardiogram shows regular P waves, a constant PR interval of 0.16 seconds in the conducted beats, and occasional P waves with no QRS complex after them, with no lengthening of the PR beforehand. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: In complete block no P waves conduct, and P waves and QRS complexes are unrelated. Here most P waves conduct with a fixed PR of 0.16 seconds and only some drop. Tell: a constant PR in conducted beats rules out complete block.

Correct. Regular P waves, a constant PR of 0.16 seconds in conducted beats and occasional P waves with no QRS, with no PR lengthening beforehand, is Mobitz type II block. Her lightheaded spells fit symptoms of bradycardia, and her long-standing hypertension and diabetes fit its most common cause, His-Purkinje disease.
First-degree block has a PR over 0.20 seconds and never drops a beat. Her PR is a normal 0.16 seconds, and some P waves fail to conduct. Tell: a normal PR with dropped beats is not first degree.

Mobitz type I lengthens the PR progressively before each dropped beat. Here the PR stays constant at 0.16 seconds with no lengthening before the drop, which marks Mobitz type II. Tell: watch the PR before the dropped beat; constant means type II.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
C.q: Which imaging test is now recommended for risk stratification of complicated or recurrent pericarditis?
opts: Correct. Cardiac magnetic resonance is now recommended for risk stratification of complicated or recurrent pericarditis. Edema or late gadolinium enhancement on it also identifies inflammatory, potentially reversible constriction before committing to pericardiectomy.

Coronary angiography is not the recommended study for stratifying pericarditis; that role belongs to cardiac magnetic resonance, which can show pericardial edema and late gadolinium enhancement. Tell: the question asks about pericardial inflammation, so pick the test that images the inflamed pericardium.

A plain chest radiograph is not the recommended risk-stratification test and cannot show pericardial edema or late gadolinium enhancement. Cardiac magnetic resonance fills that role for complicated or recurrent pericarditis. Tell: risk stratification here depends on seeing active inflammation, which needs magnetic resonance.

A ventilation-perfusion scan has no stated role in pericarditis. For complicated or recurrent disease, cardiac magnetic resonance is recommended because edema or late gadolinium enhancement shows active, potentially reversible pericardial inflammation. Tell: choose the scan that looks at the pericardium, not the lungs.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
C.q: Constriction that persists after a coexisting pericardial effusion has been drained defines which entity?
opts: Cardiac tamponade is pericardial fluid under pressure compressing the heart, so removing the fluid removes the problem. Constriction that remains after drainage points to effusive-constrictive pericarditis. Tell: if drainage fixes it, it was tamponade; if constriction persists, the pericardium itself is scarred.

Recurrent pericarditis is defined by timing: symptoms return after a symptom-free interval of 4 to 6 weeks or longer. It says nothing about constriction persisting after drainage, which defines effusive-constrictive pericarditis. Tell: recurrence is about time; persistence after drainage is about a stiff pericardium.

Correct. Effusive-constrictive pericarditis combines underlying constriction with a coexisting effusion, usually with tamponade, and it is recognized when constriction persists after the effusion is drained. Draining the fluid relieves the effusion but not the scarred, noncompliant pericardium.

A loculated posterior effusion describes where fluid collects, not a constrictive process. Constriction persisting after an effusion is drained is the definition of effusive-constrictive pericarditis: underlying constriction plus a coexisting effusion. Tell: the stem describes what remains after drainage, and that is constriction.

C.q: A 45-year-old woman has a catheter-related deep vein thrombosis of the right arm and asks how likely a pulmonary embolism is compared with a leg clot. Which statement is accurate?
opts: About 3% for arm and leg clots alike

About 3% for both sites ignores that the risk differs by location. Pulmonary embolism occurs in up to 6% of upper-extremity clots like her catheter-related one, but in 15% to 30% of lower-extremity clots; the tell is that leg clots carry several times the risk.
15 to 30%, versus up to 6% for leg clots

This reverses the two figures. Pulmonary embolism complicates 15% to 30% of lower-extremity deep vein thromboses and only up to 6% of upper-extremity ones, so her arm clot carries the lower risk, not the higher.
Under 1% for arm clots, 6% for leg clots

Both numbers are too low, and the leg figure is off most: pulmonary embolism occurs in 15% to 30% of lower-extremity clots, not 6%. Up to 6% is the figure for upper-extremity clots like hers, so this choice moves the arm number onto the leg.
Up to 6%, versus 15 to 30% for leg clots

Correct. Pulmonary embolism occurs in up to 6% of upper-extremity deep vein thromboses (DVTs), versus 15% to 30% of lower-extremity ones, so her catheter-related arm clot carries the lower risk. Arm clots are only 5% to 10% of all DVTs and are most often caused by pacemakers, defibrillators or central venous catheters.

C.q: A 68-year-old man who smoked for 40 years has no symptoms, but a widened, pulsatile aorta is felt on routine abdominal examination. Which is the study of choice for initial screening for an aneurysm?
opts: A plain film shows a calcified outline in only about 75% of aneurysms and misses the 25% that are not calcified. Abdominal ultrasound is the screening study of choice for his suspected aneurysm. A test that misses a quarter of cases cannot screen.

Computed tomography angiography is the best diagnostic and pre-intervention planning study, used once repair is being considered. For this asymptomatic smoker with a pulsatile aorta on examination, initial screening uses abdominal ultrasound. Planning comes after screening.

Correct. A widened, pulsatile aorta found on routine examination of an asymptomatic 68-year-old smoker calls for screening, and abdominal ultrasound is the diagnostic study of choice for initial screening for an aneurysm. It is also used for serial documentation of aneurysm size.

Magnetic resonance imaging is comparable to computed tomography without dye or ionizing radiation and suits stable patients with a dye allergy. He has no allergy, and the first step is screening with abdominal ultrasound. Magnetic resonance is the alternative, not the starting test.

C.io: Demonstrate understanding of modified Duke diagnostic criteria.
C.q: Which combination of modified Duke criteria establishes definite infective endocarditis?
opts: One major plus one minor criterion makes endocarditis possible, not definite. To reach definite with only one major criterion, three minor criteria are needed alongside it. Tell: definite is two major, one major plus three minor, or five minor.

Three minor criteria alone make endocarditis possible, not definite. Definite requires five minor criteria, one major plus three minor, or two major. Tell: possible is one major plus one minor or three minor; more criteria are needed to reach definite.

Correct. Definite infective endocarditis is documented by two major criteria, one major plus three minor criteria, or five minor criteria. One major with three minor is the middle of those three combinations, so it establishes a definite diagnosis.

Two minor criteria fall short even of possible, which needs three minor criteria or one major plus one minor. Definite needs five minor, one major plus three minor, or two major. Tell: two minor criteria reach neither threshold.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
C.q: A 27-year-old man admitted with presumed viral myocarditis keeps deteriorating despite full medical treatment. Coronary angiography is normal, and valvular, toxic and ischemic causes of heart failure have been excluded. Which test establishes the diagnosis?
opts: Cardiac angiography rules out coronary ischemia as a cause of new-onset heart failure, and his was already normal. Endomyocardial biopsy is what establishes myocarditis. Tell: repeating the exclusion step adds nothing; the next step is tissue.

Correct. Endomyocardial biopsy is the gold standard and is used to establish the diagnosis once other causes of heart failure are excluded, as his have been. It is recommended in acute deterioration of heart function of unknown origin that is not responding to medical treatment, which describes his course.

The chest X-ray in myocarditis is nonspecific and may only show cardiomegaly. Endomyocardial biopsy is the gold standard that establishes the diagnosis. Tell: a nonspecific film cannot establish a specific diagnosis.

Serum troponin indicates cardiac myonecrosis but does not identify its cause, so it cannot establish myocarditis. Endomyocardial biopsy is the gold standard. Tell: his deterioration despite treatment, with other causes excluded, is the textbook indication for biopsy.

C.io: Identify medical care strategies for cardiomyopathies for the following populations. 8. adolescent 9. adult 10. elderly
C.q: When is hospice referral appropriate in cardiomyopathy?
opts: A diagnosis in adolescence is not a hospice trigger; hospice referral belongs to end-stage cardiomyopathy. Earlier care is rehabilitative: cardiac rehabilitation, education on medications and nutrition, and psychological support. Tell: hospice is tied to the stage of disease, not the age at diagnosis.

Correct. Hospice referral is part of palliative care in end-stage cardiomyopathy. Palliative care also covers symptom management for dyspnea, fatigue and edema, advance care planning, goals-of-care discussions and support for caregivers and family.

A first arrhythmia is not end-stage disease. Hospice referral is reserved for end-stage cardiomyopathy, and palliative care discussions in the elderly come in advanced stages. Tell: hospice follows end-stage disease, not a single event.

Sodium restriction is not a marker of disease stage, and hospice referral is not tied to it. Hospice referral is appropriate in end-stage cardiomyopathy, within palliative care that also covers symptom management and advance care planning. Tell: look for the word end-stage.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
C.q: A 69-year-old man has long-standing constrictive pericarditis with marked edema and ascites despite diuretics. A computed tomography scan shows a thick, heavily calcified pericardium. Which treatment offers definitive relief?
opts: Correct. Long-standing constriction with edema and ascites despite diuretics and a thick, heavily calcified pericardium is established disease, and constrictive pericarditis is often a surgical disease. Pericardiectomy, removal of part or most of the pericardium, gives a 5-year survival of nearly 80% and a 10-year survival of nearly 60%.

Pericardiocentesis drains pericardial fluid, but his problem is a thick, calcified pericardium, not an effusion, so there is nothing to drain. Established constriction is often a surgical disease, treated with pericardiectomy. Tell: fluid is drained; a scarred, calcified sac is removed.

Transplantation is not a listed treatment for constriction. The disease sits in the pericardium, and pericardiectomy, removing part or most of it, is the surgical treatment that improves survival. Tell: remove the scarred sac, not the heart; earlier surgery is associated with better outcomes.

Colchicine with nonsteroidal drugs for 2 to 3 months is a trial for early, hemodynamically stable constriction. His disease is long-standing, refractory to diuretics and heavily calcified, so medical therapy will not give definitive relief. Tell: early and stable means a drug trial; late and calcified means pericardiectomy.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
C.q: What is the first-line treatment for acute, symptomatic, hemodynamically unstable bradycardia?
opts: Amiodarone may be tried for chemical cardioversion of focal atrial tachycardia, a fast rhythm, and is not used to raise a slow rate. Unstable bradycardia is treated with atropine first, then a temporary pacemaker. Tell: amiodarone belongs to the fast-rhythm toolbox; atropine to the slow.

Correct. Acute, symptomatic, hemodynamically unstable bradycardia is treated first with atropine. If it fails, a temporary pacemaker follows; chronic symptomatic bradycardia is managed with a permanent pacemaker, and asymptomatic bradycardia is not treated at all.

Adenosine is used in stable supraventricular tachycardia after a vagal maneuver, to convert the rhythm or slow it enough to reveal P waves. Slowing a heart that is already too slow and causing instability is the opposite of the goal. Tell: adenosine treats fast narrow rhythms; atropine treats unstable slow ones.

A permanent pacemaker is the treatment for chronic, symptomatic bradycardia, not the first step in an acute, unstable episode. The acute sequence is atropine first, then a temporary pacemaker. Tell: acute and unstable means atropine; chronic and symptomatic means a permanent pacemaker.

Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
C.q: A 34-year-old woman has visible, dilated, tortuous veins of the thigh and calf that are tender to palpation, with aching heaviness after prolonged standing. Which is the most common predisposing factor for her condition?
opts: Correct. Her dilated, tortuous, tender thigh and calf veins with aching heaviness after standing describe varicose veins. Among the risk factors, family history is named the most common predisposing factor for unwanted leg veins, ahead of prolonged standing, heavy lifting and pregnancy.

Heavy lifting causes periods of high venous pressure and is a real risk factor for varicose veins, but it is not the most common one. Family history is named the most common predisposing factor, so it outranks lifting even in a patient who lifts.
Women are at higher risk after pregnancy, so a recent pregnancy is a recognized contributor. The question asks for the most common predisposing factor, and that is family history, not pregnancy.

Prolonged standing produces periods of high venous pressure and also brings on her aching, but it is a contributing risk factor rather than the most common one. Family history is named the most common predisposing factor for unwanted leg veins.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
C.q: A 41-year-old man with obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy comes to the emergency department with exertional chest pressure. His electrocardiogram shows left ventricular hypertrophy without acute changes, and a clinician reaches for a chest pain order set. Which medication should be avoided?
opts: Amiodarone is used in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy to reduce the incidence and risk of sudden cardiac death and to convert atrial fibrillation and flutter. It is not the drug to avoid; nitroglycerin is. Tell: the avoided drugs are nitrates and positive inotropes.

Correct. In obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, drugs that reduce preload or afterload, such as nitrates, may increase symptoms by aggravating outflow tract obstruction, so nitroglycerin from a chest pain order set should be avoided if possible. A beta blocker such as metoprolol is the initial medication for his obstruction instead.

Metoprolol, a beta blocker, is the initial medication for outflow tract obstruction; it reduces heart rate and enhances diastolic filling. It is used, not avoided. Tell: the danger in a chest pain order set for this disease is the nitrate.

Verapamil, a nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker, treats outflow tract obstruction as a negative chronotrope and inotrope. The drug to avoid is the nitrate, which reduces preload and afterload. Tell: drugs that slow and soften the heart help; drugs that unload it hurt.

C.q: A 70-year-old woman with pneumonia and severe hypoxia becomes unresponsive. No pulse can be felt, yet the monitor shows a regular, narrow-complex rhythm at 80 with a P wave before every QRS. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: The tracing looks like normal sinus rhythm, but she has no pulse. An organized rhythm you would expect to produce a pulse, without perfusing beats, is pulseless electrical activity, a cardiac arrest. Tell: the pulse check, not the monitor, decides the diagnosis.
ruled out by a stated finding

Asystole is a flat line with no P waves and no QRS complexes. This monitor shows a regular, narrow-complex rhythm with P waves, which without a pulse is pulseless electrical activity. Tell: pulseless electrical activity is not the same as asystole.
ruled out by a stated finding

Ventricular fibrillation is chaotic, uncoordinated activity with no organized QRS complexes. This monitor shows regular, narrow complexes with a P wave before each. Tell: organized complexes rule out fibrillation.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. A regular rhythm at 80 with a P wave before every QRS, which you would expect to produce a pulse, with no pulse is pulseless electrical activity, not asystole. Her severe hypoxia from pneumonia fits one of its two leading causes in adults (hypoxia and hypovolemia), and it is unshockable.

C.q: A 47-year-old woman 5 days after hip surgery has sudden dyspnea, chest pain and a heart rate of 118. Her new electrocardiogram shows a QRS of 0.14 seconds with an rsR' pattern (a second upward deflection) in V1 to V3. Which underlying problem best explains the new conduction finding?
opts: Aortic stenosis is a named cause of left bundle branch block rather than right. Her rsR' pattern in V1 to V3 is right bundle branch block, and its sudden onset after surgery fits pulmonary embolism. Tell: rsR' in V1 means right, which points to the right ventricle.

Lyme carditis is a named cause of atrioventricular blocks rather than right bundle branch block, and nothing here suggests a tick exposure. A sudden new right bundle branch block after surgery fits a pulmonary embolism. Tell: match the cause to the acute postoperative story.

Correct. A QRS of 0.14 seconds with an rsR' pattern in V1 to V3 is right bundle branch block. A sudden increase in right ventricular pressure from a pulmonary embolism is a named cause, and sudden dyspnea, chest pain and a heart rate of 118 five days after hip surgery fit that picture.

An accessory pathway is not among the listed causes of right bundle branch block. Her wide QRS with an rsR' pattern in V1 to V3 (the bunny ears of right bundle branch block) appearing suddenly after surgery fits a pulmonary embolism. Tell: rsR' in V1 means right, and a sudden postoperative onset points to the lungs.

C.q: At what age does aortic dissection usually occur outside Marfan syndrome?
opts: Correct. The stem sets Marfan syndrome aside, and outside that exception aortic dissection usually occurs in the 60s and 70s. Males are affected more than females, a history of hypertension is present in most cases, and the most common predisposing factor is degeneration of medial collagen and elastin.

A dissection in the 20s or 30s is the pattern the stem excludes: Marfan syndrome, the classic medial degeneration, is the stated exception to the usual age. Without it, dissection usually occurs in the 60s and 70s. Young age should make you think of Marfan syndrome, not the typical patient.

Over 90 overshoots the usual window. Outside Marfan syndrome, aortic dissection clusters in the 60s and 70s, typically in a man with a history of hypertension. The incidence figure is a decade band in later adult life, not extreme old age.

A dissection in the 40s or 50s is earlier than the usual pattern once Marfan syndrome is set aside. The typical patient is in the 60s to 70s, male more often than female, and usually has a history of hypertension. Remember the age band and the hypertension history together.

C.q: A 65-year-old woman has new atrial fibrillation at 146 with palpitations. She is alert, her blood pressure is 132/84, and she has no chest pain or breathlessness. Which is the most appropriate initial treatment?
opts: Correct. New atrial fibrillation at 146 is rapid ventricular response, and with a blood pressure of 132/84, a clear mind and no chest pain or breathlessness she is hemodynamically stable. Stable atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response is treated with intravenous rate control, with anticoagulation planned for all.

Synchronized cardioversion is for hemodynamically unstable atrial fibrillation, such as with severe heart failure, hypotension or an acute myocardial infarction. She is alert with a blood pressure of 132/84 and no chest pain or breathlessness. Tell: a fast rate alone is not instability; check blood pressure and symptoms.

Mapping and ablation is a later option in atrial fibrillation management, not the first treatment of a new rapid ventricular response. Her immediate need is to slow the rate with intravenous rate control. Tell: new, fast and stable atrial fibrillation starts with intravenous rate control.

Atropine is first line for acute, symptomatic, unstable bradycardia, a slow rhythm. Her atrial fibrillation is already fast at 146, so raising the rate is the opposite of the goal. Tell: atropine is for slow and unstable; a stable rapid ventricular response needs intravenous rate control.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
D.q: A 63-year-old woman whose hypotension was relieved by pericardiocentesis for a malignant effusion asks about her outlook. Which statement best describes her prognosis?
opts: The amount of fluid removed is not what sets her outlook; for pericardial effusion and tamponade, long-term prognosis depends on the underlying cause, here cancer. A palliative care consult is recommended for malignant effusions to improve outcomes and quality of life. Tell: ask what caused the fluid, not how much there was.
Drainage has cured her for good

Pericardiocentesis is the definitive treatment for the tamponade itself, but a symptomatic malignant effusion often recurs within months, and her long-term outlook rests on the cancer. Recurrent effusions may need a pericardial window. Tell: drainage fixes the acute compression; the cause decides what happens next.
The underlying cancer will drive it

Correct. Her tamponade was promptly relieved, so her short-term outcome is often good, but long-term prognosis depends on the underlying cause. A symptomatic malignant effusion carries a limited life expectancy, a median of 2 to 4 months, often with recurrent effusion in that time, and a palliative care consult is recommended.

Her effusion is malignant, and prognosis for a pericardial effusion depends on the underlying cause, so it cannot be borrowed from other causes. A symptomatic malignant effusion carries a median life expectancy of 2 to 4 months. Tell: the same drainage can lead to very different outlooks because the cause sets the prognosis.

D.q: A 71-year-old man hospitalized for six days with pneumonia develops swelling of the left calf. His team considers using the Wells criteria to estimate his probability of deep vein thrombosis. Which statement about applying the Wells criteria to him is accurate?
opts: A low score replaces all testing

A Wells score sorts the clinical likelihood of deep vein thrombosis into low, moderate or high; it does not stand in for testing. The decisive clue here is his setting: the criteria are used only for outpatients and emergency department patients, not for inpatients like him.
Meant for outpatient or emergency use

Correct. The Wells criteria for deep vein thrombosis (DVT) are used only in the outpatient and emergency department settings, not for inpatients, and the score is less useful in hospitalized patients. He has been in hospital for six days, so the score does not fit his setting.

This reverses the truth: the Wells score is less useful in hospitalized patients and is used only in the outpatient and emergency department settings. Six days in hospital places him in exactly the group it was not designed for.

The Wells items describe the leg, such as calf swelling over 3 cm, swelling of the entire leg and pitting edema confined to the symptomatic leg. The real problem for him is the inpatient setting, since the score is used only for outpatients and emergency department patients.

D.q: A 74-year-old woman has episodes of lightheadedness. Her office electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm at 64, but her family has noticed a slow pulse during the spells. Which is the most appropriate next diagnostic step?
opts: Urgent coronary angiography does not answer the question her case raises, which is whether her spells correlate with episodes of bradycardia. Sinus node ischemia is one cause of sick sinus syndrome, but intermittent slow spells are first captured with a 24-hour ambulatory recording. Tell: intermittent symptoms with a normal office tracing need ambulatory monitoring.

A permanent pacemaker is placed in sick sinus syndrome once symptomatic bradycardia is confirmed, meaning the symptoms correlate with episodes of slow rate. That link has not yet been shown, since her office tracing is normal at 64. Tell: document the slow rate during symptoms before committing to a device.

Correct. An older woman with lightheaded spells, a normal office tracing and a slow pulse during the spells suggests sick sinus syndrome, and the key step is to confirm whether symptoms correlate with episodes of bradycardia. A 24-hour ambulatory recording does that; with correlation a permanent pacemaker follows, without it observation is appropriate.

Observation is appropriate in sick sinus syndrome only if symptoms turn out not to correlate with bradycardia. Her family has noticed a slow pulse during her spells, so that link has to be tested by monitoring before she is reassured. Tell: reassurance comes after monitoring, not instead of it.

D.io: Identify medical care strategies for pericardial disease in the lecture topic list for the following populations. 9. adult 10. elderly
D.q: An 84-year-old woman spent 9 days in the hospital for a large pericardial effusion that needed two procedures. She is now weak and needs help to walk. Besides cardiology and cardiothoracic surgery, which service is most appropriate before she goes home?
opts: Correct. Rehabilitation is listed alongside cardiology and cardiothoracic surgery in the care of older adults with pericardial disease. At 84, weak and needing help to walk after 9 days and two procedures, she fits that need, and older adults also carry higher morbidity and mortality with surgical interventions.

Genetic evaluation is not part of the care of older adults with pericardial disease. The services listed for this group are rehabilitation and cardiology or cardiothoracic surgery, and her new weakness and need for help walking point to rehabilitation. Tell: her problem is function, so choose the service that restores function.

Nothing in her story points to an infection, and the problem to solve before discharge is her weakness and need for help walking. Rehabilitation is the service listed for older adults with pericardial disease, alongside cardiology and cardiothoracic surgery. Tell: pick the service that matches the problem in front of you.

Nothing suggests kidney disease, and her pressing problem is deconditioning: she is weak and needs help to walk after a 9-day stay and two procedures. Rehabilitation is among the services listed for older adults with pericardial disease. Tell: loss of function after a long, procedure-heavy stay calls for rehabilitation.

D.q: A 72-year-old man has fatigue, shortness of breath on exertion and palpitations. His electrocardiogram shows every P wave conducted to a narrow QRS with a constant PR interval of 0.34 seconds. No offending drug or reversible cause is found. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Intravenous magnesium breaks torsades de pointes, a polymorphic ventricular tachycardia; it does nothing for a slow conduction delay. Symptomatic first-degree block with a PR over 0.3 seconds and no reversible cause is treated with a permanent pacemaker. Tell: magnesium is for a long QT, not a long PR.

Correct. His fatigue, shortness of breath and palpitations fit symptomatic first-degree block, and his PR of 0.34 seconds is above the 0.3-second threshold. With no offending drug or reversible cause, a permanent pacemaker is considered for symptomatic patients or a PR greater than 0.3 seconds.

Synchronized cardioversion terminates tachycardias with a pulse. His problem is a conduction delay: a constant PR of 0.34 seconds with every beat conducted to a narrow QRS. A delay like this is paced, not shocked. Tell: a long PR is a pacing problem.

Reassurance fits the asymptomatic majority with first-degree block, but this man has fatigue, exertional dyspnea and palpitations with a PR of 0.34 seconds. Symptoms with a PR above 0.3 seconds make him a candidate for a permanent pacemaker. Tell: symptoms plus a PR over 0.3 change the plan.

D.q: A 72-year-old woman has ischemic rest pain and a nonhealing toe ulcer, with an ankle-brachial index of 0.3. Angiography shows a long femoral-popliteal occlusion. Which treatment is principally used for her degree of disease?
opts: Correct. Rest pain, a nonhealing toe ulcer and an index of 0.3 mean severe critical limb ischemia. A bypass graft, using a saphenous vein or synthetic graft to bypass the diseased segment, here a long femoral-popliteal occlusion, is principally used to treat severe critical leg ischemia and is highly effective.

Exercise therapy improves walking distance in claudication, but her rest pain, nonhealing ulcer and index of 0.3 mean critical limb ischemia. The treatment principally used for that degree of disease is a bypass graft. Exercise alone cannot heal tissue loss.

Pentoxifylline is a xanthine derivative that helps blood flow through narrowed arteries in chronic disease. It cannot rescue a limb with rest pain, an ulcer and a long occlusion. Bypass grafting is the principal treatment for severe critical leg ischemia.

Intravenous heparin is the medical therapy for acute peripheral arterial occlusion. Her chronic critical limb ischemia with a long femoral-popliteal occlusion is principally treated with a bypass graft. Anticoagulation alone does not restore flow past a long occlusion.

D.q: What does gadolinium add to magnetic resonance imaging in suspected myocarditis?
opts: Magnetic resonance imaging cannot grow or identify a virus. Gadolinium improves the visibility and extent of inflammation, and the tissue diagnosis comes from endomyocardial biopsy, the gold standard. Tell: imaging shows where and how much inflammation; biopsy establishes the diagnosis.

Troponin is a serum blood test, the indicator of cardiac myonecrosis, and is not measured by imaging. Gadolinium improves the visibility and extent of inflammation on magnetic resonance imaging. Tell: necrosis is measured in blood; inflammation is shown on enhanced imaging.

Ruling out coronary disease is the job of cardiac angiography, which excludes coronary ischemia as a cause of new-onset heart failure. Gadolinium in magnetic resonance imaging improves the visibility of inflammation and its extent. Tell: angiography looks at the coronaries; gadolinium imaging looks at inflamed muscle.

Correct. In suspected myocarditis, gadolinium-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) improves the visibility of inflammation and shows its extent in the myocardium. It sits in the work-up beside troponin, the electrocardiogram, echo and angiography, with endomyocardial biopsy as the gold standard.

D.q: A 70-year-old woman has Mobitz type II block found on a routine tracing; she has no symptoms. Her family prefers to avoid procedures. Which approach should be avoided?
opts: A permanent pacemaker is the definitive treatment for Mobitz type II, so it is the approach to pursue, not avoid. Observation alone is what should be avoided. Tell: the question asks which option is unsafe.

Referral to cardiology is appropriate, since a permanent pacemaker is the definitive treatment. The approach to avoid is simple observation of Mobitz type II, which is dangerous even without symptoms. Tell: referral moves toward the right treatment, so it is not the one to avoid.

Correct. Observation without pacing should be avoided: Mobitz type II is considered dangerous even without symptoms because of its unpredictable progression to complete block and poor prognosis, with a higher risk of sudden cardiac death. The definitive treatment is a permanent pacemaker, even for a symptom-free patient.

Reviewing her medication list is reasonable and harmless. What should be avoided is observation without a pacemaker, because Mobitz type II is dangerous even without symptoms. Tell: the question asks which step to avoid, and a safe, sensible step never fits that.

D.q: A 26-year-old woman with obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is leaving for a summer hiking trip in a hot climate. She takes a beta blocker and asks how to lower her risk of symptoms while away. Which counseling point is most appropriate?
opts: Correct. Patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy are advised to maintain hydration and avoid dehydration, which matters on a hot-weather hiking trip. The same education covers avoiding excess alcohol and keeping to mild to moderate, noncompetitive recreational activity.
Restrict fluids to soften the murmur

Fluid restriction contradicts the advice to maintain hydration and avoid dehydration, and softening the murmur is not a goal of self-care. Tell: a hot-climate trip makes hydration the key counseling point, along with avoiding excess alcohol.
Use alcohol to relax at the campsite

Patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy are taught to avoid excess alcohol consumption, alongside maintaining hydration. Using alcohol to relax at camp contradicts that advice. Tell: in this disease alcohol appears only on the avoid list.
Take extra diuretic on hot days

Extra diuretic in the heat runs straight against the advice to maintain hydration and avoid dehydration. Tell: in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, anything that dries the patient out works against the self-care she has been taught, which also includes avoiding excess alcohol.

D.q: An 80-year-old man is brought in dizzy and confused, with a blood pressure of 78/44. His electrocardiogram shows P waves at 76 and wide QRS complexes at 32, with no relationship between them. Which is the most appropriate emergent treatment?
opts: A permanent pacemaker is the definitive treatment for complete block, but this man is confused with a blood pressure of 78/44, so he needs emergent transcutaneous pacing first. Tell: 'emergent' points to the temporary bridge, not the permanent device.

Correct. P waves at 76 and wide QRS complexes at 32 with no relationship are third-degree (complete) block. His confusion and blood pressure of 78/44 call for emergent treatment: atropine or epinephrine, both controversial, or transcutaneous pacing, followed definitively by a permanent pacemaker.

Intravenous amiodarone treats ventricular tachycardia, a fast wide rhythm. His wide complexes at 32 are a slow escape rhythm from complete block, which needs transcutaneous pacing. Tell: a slow wide rhythm is an escape rhythm, not tachycardia.

Synchronized cardioversion shocks an unstable tachycardia; this is a slow escape rhythm at 32 from complete block. An unstable patient with complete block needs transcutaneous pacing. Tell: pace the slow, shock the fast.

D.q: A 70-year-old woman with heart failure is admitted with a tender, swollen left calf, and duplex ultrasound confirms deep vein thrombosis. Her daughter asks why heart failure raises the risk of a clot. Which Virchow triad component should the clinician name?
opts: An elevated platelet count is not one of the three Virchow components, which are venous stasis, a hypercoagulable state and endothelial injury. Heart failure is placed under venous stasis, the component of altered blood flow.

A hypercoagulable state is a clotting tendency, inherited (factor V Leiden, protein C or S deficiency) or acquired (cancer, estrogen, pregnancy). Heart failure is grouped instead with immobilization and venous insufficiency under venous stasis, the altered blood flow component.

Correct. Heart failure is listed under venous stasis, the Virchow triad component of altered blood flow, alongside immobilization and venous insufficiency. Her heart failure raises clot risk through stasis; it is neither an injury to the vein wall nor an inherited or acquired clotting tendency.
Endothelial injury comes from trauma, surgery, intravenous drug use or burns. Heart failure does not damage the vessel lining; it is listed under venous stasis, the component of altered blood flow.
