D.q: A 19-year-old woman with a week of fever and myalgia now has severe breathlessness. She is cold and clammy with a blood pressure of 78/50, heart rate 128, raised jugular venous pressure and crackles throughout both lungs. Myocarditis is suspected. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Endomyocardial biopsy is the gold standard, but it is used once other causes of heart failure are excluded and is not done before support in a patient this unstable. Aggressive hemodynamic stabilization comes first. Tell: diagnosis can follow; her blood pressure of 78/50 cannot wait.

Correct. She is hypotensive at 78/50, tachycardic, cold and clammy with raised jugular venous pressure and crackles, a patient in shock. Supportive care is the mainstay of myocarditis treatment, directed toward the clinical scenario, and this scenario requires aggressive hemodynamic stabilization first.

Outpatient follow-up is unsafe for a patient with a blood pressure of 78/50, a heart rate of 128 and pulmonary crackles. Treatment is directed toward the clinical scenario and may require aggressive hemodynamic stabilization, which comes first. Tell: hypotension and cold, clammy skin rule out sending her home.

Exercise testing does not belong in the care of a patient with a blood pressure of 78/50 and crackles throughout both lungs. Myocarditis treatment is directed toward the clinical scenario, and hers calls for aggressive hemodynamic stabilization. Tell: an unstable patient is stabilized before any grading.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. D.q: An 81-year-old man has known tachy-brady syndrome (a fast rhythm alternating with slow rates and pauses) and asks which fast rhythm is behind his palpitations. An ambulatory monitor is arranged. Which rhythm is it most likely to record during the fast episodes?
opts: Atrial flutter is an organized atrial rhythm with sawtooth waves at an atrial rate of 250 or more, but it is not the named most-common fast rhythm of tachy-brady syndrome. That is atrial fibrillation. Tell: in tachy-brady syndrome, expect an irregularly irregular fast phase, not a regular sawtooth.

Correct. In tachy-brady syndrome, the form of sick sinus syndrome in which a fast rhythm alternates with slow rates or pauses, the tachyarrhythmia is most commonly atrial fibrillation. During his fast episodes the monitor would most likely show an irregularly irregular rhythm without P waves.

A junctional rhythm is a slow, regular rhythm usually at 40 to 60 with inverted or hidden P waves, and it can follow sinus arrest. It could appear in his slow phases, not his fast ones. Tell: junctional rhythm belongs to the brady side; atrial fibrillation is the usual tachy side.

Ventricular tachycardia can be the fast rhythm in some patients with tachy-brady syndrome, who then need a permanent pacemaker with an implantable defibrillator. It is not the most common one; atrial fibrillation is. Tell: ventricular tachycardia changes the device, not the most likely rhythm.

D.io: Discuss indications and antibiotic regimens for subacute bacterial endocarditis prophylaxis.
D.q: A 63-year-old man with a prosthetic aortic valve is having a tooth extracted tomorrow. He has no drug allergies and takes pills without difficulty. Which prophylaxis is most appropriate?
opts: Correct. His prosthetic aortic valve is on the list of conditions for which prophylaxis is reasonable, and a tooth extraction manipulates the gums and roots of the teeth. With no allergy and no trouble swallowing, the regimen is a single dose of oral amoxicillin 2 g 30-60 minutes before the procedure.

Prophylaxis is indicated. Prosthetic cardiac valves are on the list of qualifying conditions, and an extraction is a dental procedure that manipulates the gums or roots of the teeth. Tell: no prophylaxis fits procedures like dental radiographs or orthodontic adjustments, not an extraction.
ruled out by a stated finding

Clindamycin is no longer recommended for endocarditis prophylaxis because of the risk of Clostridioides difficile infection. He has no allergy and can take pills, so oral amoxicillin is the standard. Tell: clindamycin is never the answer in the current regimen.

Prophylaxis is a single dose given 30-60 minutes before the procedure, not a week of antibiotics afterward. The drug is right, but the timing and duration are wrong. Tell: a correct prophylactic regimen is one dose, given before.

D.q: A 58-year-old woman has a slow sinus rhythm at 38 six hours after an inferior myocardial infarction. She feels faint and her blood pressure is 80/50. Each narrow QRS has a normal P wave before it. Which drug should be given first?
opts: Metoprolol is a beta blocker, and beta blockers are a listed cause of sinus bradycardia, so it would slow her further at a rate of 38. Beta blockers are used for fast rhythms, such as rate control in stable atrial flutter. Tell: a hypotensive, faint patient with a slow sinus rate needs atropine, not a rate-slowing drug.

Diltiazem is a nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker, a class listed with beta blockers and digoxin as a drug cause of sinus bradycardia. Giving it at a rate of 38 with a blood pressure of 80/50 would deepen the problem. Tell: drugs that cause bradycardia never rescue it; atropine does.

Adenosine is used in stable supraventricular tachycardia after a vagal maneuver, to convert the rhythm or slow it enough to reveal P waves. Slowing a sinus rhythm already at 38 is the opposite of what she needs. Tell: adenosine is for a fast narrow rhythm; unstable sinus bradycardia gets atropine.

Correct. A sinus rhythm at 38 with a normal P wave before each narrow QRS, faintness and a blood pressure of 80/50 is acute, symptomatic, hemodynamically unstable sinus bradycardia; sinus node ischemia is a listed cause, fitting the infarction. Atropine is first line, followed by a temporary pacemaker if it fails.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
D.q: A 69-year-old woman with long-standing hypertension has a preoperative 12-lead electrocardiogram, which is shown. The QRS lasts 0.16 seconds. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Ventricular tachycardia is a regular wide rhythm at 100 to 250 with no P waves. This preoperative tracing shows wide complexes at a normal rate with a deep S wave in V1, the pattern of a bundle branch block. Tell: wide at a normal rate means slowed conduction, not tachycardia.

This tracing does not show a pre-excitation pattern; its deep, dominant S waves in V1 and broad, upright lateral complexes are a bundle branch block. Tell: a QRS over 0.12 seconds with a deep S in V1 and no lateral Q waves is left bundle branch block.

Right bundle branch block gives an rsR' pattern ('bunny ears') in V1 to V3 and a slurred S wave in I and aVL. Here V1 to V3 are deep and downward. Tell: bunny ears in V1 mean right; a deep S in V1 means left.

Correct. A QRS of 0.16 seconds with a deep, dominant S wave in V1 (rS pattern) and broad, upright, monophasic lateral complexes without Q waves in I, V5 and V6 is left bundle branch block. Chronic hypertension, her long-standing condition, is a named cause.
D.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram with wide complexes, deep downward complexes in V1 to V3 and broad upright complexes in the lateral leads

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
D.q: A 74-year-old man with diabetes is told his new palpitations come from atrial fibrillation. Which description best fits his electrocardiogram?
opts: Irregular, with three or more P-wave shapes

Irregular beats with three or more P-wave shapes in the same lead describe multifocal atrial tachycardia, from multiple atrial foci, with one P wave per QRS. Atrial fibrillation has no P waves to count. Tell: in an irregular rhythm, changing P shapes mean multifocal; absent P waves mean fibrillation.
Regular, with a P wave before each beat

A regular rhythm with a uniform P wave before each QRS describes a sinus rhythm, such as sinus tachycardia. Atrial fibrillation has absent P waves and is irregularly irregular. Tell: regularity with a P wave before every beat rules atrial fibrillation out.
Irregularly irregular, with no P waves

Correct. Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular with absent P waves and no PR interval, and the QRS stays narrow. The rate is often 110 to 160 but can be under 80 or over 200, and diabetes, as in this man, is one of the conditions in which it is commonly seen.
Regular, with sawtooth waves between beats

Regular sawtooth waves between beats describe atrial flutter, in which the atria fire at 250 or more and the node blocks some impulses, most often 2:1. Atrial fibrillation has no organized atrial waves and an irregularly irregular rhythm. Tell: organized sawtooth means flutter; no P waves and no regularity mean fibrillation.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following arterial occlusive disease and aortic aneurysm: 2. Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
D.q: A 71-year-old man's asymptomatic abdominal aortic aneurysm measured 4.1 cm six months ago and now measures 4.8 cm. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Imaging every 6 to 12 months is the surveillance plan for a 4.0 to 5.4 cm aneurysm that is not growing rapidly. His grew 0.7 cm in six months, beyond the 0.5 cm rapid-growth threshold that calls for repair. The growth rate overrides the size-based interval.

Three-yearly ultrasound is for aneurysms of 3.0 to 3.9 cm. His is 4.8 cm and grew 0.7 cm in six months, which exceeds the 0.5 cm rapid-growth criterion for repair. Both size and growth rule out the longest interval.

Correct. Evidence of rapid growth, 0.5 cm in six months, means the aneurysm should be repaired. His grew from 4.1 to 4.8 cm, a 0.7 cm increase in six months, so repair is indicated even though 4.8 cm is below the size thresholds of 5.0 cm in women and over 5.5 cm in men.

Size is only one trigger; rapid growth is another. His aneurysm grew 0.7 cm in six months, more than the 0.5 cm in six months that defines rapid growth, so it should be repaired now. Waiting for 5.5 cm ignores the growth criterion.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
D.q: A 59-year-old man is on day 6 of antibiotics for aortic valve endocarditis. He still has fevers, and today's electrocardiogram shows a new conduction block not present on admission. Which complication best explains the new conduction abnormality?
opts: Rupture of the chordae tendineae causes a new murmur from valvular damage and can lead to heart failure, but it does not interrupt the conduction system. Tell: a new conduction block points to an abscess extending into the upper ventricular septum, not to a chordal problem.

Correct. Persistent fever on day 6 with a new conduction block suggests a perivalvular abscess, meaning infection that extends beyond the valve leaflets into myocardial tissue. When the abscess extends into the upper ventricular septum, it interrupts the conduction system.

Extension of an abscess into the epicardium causes pericarditis, not a conduction block. Conduction is interrupted when the abscess extends into the upper ventricular septum instead. Tell: epicardium means pericarditis; upper septum means heart block.

Septic emboli to the lungs would cause lung findings, not a new conduction block on the electrocardiogram. A block appearing during treatment points to a perivalvular abscess extending into the upper ventricular septum. Tell: an electrical change localizes the problem to the septum, not the lungs.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
D.q: A 72-year-old woman has 6 weeks of aching and stiffness in her shoulders and hips, fatigue and a low-grade fever. Her erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein are high, but no murmur is heard and three sets of blood cultures are negative. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. Six weeks of shoulder and hip aching and stiffness, fatigue, low-grade fever and a high erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein fit polymyalgia rheumatica, which mimics endocarditis through myalgia and elevated inflammatory markers. The absent murmur and three negative culture sets argue against endocarditis.

Atrial myxoma mimics endocarditis with fever and a new murmur, such as a tumor plop or mid-diastolic rumble. She has no murmur at all. Tell: a myxoma announces itself with a new murmur; girdle aching with high inflammatory markers points to polymyalgia rheumatica.
ruled out by a stated finding

Antiphospholipid syndrome mimics endocarditis through thromboemboli and cardiac valve disease. She has neither, only shoulder and hip aching with high inflammatory markers. Tell: clots and valve lesions suggest antiphospholipid syndrome; proximal myalgia with elevated markers suggests polymyalgia rheumatica.

Subacute endocarditis would be supported by a new murmur and positive blood cultures; she has no murmur and three negative culture sets. Without positive cultures or echocardiographic evidence she meets no major Duke criterion. Tell: proximal stiffness with high inflammatory markers and clean cultures points away from endocarditis.
ruled out by a stated finding

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following arterial occlusive disease and aortic aneurysm: 2. Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
D.q: A 68-year-old man with hypertension and an acute dissection has had his systolic pressure lowered to 110 mmHg and his pain controlled. Which definitive treatment removes the diseased segment?
opts: Carotid endarterectomy removes plaque from the carotid artery and is the gold standard for high-grade carotid stenosis. A dissected aorta is repaired by grafting and replacing the diseased portion. The procedure must match the vessel and the lesion.

Correct. With his systolic pressure at 110 mmHg, inside the 100 to 120 mmHg target, and his pain controlled, the definitive step is surgery: grafting and replacing the diseased portion of the aorta. Blood pressure reduction stops progression, but only the graft removes the diseased segment.

Catheter-directed thrombolysis dissolves arterial clot in acute limb ischemia of under 14 days. A dissection is a torn aortic wall, not a clot, and is definitively treated by grafting and replacing the diseased aorta. Lysis has no role in a dissection.

Ultrasound-guided thrombin injection seals the leak of a pseudoaneurysm by promoting clot. A dissection needs the diseased aorta surgically grafted and replaced. Thrombin treats a small cavity outside an artery, not a dissected aorta.
D.cite: Arterial Occlusive Diseaase and Aneurysms - Carter.pptx, Slide 118

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
D.q: A 24-year-old marathon runner has an electrocardiogram at a sports physical. He has no symptoms. The PR interval grows longer with each beat until one P wave is not followed by a QRS complex, and then the cycle repeats. The QRS complexes are narrow. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Mobitz type II drops QRS complexes without warning while the PR stays constant. Here the PR lengthens before each drop in a repeating cycle, which marks Mobitz type I. Tell: a lengthening PR before the drop is type I; a constant PR is type II.

Correct. A PR interval that grows longer with each beat until a P wave is not conducted, then repeats, with narrow QRS complexes, is Mobitz type I (Wenckebach) block. In a symptom-free marathon runner, increased vagal tone from an overreactive vagus nerve is a named cause, and the block needs no treatment.
First-degree block has a long but constant PR and never drops a beat. Here the PR changes from beat to beat and a P wave fails to conduct. Tell: any dropped beat moves the rhythm beyond first degree.

Complete block has no relationship between P waves and QRS complexes, with two separate rates. Here the PR changes in an orderly, repeating pattern tied to each drop. Tell: a predictable PR pattern means the atria and ventricles are still linked.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following arterial occlusive disease and aortic aneurysm: 2. Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
D.q: A 70-year-old man who had a large anterior myocardial infarction three weeks ago develops sudden pain and coldness of his right leg with absent foot pulses. Which cardiac finding is the most likely embolic source?
opts: Valve calcification is not a named embolic source. After his large myocardial infarction three weeks ago, a left ventricular thrombus is the classic origin of an embolus to the leg. The heart is the source in 80 to 90% of cases, through clot rather than calcium.

Fluid around the heart is not an embolic source. The cardiac sources named for limb emboli are atrial fibrillation and left ventricular thrombus after a myocardial infarction. His recent large infarction points to a ventricular clot.

Correct. Thromboemboli are the most common emboli in acute limb ischemia, and the heart is the source in 80 to 90% of cases, for example atrial fibrillation or a left ventricular thrombus after a myocardial infarction. His large anterior infarction three weeks ago makes a ventricular thrombus the likely source.

A septal scar is not a recognized embolic source here. After a myocardial infarction, a left ventricular thrombus can dislodge, travel distally and occlude a smaller artery. His three-week-old anterior infarction makes the ventricle the likely source.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
D.q: A 64-year-old woman with dilated cardiomyopathy has breathlessness on exertion and peripheral edema. On examination her neck veins distend when firm pressure is held over her right upper abdomen, a sign called hepatojugular reflux (neck-vein distension with firm pressure over the liver). Which additional finding is expected with this degree of congestion?
opts: A pulsatile mass in the epigastrium

A pulsatile epigastric mass is not among the congestive findings. With hepatojugular reflux, the expected gastrointestinal findings of dilated cardiomyopathy are congestive hepatomegaly and ascites. Tell: venous congestion enlarges the liver and fills the abdomen with fluid; it does not create a pulsating mass.

Flank bruising has nothing to do with venous congestion. Dilated cardiomyopathy with hepatojugular reflux is expected to show congestive hepatomegaly and ascites, along with dependent pitting edema. Tell: congestion causes swelling and enlargement, not bruising.

Correct. Alongside hepatojugular reflux, the gastrointestinal findings of dilated cardiomyopathy include congestive hepatomegaly and ascites. They reflect venous congestion, which also gives jugular vein distention, an enlarged liver and spleen, and dependent pitting edema like hers.

A small liver is the opposite of what congestion does: in dilated cardiomyopathy the gastrointestinal findings are congestive hepatomegaly, hepatojugular reflux and ascites, with the liver and spleen enlarged from venous congestion. Tell: hepatojugular reflux and an enlarged liver travel together.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
D.q: A 62-year-old woman treated for breast cancer 2 years ago has 3 weeks of fatigue and exertional dyspnea. Her blood pressure is 128/80 without hypotension. The chest radiograph shows an enlarged, water-bottle (globular) cardiac silhouette with clear lung fields. Which test is required to confirm a pericardial effusion?
opts: Coronary angiography is not part of the initial workup of a suspected effusion and does not confirm one; confirmation requires an echocardiogram. The workup pairs history, examination, electrocardiogram, chest radiograph and basic labs with transthoracic echocardiography. Tell: the confirming test must image the pericardial space.

Her radiograph already suggests an effusion, and a second film adds nothing: a chest radiograph can suggest a pericardial effusion but cannot confirm it. An echocardiogram is required for confirmation. Tell: separate the suggestive tests (examination, electrocardiogram, radiograph) from the confirming one (echocardiogram).

Correct. Her breast cancer history, 3 weeks of fatigue and dyspnea, and a globular silhouette with clear lungs suggest an effusion, but clinical evaluation, electrocardiogram and chest radiograph can only suggest it. An echocardiogram is required to confirm a pericardial effusion, and transthoracic echocardiography is part of the initial workup.

An electrocardiogram belongs in the initial workup and may suggest an effusion, but like the chest radiograph it cannot confirm one. Confirmation requires an echocardiogram. Tell: the electrocardiogram and radiograph raise the suspicion; the echocardiogram settles it.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
D.q: A 35-year-old man who recently moved from a region where tuberculosis is common has effusive pericarditis. Pericardial fluid is positive on acid-fast stain. Which treatment may significantly reduce his progression to constriction?
opts: Anti-inflammatory drugs alone leave the tuberculosis untreated, and it is treatment of the tuberculosis that may significantly reduce progression to constriction. Nonsteroidal drugs with colchicine are a time-limited 2 to 3 month trial for early, stable constriction, not an indefinite plan. Tell: when the cause is known and treatable, treat the cause.

Correct. He comes from a region where tuberculosis is common and his pericardial fluid is positive on acid-fast stain, so tuberculosis is the underlying etiology. When tuberculosis is the cause, treating it may significantly reduce progression to constrictive pericarditis.

Pericardiectomy, removal of part or most of the pericardium, treats constriction once it is established; he has effusive pericarditis, not constriction yet. Treating the tuberculosis is what may significantly reduce progression to constriction. Tell: the question asks how to prevent constriction, not how to remove a constricted pericardium.

Diuretics relieve fluid overload in constriction but leave the infection untreated, so they cannot change its course. In tuberculous pericarditis, antituberculous treatment may significantly reduce progression to constriction. Tell: diuretics treat congestion; only treating the cause changes the course.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
D.q: A 58-year-old woman received mediastinal radiation and chemotherapy for a chest cancer 15 years ago. She now has progressive exercise intolerance, orthopnea (breathlessness lying flat), ascites and swollen legs. Echocardiogram shows stiff ventricles of normal size, marked atrial enlargement and abnormal diastolic function with a preserved ejection fraction. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Acute myocarditis does not fit a slow course years after cancer treatment. Mediastinal radiation and chemotherapy are named causes of restrictive cardiomyopathy, which often presents at an advanced stage with pronounced cardiopulmonary symptoms. Tell: a remote treatment history plus stiff ventricles points to restriction.

Dilated cardiomyopathy would show dilated ventricles, but hers are normal in size with a preserved ejection fraction. Her stiff ventricles, marked atrial enlargement and abnormal diastolic function after mediastinal radiation and chemotherapy fit restrictive cardiomyopathy. Tell: normal-sized ventricles plus big atria means restrictive.

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is not linked to radiation or chemotherapy, and her picture is stiff ventricles of normal size with big atria. Treatment-related cardiotoxicity, through inflammation and fibrosis, causes restrictive cardiomyopathy. Tell: prior mediastinal radiation and chemotherapy is the named restrictive clue.

Correct. Mediastinal radiation and chemotherapy are treatment-related causes of restrictive cardiomyopathy, with chemotherapy leading to inflammation, then fibrosis and restriction. These patients may have a prior history of radiation or chemotherapy and often present at an advanced stage, as she does with stiff ventricles and big atria.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
D.q: A 61-year-old man with a long QT has recurrent runs of torsades de pointes (QRS complexes that twist around the baseline). Between runs he is alert, with a pulse and a normal blood pressure. Which is the first treatment?
opts: Procainamide prolongs the QT and is avoided in torsades de pointes, like amiodarone. The first treatment in a conscious patient is intravenous magnesium. Tell: torsades is treated with magnesium, never with a drug that lengthens the QT.

Metoprolol is avoided in torsades de pointes: beta blockers cause bradycardia, lengthening the R-to-R interval and indirectly prolonging the QT. Intravenous magnesium is the first treatment. Tell: slowing the heart worsens torsades.
Amiodarone prolongs the QT and is avoided in torsades de pointes. In an alert patient with a pulse, intravenous magnesium comes first. Tell: drugs that lengthen the QT are off the table in torsades.

Correct. Between runs he is alert with a pulse and a normal blood pressure, so his torsades de pointes is treated with intravenous magnesium to break it, followed by more magnesium as an infusion. Amiodarone, procainamide and beta blockers are avoided; lidocaine is the one antiarrhythmic that can be used.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
D.q: Which causes should be checked first in a patient with frequent premature ventricular contractions?
opts: Hyperlipidemia and obesity are not on the list of causes of premature ventricular contractions. The listed causes are hypoxemia and electrolyte imbalance (low potassium, low magnesium, high calcium), plus alcohol, caffeine and stimulants. Tell: choose the causes that can be measured and corrected at the bedside.

Hypertension and diabetes are not among the listed causes of premature ventricular contractions; they feed the degenerative conduction disease behind heart block. Frequent premature beats call first for checks of what is fixable now: oxygenation and potassium, magnesium and calcium.

Dehydration and fever are not on the list of causes of premature ventricular contractions. The named causes are hypoxemia and electrolyte imbalance, plus alcohol, caffeine and stimulants. Tell: the first checks are an oxygen level and an electrolyte panel, not a volume or temperature workup.

Correct. Frequent premature ventricular contractions should prompt a search for their named causes: hypoxemia and electrolyte imbalance (hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypercalcemia). These beats occur with or without structural heart disease, and alcohol, caffeine and stimulants are other triggers to ask about.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
D.q: Where are patients with Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy admitted?
opts: No surgical treatment is part of the plan; diagnosis is by cardiac catheterization, and treatment is empiric and supportive, with beta blockers, anticoagulation for a left ventricular thrombus or diuretics for heart failure. Admission is to cardiology. Tell: catheterization and acute coronary syndrome protocols belong to cardiology.

Correct. Takotsubo cardiomyopathy mimics acute coronary syndrome with no initial reliable differences, so evaluation and treatment follow established acute coronary syndrome protocols and the patient is admitted to cardiology. Care is then empiric and supportive, and most patients completely recover.

Sending the patient home ignores that troponin is usually elevated, the electrocardiogram shows ST elevation and the picture cannot be told from acute coronary syndrome early on. Patients are admitted to cardiology. Tell: anything managed by acute coronary syndrome protocols is admitted.

Psychiatric admission misses the cardiac problem: the patient has elevated troponin, ST changes and wall-motion abnormalities that mimic acute coronary syndrome, so admission is to cardiology. Tell: until catheterization shows normal coronary arteries, this is treated as acute coronary syndrome.

D.io: Identify medical care strategies for ventricular dysrhythmias for the following populations. 3. adult 4. elderly
D.q: An 82-year-old woman has an electrocardiogram at a routine visit and has no symptoms. The rhythm is regular at 70, every P wave is followed by a narrow QRS, and the PR interval is a constant 0.26 seconds. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. A regular rhythm with every P wave followed by a narrow QRS and a constant PR of 0.26 seconds (over 0.20) is first-degree atrioventricular block. The vast majority cause no symptoms, and at 82 the most common cause, age-related degeneration of the conduction system, fits; no treatment is needed.

Mobitz type II has a constant PR, usually in the normal range, with randomly dropped QRS complexes. Every one of her P waves is followed by a QRS, and her PR of 0.26 seconds is long. Tell: no dropped beats means no second-degree block.
ruled out by a stated finding
Mobitz type I lengthens the PR progressively until a QRS drops. Her PR is long but constant at 0.26 seconds, and every P wave conducts. Tell: a constant PR with no drops is first degree.
ruled out by a stated finding

Third-degree block shows P waves with no relationship to the QRS complexes and a ventricular rate usually under 40. She conducts every P wave at a rate of 70. Tell: a fixed PR before every QRS rules out complete block.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
D.q: How is hemodynamically stable atrial flutter treated first?
opts: Catheter ablation is the definitive management of atrial flutter, which has a substantial recurrence rate, but it is not the first step for a stable patient. Stable flutter starts with rate control using a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker. Tell: the first step is rate control; ablation is the definitive end point.

Repeated adenosine belongs to the sequence for stable supraventricular tachycardia after a vagal maneuver, not to the listed treatment of atrial flutter. Stable flutter is rate controlled with a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker. Tell: flutter has its own sequence, rate control if stable and synchronized cardioversion if unstable.

Synchronized cardioversion is for hemodynamically unstable atrial flutter, and an elective outpatient cardioversion comes only after 21 days of anticoagulation. The question specifies a stable patient, who starts with rate control. Tell: stable flutter gets a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker first; unstable flutter gets the shock.

Correct. Hemodynamically stable atrial flutter is treated first with rate control using a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker, while an unstable patient gets synchronized cardioversion. Rate control is harder to achieve in flutter than in atrial fibrillation, and anticoagulation is part of management.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
D.q: A 52-year-old man has an electrocardiogram before a dental procedure. Among normal sinus beats at 74 is an occasional early, narrow QRS preceded by a P wave that is inverted in II, III and aVF, with a PR interval under 0.12 seconds. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: A premature ventricular contraction begins in the ventricles and is early, wide and bizarre with no P wave. This early beat is narrow and carries an inverted P wave with a short PR. Tell: a narrow early beat with a P wave is supraventricular; a wide, bizarre one without a P wave is ventricular.
ruled out by a stated finding

A premature atrial contraction begins in the atria and shows an early, abnormally shaped P wave before a narrow QRS. A P wave inverted in II, III and aVF with a PR under 0.12 seconds is the junctional pattern instead. Tell: inversion in II, III and aVF with a short PR places the early beat in the junction, not the atria.

Wolff-Parkinson-White shows pre-excitation, a short PR interval with a slurred QRS upstroke (delta wave), on tracings in normal sinus rhythm. Here the sinus beats are normal and only the occasional early beat has a short PR, with an inverted P wave. Tell: pre-excitation marks the sinus beats; a junctional premature beat is a one-off.

Correct. An occasional early, narrow QRS whose P wave is inverted in II, III and aVF with a PR under 0.12 seconds comes from the atrioventricular junction: a premature junctional contraction. When the top of the node fires first, the atria beat before the ventricles and the PR is short; most people with these beats have no symptoms.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
D.q: From which point is the typical 4-6 week course of antibiotics for infective endocarditis counted?
opts: Correct. Antibiotic therapy must be bactericidal and prolonged, typically 4-6 weeks counted from the first NEGATIVE blood culture. All bacteria in the vegetation must be killed, so the count begins only once cultures have turned negative.

The first positive culture marks the diagnosis, not the start of the count. Therapy runs typically 4-6 weeks from the first negative blood culture, so days of persistent bacteremia do not count toward the course. Tell: the clock starts at culture clearance, not at diagnosis.

Fever resolution is not the anchor for the course. The typical 4-6 weeks of bactericidal, parenteral therapy are counted from the first negative blood culture. Tell: the marker is microbiologic (a negative culture), not clinical (the fever breaking).

Admission day is not the anchor. The typical 4-6 week bactericidal course is counted from the first negative blood culture, which may come days after admission. Tell: the count starts when cultures clear, not when the patient arrives.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
D.q: A 26-year-old man has a sudden, regular narrow complex tachycardia at 230 with retrograde (inverted) P waves. An electrocardiogram taken last year in normal sinus rhythm showed a short PR interval and a delta wave (a slurred QRS upstroke). Which diagnosis is most likely?
opts: Sinus tachycardia is regular at over 100 to 160 with a uniform P wave before every QRS, driven by a physiologic or pathologic process. A sudden rate of 230 with retrograde P waves is beyond that range and points to reentry. Tell: retrograde P waves and a rate over 200 do not come from the sinus node.
ruled out by a stated finding

Nodal reentrant tachycardia is a circuit within the atrioventricular node, usually at 140 to 180 with hidden P waves. It needs no accessory pathway, so it does not explain the short PR and delta wave on his sinus tracing. Tell: prior pre-excitation plus a rate above 200 points to accessory pathway reentry rather than nodal reentry.

Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular with absent P waves, the exception among supraventricular tachycardias, which are otherwise regular. His rhythm is regular with retrograde P waves, and his prior pre-excitation points to an accessory pathway. Tell: regular with retrograde P waves after pre-excitation is atrioventricular reentry.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Pre-excitation, a short PR interval and delta wave, on last year's tracing in normal sinus rhythm points to an accessory pathway (bundle of Kent) and the potential for atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia. That rhythm is regular and narrow, above 100 and usually 200 to 300, with hidden or retrograde P waves, matching his rate of 230.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
D.q: What is the first-line treatment for stable supraventricular tachycardia?
opts: Immediate synchronized cardioversion, a timed shock at decreased voltage, is for hemodynamically unstable supraventricular tachycardia, the less common presentation. A stable patient starts with a vagal maneuver. Tell: the word stable points to the vagal maneuver; unstable points to the shock.

Adenosine is the second step in stable supraventricular tachycardia, used if a vagal maneuver fails, and it may be repeated once. It may convert the rhythm to normal sinus rhythm or slow it enough to reveal P waves. Tell: first line means before any drug, which is the vagal maneuver.

Intravenous procainamide is used when Wolff-Parkinson-White is known or adenosine reveals atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White, the setting in which adenosine must never be used. Ordinary stable supraventricular tachycardia starts with a vagal maneuver. Tell: procainamide answers pre-excited atrial fibrillation, not routine supraventricular tachycardia.

Correct. Stable supraventricular tachycardia is treated first with a vagal maneuver. Adenosine follows, and may be repeated once, to convert the rhythm or slow it enough to see P waves; a hemodynamically unstable patient instead gets immediate synchronized cardioversion.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
D.q: A 61-year-old woman with heart failure has palpitations. A 48-hour monitor shows several runs of 4 to 8 identical wide QRS beats, each lasting a few seconds, without hemodynamic compromise. Which is the first-line drug?
opts: Correct. Runs of 4 to 8 identical wide beats lasting a few seconds without compromise are non-sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia, often seen with heart failure. Because she has palpitations, it is symptomatic, and the first-line drug is a beta blocker such as metoprolol or carvedilol, with catheter ablation next if needed.

Adenosine is not among the drugs named for ventricular tachycardia. Symptomatic non-sustained ventricular tachycardia is treated first with a beta blocker such as metoprolol or carvedilol. Tell: the first drug for symptomatic non-sustained runs is a beta blocker.

Intravenous magnesium breaks torsades de pointes, a polymorphic rhythm; her runs are identical wide beats, so they are monomorphic. Symptomatic non-sustained runs start with a beta blocker. Tell: identical complexes do not call for magnesium.

Digoxin is not named for ventricular tachycardia. A beta blocker such as metoprolol or carvedilol is the first-line drug for symptomatic non-sustained runs, followed by catheter ablation if it fails or is not tolerated. Tell: beta blocker, then ablation, then an antiarrhythmic.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
D.q: A 26-year-old healthy man has an incidental right bundle branch block on a pre-employment electrocardiogram. His examination and echocardiogram are normal, and he asks whether this means he has heart disease. Which answer is most accurate?
opts: It proves a past heart attack

Right bundle branch block does not prove a past heart attack. Ischemic heart disease is one listed cause, but the block may occur with no apparent underlying heart disease, as in this healthy man. Tell: his normal echocardiogram argues against old damage.

Nothing says an isolated right bundle branch block inevitably becomes complete block. It may occur with no apparent heart disease, and prognosis depends on the presence and type of underlying heart disease. Tell: in a healthy man with a normal heart, the outlook follows his normal heart.
A pacemaker is not indicated for an isolated, silent right bundle branch block. Treatment depends on the underlying condition, and he has none. Tell: no symptoms and a normal heart mean no device.
It can occur without heart disease

Correct. A new right bundle branch block is not always pathological and may occur in people with no apparent underlying heart disease. With a normal examination and echocardiogram, this young man can be reassured; treatment depends on any underlying condition, and the block itself is usually asymptomatic.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
D.q: A 29-year-old woman has had a resting heart rate of 105 to 115 for a year. Thyroid tests, a blood count, a drug screen and an echocardiogram are normal, and she takes no medications or stimulants. Her electrocardiogram shows a normal P wave before every narrow QRS. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Atrial flutter with 2:1 block shows two sawtooth waves for every QRS, at an atrial rate of 250 or more. She has one normal P wave before each QRS at about 110. Tell: one normal P wave per QRS is sinus; two sawtooth waves per QRS is flutter.

Nodal reentrant tachycardia is a paroxysmal, regular narrow tachycardia, usually 140 to 180, with hidden P waves. Hers is a persistent rate of 105 to 115 for a year with normal P waves visible before every QRS. Tell: sudden episodes with hidden P waves mean nodal reentry; a steady sinus rate with visible P waves does not.

Correct. A resting rate of 105 to 115 for a year with a normal P wave before every narrow QRS is sinus tachycardia, and normal thyroid tests, blood count, drug screen and echocardiogram with no medications or stimulants exclude the secondary causes. A sinus tachycardia that stays unexplained after that is inappropriate sinus tachycardia, a diagnosis of exclusion.

Focal atrial tachycardia comes from a single ectopic focus outside the sinus node, with a consistently abnormal P wave, usually at 150 to 250, and abrupt-onset palpitations. Her P waves are normal and her rate is a steady 105 to 115. Tell: a normal P-wave shape points to the sinus node; an abnormal one points to an ectopic focus.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following arterial occlusive disease and aortic aneurysm: 2. Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
D.q: What does the word part "athero" in atherosclerosis refer to?
opts: The clot at a site of rupture

The clot that forms at a plaque rupture is thrombosis, a later event in the plaque's life. Athero comes from the Greek for gruel or paste and refers to the fatty material in the core of the plaque. Think of the soft, pasty core, not the clot that forms after rupture.
The fibrous cap over the plaque

The fibrous tissue that forms over the plaque is what the sclerosis half of the word describes: hardness, the stiffening of the arterial wall. Athero, gruel or paste, names the soft fatty core underneath. Split the word: athero for the core, sclerosis for the cap.
The fatty core of the plaque

Correct. Athero is Greek for gruel or paste and refers to the fatty material in the core of the plaque. Sclerosis, meaning hardness, refers to the stiffening of the arterial wall by the fibrous tissue that forms over the plaque. The plaque itself begins as a fatty streak.
The calcium in the arterial media

Calcium in the arterial media is medial calcific sclerosis (Mönckeberg sclerosis), a separate one of the three processes grouped under arteriosclerosis. Athero, gruel or paste, refers to the fatty material in the plaque's core. Medial calcification is a different process, not a word part of atherosclerosis.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following venous disorders: 2. Deep vein thrombosis 3. Phlebitis a. Thrombophlebitis Septic thrombophlebitis 4. Arteriovenous fistula of the extremity a. Acquired (e.g. trauma, iatrogenic) b. Created (i.e. for hemodialysis) 5. Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
D.q: A 63-year-old man with a peripherally inserted central catheter for chemotherapy develops a tender cord in the upper arm. Venous duplex ultrasound shows extensive clot burden in a superficial vein. He has active cancer and a prior deep vein thrombosis. Which therapy should be added to compresses and an anti-inflammatory drug?
opts: Correct. His duplex ultrasound shows extensive clot burden, and active cancer with a prior deep vein thrombosis puts him at higher risk of thrombosis. In that setting anticoagulation may be added to warm compresses and an anti-inflammatory drug, using unfractionated heparin, enoxaparin (a low molecular weight heparin) or fondaparinux.

Systemic corticosteroids are not part of the treatment of superficial thrombophlebitis, which uses warm compresses, compression, elevation and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs such as ibuprofen. His extensive clot and high thrombotic risk call for anticoagulation instead.

Aspirin alone is not among the agents used for this problem. With extensive clot burden or intermediate or higher thrombotic risk, as with his active cancer and prior clot, the added therapy is unfractionated heparin, enoxaparin or fondaparinux.

Antibiotics are not part of the plan, since nothing in the stem describes infection within the vein. His ultrasound shows extensive clot, and with active cancer and a prior deep vein thrombosis the added treatment is anticoagulation with a heparin or fondaparinux.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
D.q: A 66-year-old woman in torsades de pointes (a polymorphic rhythm whose QRS complexes twist around the baseline) becomes unresponsive with a blood pressure of 60/30 and only a faint pulse. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Synchronized cardioversion needs a consistent QRS to time the shock to, and a polymorphic rhythm such as torsades has none. A hemodynamically unstable patient in torsades is defibrillated. Tell: polymorphic rhythms are never synchronized.

Transcutaneous pacing treats slow, blocked rhythms, not a fast polymorphic one. Unresponsive with a blood pressure of 60/30, she is unstable and needs defibrillation. Tell: pace the slow, shock the fast.

Correct. Unresponsive with a blood pressure of 60/30, she is hemodynamically unstable, and an unstable patient in torsades de pointes is defibrillated (unsynchronized cardioversion). Magnesium is the drug for a conscious patient, and amiodarone, procainamide and beta blockers are avoided because they prolong the QT.

Intravenous lidocaine is the one antiarrhythmic that can be used in torsades de pointes, but a drug is not the step for an unstable patient. Unresponsive with a blood pressure of 60/30, she needs defibrillation. Tell: instability moves torsades from drugs to a shock.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following venous disorders: 2. Deep vein thrombosis 3. Phlebitis a. Thrombophlebitis Septic thrombophlebitis 4. Arteriovenous fistula of the extremity a. Acquired (e.g. trauma, iatrogenic) b. Created (i.e. for hemodialysis) 5. Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
D.q: A 66-year-old man has long-standing pitting edema of the lower leg with brown pigmentation and a healed medial ankle ulcer. Duplex ultrasound shows thickened, scarred valve leaflets and chronic obstruction of the femoral vein. He does not recall any leg clot. Which is the most likely cause of his condition?
opts: Correct. Thickened, scarred valve leaflets with chronic obstruction of the femoral vein are the post-thrombotic picture, and prior deep vein thrombosis (DVT) is one of the most common causes of chronic venous insufficiency. Not recalling a clot does not exclude it: about 25% of these patients have no known history of DVT.

Progressive superficial venous reflux is another common cause, but in it the valves fail because they sit in a dilated vein. His leaflets are thickened and scarred with chronic proximal obstruction, which is the post-thrombotic pattern of a prior deep vein thrombosis.

Neoplastic obstruction of the pelvic veins is listed only among the other, less common causes. His duplex shows scarred valve leaflets and chronic obstruction of the femoral vein, the post-thrombotic findings that point to a prior deep vein thrombosis.

A congenital or acquired arteriovenous fistula is one of the less common causes of chronic venous insufficiency. Thickened, scarred leaflets with chronic femoral vein obstruction are post-thrombotic changes, so this is secondary disease from a prior deep vein thrombosis, even without a remembered clot.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following venous disorders: 2. Deep vein thrombosis 3. Phlebitis a. Thrombophlebitis Septic thrombophlebitis 4. Arteriovenous fistula of the extremity a. Acquired (e.g. trauma, iatrogenic) b. Created (i.e. for hemodialysis) 5. Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
D.q: A 33-year-old woman eight weeks postpartum has mild calf aching and a low pretest probability of deep vein thrombosis. Her clinician orders a D-dimer. Which characteristic makes a negative result useful for excluding a clot?
opts: D-dimer is a blood test whose elevation implies increased fibrinolysis; it does not visualize a clot. Seeing the thrombus is the job of venous duplex ultrasound, which has replaced contrast venography, while the D-dimer's value lies in its sensitivity.

D-dimer is sensitive but not specific, so a positive result cannot confirm a clot. Its value for excluding a clot in a low-probability patient like her comes from high sensitivity, which makes a negative result reliable.

A blood test cannot measure how a vein compresses; that would take imaging such as venous duplex ultrasound. D-dimer reflects fibrinolysis, and it excludes a clot in low-probability patients through its sensitivity.

Correct. With a low pretest probability she starts with a D-dimer, and a negative result lets the clinician stop because the test is sensitive. Sensitivity is what makes it a rule-out test for deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism; it is not specific, so a positive result would still need ultrasound.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following arterial occlusive disease and aortic aneurysm: 2. Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
D.q: A 70-year-old woman with long-standing hypertension has three months of progressive hoarseness. A chest radiograph shows widening of the mediastinal shadow. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: A descending thoracic aneurysm compresses the trachea or esophagus, causing dyspnea, stridor, wheezing, cough or dysphagia. Her symptom is hoarseness, which localizes the aneurysm to the arch through the recurrent laryngeal nerve. Match the symptom to the segment.

Correct. Thoracic aneurysm symptoms depend on location, and an arch aneurysm causes hoarseness through the recurrent laryngeal nerve. Her long-standing hypertension is the common history, and the widened mediastinal shadow on chest radiograph is a typical finding.

An ascending thoracic aneurysm causes aortic regurgitation and heart failure rather than hoarseness. Her progressive hoarseness localizes the aneurysm to the arch, where it involves the recurrent laryngeal nerve. Valve problems point to the ascending aorta.

An abdominal aortic aneurysm causes abdominal, back or flank pain and cannot widen the mediastinal shadow or affect the recurrent laryngeal nerve. Her hoarseness and mediastinal widening place the aneurysm in the chest, at the arch. The chest film finding rules out the abdomen.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
D.q: A 66-year-old man with a prior myocardial infarction wears a 24-hour monitor. It shows several runs of 5 to 8 consecutive wide, identical beats at 150, each lasting under 10 seconds and stopping on its own. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Sustained ventricular tachycardia lasts 30 seconds or more or causes hemodynamic collapse sooner. His runs stop on their own in under 10 seconds without collapse. Tell: under 30 seconds with no collapse means non-sustained.

Premature atrial contractions are single early beats with an abnormally shaped P wave. His runs are wide, identical and consecutive, which places them in the ventricles. Tell: consecutive wide beats are ventricular tachycardia.

Correct. Three or more consecutive premature ventricular contractions are ventricular tachycardia, and runs lasting under 30 seconds are non-sustained. His identical QRS shapes make it monomorphic, which is often seen with heart disease such as a prior myocardial infarction.

Ventricular fibrillation is uncoordinated activity with no pulse and no perfusion. His runs are organized, identical wide beats at 150 that stop on their own. Tell: identical complexes and self-termination rule out fibrillation.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
D.q: Which is the most common site of infective endocarditis?
opts: Correct. Infective endocarditis most commonly affects the heart valves. The endocardium is the inner membrane that lines the heart chambers and covers the valve cusps, and vegetations most often form on native or prosthetic valves.

The low-pressure side of a ventricular septal defect is a listed site, but it is not the most common one; the heart valves are. Tell: valves come first, while septal defects, endocardium damaged by abnormal jets or foreign bodies, and intracardiac devices are the other listed sites.

Intracardiac devices are a listed site, with vegetations on pacemakers and implantable cardioverter defibrillators in cardiovascular implantable electronic device endocarditis, but they are not the most common site. Tell: the heart valves remain the most common site of infection.

The pericardial sac is not part of the endocardium, which is the inner membrane lining the heart chambers and covering the valve cusps. Endocarditis is inflammation of the endocardium, most commonly on the heart valves. Tell: endo means inside the heart; the pericardium surrounds it.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
D.q: A 23-year-old competitive cyclist has a regular rhythm at 50 with narrow QRS complexes and no visible P waves on a screening electrocardiogram. He has no symptoms, and his echocardiogram is normal. Which is the most appropriate management?
opts: His training is the likely reason for the rhythm, since increased vagal tone in well-conditioned athletes is a recognized cause of junctional rhythm. Junctional rhythm is generally well tolerated and needs no treatment when asymptomatic in an otherwise healthy person. Tell: an asymptomatic athlete with a normal heart needs no restriction.

Correct. A regular, narrow-complex rhythm at 50 with no visible P waves is a junctional rhythm, usually 40 to 60, and it can be seen in healthy people with increased vagal tone, such as well-conditioned athletes. With no symptoms and a normal echocardiogram in an otherwise healthy cyclist, no treatment is needed.

Atropine is used when a junctional rhythm comes from digitalis toxicity, and as first-line treatment for acute, unstable bradycardia. This cyclist has no symptoms, no drug exposure and a normal heart. Tell: atropine needs a cause like digoxin toxicity or instability, and a healthy athlete has neither.

A permanent pacemaker is for a junctional rhythm caused by complete or high-grade atrioventricular block or by sick sinus syndrome. This cyclist's rhythm comes from high vagal tone in a normal heart and causes no symptoms. Tell: management depends on the cause, and a healthy, asymptomatic athlete needs none.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
D.q: A 22-year-old man has sudden palpitations and lightheadedness. He is alert, with a blood pressure of 112/70. His 12-lead electrocardiogram is shown. Which drug is the most appropriate?
opts: Intravenous rate control is the step for ordinary, stable atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response, which has narrow complexes. His irregular, wide complexes of changing width show conduction down an accessory pathway, which is treated with intravenous procainamide. Tell: wide, irregular and very fast means pre-excited fibrillation, not routine rate control.

Correct. The tracing shows a very fast, irregular rhythm with wide complexes of changing width, which is atrial fibrillation conducting with Wolff-Parkinson-White (pre-excited atrial fibrillation). He is alert with a blood pressure of 112/70, and in this setting intravenous procainamide is used, never adenosine.

Adenosine must never be used when atrial fibrillation runs with Wolff-Parkinson-White; it is first line only for ordinary orthodromic reentry. His irregular, wide-complex rhythm of changing width is pre-excited atrial fibrillation. Tell: irregular wide complexes in a young man with palpitations rule adenosine out and point to procainamide.

Lidocaine is not the listed drug for this rhythm. The look-alike wide rhythm, ventricular tachycardia, is regular at 150 to 200, whereas this one is irregular with rates approaching 300, which marks atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White, treated with intravenous procainamide. Tell: irregularity separates the two.
D.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram of a very rapid, irregular rhythm with wide complexes whose width and height vary from beat to beat

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
D.q: A 62-year-old man collapses in a hospital hallway. He is unresponsive with no pulse, and cardiopulmonary resuscitation is started. His monitor strip is shown. Which is the most important next step?
opts: Correct. Chaotic, uncoordinated activity with no organized QRS complexes and no pulse is ventricular fibrillation. It is treated as cardiac arrest: defibrillation (unsynchronized cardioversion) as soon as possible, then 2 minutes of cardiopulmonary resuscitation, with epinephrine every 3 to 5 minutes and amiodarone if it persists.

Transcutaneous pacing is the emergent treatment for unstable bradycardia from high-grade block. This pulseless, chaotic rhythm is ventricular fibrillation and needs defibrillation. Tell: a pulseless, chaotic strip is shocked, not paced.

Intravenous amiodarone is added when ventricular fibrillation persists after shocks and epinephrine. The first priority is defibrillation as soon as possible. Tell: shock first; antiarrhythmics come later.

Synchronized cardioversion times the shock to a QRS complex, so it is for a tachycardia with a pulse. Ventricular fibrillation has no QRS to time to and no pulse, so it needs defibrillation. Tell: no QRS and no pulse mean an unsynchronized shock.
D.alt: Rhythm strip of continuous, irregular, low-to-medium waves with no recognizable P waves or complexes

D.io: Identify medical care strategies for venous disorders in the lecture topic list for the following populations.
D.q: Advancing age raises deep vein thrombosis risk above which age?
opts: Thirty years is decades below the cutoff, since age counts as a deep vein thrombosis risk factor only past 60 years. At 30, risk comes from other listed factors such as estrogen-containing contraceptives or the first 6 to 12 weeks postpartum.
Fifty years is close but below the listed threshold. Risk from age is given as age over 60 years, so a patient between 50 and 60 is still under the line for age as a deep vein thrombosis risk factor.

Correct. Age over 60 years is listed among the other risk factors for deep vein thrombosis (DVT), alongside being overweight or obese, smoking, heart failure and a personal or family history of DVT or pulmonary embolism.

Seventy-five years overshoots the threshold. Age already counts as a deep vein thrombosis risk factor once a patient is over 60 years, so waiting for 75 would miss fifteen years in which age is already adding risk.
