D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
D.q: A 64-year-old man has restrictive cardiomyopathy confirmed on imaging, but cardiac magnetic resonance imaging and genetic testing have not identified a cause. His team is considering endomyocardial biopsy. When is biopsy performed in this condition?
opts: When imaging and genetic tests are negative

Correct. In restrictive cardiomyopathy, endomyocardial biopsy is performed when all imaging studies and genetic testing are negative, or when a tissue sample is likely to confirm or exclude a diagnosis that would change management. His negative magnetic resonance imaging and genetic testing meet the first condition.
As the first test in every suspected case

Biopsy is not the first test. The echocardiogram, then cardiac magnetic resonance imaging when no cause is found, come first, and biopsy follows negative imaging and genetic testing. Tell: biopsy sits at the end of the sequence, after the noninvasive tests.
Never, since it cannot change management

Biopsy is performed precisely when a tissue sample could confirm or exclude a diagnosis that would change clinical management, or when imaging and genetic testing are negative. Tell: never contradicts the stated indications, and his situation matches one of them.
Only after cardiac transplantation is done

Biopsy belongs to the diagnostic work-up, done when imaging and genetic testing are negative or when tissue could change management, not only after transplantation. Tell: his team is still searching for a cause, which is exactly when biopsy is used.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
D.q: A 58-year-old woman with acute endocarditis asks why the team is so worried when she felt well a week ago. Which statement about untreated acute endocarditis is accurate?
opts: It is mainly a lung infection

Acute endocarditis is a hectically febrile illness that rapidly damages cardiac structures and seeds extracardiac sites; the lung is only one of several embolic targets, along with the spleen, kidney and liver. Tell: the infection sits on the endocardium and spreads outward, so it is a heart infection, not mainly a lung one.

Smoldering harmlessly is wrong on both counts. Even subacute endocarditis is gradually progressive over weeks or months, and acute disease rapidly damages cardiac structures. Tell: she was well a week ago, the rapid acute pattern that kills within weeks if untreated.

Acute endocarditis does not resolve on its own; if untreated, it progresses to death within weeks. Tell: a virulent, invasive organism that rapidly damages the heart and seeds extracardiac sites demands treatment, and spontaneous resolution is not part of either form.
It can be fatal within weeks

Correct. She felt well a week ago, the rapid onset typical of acute disease (typically 3-10 days, with high fevers and systemic toxicity). A virulent organism rapidly damages cardiac structures and seeds extracardiac sites, and if untreated, acute endocarditis progresses to death within weeks.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
D.q: A 28-year-old man had a cold 10 days ago. He now has sharp, pleuritic (worse with a deep breath) substernal chest pain that is worse lying flat and eases when he leans forward. A pericardial friction rub (a scratchy, squeaking sound) is heard at the left sternal border, and the electrocardiogram shows widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression and ST depression in aVR. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Myocardial infarction is a common differential, but pericardial pain is pleuritic and positional, unlike infarction, and his tracing shows the widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression and reciprocal aVR changes that characterize pericarditis. A friction rub is highly specific for pericarditis. Tell: diffuse concave ST elevation plus PR depression points to the pericardium.

Pleuritis is a common differential, but a pleural rub is heard only during inspiration, while his is a pericardial rub at the left sternal border. Widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression also places the problem in the pericardium. Tell: a rub at the left sternal border plus diffuse ST changes means pericarditis.

Correct. Sharp pleuritic substernal pain that is worse supine and eased by leaning forward, a friction rub at the left sternal border, and widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression and reciprocal ST depression in aVR meet three of the four criteria; two suffice. A preceding cold fits, since most idiopathic cases are likely viral.

Pulmonary embolism is a less common differential for this chest pain, and nothing here fits it better than pericarditis: the pain eases on leaning forward, a friction rub is present, and the tracing shows widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression. Tell: positional pain plus a rub plus diffuse ST elevation meets the pericarditis criteria.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
D.q: Which external device detects and shocks fatal ventricular arrhythmias while worn on the body?
opts: Transcutaneous pacing pads pace a slow heart in an emergency, such as Mobitz type II or complete block; they do not detect and shock fatal fast rhythms, and they are not worn day to day. Tell: the worn device that shocks is the wearable cardioverter-defibrillator (LifeVest).

An implantable loop recorder sits under the skin and only records the rhythm; it is not worn on the body and cannot shock. Tell: the external device that both detects and shocks fatal rhythms is the wearable cardioverter-defibrillator (LifeVest).
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. A wearable (external) cardioverter-defibrillator, the LifeVest, is worn on the body and, like an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD), detects fatal arrhythmias and delivers a shock to prevent sudden cardiac death. The implanted version is the alternative, and newer implanted devices can also pace.

A Holter monitor records the rhythm while worn, but it cannot deliver a shock. The wearable cardioverter-defibrillator (LifeVest) detects fatal arrhythmias and shocks them. Tell: recording alone is not treatment; the stem asks for a device that shocks.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following arterial occlusive disease and aortic aneurysm: 2. Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
D.q: A 67-year-old woman had a 20-minute episode of right arm weakness and slurred speech that fully resolved. A left carotid bruit is heard. Which is the best initial test for her carotid arteries?
opts: Correct. Her 20-minute episode of right arm weakness and slurred speech that fully resolved, with a left carotid bruit, points to carotid disease. Duplex ultrasonography is the most widely used initial screening tool and is also used to monitor patients serially for progression or after intervention.

The ankle-brachial index is the initial test for peripheral artery disease in the legs. Her transient right arm weakness and slurred speech with a left carotid bruit need carotid imaging, starting with duplex ultrasonography. A leg test does not evaluate the carotids.

Digital subtraction angiography is the invasive gold standard, but it is not used for screening; it guides therapeutic interventions. Her first carotid test after a transient episode and a bruit is duplex ultrasonography. Gold standard and first test are different roles.

Chest computed tomography is not among the carotid studies; carotid evaluation uses duplex ultrasonography first, then computed tomography or magnetic resonance angiography of the cervical and intracranial vessels. Her symptoms and bruit call for duplex. A chest scan misses the neck.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following arterial occlusive disease and aortic aneurysm: 2. D.q: A 71-year-old man is scheduled for a femoral-popliteal bypass graft using his saphenous vein. He asks what can go wrong. Which complications should he be counseled about?
opts: Correct. Bypass graft surgery, here a femoral-popliteal bypass with his saphenous vein, is invasive and highly effective, but its complications include myocardial infarction and stroke, infection of the graft and peripheral embolization. These are what he should be counseled about.

Kidney stones and gout are not listed complications of bypass surgery. The complications of a bypass graft are myocardial infarction and stroke, infection of the graft and peripheral embolization. Counsel on the cardiovascular and graft risks.

Hoarseness and dysphagia are compression symptoms of thoracic aortic aneurysms of the arch and descending aorta, not risks of a leg bypass. His counseling should cover myocardial infarction, stroke, graft infection and peripheral embolization. Match symptoms to the anatomy involved.

Heart block is not among the listed bypass complications. The named risks are myocardial infarction and stroke, infection of the graft and peripheral embolization. A cardiac complication does appear, but it is infarction, not a conduction problem.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
D.q: A 47-year-old man has new dilated cardiomyopathy with an ejection fraction of 30%. He reports fatigue, heat intolerance and weight loss, and the conjunctivae look pale. Which initial laboratory tests are most useful for finding a contributing cause?
opts: Lipase and amylase are not part of the dilated cardiomyopathy work-up. The listed tests are a complete blood count for anemia, a metabolic panel, liver function and thyroid function. Tell: heat intolerance, weight loss and pallor match thyroid tests and a blood count.
Blood cultures and a throat swab

Cultures are not part of the dilated cardiomyopathy laboratory panel, and nothing in his story points to infection. The panel is a complete blood count for anemia, a metabolic panel for electrolytes and renal function, liver function and thyroid function. Tell: his heat intolerance and pallor match thyroid tests and a blood count.

Neither test is part of the listed work-up. His clues match two tests that are: thyroid function for heat intolerance and weight loss, and a complete blood count for pale conjunctivae. Tell: hyperthyroidism is on the dilated cardiomyopathy differential, so thyroid function is checked.
Thyroid function and a blood count

Correct. His heat intolerance and weight loss raise hyperthyroidism, which is on the dilated cardiomyopathy differential, and his pale conjunctivae raise anemia. The initial work-up includes thyroid function and a complete blood count to evaluate for anemia, along with a metabolic panel and liver function.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
D.q: A 41-year-old woman is being treated for acute pericarditis with an anti-inflammatory and colchicine. She asks whether she may take brisk walks while recovering. Which heart rate ceiling should guide her activity?
opts: A ceiling of 60 beats per minute is not the stated limit. During recovery her maximal heart rate is kept under 100 beats per minute, with strenuous activity avoided until symptoms resolve and C-reactive protein normalizes, and for at least 1 month after diagnosis. Tell: the number to remember is 100.

Correct. Strenuous physical activity is avoided until her symptoms resolve and C-reactive protein normalizes, for at least 1 month after diagnosis, and activity is kept to a maximal heart rate under 100 beats per minute. Any walking during recovery should stay within that ceiling.

A ceiling of 150 beats per minute would allow the strenuous exertion that is to be avoided during recovery. The limit is a maximal heart rate under 100 beats per minute, kept for at least 1 month and until symptoms resolve and C-reactive protein normalizes. Tell: 150 is a workout target, not a recovery ceiling.
No limit if she feels well

How she feels is not the only guide: the restriction lasts until symptoms resolve and C-reactive protein normalizes, and for at least 1 month after diagnosis, with a maximal heart rate under 100 beats per minute. Tell: feeling well meets one condition, but the C-reactive protein and the 1-month minimum must also be met.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
D.q: A 33-year-old man has had a regular, narrow-complex tachycardia at 190 for an hour. He is alert, with a blood pressure of 124/80. A properly performed vagal maneuver has not converted it. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: A permanent pacemaker treats chronic symptomatic bradycardia, such as sick sinus syndrome with symptomatic slow rates. He has a fast, regular narrow tachycardia that a pacemaker would not end. Tell: pacemakers answer slow rhythms; a stable supraventricular tachycardia after a failed vagal maneuver gets adenosine.

Synchronized cardioversion is immediate treatment for hemodynamically unstable supraventricular tachycardia, the less common presentation. He is alert with a blood pressure of 124/80, so he is stable and the next step is adenosine. Tell: failure of a vagal maneuver alone does not make him unstable.

Correct. He is stable, alert with a blood pressure of 124/80, and a properly performed vagal maneuver has failed, so adenosine is next for this supraventricular tachycardia. It may be given twice if needed and may convert the rhythm to normal sinus rhythm or at least slow it so any P waves can be seen.

Intravenous procainamide is used when Wolff-Parkinson-White is known or adenosine reveals atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White, an irregular, wide rhythm. His rhythm is regular and narrow with no pre-excitation described. Tell: a regular narrow rhythm after a failed vagal maneuver goes to adenosine.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
D.q: Which bacterial cause of pericarditis is linked to rheumatic pancarditis?
opts: Histoplasma is not a bacterium; it is listed among the fungal causes of pericarditis with Aspergillus, Blastomyces, Coccidioides and Candida. The bacterial cause tied to rheumatic pancarditis is Streptococcus. Tell: the stem asks for a bacterium, which removes the fungal option first.

Correct. Among the bacterial causes of pericarditis, Streptococcus is the one tied to rheumatic pancarditis. The other bacterial causes listed are Staphylococcus, Pneumococcus, Haemophilus, Mycoplasma and Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

Mycoplasma is a listed bacterial cause of pericarditis, but rheumatic pancarditis is tied to Streptococcus, not Mycoplasma. The bacterial list is Staphylococcus, Pneumococcus, Streptococcus, Haemophilus, Mycoplasma and Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Tell: only Streptococcus carries the rheumatic label.

Staphylococcus is a listed bacterial cause of pericarditis, but it carries no rheumatic link; the bacterium tied to rheumatic pancarditis is Streptococcus. Bacterial disease is uncommon overall, with purulent pericarditis about 2 to 3% of cases in published series. Tell: rheumatic means Streptococcus.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following venous disorders: 2. Deep vein thrombosis 3. Phlebitis a. Thrombophlebitis Septic thrombophlebitis 4. Arteriovenous fistula of the extremity a. Acquired (e.g. trauma, iatrogenic) b. Created (i.e. for hemodialysis) 5. Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
D.q: Andexanet alfa is the reversal agent for which pair of anticoagulants?
opts: Unfractionated heparin and low molecular weight heparins such as enoxaparin are reversed with protamine sulfate, not andexanet alfa. Andexanet alfa is matched to apixaban and rivaroxaban instead.

Each of these has its own reversal agent: dabigatran is reversed by idarucizumab, and warfarin by 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate, fresh frozen plasma or vitamin K. Andexanet alfa reverses apixaban and rivaroxaban.
Dabigatran is reversed by idarucizumab, not andexanet alfa, and fondaparinux is not among the drugs andexanet alfa reverses. Its pair is apixaban and rivaroxaban, with off-label use for edoxaban.

Correct. Andexanet alfa (Andexxa) is the reversal agent for apixaban and rivaroxaban when either causes life-threatening or intracranial hemorrhage, the most serious adverse effect of anticoagulation. It is also used off-label for edoxaban.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
D.q: A 61-year-old man's frequent premature atrial contractions are shown on monitoring to trigger his episodes of atrial fibrillation. Referral for which procedure is most appropriate?
opts: Correct. His premature atrial contractions are frequent and monitoring shows them triggering atrial fibrillation, the two settings in which catheter ablation is used. Otherwise, persistent symptomatic premature atrial contractions are treated with a beta blocker such as metoprolol if not contraindicated.

A permanent pacemaker treats chronic symptomatic bradycardia, such as sick sinus syndrome with symptomatic slow rates. His problem is early atrial beats that set off atrial fibrillation, not a slow rate. Tell: premature atrial beats that trigger fibrillation are targeted by catheter ablation.

Septal myectomy is not a treatment for premature atrial contractions. When these beats are frequent or are shown to trigger atrial fibrillation, as on his monitor, catheter ablation is the procedure used. Tell: the procedure has to target the early atrial beats themselves, which ablation does.

Carotid endarterectomy is not a treatment for premature atrial contractions, which arise in the atria. When they are frequent or trigger atrial fibrillation, catheter ablation is the listed procedure. Tell: an arrhythmia trigger is treated at its source in the heart, by ablation.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following venous disorders: 2. Deep vein thrombosis 3. Phlebitis a. Thrombophlebitis Septic thrombophlebitis 4. Arteriovenous fistula of the extremity a. Acquired (e.g. trauma, iatrogenic) b. Created (i.e. for hemodialysis) 5. Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
D.q: A 66-year-old woman has a large arteriovenous fistula of the thigh and a positive Nicoladoni-Branham sign (slowing of the heart rate when the fistula is compressed). Her resting pulse is 88 beats per minute. Which action should the examiner avoid?
opts: Listening over it for a bruit

Listening over the fistula does not compress it, so it cannot set off the reflex slowing of the heart. The diagnosis of an arteriovenous fistula is made by physical examination, and only compression of a large fistula triggers the Nicoladoni-Branham response.
Feeling for a thrill over it

Feeling for a thrill does not hold the fistula closed, so it does not provoke the reflex drop in heart rate. Physical examination is how an arteriovenous fistula is diagnosed; the maneuver to avoid is sustained compression of a large fistula.

Checking the pulses below the fistula is part of a complete vascular examination and helps detect ischemia, one of the complications to watch for. It does not compress the fistula, so it carries no risk of the reflex slowing that compression causes.

Correct. Her positive Nicoladoni-Branham sign means that compressing this large arteriovenous (AV) fistula reflexly slows her heart rate. Holding it compressed is the one action here that provokes that reflex, so sustained compression is what the examiner should avoid.

D.io: Identify medical care strategies for cardiomyopathies for the following populations. 8. adolescent 9. adult 10. elderly
D.q: A 79-year-old man with cardiomyopathy has become lightheaded on standing since his medications were increased at his last visit. He is frail and has lost weight. Which parts of his drug therapy call for particular caution at his age?
opts: Sodium restriction is a lifestyle modification listed for adults, not a drug, so it is not the drug therapy the question asks about. The medications singled out for caution in the elderly are diuretics and vasodilators. Tell: his symptoms began when medications were increased.

Correct. Age-specific care for elderly patients calls for cautious use of diuretics and vasodilators, with therapy tailored to comorbidities and frailty and a focus on symptom control and quality of life. His lightheadedness on standing after a dose increase, with frailty and weight loss, is the situation that caution targets.

Device therapy is part of adult cardiomyopathy care, but device checks are not drug therapy and do not explain lightheadedness after a medication increase. The elderly list calls for cautious use of diuretics and vasodilators. Tell: link his symptom to the drug change.

Home-based rehabilitation is an option for elderly or mobility-limited patients and is not a drug. Caution in the elderly applies to diuretics and vasodilators. Tell: the question asks about drug therapy, and the elderly list names two drug classes.

D.io: Identify medical care strategies for atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias for the following populations. 3. adult 4. elderly
D.q: A 77-year-old woman with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is admitted in respiratory failure. Her rhythm is irregular at 125, with a P wave before every narrow QRS in at least three different shapes. Which is the mainstay of management for this rhythm?
opts: Long-term anticoagulation is part of managing atrial fibrillation, guided by stroke-risk and bleeding-risk scores. Her rhythm has a P wave before every QRS in three shapes, which is multifocal atrial tachycardia, not fibrillation, and it is managed by treating its cause. Tell: discrete P waves in several shapes mean multifocal; absent P waves mean fibrillation.

Synchronized cardioversion is used for hemodynamically unstable tachycardias, such as unstable focal atrial tachycardia. Multifocal atrial tachycardia is driven by the acute illness itself, so the mainstay is treating the lung disease. Tell: multifocal atrial tachycardia is a marker of how sick the patient is, and treating the cause is the fix.

Catheter ablation is usually curative, about 90 percent, for focal atrial tachycardia, which has one ectopic focus. Her rhythm comes from several foci provoked by acute respiratory failure. Tell: one abnormal P shape can be ablated; three or more shapes driven by illness are treated at the cause.

Correct. An irregular rhythm at 125 with a P wave before every narrow QRS in at least three shapes is multifocal atrial tachycardia, here in severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with respiratory failure. Management is treating the underlying condition; a beta blocker or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker may be added in hospital but is not suitable long term.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
D.q: Pericarditis symptoms that persist beyond 4 to 6 weeks, up to 3 months, without a sustained remission define which form?
opts: Correct. Incessant pericarditis is defined by symptoms that persist for more than 4 to 6 weeks and up to 3 months without a sustained remission. Beyond 3 months the course is labeled chronic, and a return after a symptom-free interval of 4 to 6 weeks or longer is recurrent.

Constrictive pericarditis is a structural diagnosis, fibrous scarring with loss of pericardial elasticity, not a time label. Unbroken symptoms from 4 to 6 weeks up to 3 months define incessant pericarditis. Tell: duration words (acute, incessant, chronic, recurrent) describe pericarditis courses; constriction describes a stiff sac.

Chronic pericarditis is the label once symptoms persist for more than 3 months. Persistence from 4 to 6 weeks up to 3 months without remission is incessant. Tell: 3 months is the dividing line; under it, unbroken symptoms are incessant, and over it they are chronic.

Recurrent pericarditis needs a symptom-free interval of 4 to 6 weeks or longer before symptoms return. Symptoms that never remit for up to 3 months define incessant pericarditis instead. Tell: a gap without symptoms means recurrent; no gap means incessant or chronic.

D.io: Identify medical care strategies for infective endocarditis for the following populations. 8. infant 9. child 10. adolescent 11. adult 12. elderly
D.q: A 17-year-old who injects drugs has fever, rigors and a tricuspid valve vegetation. Which organism is most likely?
opts: Coagulase-negative staphylococci are linked to prosthetic material, recent surgery and neonatal catheter-related disease. This adolescent has no device; he injects drugs. Tell: injection drug use in an adolescent points to Staphylococcus aureus.

Correct. Adolescents increasingly resemble adults, including injection drug use-associated Staphylococcus aureus disease. His drug use, fever with rigors and a tricuspid valve vegetation fit that adult-type profile rather than the viridans streptococcal disease of younger children.

Viridans group streptococci are the most common organisms in children over 1 year with congenital heart disease, who have indolent disease. This 17-year-old injects drugs, which shifts the organism toward Staphylococcus aureus. Tell: congenital heart disease in a child means viridans; injection drug use in an adolescent means Staphylococcus aureus.

Candida is a neonatal and infant organism, tied to central venous catheters, hyperalimentation, neonatal intensive care and prematurity. None of those apply to a 17-year-old who injects drugs. Tell: Candida belongs to the catheter-bearing infant, not the adolescent who injects drugs.

D.io: Demonstrate understanding of modified Duke diagnostic criteria.
D.q: A 70-year-old man has a fever of 38.9 °C (102.0 °F). Two separate blood cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus, a transesophageal echocardiogram shows no vegetation, and he has no predisposing heart condition, no drug use and no skin, eye or kidney findings. How is his case classified under the modified Duke criteria?
opts: Nothing here rules endocarditis out: two separate blood cultures growing Staphylococcus aureus meet a major criterion, and his fever is a minor criterion. One major plus one minor makes endocarditis possible. Tell: a clean echocardiogram removes one major criterion, not the diagnosis.

Criteria are met. Staphylococcus aureus is a typical organism, so two separate positive cultures meet the major blood culture criterion, and a fever of 38.9 °C is above the 38.0 °C minor threshold. Tell: count the cultures first, because two separate positives of a typical organism are a major criterion.

Definite needs two major criteria, one major plus three minor, or five minor. He has only one major (the cultures) and one minor (fever), because the echocardiogram is negative and he has no predisposition, vascular or immunologic findings. Tell: a second major criterion is missing.

Correct. He meets one major criterion, a typical organism (Staphylococcus aureus) in two separate blood cultures, and one minor criterion, fever of 38.9 °C (102.0 °F). The negative transesophageal echocardiogram and absent predisposition, vascular and immunologic findings add nothing, so one major plus one minor is possible endocarditis.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following arterial occlusive disease and aortic aneurysm: 2. Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
D.q: Which pseudoaneurysms may be managed by watching and waiting?
opts: Over 5 cm is the wrong direction: watch and wait is the plan for pseudoaneurysms under 2 cm, which may thrombose and regress on their own. A pseudoaneurysm that needs treatment is sealed with ultrasound-guided thrombin injection. Small means wait; larger means thrombin.

Location is not the criterion. The common site of pseudoaneurysm is the femoral artery after cardiac catheterization, and watch and wait is chosen by size: under 2 cm in diameter, it may thrombose and regress on its own. Size, not site, decides.

Correct. A pseudoaneurysm under 2 cm in diameter may undergo spontaneous thrombosis and regression, so watch and wait is appropriate. Otherwise, ultrasound-guided injection of thrombin, which promotes clot, seals the leak.

Pain from swelling or nerve compression is the presenting symptom of a pseudoaneurysm, not the criterion for waiting. Watch and wait is chosen for pseudoaneurysms under 2 cm in diameter, which may undergo spontaneous thrombosis and regression. The deciding factor is a diameter under 2 cm.

E.io: Identify medical care strategies for infective endocarditis for the following populations. 8. infant 9. child 10. adolescent 11. adult 12. elderly
E.q: A 9-year-old with unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease is scheduled for a tonsillectomy. Which is the most appropriate step regarding endocarditis?
opts: Both the child and the procedure qualify. Unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease is a high-risk pediatric condition, and a tonsillectomy is an invasive respiratory procedure with mucosal incision. Tell: prophylaxis requires a high-risk condition AND a qualifying procedure, and both are present here.

Prophylaxis is a single dose given 30-60 minutes before the procedure, not afterward. This child qualifies: unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease plus a tonsillectomy that incises respiratory mucosa. Tell: a dose given afterward is not prophylaxis.

Correct. Unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease, including palliative shunts and conduits, is a high-risk pediatric condition, and tonsillectomy is an invasive respiratory procedure with mucosal incision. Both conditions are met, so prophylaxis is given as a single dose 30-60 minutes before surgery.

Canceling is not the recommendation. A high-risk child undergoing an invasive respiratory procedure receives prophylaxis beforehand and proceeds with surgery. Tell: high-risk heart disease changes the antibiotic plan, not whether the tonsillectomy happens.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
E.q: A 27-year-old woman has had 20 minutes of sudden palpitations. Her heart rate is 188, blood pressure 122/76, and she is alert with no chest pain or breathlessness. The electrocardiogram shows a regular narrow complex tachycardia with no visible P waves. Which is the most appropriate first step?
opts: Intravenous procainamide is used when Wolff-Parkinson-White is known or adenosine reveals atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White; it is not a first step. Her rhythm is regular and narrow with no pre-excitation described. Tell: a stable regular narrow tachycardia starts with a vagal maneuver.

Correct. A sudden, regular narrow complex tachycardia at 188 with no visible P waves is supraventricular tachycardia, and with a blood pressure of 122/76, a clear mind and no chest pain or breathlessness she is stable. A vagal maneuver is first line, followed by adenosine, which may slow the rhythm enough to show P waves.

Immediate synchronized cardioversion is for hemodynamically unstable supraventricular tachycardia. She is alert, with a blood pressure of 122/76 and no chest pain or breathlessness, so she is stable. Tell: a fast rate alone is not instability; look at blood pressure and mental status.

Adenosine is the second step for stable supraventricular tachycardia, given if a vagal maneuver fails, and it may be repeated once. The question asks for the first step, which needs no drug. Tell: vagal maneuver first, then adenosine.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
E.q: A 17-year-old soccer player had an episode of racing heartbeat that stopped on its own. His resting tracing, taken in sinus rhythm, is shown. Which description best fits this tracing?
opts: Progressively longer PR, then a dropped beat

A PR interval that lengthens until a beat drops is not what this tracing shows; every P wave here is followed by a QRS. The striking features are a short PR and a slurred start to each QRS (delta wave), which is pre-excitation. Tell: look at the start of the QRS; a slurred upstroke means an accessory pathway.
Long PR with every P wave conducted

A long PR interval is not this tracing; the P wave runs almost straight into the QRS, so the PR is short, under 0.12 seconds. Combined with the slurred QRS upstroke (delta wave), that short PR marks pre-excitation through an accessory pathway. Tell: in Wolff-Parkinson-White the PR is short, never long.
Irregular rhythm with no P waves

An irregular rhythm with no P waves describes atrial fibrillation. This tracing was taken in sinus rhythm, with a P wave before every QRS. Tell: in sinus rhythm the clues to an accessory pathway are a short PR and a delta wave, not irregularity.
ruled out by a stated finding
Short PR with a slurred QRS upstroke

Correct. On his resting tracing in sinus rhythm, the P wave runs almost straight into a QRS whose upstroke is slurred: a short PR interval with a delta wave. That is pre-excitation, consistent with an accessory pathway (bundle of Kent) and Wolff-Parkinson-White, which fits his self-terminating episode of racing heartbeat.
E.alt: Close-up rhythm strip of three beats, each with a small P wave running into a QRS whose upstroke is gradual before the main spike

Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
E.q: A 68-year-old man is brought in confused, with a blood pressure of 76/40. The monitor shows a slow, regular rhythm at 36 with a normal P wave before every narrow QRS. Which is the first-line treatment?
opts: Synchronized cardioversion, a timed shock at decreased voltage, treats hemodynamically unstable tachycardias such as supraventricular tachycardia or atrial fibrillation. His rhythm is slow at 36, the opposite problem. Tell: unstable and fast means a synchronized shock; unstable and slow means atropine.

Correct. A slow, regular rhythm at 36 with a normal P wave before every narrow QRS is sinus bradycardia, and confusion with a blood pressure of 76/40 make it acute, symptomatic and hemodynamically unstable. Atropine is first line; if it fails, a temporary pacemaker follows.

A permanent pacemaker is for chronic, symptomatic bradycardia, not the first step in an acute, unstable episode. The acute sequence is atropine, then a temporary pacemaker if atropine fails. Tell: acute and unstable means atropine first; a permanent device comes later if the problem is chronic.

Adenosine is used in stable supraventricular tachycardia after a vagal maneuver, to convert the rhythm or slow it enough to reveal P waves. Slowing a rhythm already at 36 in a confused, hypotensive man is the opposite of the goal. Tell: adenosine is for fast narrow rhythms; atropine is for unstable slow ones.

E.q: A 59-year-old man with three coronary stents and no valve disease needs a tooth extracted. He asks whether he needs antibiotics before the procedure. Which advice is most accurate?
opts: Amoxicillin is the standard oral regimen only for patients with a qualifying condition, such as prosthetic valves or valve-repair material, previous endocarditis, certain congenital heart disease or cardiac transplant with valve regurgitation. Coronary stents are not on that list. Tell: the condition, not the extraction alone, triggers prophylaxis.

Postponing the extraction serves no purpose, because coronary stents are not among the conditions that warrant endocarditis prophylaxis. Tell: the qualifying list is valve-related (prosthetic valves, repair material, prior endocarditis, certain congenital disease, transplant valve regurgitation), not coronary.

Correct. Prophylaxis is reasonable only for patients with prosthetic valves or valve-repair material, previous endocarditis, certain unrepaired or residual congenital heart disease, or cardiac transplant with valve regurgitation. Three coronary stents with no valve disease are not on that list, so no antibiotic is needed even for an extraction.

Clindamycin is no longer recommended for endocarditis prophylaxis because of the risk of Clostridioides difficile infection, and he needs no prophylaxis at all. Tell: coronary stents without valve disease are not a qualifying condition, so giving no drug is the right answer.

E.q: Which electrolyte disturbances are named triggers of premature ventricular contractions?
opts: Low calcium is the wrong direction: hypercalcemia, not hypocalcemia, is the named trigger of premature ventricular contractions, and sodium is not on the list. The named imbalances are hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia and hypercalcemia. Tell: potassium and magnesium low, calcium high.

Correct. Hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia, along with hypercalcemia, are the electrolyte imbalances named as causes of premature ventricular contractions, together with hypoxemia, alcohol, caffeine and stimulants. These beats occur with or without structural heart disease.

Phosphate and chloride are not named triggers. The electrolyte imbalances listed are hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia and hypercalcemia, along with hypoxemia, alcohol, caffeine and stimulants. Tell: the electrolytes to check are potassium, magnesium and calcium.

High potassium and low sodium are not the named triggers; potassium matters here when it is low. The list is hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia and hypercalcemia. Tell: remember potassium and magnesium low, calcium high.

E.q: A 58-year-old man with suspected tamponade has distended jugular veins and a blood pressure of 88/60. He has leg edema, and drainage is being arranged. Which drug class should be avoided?
opts: Antibiotics are not part of tamponade management unless an infection is identified, in which case further management targets the underlying etiology after drainage. They do not threaten his preload the way a diuretic would. Tell: the class to avoid is the one that undoes the fluid support his compressed heart needs.

Intravenous fluid resuscitation is given in tamponade to increase preload and prevent right ventricular collapse, a temporizing measure until drainage. It is part of his treatment, not something to avoid. Tell: in tamponade, adding volume helps and removing volume hurts.

Nothing about his tamponade makes local anesthetics a concern, and needle drainage is the planned definitive treatment. The danger lies in lowering preload, which fluid resuscitation is meant to support until pericardiocentesis. Tell: ask which drug class opposes the fluid support his heart depends on.

Correct. In tamponade, intravenous fluids are given to increase preload and prevent right ventricular collapse while drainage is arranged, so a diuretic, which works against that goal, should be avoided despite his leg edema. Expedient pericardiocentesis is the definitive treatment.

E.q: A 64-year-old woman has two weeks of exertional breathlessness and chest pressure. Her electrocardiogram shows a left bundle branch block; a tracing from last year was normal. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Correct. A left bundle branch block absent a year ago is new, and a new left bundle branch block should always be considered a sign of pathology, an ST-elevation myocardial infarction equivalent. With exertional breathlessness and chest pressure, she needs evaluation for underlying heart disease rather than reassurance.

Synchronized cardioversion terminates tachycardias; a conduction block is not shocked. A new left bundle branch block is a sign of pathology that needs evaluation for heart disease. Tell: there is no fast rhythm to convert.

Some new right bundle branch blocks occur without heart disease, but a new left bundle branch block is always considered a sign of pathology. With new exertional symptoms, she needs evaluation, not reassurance. Tell: a new right block can be benign; a new left block never is.

A pacemaker is not the next step: left bundle branch block is usually left untreated, and a biventricular pacer is reserved for symptomatic block with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. Her new block first needs evaluation for underlying disease. Tell: evaluate before any device.

E.q: A 64-year-old woman must stay in bed for several days after major abdominal surgery. Her team wants a preventive measure aimed at the venous stasis component of the Virchow triad. Which measure is most appropriate?
opts: Warm compresses act on the skin and do nothing to keep blood moving in the deep veins of an immobilized leg. For a patient confined to bed after surgery, the preventive device is intermittent pneumatic compression, whose cuffs squeeze the leg in sequence.

An inferior vena cava filter does not keep blood moving in the legs, so it does not address venous stasis. Prevention aimed at stasis in a bedbound postoperative patient is intermittent pneumatic compression.

Thrombolysis with tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) treats an existing clot and is helpful for a large proximal deep vein thrombosis or a pulmonary embolism in a hemodynamically stable patient. She has no clot yet; preventing stasis after surgery calls for intermittent pneumatic compression.

Correct. She will be immobilized in bed after major surgery, which is exactly when intermittent pneumatic compression is used to prevent deep vein thrombosis (DVT). The cuffs inflate in sequence from the lower leg upward, moving blood out of the leg and countering venous stasis.

E.q: A 70-year-old man with prior cardiac surgery has a regular rhythm at 150 with sawtooth atrial waves, two for every narrow QRS. He is alert, with a blood pressure of 128/78. Which is the most appropriate initial treatment?
opts: Correct. A regular rate of 150 with two sawtooth waves for every narrow QRS is atrial flutter with 2:1 block, and prior cardiac surgery is a common setting. He is alert with a blood pressure of 128/78, so stable flutter is treated with a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker for rate control, which is harder to achieve than in atrial fibrillation.

Intravenous procainamide is used when Wolff-Parkinson-White is known or adenosine reveals atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White. His rhythm is atrial flutter with 2:1 block and no pre-excitation. Tell: stable flutter is rate controlled with a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker.

Synchronized cardioversion is for hemodynamically unstable atrial flutter. He is alert with a blood pressure of 128/78, so rate control comes first, and an elective outpatient cardioversion would follow 21 days of anticoagulation. Tell: stable flutter gets rate control; unstable flutter gets the shock.

A permanent pacemaker treats chronic symptomatic bradycardia, not a fast atrial rhythm. His flutter at 150 needs rate control now, with ablation as the definitive management later. Tell: a pacemaker does not treat a fast rhythm; flutter gets rate control, then ablation.

E.q: In unstable Mobitz type II block, when medications are not used or do not work, which is the emergent measure?
opts: Correct. Unstable Mobitz type II is treated emergently with atropine or epinephrine (both no longer contraindicated but highly controversial) or transcutaneous pacing. When medications are not used or do not work, transcutaneous pacing is the emergent measure, bridging the patient to the definitive permanent pacemaker.

Vagal maneuvers raise vagal tone, which is itself a named cause of milder atrioventricular blocks, so they could only slow conduction further. Unstable Mobitz type II needs transcutaneous pacing when drugs fail. Tell: a slow, blocked rhythm is paced.

Synchronized cardioversion treats unstable tachycardias with a pulse. Unstable Mobitz type II is a slow rhythm from a block that usually sits at the bundle of His, so it needs pacing. Tell: pace the slow, shock the fast.

Defibrillation is for ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia. Unstable Mobitz type II, a slow rhythm with a pulse, is paced transcutaneously when medications fail. Tell: a pulse and a slow rate point to pacing, never a shock.

E.q: A 66-year-old man has right-sided heart failure with a raised jugular venous pressure and ascites. Echocardiogram shows abnormal diastolic filling, normal-sized ventricles and big atria, but the team cannot tell restrictive cardiomyopathy from constrictive pericarditis. Which test is used to differentiate them?
opts: Echocardiography alone is not definitive for this distinction, so repeating it adds little. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging is used to differentiate them, showing pericardial thickening in pericarditis. Tell: a test that could not settle the question once will not settle it on repeat.

Rhythm monitoring records rhythm, which in restrictive disease often shows atrial fibrillation or conduction disorders, but it does not show the pericardium. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging differentiates the two by showing pericardial thickening in pericarditis. Tell: telling these apart needs an image of the pericardium.

Correct. Echocardiography alone is not definitive because restrictive cardiomyopathy and constrictive pericarditis look alike, as in this man with big atria and abnormal diastolic filling. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging is used to differentiate them, showing pericardial thickening in pericarditis.

An exercise echo is still an echocardiogram, and echo alone is not definitive for separating restrictive cardiomyopathy from constrictive pericarditis. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging is used, showing pericardial thickening in pericarditis. Tell: the answer is a different modality, not a different echo.

E.q: A 34-year-old woman without diabetes has ulcers on the posterior aspect of both lower legs. Her pedal pulses are strong, and there are no varicose veins, brown pigmentation or leg swelling. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. Bilateral ulcers on the posterior aspect of the lower legs are the pattern of erythema induratum on the differential of leg ulcers. Her strong pulses argue against arterial ulcers, the lack of diabetes against neuropathic ulcers, and the absence of varicose veins, pigmentation and swelling against venous disease.

Diabetic neuropathic ulcers belong to patients with diabetes, and she has none. Ulcers on the posterior aspect of both lower legs, in a woman with strong pulses, are the distribution of erythema induratum.

Venous ulcers occur at the medial ankle in a leg with chronic venous hypertension, typically with edema and brown pigmentation. She has no swelling, pigmentation or varicose veins, and her ulcers are posterior and bilateral, the pattern of erythema induratum.

Arterial insufficiency ulcers are painful, usually (not always) on the lateral aspect of the ankle, and come with weak pulses. Her strong pedal pulses and bilateral posterior ulcers point to erythema induratum instead.

Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
E.q: A 70-year-old man arrives with a suddenly cold, pale, pulseless left foot. Vascular surgery has been called. Which medical therapy should be started?
opts: Aspirin is an antiplatelet agent used in chronic peripheral artery disease. The medical therapy for an acute arterial occlusion is anticoagulation with intravenous heparin. An oral antiplatelet alone is not the acute treatment.

Cilostazol is an oral drug that suppresses platelet aggregation and dilates vessels to improve walking distance in chronic claudication. A suddenly cold, pale, pulseless foot is acute limb ischemia, anticoagulated with intravenous heparin while vascular surgery acts. Chronic drugs do not treat acute occlusion.

Correct. A suddenly cold, pale, pulseless foot is acute peripheral arterial occlusion, and its medical therapy is anticoagulation with intravenous heparin, started alongside the immediate vascular surgery consult. Diagnostic testing then depends on the category of ischemia.

Pentoxifylline is a xanthine derivative that helps blood flow through narrowed arteries in chronic disease. Acute arterial occlusion needs intravenous heparin anticoagulation alongside the vascular surgery consult. An oral chronic agent does not fit this emergency.

E.q: A 63-year-old man ran out of his metoprolol four days ago. He feels his heart racing, and his pulse is 118 and regular, with a normal P wave before every narrow QRS. He has no fever and is not bleeding. Which is the most likely cause of his tachycardia?
opts: Correct. A regular rate of 118 with a normal P wave before every narrow QRS is sinus tachycardia, and abrupt withdrawal of a beta blocker or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker is a listed drug cause. Running out of metoprolol four days ago, with no fever or bleeding to explain the rate, fits that cause.

Increased vagal tone is not among the listed causes of sinus tachycardia, which are physiologic, pathologic or drug-related, including abrupt beta blocker withdrawal. A slow sinus rate, sinus bradycardia, is the adaptive response seen in well-conditioned athletes. Tell: a fast sinus rate four days after stopping metoprolol is withdrawal.

Hypothyroidism is a listed cause of sinus bradycardia and sick sinus syndrome, so it slows the sinus rate. His rate is fast at 118 and began after he ran out of metoprolol. Tell: hyperthyroidism, not hypothyroidism, sits on the sinus tachycardia list.

Increased intracranial pressure is a listed cause of sinus bradycardia, not sinus tachycardia. His fast sinus rate began after he stopped metoprolol, a listed drug-withdrawal cause. Tell: raised intracranial pressure slows the sinus node; beta blocker withdrawal speeds it.

E.q: Which adverse effect of corticosteroids is a particular concern for older adults with pericarditis?
opts: Hearing loss is not the corticosteroid concern named for older adults with pericarditis; the named risk is osteoporosis. Other age-specific cautions include anti-inflammatory drugs on the Beers list and dose reduction of colchicine. Tell: in older adults, steroids are a bone problem.

Correct. In older adults with pericarditis, corticosteroids raise osteoporosis risk, which makes them a particular concern in this group. That sits beside the other age-specific cautions: anti-inflammatory drugs on the Beers list and colchicine considered for dose reduction.

Hypoglycemia is not the corticosteroid concern named for older adults with pericarditis; the stated risk is osteoporosis. In recurrent disease, prednisone is mainly kept for patients with underlying systemic autoimmune disease. Tell: the older-adult steroid warning is about bone strength.

Bradycardia is not the corticosteroid effect flagged for older adults with pericarditis; the flagged risk is osteoporosis. Age also calls for caution with anti-inflammatory drugs and a possible colchicine dose reduction. Tell: link steroids in older adults to fragile bones, not to heart rate.

E.q: A 68-year-old man with coronary artery disease has frequent premature atrial contractions (early beats with abnormal P waves) on a monitor. Which sustained rhythm may these beats go on to precede in him?
opts: Complete heart block is not among the rhythms premature atrial contractions are listed as preceding. In a patient with heart disease they may lead into paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia, atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter. Tell: premature atrial beats lead into fast atrial rhythms, not into block.

Multifocal atrial tachycardia arises in acutely ill patients with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or heart failure, not as the sequel of premature atrial contractions. In heart disease these beats may precede supraventricular tachycardia, atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter. Tell: the listed sequels are fibrillation, flutter and supraventricular tachycardia.

Ventricular fibrillation is not among the rhythms premature atrial contractions are listed as preceding; these beats begin in the atria and lead into atrial rhythms. In heart disease they may precede supraventricular tachycardia, atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter. Tell: an atrial trigger leads into an atrial rhythm.

Correct. In patients with heart disease, such as his coronary artery disease, premature atrial contractions may precede paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia, atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter. Because his are frequent, the next step is also to look for underlying structural heart disease.

E.q: A 74-year-old woman with no symptoms and normal exercise tolerance has a routine electrocardiogram showing a constant PR interval of 0.24 seconds, with every P wave conducted to a narrow QRS complex. Which is the most appropriate management?
opts: A beta blocker is itself a named cause of first-degree block, so it could only lengthen her PR further, and it treats nothing here. Asymptomatic first-degree block needs no treatment. Tell: rate-slowing drugs appear on the cause list, not the treatment list.

A permanent pacemaker is considered for symptomatic first-degree block or a PR over 0.3 seconds. She has no symptoms and a PR of 0.24 seconds. Tell: no symptoms and a PR under 0.3 seconds mean no device.

Correct. Her constant PR of 0.24 seconds with every P wave conducted to a narrow QRS is first-degree block, and she has no symptoms. No treatment is needed unless debilitating or heart failure symptoms develop, and a permanent pacemaker is considered only for symptoms or a PR over 0.3 seconds.

Transcutaneous pacing is an emergency bridge for unstable high-grade blocks such as Mobitz type II or complete block, not for a stable, silent first-degree block. She needs no treatment. Tell: emergency pacing needs an unstable patient.

E.q: A 44-year-old man began having pleuritic (worse with a deep breath) pericardial pain 8 weeks ago. Despite treatment the symptoms have never fully gone away, with no symptom-free interval. Which term best describes his course?
opts: Recurrence requires symptoms to return after a symptom-free interval of 4 to 6 weeks or longer, and he has never had such an interval. Unbroken symptoms at 8 weeks are incessant. Tell: no symptom-free gap, no recurrence.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. His symptoms have persisted for 8 weeks, beyond the 4 to 6 weeks of acute pericarditis but short of 3 months, with no symptom-free interval. Symptoms persisting more than 4 to 6 weeks and up to 3 months without a sustained remission define incessant pericarditis.

Chronic pericarditis requires symptoms for more than 3 months. At 8 weeks without remission he sits in the incessant window, beyond 4 to 6 weeks but under 3 months. Tell: count the weeks; chronic starts only after 3 months.
ruled out by a stated finding

Effusive-constrictive pericarditis is underlying constriction with a coexisting effusion, recognized when constriction persists after drainage; it is a structural diagnosis, not a time label. He has unremitting pain at 8 weeks, which is incessant pericarditis. Tell: his stem gives a duration, with no effusion or drainage.

Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
E.q: A 76-year-old woman had a mechanical mitral valve placed 4 years ago. She has 5 weeks of low-grade fever and fatigue, and blood cultures are pending. Which organism is most likely in her prosthetic valve infection?
opts: Correct. Her mechanical valve was placed 4 years ago, so this is late prosthetic valve endocarditis, which is caused by Streptococcus viridans. The 5-week course of low-grade fever and fatigue also fits, since viridans streptococci are a classic subacute organism; early infection would instead be staphylococcal.

Escherichia coli is not among the listed prosthetic valve organisms or the usual acute or subacute causes. Late prosthetic valve infection, years after surgery, is caused by viridans streptococci. Tell: years after valve surgery, think oral-source streptococci, not a bowel gram-negative rod.

Candida is the fungal cause of endocarditis and is not the expected organism for late prosthetic valve infection, which is Streptococcus viridans. Tell: a prosthesis infected years after surgery with a smoldering course points to viridans streptococci, not a fungus.

Staphylococcus epidermidis, a coagulase-negative staphylococcus, is the classic EARLY prosthetic valve organism, along with Staphylococcus aureus. Her valve was placed 4 years ago, which makes this late disease from viridans streptococci. Tell: early after surgery means skin staphylococci; years later means viridans.

E.q: A 55-year-old man with symptomatic varicose veins has a duplex ultrasound showing significant saphenous vein reflux. Which referral is most appropriate?
opts: A cardiologist is not the referral for superficial venous reflux; his problem is in the leg veins, usually the great saphenous vein in varicose veins. Significant saphenous reflux is one of the triggers for referral to a vascular specialist.

A hematologist does not manage saphenous reflux, which arises from venous reflux and venous hypertension in the leg veins rather than from a blood disorder. Referral to a vascular specialist is indicated for significant saphenous reflux.

An orthopedic surgeon does not treat venous reflux. Significant saphenous reflux on duplex ultrasound is a reason for referral to a vascular specialist, who can consider surgery aimed at restoring proper flow and lowering venous hypertension.

Correct. Significant saphenous reflux is one of the reasons to refer to a vascular specialist, along with arterial insufficiency, nonhealing or recurrent ulcers, persistent stasis dermatitis and diagnostic uncertainty. Varicose veins usually involve the great saphenous vein, so his reflux sits in the vein most often affected.

E.io: Identify medical care strategies for atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias for the following populations. 3. adult 4. elderly
E.q: A 79-year-old woman has spells of a racing heartbeat followed by near-fainting. Her ambulatory monitor strip is shown, and her near-fainting spells match the long pauses. Which is the most appropriate management?
opts: Observation is appropriate in sick sinus syndrome only when symptoms do not correlate with episodes of bradycardia. Her near-fainting spells match the long pauses on her monitor. Tell: correlation between symptoms and pauses moves management from watching to a permanent pacemaker.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Bursts of a racing rhythm that stop into long pauses are tachy-brady syndrome, a form of sick sinus syndrome, and her near-fainting matches the pauses. When symptoms correlate with the bradycardia, a permanent pacemaker is the treatment, and tachy-brady syndrome often needs one.

Atropine is first line for acute, symptomatic, hemodynamically unstable bradycardia, a short-term rescue. Her problem is recurrent, documented pauses from a diseased sinus node, which needs a permanent pacemaker. Tell: acute and unstable means atropine; recurrent and symptomatic means a permanent pacemaker.

Adenosine is used for stable supraventricular tachycardia after a vagal maneuver, to convert the rhythm or slow it. Her near-fainting comes from the pauses, and slowing her heart would not help them. Tell: in tachy-brady syndrome, symptoms that match the pauses call for a permanent pacemaker.
E.alt: Three rows of a rhythm strip: bursts of rapid narrow complexes that stop abruptly, then long flat pauses before slower beats resume

E.q: After a positive D-dimer in the low likelihood Wells category, which test comes next?
opts: Stopping is the response to a negative D-dimer in the low-likelihood group, not a positive one. A positive result reflects increased fibrinolysis, which is not specific for a clot, so it must be followed by ultrasound.

Correct. In a low-likelihood patient, a negative D-dimer ends the work-up, but a positive one leads to ultrasound, because D-dimer is sensitive but not specific. A negative ultrasound then stops the evaluation, and venous duplex ultrasound has replaced contrast venography as the imaging test.

Repeating the D-dimer adds nothing, since the test is sensitive but not specific and a second positive would still not confirm a clot. The next step after a positive result is venous duplex ultrasound.
Contrast ascending venography is the definitive gold standard but has been replaced by venous duplex ultrasound. After a positive D-dimer, ultrasound is the next test, not venography.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
E.q: Which laboratory test evaluates for anemia in suspected dilated cardiomyopathy?
opts: Correct. The complete blood count (CBC) is the test that evaluates for anemia in suspected dilated cardiomyopathy. The rest of the initial panel has its own targets: a comprehensive metabolic panel for electrolytes and renal function, liver function tests and thyroid function.

Thyroid function is checked because hyperthyroidism is on the dilated cardiomyopathy differential, but it does not detect anemia. The complete blood count does. Tell: match each test to its target, and anemia belongs to the blood count.

Liver function tests are in the work-up, but they look for elevation in alcoholic disease or hemochromatosis, not for anemia. Anemia is evaluated with the complete blood count. Tell: blood count for anemia; liver tests for alcohol or iron-related disease.

The comprehensive metabolic panel evaluates electrolytes and renal function, not anemia. Anemia is evaluated with a complete blood count. Tell: the metabolic panel covers salts and kidneys, while anemia is read from the blood count.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following arterial occlusive disease and aortic aneurysm: 2. Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
E.q: What defines aortic dissection?
opts: Dilation involving all three layers of the wall is a true aneurysm, saccular or fusiform. Aortic dissection instead separates the wall layers after an intimal tear, creating a false lumen in the media where blood can pool. Dilation versus separation is the distinction.
A cavity outside the vessel wall

A blood-filled cavity outside the vessel wall is a pseudoaneurysm (false aneurysm), formed when an arterial rupture is sealed as the cavity thromboses. Aortic dissection starts with an intimal tear and creates a false lumen within the media. Outside the wall is pseudoaneurysm; inside the wall is dissection.

Plaque narrowing of the lumen is atherosclerotic stenosis. Aortic dissection is a tear, not a narrowing: an intimal tear typically contained by the media, with the wall layers separating to form a false lumen. Narrowing describes plaque; a false lumen describes dissection.
An intimal tear with a false lumen

Correct. Aortic dissection forms from an intimal tear and is typically contained by the media layer. The vessel wall layers separate, creating a false lumen within the media where blood can pool. Its most common predisposing factor is degeneration of medial collagen and elastin.

Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
E.q: A 63-year-old man is admitted with an acute myocardial infarction. He has never had a cardiac procedure and has had no tick bites. On the second hospital day his monitor shows a PR interval that lengthens with each beat until a QRS complex is dropped, in a repeating pattern. Which named cause of this rhythm fits him best?
opts: Age-related degeneration of the conduction system is the most common cause of first-degree block, but it is not on the list of causes of Mobitz type I. A block that appears on the second day of an acute infarction points to atrioventricular node ischemia. Tell: the timing with his infarction is the clue.

Cardiac ablation is a named cause of Mobitz type I, but he has never had a cardiac procedure. A block that appears during an acute infarction points to atrioventricular node ischemia. Tell: the stem rules ablation out on purpose.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. A PR that lengthens until a QRS drops, in a repeating pattern, is Mobitz type I (Wenckebach). Atrioventricular node ischemia, usually after a myocardial infarction, is a named cause, and his block appeared on day 2 of an acute infarction, while the stem rules out ablation and Lyme carditis.
Lyme carditis from a tick bite

Lyme carditis is a named cause of Mobitz type I, but he has had no tick bites. A block that appears on day 2 of an acute infarction points to atrioventricular node ischemia. Tell: the exclusions in the stem leave ischemia standing.
ruled out by a stated finding

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
E.q: A 58-year-old woman had a large effusion drained for tamponade. Afterward her jugular venous pressure remains elevated and shows the Kussmaul sign (a rise on inspiration), and she remains fluid overloaded. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. An elevated jugular venous pressure with the Kussmaul sign and ongoing fluid overload after a tamponading effusion was drained show constriction persisting after drainage. Effusive-constrictive pericarditis is underlying constriction with a coexisting effusion, usually with tamponade, which is exactly this sequence.

A pericardial effusion is extra fluid in the pericardial space, and once drained nothing should remain to restrict the heart. Persistent venous congestion with the Kussmaul sign after drainage means an underlying constriction remains, which is effusive-constrictive pericarditis. Tell: what persists after drainage is the clue.
ruled out by a stated finding

Nothing points to a disease of the heart muscle; her problem appeared with a tamponading effusion and persisted after it was drained. Persistent constriction after effusion drainage is the defining feature of effusive-constrictive pericarditis. Tell: tie the findings to the drainage sequence the stem describes.

Recurrent pericarditis is a return of pericarditis symptoms after a symptom-free interval of 4 to 6 weeks or longer. She has had no interval at all; her congestion persisted straight after drainage, which marks effusive-constrictive disease. Tell: recurrence is about time; this is about what remains after drainage.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
E.q: A 63-year-old man started a new medication 2 weeks ago and now feels tired. His electrocardiogram shows a regular rate of 48 with an upright P wave before every narrow QRS and a PR interval of 0.18 seconds. Which medication class most likely explains this rhythm?
opts: Anticholinergic drugs are listed causes of sinus tachycardia, which would raise the sinus rate above 100. His sinus rhythm is slow at 48. Tell: anticholinergics speed the sinus node; beta blockers, nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers and digoxin slow it.

Beta-agonists are listed triggers of fast rhythms such as nodal reentrant tachycardia, and they do not slow the sinus node. His rhythm is sinus bradycardia at 48. Tell: a drug that slows the sinus rate below 60 belongs to the beta blocker, nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker or digoxin group.

Correct. A regular rate of 48 with an upright P wave before every narrow QRS and a PR of 0.18 seconds is sinus bradycardia. Beta blockers, nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers and digoxin are its listed drug causes, and fatigue two weeks after starting a new medication fits a beta blocker.

Stimulants are listed causes of sinus tachycardia, raising the sinus rate. A slow sinus rhythm at 48 points instead to a beta blocker, nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker or digoxin. Tell: stimulants and anticholinergics sit on the fast list; beta blockers sit on the slow list.

E.q: Which high-risk pediatric condition warrants endocarditis prophylaxis before qualifying procedures?
opts: A defect repaired years ago, no residual leak

A repaired defect is high risk only in the first 6 months after repair with prosthetic material or a device, or when residual defects sit adjacent to prosthetic material. Years later with no residual leak, it is not on the list. Tell: look for prosthetic material, a residual defect or the 6-month window.

Correct. Unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease, including palliative shunts and conduits, is on the high-risk pediatric list, along with prosthetic valves or material, prior endocarditis, the first 6 months after repair with prosthetic material, residual defects next to prosthetic material and cardiac transplant with valvulopathy.
An innocent murmur found on screening

An innocent murmur found on screening is not a high-risk condition; it involves no prosthetic material, prior infection or cyanotic lesion. Tell: the high-risk list names specific structural conditions, such as unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease, not a benign murmur.
A family history of valve disease

A family history of valve disease is not on the high-risk pediatric list, which covers the child's own heart: prosthetic valves or material, prior endocarditis, unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease and recent or residual repairs. Tell: risk comes from the patient's own lesion, not a relative's.

Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
E.q: A 76-year-old woman has episodes of lightheadedness and one faint. A 24-hour ambulatory monitor shows runs of a fast, irregular rhythm that alternate with slow rates and long pauses. Which fast rhythm is most likely on her monitor?
opts: Correct. Runs of a fast, irregular rhythm alternating with slow rates and long pauses, with lightheadedness and a faint, are tachy-brady syndrome, a form of sick sinus syndrome. The tachyarrhythmia in tachy-brady syndrome is most commonly atrial fibrillation, which fits an irregular fast run.

Ventricular fibrillation is not the listed fast rhythm of tachy-brady syndrome, and she has recurring runs she lives through between slow spells. The tachyarrhythmia there is most commonly atrial fibrillation; ventricular tachycardia occurs in some patients and calls for a pacemaker with a defibrillator. Tell: recurring irregular fast runs with pauses are atrial fibrillation.

Nodal reentrant tachycardia is a regular narrow tachycardia, usually 140 to 180, typically in women without heart disease. Her fast runs are irregular and alternate with slow rates and pauses, the pattern of tachy-brady syndrome. Tell: irregular fast runs plus pauses in an older patient point to atrial fibrillation.

Sinus tachycardia is regular with a uniform P wave before every QRS. Her fast runs are irregular, and in tachy-brady syndrome the fast rhythm is most commonly atrial fibrillation. Tell: an irregular fast phase alternating with pauses is not sinus; it is atrial fibrillation until proven otherwise.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a.
