Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
E.q: A 58-year-old woman has a regular, narrow-complex tachycardia at 210 with no visible P waves. She is confused and pale, with a blood pressure of 70/40. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: A vagal maneuver is first line only for stable supraventricular tachycardia. She is confused and pale with a blood pressure of 70/40, so she is hemodynamically unstable. Tell: instability skips the vagal maneuver and adenosine and goes straight to synchronized cardioversion.

Adenosine follows a vagal maneuver in stable supraventricular tachycardia and may convert the rhythm or slow it to reveal P waves. She is confused and hypotensive, which calls for an immediate synchronized shock rather than a drug. Tell: drugs are for the stable patient; the unstable one gets cardioversion.

An unsynchronized shock is not the treatment for unstable supraventricular tachycardia; the shock used is synchronized, meaning timed, at decreased voltage. She has a regular narrow rhythm with organized complexes to time the shock to. Tell: an organized narrow-complex rhythm in an unstable patient means synchronized cardioversion.

Correct. A regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 210 with no visible P waves is supraventricular tachycardia, and confusion, pallor and a blood pressure of 70/40 make it hemodynamically unstable. That calls for immediate synchronized cardioversion, a timed shock at decreased voltage; collapse like this is expected once the rate passes 200.

Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
E.q: A 55-year-old woman had femoral vessel puncture for an endovascular procedure two days ago. Examination of the groin shows a new bruit over the puncture site, and the surgeon suspects an iatrogenic arteriovenous fistula. Which study is used to confirm the diagnosis?
opts: A plain radiograph is not among the tests used to confirm an arteriovenous fistula. After femoral access, a suspected iatrogenic fistula is confirmed with duplex ultrasound, and computed tomography angiography or angiography can add its location and size.

A D-dimer is a blood test and gives no picture of the vessels at the puncture site, so it cannot show an abnormal artery-to-vein connection. Confirming a suspected iatrogenic fistula after femoral access takes duplex ultrasound.

Correct. Puncture of the femoral vessels for an endovascular procedure is the classic setting for an iatrogenic arteriovenous (AV) fistula, and duplex ultrasound confirms the diagnosis in suspected cases. Computed tomography angiography and angiography can also confirm a fistula and show its location and size.

The ankle-brachial index is not used to confirm an arteriovenous fistula. After groin access, the puncture site is checked with a complete lower extremity vascular examination comparing pulses with pre-procedure findings, and a suspected fistula is confirmed by duplex ultrasound.

E.q: A 52-year-old man on telemetry has a prolonged QT after starting a new medication and then develops polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (QRS complexes that vary in shape and twist around the baseline). He becomes unresponsive and pulseless. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Intravenous magnesium breaks torsades in a conscious patient. This man is unresponsive and pulseless, and a hemodynamically unstable patient with torsades is defibrillated. Tell: 'conscious' is the word that puts magnesium first.

Correct. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with a prolonged QT is torsades de pointes, and a hemodynamically unstable patient, here unresponsive and pulseless, is treated with defibrillation (unsynchronized cardioversion). Magnesium is the drug for torsades in a conscious patient; once he is pulseless, the shock comes first.

Transcutaneous pacing treats slow, blocked rhythms, not a fast polymorphic one. A pulseless patient in polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is defibrillated. Tell: an unresponsive, pulseless patient with a fast rhythm needs a shock.

Synchronized cardioversion needs a consistent QRS to time against and is used in a patient with a pulse. A pulseless polymorphic rhythm is defibrillated (unsynchronized). Tell: no pulse and a changing QRS both point to an unsynchronized shock.
ruled out by a stated finding

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
E.q: A 30-year-old man is diagnosed with acute idiopathic pericarditis after a viral illness. He is afebrile, his troponin is normal, the echocardiogram shows no effusion, and he has no contraindication to any medication. Which treatment is most appropriate?
opts: Anakinra is fourth-line therapy, after nonsteroidal drugs with colchicine, then prednisone with colchicine, then the two combined. A first uncomplicated episode starts with an anti-inflammatory drug plus colchicine. Tell: a first, low-risk episode does not usually start with an interleukin-1 blocker.

Antibiotics have no place in the regimen for idiopathic or viral pericarditis, which is anti-inflammatory therapy. He is afebrile with no effusion, so nothing suggests a bacterial process, and ibuprofen with colchicine is the initial therapy. Tell: a viral prodrome with typical findings calls for anti-inflammatory drugs, not antimicrobials.

Correct. He has acute idiopathic pericarditis after a viral illness with no high-risk features (afebrile, normal troponin, no effusion) and no contraindications. A nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug such as ibuprofen plus colchicine is the initial recommended therapy for most such patients, with gastrointestinal protection.

Prednisone with colchicine is second-line therapy, kept for refractory cases or patients with a contraindication to nonsteroidal drugs, and he has neither. Ibuprofen with colchicine comes first. Tell: the stem's statement that he has no contraindication to any medication is there to rule out the steroid.

Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
E.q: Which mimic of deep vein thrombosis presents with leg pain, erythema, fever and chills?
opts: A calf muscle pull or tear usually has an inciting injury in the history and may show bruising at the ankle. It does not explain fever and chills, which with leg pain and erythema point to cellulitis.

Lymphedema is chronic edema of the extremities, usually after pelvic surgery, malignancy or radiation therapy. Chronic swelling is its hallmark, whereas leg pain with erythema, fever and chills points to cellulitis.
A ruptured popliteal (Baker) cyst causes severe, sudden calf discomfort that can mimic a clot. Fever, chills and erythema are not its features; that combination with leg pain describes cellulitis.

Correct. Cellulitis causes leg pain with erythema and may be accompanied by fever and chills. Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) can also bring pain, warmth and erythema, so the fever and chills are the clues that tip this mimic toward infection.

Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
E.q: A 59-year-old man with native aortic valve endocarditis and a large vegetation asks whether a blood thinner would prevent a stroke. He has no other reason for anticoagulation. Which choice should be avoided?
opts: Correct. Anticoagulation is not beneficial in patients with native valve infection; it is only controversial in patients with prosthetic valves. He has native aortic valve endocarditis and no other reason for anticoagulation, so heparin or warfarin should not be started to prevent a stroke.

Monitoring renal function is not a choice to avoid, and nothing in the stem argues against checking his kidneys while infectious disease directs therapy and monitoring. The choice to avoid is anticoagulation, which is not beneficial in native valve infection. Tell: only one option lacks benefit here.

Consulting infectious disease is appropriate: infectious disease manages antibiotic therapy and outpatient monitoring pending disposition. The choice to avoid is anticoagulation, which is not beneficial with native valve infection. Tell: consultations help; the blood thinner does not.

Appropriate antibiotic therapy is the expected treatment and should continue; surgery is considered only when infection is not resolving with it. The choice to avoid is anticoagulation, which is not beneficial in native valve endocarditis such as his. Tell: stopping effective therapy is never the safe answer.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
E.q: A 74-year-old man with a prosthetic aortic valve placed 3 years ago has endocarditis, and his blood cultures grow methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. Which regimen is most appropriate?
opts: Vancomycin plus ceftriaxone is an empiric regimen used before the organism is known (subacute presentation, native valve, or prosthetic valve in place more than 1 year). His cultures already show methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus on a prosthetic valve. Tell: a known organism replaces the empiric pair with targeted combination therapy.

Penicillin G plus gentamicin is a viridans streptococcal regimen, not a staphylococcal one. Tell: penicillin G pairs with viridans streptococci, while methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus on a prosthetic valve needs vancomycin, rifampin and gentamicin.

Nafcillin replaces vancomycin only when the culture shows methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus. His strain is methicillin-resistant, so vancomycin stays in the combination with rifampin and gentamicin. Tell: susceptible means nafcillin or oxacillin; resistant means vancomycin.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Staphylococcus aureus infection of a prosthetic valve is treated with combination therapy: an antistaphylococcal drug plus rifampin and gentamicin. Because his strain is methicillin-resistant, that drug is vancomycin (nafcillin or oxacillin would be used only for a susceptible strain).

E.io: Identify medical care strategies for atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias for the following populations. 3. adult 4. elderly
E.q: A 69-year-old woman with hypertension and diabetes has newly found atrial fibrillation, now rate controlled. Her HAS-BLED (bleeding-risk) score is 1, low risk. Which tool now decides whether she needs anticoagulation?
opts: Her HAS-BLED (bleeding-risk) score has already done its job: at 1 it is low risk, so anticoagulation is okay, while a score of 3 and up would mean no anticoagulation. It cannot say whether she needs anticoagulation; stroke risk sets that. Tell: bleeding risk decides whether anticoagulation is safe, stroke risk whether it is needed.

QRS duration is a feature of the tracing, and atrial fibrillation keeps a narrow QRS under 0.12 seconds; width plays no part in the anticoagulation decision. That decision rests on stroke risk, assessed with the CHA2DS2-VASc (stroke-risk) score. Tell: anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation is about clot risk, not the intervals on the tracing.

Her heart rate guides rate control, which is already achieved. Whether she needs anticoagulation rests on the CHA2DS2-VASc (stroke-risk) score, where 0 in men or 1 in women is low risk and may not require it. Tell: the rate guides rate control; the stroke-risk score guides anticoagulation.

Correct. Her HAS-BLED (bleeding-risk) score of 1 is low risk, so anticoagulation is acceptable, and whether she needs it is set by the CHA2DS2-VASc (stroke-risk) score. A score of 0 in men or 1 in women is low risk; her age of 65 to 74 (1), female sex (1), hypertension (1) and diabetes (1) give her 4.

E.q: A 38-year-old woman notices occasional skipped beats during a stressful month of heavy coffee and wine. Her electrocardiogram shows occasional early beats with an abnormally shaped P wave and a narrow QRS, and her examination and echocardiogram are normal. Which advice is most appropriate?
opts: Catheter ablation is used when premature atrial contractions are frequent or are triggering atrial fibrillation. Hers are occasional, her heart is normal on examination and echocardiogram, and clear triggers are present. Tell: occasional beats with obvious triggers get counseling and reassurance, not a procedure.

A beta blocker such as metoprolol is for premature atrial contractions that are persistent and symptomatic, if not contraindicated. Hers are occasional and tied to coffee, wine and stress that she can cut back. Tell: start with avoiding triggers and reassurance; a beta blocker is held for persistent symptoms.

Correct. Occasional early beats with an abnormal P wave and a narrow QRS are premature atrial contractions, and in a normal heart they occur with excess alcohol, stress and caffeine, all present in her month. Management is to counsel avoidance of these precipitants and reassure her about the benign nature of the rhythm.

Anticoagulation is part of managing atrial fibrillation and atrial flutter, guided by stroke risk. She has isolated premature atrial contractions in a normal heart, which carry no such indication. Tell: early beats with a P wave are not fibrillation, and they need counseling rather than anticoagulation.

Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
E.q: A 70-year-old man has claudication after half a block despite six months of supervised exercise, smoking cessation and cilostazol, and can no longer work. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Correct. Revascularization is recommended for claudication with severe functional disability and an inadequate response to exercise or drug therapy, which fits half-block claudication despite six months of supervised exercise, smoking cessation and cilostazol. Endovascular options include angioplasty with or without stenting and atherectomy.

Amputation is the last surgical option, not the next step for a limb without tissue loss. He has disabling claudication after failed exercise and drug therapy, which is the stated indication for revascularization. Restore flow before considering removal.

Intravenous heparin is the medical therapy for acute limb ischemia, the sudden occlusion of a previously patent artery. His problem is chronic, disabling claudication despite six months of exercise and drugs, which calls for revascularization. Acute anticoagulation does not treat chronic disability.

He has already completed six months of supervised exercise with smoking cessation and cilostazol and still cannot work. An inadequate response to exercise or drug therapy with severe functional disability is the indication for revascularization. Repeating a failed program delays the indicated step.

E.q: A 45-year-old woman who drinks four cups of coffee a day feels occasional skipped beats. Her electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm at 78, interrupted by an early beat with an abnormally shaped P wave followed by a narrow QRS. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: A premature ventricular contraction begins in the ventricles and is early, wide and bizarre with no P wave. This early beat is narrow and has its own P wave in front. Tell: a P wave before a narrow early beat places it above the ventricles.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. An early beat with its own abnormally shaped P wave and a narrow QRS, interrupting sinus rhythm at 78, is a premature atrial contraction beginning in the atria. These beats can occur in normal hearts with excess caffeine, stress or alcohol, fitting her four cups of coffee a day.

A premature junctional contraction is early and narrow, but its P wave is inverted in II, III and aVF, buried in the QRS or after the QRS. This beat has an abnormally shaped P wave before the QRS, the atrial pattern. Tell: inverted, hidden or trailing P waves mean junctional; an early, oddly shaped P wave in front means atrial.

A Mobitz type I block is a conduction block, which produces a missing beat rather than an extra early one. Her tracing shows an early beat with its own abnormal P wave and a narrow QRS, which is a premature atrial contraction. Tell: an early extra beat is ectopic; a block drops a beat.

Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
E.q: A 58-year-old man on telemetry develops a run of identical wide QRS complexes at 180 per minute. Within 18 seconds his blood pressure falls to 70/40 and he loses consciousness, and the team shocks him back to sinus rhythm. How should this episode be classified?
opts: Bigeminy alternates one normal beat with one ectopic beat. A continuous run of identical wide complexes at 180 is ventricular tachycardia, defined as 3 or more consecutive premature ventricular contractions. Tell: a run is tachycardia; alternation is bigeminy.

Under 30 seconds counts as non-sustained only when the run does not cause collapse. His 18-second run dropped his pressure to 70/40 and made him lose consciousness, which by definition makes it sustained. Tell: collapse overrides the clock.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Ventricular tachycardia is sustained if it lasts 30 seconds or more or causes hemodynamic collapse in under 30 seconds. His run lasted only 18 seconds, but his pressure fell to 70/40 and he lost consciousness, so it counts as sustained; the identical complexes make it monomorphic.

Ventricular fibrillation has no organized QRS complexes, only uncoordinated activity. Identical wide complexes at a regular 180 are monomorphic ventricular tachycardia. Tell: identical complexes rule out fibrillation.

E.q: A 52-year-old man starts outpatient treatment for deep vein thrombosis with low molecular weight heparin injections overlapped with warfarin. The injections continue for at least five days and until his international normalized ratio is above which value?
opts: Above 1 is too low a target; the overlap of injections with warfarin continues for at least 5 days and until the international normalized ratio is above 2. Stopping at a value just above 1 ends the heparin before warfarin has reached the required level.

Correct. For outpatient treatment, low molecular weight heparin (enoxaparin) or fondaparinux is given for at least 5 days, overlapping with warfarin, until the international normalized ratio (INR) is above 2. Inpatient unfractionated heparin uses the same cutoff, overlapping warfarin until the INR has been above 2 for at least 24 hours.

Above 3 overshoots the threshold. The heparin and warfarin overlap ends after at least 5 days once the international normalized ratio is above 2, so waiting for 3 would extend the injections beyond what is required.

Above 4 is well past the threshold. The overlap continues for at least 5 days and until the international normalized ratio is above 2, the same cutoff used when unfractionated heparin is overlapped with warfarin in hospital.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
E.q: A 67-year-old former smoker with weight loss has a large pericardial effusion. Lung cancer is suspected, and pericardiocentesis is performed. Which study of the pericardial fluid best addresses this suspicion?
opts: Gram stain looks for bacteria and suits suspected purulent pericarditis, not a suspected lung cancer. His smoking history and weight loss point to malignancy, which cytology addresses. Tell: match each fluid study to its suspicion: Gram stain and culture for infection, acid-fast studies for tuberculosis, cytology for cancer.

Cell count and differential are rarely helpful in establishing the diagnosis, so they cannot answer the question of malignancy. Cytology is the fluid study directed at a suspected cancer. Tell: the one fluid test described as rarely helpful is unlikely to be the best answer.

Correct. A former smoker with weight loss and a large effusion raises suspicion of lung cancer, a malignancy to evaluate for in the effusion workup. Of the studies sent on pericardial fluid (cell count, Gram stain, bacterial and fungal culture, acid-fast stain with mycobacterial culture, and cytology), cytology is the one aimed at malignant cells.

Fungal culture looks for a fungal infection, and nothing here suggests one. His smoking, weight loss and large effusion raise suspicion of lung cancer, which cytology addresses. Tell: cultures answer infection questions; cytology answers the cancer question.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following arterial occlusive disease and aortic aneurysm: 2. Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
E.q: A 66-year-old man with a known ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm develops a new diastolic murmur, exertional dyspnea and leg swelling. Which complication does the aneurysm's location explain?
opts: Recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement, with hoarseness, comes from an arch aneurysm. His ascending aneurysm explains aortic regurgitation and heart failure, matching the diastolic murmur, exertional dyspnea and leg swelling. He has no hoarseness.

Correct. An ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm can cause aortic regurgitation and heart failure. That explains his new diastolic murmur, exertional dyspnea and leg swelling, while arch aneurysms cause hoarseness and descending ones cause compression symptoms.

Tracheal compression, with dyspnea, stridor and wheezing, comes from a descending thoracic aneurysm. His ascending location explains aortic regurgitation with heart failure, which fits a diastolic murmur and leg swelling. Stridor would point to the descending aorta.

Esophageal compression with dysphagia is an effect of a descending thoracic aneurysm. An ascending aneurysm produces aortic regurgitation and heart failure, matching his murmur, breathlessness and edema. He has no swallowing complaint.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
E.q: What is the etiology of Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy?
opts: Plaque rupture is exactly what is absent: the syndrome mimics acute coronary syndrome, but angiographic evidence of coronary artery disease or acute plaque rupture is not found. The etiology is unknown. Tell: a ruptured plaque would make it acute coronary syndrome, not Takotsubo.

Viral infection is not the cause; the etiology is unknown, and the recognized risk factor is a significant emotional or physical stressor rather than an illness. Tell: the history to look for is a stressor such as the death of a loved one, bad financial news, a natural disaster or surgery.

Amyloid is not the cause; the dysfunction is transient and regional, principally in the left ventricle, and no deposit is involved. The etiology is unknown, with a significant emotional or physical stressor as the risk factor. Tell: Takotsubo is transient and follows a stressor.

Correct. The etiology of Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy is unknown. What is known is the risk factor, a significant emotional or physical stressor such as the death of a loved one, bad financial news or surgery, and that 90% of cases are postmenopausal women.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following arterial occlusive disease and aortic aneurysm: 2. Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
E.q: A 72-year-old man has an asymptomatic abdominal aortic aneurysm measuring 4.2 cm, unchanged from last year. Which follow-up is most appropriate?
opts: Emergency surgery is for a ruptured aneurysm. His is asymptomatic, 4.2 cm and unchanged from last year, so it is followed with imaging every 6 to 12 months. Nothing in the stem suggests rupture or rapid growth.

Correct. Surveillance frequency depends on size: an aneurysm of 4.0 to 5.4 cm is imaged with ultrasound or computed tomography every 6 to 12 months. His 4.2 cm aneurysm is asymptomatic and unchanged from last year, so it has no growth trigger for repair.

At 4.2 cm and unchanged, he is below every repair trigger: 5.0 cm or larger in women, over 5.5 cm in men, or growth of 0.5 cm in six months. He needs surveillance, not surgery. Check both size and growth before choosing repair.

Three-yearly ultrasound is for aneurysms of 3.0 to 3.9 cm. At 4.2 cm he has crossed into the 4.0 to 5.4 cm range, which shortens the interval to every 6 to 12 months. Crossing 4.0 cm tightens surveillance.

E.q: A 66-year-old woman with dilated cardiomyopathy develops a new holosystolic murmur heard best at the apex that radiates to the left axilla. Her ventricle has continued to enlarge on serial echocardiograms. Which complication best accounts for the new murmur?
opts: Correct. As the ventricle in dilated cardiomyopathy keeps dilating, the valve apparatus is distorted, and mitral regurgitation (which appears earlier) and tricuspid regurgitation commonly develop. Her new holosystolic apical murmur is that mitral regurgitation, and rising end-systolic volumes then drive further dilation.
Outflow obstruction from a thick septum

A thick septum does not fit dilated cardiomyopathy, which increases cardiac mass with little or no wall hypertrophy. Her new murmur is mitral regurgitation from distortion of the valve apparatus. Tell: an enlarging, dilated ventricle stretches the valve rather than obstructing outflow.

Pericardial thickening is not a complication of dilated cardiomyopathy. Her new murmur reflects valve regurgitation from a distorted valve apparatus as the ventricle dilates, with mitral regurgitation appearing earlier. Tell: a new murmur in an enlarging ventricle means a distorted, leaking valve.

Tricuspid regurgitation also develops in dilated cardiomyopathy, but mitral regurgitation appears earlier, matching a new murmur heard best at the apex. Tell: the mitral valve is the first to leak as the ventricle dilates, and her murmur is apical.

E.io: Identify medical care strategies for cardiomyopathies for the following populations. 8. adolescent 9. adult 10. elderly
E.q: A 15-year-old boy is seen for a sports physical. He has no symptoms, but his father was recently diagnosed with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, which is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. Which strategy for this adolescent is most appropriate?
opts: Screening is listed as an adolescent strategy, so waiting until adulthood skips the step meant for his age. Genetic screening for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is the fit. Tell: the age-specific list places genetic screening in adolescence, and he is 15.
An endomyocardial biopsy at this visit

Biopsy is not part of the adolescent strategy, and he has no symptoms. Genetic screening for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is the listed approach for adolescents, with activity restriction if high risk. Tell: an asymptomatic relative is screened, not biopsied.

Correct. Age-specific care for adolescents includes genetic screening for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, which fits a 15-year-old whose father has the autosomal dominant disease. Activity restriction is added for high-risk individuals, with medication for symptoms and an implantable defibrillator in select cases.
A routine chest radiograph each year

A yearly chest radiograph is not among the adolescent strategies. The listed approach is genetic screening for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, with activity restriction for high-risk individuals. Tell: with an affected father and a dominant pattern, the screening tool is genetic.

Deep vein thrombosis 3. Phlebitis a. Thrombophlebitis Septic thrombophlebitis 4. Arteriovenous fistula of the extremity a. Acquired (e.g. trauma, iatrogenic) b. Created (i.e. for hemodialysis) 5. Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
E.q: A 57-year-old man with superficial thrombophlebitis of the calf was started on compresses, elevation and an anti-inflammatory drug. At his recheck nine days later, the tender cord has lengthened and the redness has spread up the leg. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Continuing unchanged ignores the finding that matters: his cord has lengthened and the redness has spread at the 9-day recheck. Worsening signs at that visit call for a repeat duplex ultrasound, and an extensive clot would then justify anticoagulation.
Place an inferior vena cava filter

An inferior vena cava filter is not part of the management of superficial thrombophlebitis, which uses compresses, compression, elevation and anti-inflammatory drugs, with anticoagulation for extensive clot. His worsening signs call for a repeat duplex ultrasound first.

Another four-week wait would leave a worsening clot unassessed. The recheck at 7 to 10 days has already shown progression, and persistence or worsening at that point triggers a repeat duplex ultrasound, not a further delay.

Correct. He had the standard recheck within 7 to 10 days, and the cord has lengthened and the redness spread, so his signs are worsening. Persistence or worsening at that recheck calls for a repeat duplex ultrasound; if it shows extensive clot burden, anticoagulation may be started.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
E.q: A 66-year-old man with subacute endocarditis has a fundoscopic examination that shows Roth spots (white-centered retinal hemorrhages). What process causes these spots?
opts: Hypertensive retinal change is not the mechanism of Roth spots. In endocarditis, Roth spots are white-centered hemorrhages caused by vasculitis affecting the small arteries of the retina. Tell: a white-centered retinal hemorrhage in a patient with endocarditis is a Roth spot from small-vessel vasculitis.

Optic nerve swelling is not what Roth spots are; they are white-centered retinal hemorrhages. The cause is vasculitis affecting the small arteries of the retina. Tell: Roth spots are hemorrhages in the retina, not swelling of the optic nerve.

No trauma or detachment is part of this picture; he has subacute endocarditis with no injury described. Roth spots arise from vasculitis affecting the small arteries of the retina. Tell: in endocarditis, think vasculitis for white-centered retinal hemorrhages.

Correct. Roth spots are white-centered hemorrhages produced by vasculitis affecting the small arteries of the retina. In this man with subacute endocarditis they are the eye finding of the disease, alongside exam findings such as splinter hemorrhages, petechiae, Osler nodes and Janeway lesions.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
E.q: A 35-year-old woman has abrupt-onset palpitations. Her electrocardiogram shows a regular, narrow-complex rhythm at 170, with one P wave of the same abnormal shape before every QRS. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Sinus tachycardia has a uniform, normal P wave before every QRS and runs at over 100 to 160. Her P waves have an abnormal shape and her rate is 170 with an abrupt onset. Tell: the P-wave shape decides it; normal means sinus, consistently abnormal means an ectopic atrial focus.
ruled out by a stated finding

Nodal reentrant tachycardia is a reentry circuit within the atrioventricular node, and its P waves are hidden. She has a visible abnormal P wave before every QRS. Tell: when you can see an abnormal P wave before each QRS, the rhythm is atrial; hidden P waves point to the node.

Multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular, with at least three different P-wave shapes in the same lead, and occurs in acutely ill patients with lung disease or heart failure. Her rhythm is regular with one P-wave shape. Tell: one abnormal shape in a regular rhythm is focal; three or more shapes in an irregular rhythm is multifocal.

Correct. A regular, narrow-complex rhythm at 170 with one consistently abnormal P wave before every QRS comes from a single ectopic focus in the atria outside the sinus node: focal atrial tachycardia. It usually runs at 150 to 250, and most people report abrupt-onset palpitations, as she does.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
E.q: An irregular, wide-complex tachycardia with some rates approaching 300 appears in someone with a known accessory pathway. Which intravenous drug is used?
opts: Correct. An irregular, wide-complex tachycardia with some rates approaching 300 in someone with a known accessory pathway is atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White. When Wolff-Parkinson-White is known, intravenous procainamide is used, and adenosine must never be given.

Intravenous magnesium is not the listed drug for atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White. An irregular, wide tachycardia in someone with a known accessory pathway is treated with intravenous procainamide. Tell: a known pathway plus irregular wide complexes means procainamide.

Adenosine must never be used when Wolff-Parkinson-White is known or atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White appears; it is first line only for ordinary orthodromic reentry. This irregular, wide rhythm with a known accessory pathway is that exception. Tell: a known accessory pathway plus a fast irregular rhythm rules adenosine out.

Atropine is first line for acute, symptomatic, unstable bradycardia, a slow rhythm. This tachycardia already approaches 300, the opposite problem. Tell: atropine is for slow and unstable rhythms; pre-excited atrial fibrillation is treated with procainamide.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
E.q: In sinus arrhythmia, how does the heart rate change with breathing?
opts: A P-wave shape that varies in an irregular rhythm suggests multiple atrial foci, as in multifocal atrial tachycardia, which needs at least three shapes. Sinus arrhythmia keeps uniform P waves, and its rate does change, rising with inspiration and falling with expiration. Tell: in sinus arrhythmia the rate moves and the P wave stays the same.
Faster in both phases of the breath

The rate does not rise throughout the breath; it rises with inspiration and falls with expiration, which is what makes sinus arrhythmia irregular with a pattern. A rate that stayed fast in both phases would simply be a faster sinus rhythm. Tell: the pattern has two directions, up on the way in and down on the way out.
Slower on inspiration, faster on expiration

This reverses the pattern. In sinus arrhythmia the sinus rate rises during inspiration and falls during expiration, with uniform P waves throughout. Tell: inspiration speeds and expiration slows, so the beats crowd together as the breath comes in and spread apart as it goes out.
Faster on inspiration, slower on expiration

Correct. Sinus arrhythmia is a normal, physiologic rhythm that is irregular with a pattern: the rate speeds up with inspiration and slows with expiration. Every beat keeps a uniform P wave and a narrow QRS, and the rate stays within 60 to 100.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
E.q: Which complete blood count pattern is expected in infective endocarditis?
opts: Eosinophilia and macrocytic anemia are not the expected pattern. The complete blood count with differential shows leukocytosis and anemia of chronic disease with a normal mean corpuscular volume. Tell: the anemia is normocytic, so large red cells point elsewhere.

Correct. The complete blood count with differential in infective endocarditis shows leukocytosis and anemia of chronic disease with a normal mean corpuscular volume, that is, a normocytic anemia. Alongside it, urinalysis may show hematuria, proteinuria and pyuria.

Leukopenia with microcytic anemia gets the white count direction and the red cell size wrong. Endocarditis shows leukocytosis with anemia of chronic disease and a normal mean corpuscular volume. Tell: the white count goes up, and the anemia is normocytic, not microcytic.

Polycythemia is not expected; endocarditis causes an anemia of chronic disease with a normal mean corpuscular volume, and the white count is raised (leukocytosis), not normal. Tell: both cell lines move, with white cells up and red cells down.

E.io: Demonstrate understanding of modified Duke diagnostic criteria.
E.q: A 58-year-old man with a prosthetic aortic valve has a fever of 38.6 °C (101.5 °F) and conjunctival petechiae (pinpoint hemorrhages on the conjunctiva). No blood cultures or echocardiogram have been done yet. How is his case classified under the modified Duke criteria?
opts: Correct. He has three minor criteria: a predisposing heart condition (prosthetic aortic valve), fever of 38.6 °C (101.5 °F), above 38 °C, and an embolic phenomenon, conjunctival hemorrhage. With no cultures or echocardiogram there is no major criterion, and three minor criteria make endocarditis possible.

Criteria are met: fever above 38 °C, the prosthetic valve as a predisposing heart condition, and conjunctival hemorrhages as an embolic phenomenon are each a minor criterion. Tell: count every minor item from the history and exam, even before cultures or echocardiography are done.

Definite needs two major criteria, one major plus three minor, or five minor. He has three minor criteria and no major criterion yet, because cultures and echocardiography have not been done. Tell: three minor criteria stop at possible.

Nothing here excludes endocarditis; with no cultures or echocardiogram the workup has barely begun. His three minor criteria make it possible, and blood cultures (three sets from separate sites) and transesophageal echocardiography come next. Tell: ruled out requires evidence against the disease, not missing tests.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following arterial occlusive disease and aortic aneurysm: 2. Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
E.q: A 68-year-old man has a 3.1 cm femoral pseudoaneurysm that has persisted since his catheterization. Which treatment seals the leak?
opts: Correct. His pseudoaneurysm is 3.1 cm, larger than the under-2 cm size that may thrombose and regress spontaneously, and it has persisted. Ultrasound-guided injection of thrombin, which promotes clot, seals the leak. Watch and wait is reserved for those under 2 cm.
Heparin prevents the clotting that seals a pseudoaneurysm cavity. The leak is sealed by ultrasound-guided thrombin injection, which promotes clot. Anticoagulation works against the treatment goal.

Catheter-directed thrombolysis dissolves clot in acute limb ischemia of under 14 days, the opposite of what a pseudoaneurysm needs. A pseudoaneurysm is sealed by promoting clot, with ultrasound-guided thrombin injection. Lysis would keep the leak open.

Watchful waiting is for pseudoaneurysms under 2 cm, which may undergo spontaneous thrombosis and regression. His is 3.1 cm and has persisted since catheterization, so the leak should be sealed with ultrasound-guided thrombin. Size over 2 cm and persistence both argue against waiting.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following arterial occlusive disease and aortic aneurysm: 2. Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
E.q: Carotid angioplasty with stenting is chosen for which patients?
opts: Correct. Carotid angioplasty with stenting is less invasive, most commonly performed through the right or left common femoral artery, so it allows intervention in poor surgical candidates. Carotid endarterectomy, removal of plaque through a surgical incision, remains the gold standard for high-grade stenosis in patients fit for surgery.

Stenosis under 50% is low grade, and both symptomatic and asymptomatic patients with it are managed medically with antiplatelets, comorbidity control and smoking cessation. Stenting is a revascularization option for patients who need intervention but are poor surgical candidates. Low-grade stenosis is not an intervention question.

Asymptomatic disease alone does not trigger intervention: surgery is advised for asymptomatic stenosis only above 80% with a life expectancy over five years, and others are managed medically. Stenting is singled out for poor surgical candidates. The deciding feature is surgical risk, not symptom status.

A life expectancy under five years argues against intervention for asymptomatic stenosis, since surgery there requires a life expectancy over five years. Stenting is chosen because it is less invasive for poor surgical candidates, not because survival is short. Short survival points toward medical management.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
E.q: A 25-year-old woman has newly diagnosed hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with a septum of 2.2 cm and occasional palpitations. Her cardiologist wants to judge her risk of ventricular arrhythmia and sudden cardiac death. Which test assesses that risk?
opts: Catheterization is not required for diagnosis and is obtained when invasive therapy, a pacemaker or surgery, is planned. Arrhythmia and sudden death risk are assessed with 24 to 48 hours of ambulatory electrocardiogram monitoring. Tell: no procedure is planned, so catheterization has no role.

Genetic testing is available in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy but does not influence treatment, and it is not the test for arrhythmia risk. Ambulatory electrocardiogram monitoring for 24 to 48 hours assesses that risk. Tell: to judge ventricular arrhythmia risk, record the rhythm.

Correct. Ambulatory electrocardiogram monitoring for 24 to 48 hours should be performed in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy to assess the risk of ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death, the question her cardiologist is asking. Antiarrhythmics such as amiodarone are then used for sudden death prevention.

A chest radiograph does not record rhythm and cannot grade arrhythmia risk. Ambulatory electrocardiogram monitoring for 24 to 48 hours assesses the risk of ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death. Tell: arrhythmia risk is measured by recording the rhythm.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
E.q: A 29-year-old woman has acute pericarditis with a friction rub (a scratchy, squeaking sound) and widespread ST elevation. Her clinician wants laboratory values that confirm inflammation and can guide the length of therapy. Which pair of tests is most appropriate?
opts: Neither test is in the initial laboratory workup of acute pericarditis, which lists complete blood count, troponins, erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein, with further testing case by case. Tell: the markers of pericardial inflammation in the workup are the sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein.

Pancreatic and liver enzymes do not measure pericardial inflammation; gastritis and peptic ulcer disease are on the differential, but her rub and widespread ST elevation already establish pericarditis. The inflammatory pair in the workup is sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein. Tell: measure the inflammation you have diagnosed.

Correct. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein are the inflammatory markers in the initial laboratory workup of acute pericarditis, alongside a complete blood count and troponins. With her rub and widespread ST elevation confirming the diagnosis, they are the pair that measures the inflammation itself.

Neither appears in the initial laboratory workup for acute pericarditis. Pulmonary embolism is a less common differential, but her rub and widespread ST elevation fit pericarditis, and inflammation is measured with sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein. Tell: pick the markers of inflammation, not of clotting or cardiac strain.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
E.q: A 70-year-old woman with right-sided heart failure has atrial flutter (sawtooth flutter waves) with a ventricular rate of 140. She is alert, with a blood pressure of 124/78 and no chest pain. Which is the most appropriate initial treatment?
opts: Synchronized cardioversion is for hemodynamically unstable atrial flutter, and an elective outpatient cardioversion comes only after 21 days of anticoagulation. She is alert with a normal blood pressure and no chest pain. Tell: stable flutter starts with rate control; instability is what earns the shock.
A beta or calcium channel blocker

Correct. Sawtooth flutter waves with a ventricular rate of 140 in a woman with right-sided heart failure are atrial flutter, and she is alert with a blood pressure of 124/78 and no chest pain, so she is stable. Stable flutter is rate controlled with a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker, though control is harder to achieve than in atrial fibrillation.

A permanent pacemaker treats chronic symptomatic bradycardia, a slow rate. Her flutter has a ventricular rate of 140, which needs slowing with a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker. Tell: a pacemaker does not treat a fast atrial rhythm; ablation is the definitive step for flutter.

Adenosine, repeated once if needed, is the second step for stable supraventricular tachycardia after a vagal maneuver; it is not the listed treatment for atrial flutter. Stable flutter is rate controlled with a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker. Tell: once sawtooth waves are visible, the diagnosis is made and rate control follows.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
E.q: A 55-year-old man has a preoperative electrocardiogram and no symptoms. The rhythm is sinus at 72, the QRS lasts 0.16 seconds, V1 to V3 show an rsR' pattern (a second upward deflection, bunny ears), and there is a slurred S wave in I and aVL. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Left bundle branch block widens the QRS with a dominant S wave (rS) in V1 and monophasic R waves in the lateral leads. An rsR' in V1 to V3 with a slurred S in I and aVL is right bundle branch block. Tell: bunny ears in V1 mean right; a deep S in V1 means left.

Correct. A QRS over 0.12 seconds (here 0.16) with an rsR' pattern (bunny ears) in V1 to V3 and a slurred S wave in I and aVL is right bundle branch block. It is usually asymptomatic, its treatment depends on any underlying condition, and a new block is not always pathological.

Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome does not produce rsR' in V1 to V3 with a slurred S in I and aVL. Those findings, with a QRS of 0.16 seconds, are the criteria for right bundle branch block. Tell: bunny ears in the right precordial leads mean right bundle branch block.

Ventricular tachycardia is a regular wide rhythm at 100 to 250 with no P waves. He is in sinus rhythm at 72, so the wide QRS is a conduction delay, here right bundle branch block. Tell: a wide QRS at a normal sinus rate is a bundle branch block.
ruled out by a stated finding

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. E.q: A 62-year-old man was shocked out of unstable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia 3 days ago and is now stable in sinus rhythm. Which is the most appropriate long-term measure to prevent sudden cardiac death?
opts: Catheter ablation of an accessory pathway does not protect against recurrent ventricular tachycardia. After life-threatening ventricular tachycardia, most patients need an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) for secondary prevention of sudden cardiac death. Tell: the long-term safeguard is a device that shocks.

Correct. He survived unstable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia, so once stabilized he, like most such patients, needs an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) for secondary prevention of sudden cardiac death. Its sensing electrodes detect fatal arrhythmias and it delivers a shock; newer devices can also pace.

A pill-in-the-pocket drug does not prevent sudden cardiac death after life-threatening ventricular tachycardia. Most survivors need an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) for secondary prevention. Tell: protection against a lethal rhythm needs a device that detects and shocks it.

A permanent pacemaker treats slow rhythms and blocks; it cannot shock a recurrence of ventricular tachycardia. He needs an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD), and newer models can also pace. Tell: pacemakers pace slow hearts; defibrillators shock fast ones.

E.q: A 30-year-old marathon runner has no symptoms. A lead II tracing taken at rest is shown; the rate is 48. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Sinus bradycardia, which is also seen in conditioned athletes, keeps a uniform P wave before every QRS with a PR of 0.12 to 0.20 seconds. This tracing shows no P wave before any complex. Tell: same slow rate in the same kind of patient, so look for the P wave; hidden P waves mean junctional.
ruled out by a stated finding

Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular with absent P waves, often at 110 to 160. These complexes are slow, at 48, and evenly spaced. Tell: both lack visible P waves, but a regular slow rhythm is junctional, while fibrillation is irregularly irregular.

Complete atrioventricular block is one cause of a junctional rhythm, and then a permanent pacemaker is needed, but nothing here suggests block: he is an asymptomatic runner with increased vagal tone. The tracing shows regular narrow complexes at 48 with hidden P waves. Tell: the question asks for the rhythm on the strip, and that is junctional.

Correct. The lead II tracing shows evenly spaced, narrow QRS complexes at 48 with no P wave before any of them because the P waves are hidden in the QRS: a junctional rhythm, usually 40 to 60. It can be seen in healthy people with increased vagal tone, such as this well-conditioned runner, and needs no treatment when asymptomatic.
E.alt: Lead II rhythm strip of five narrow complexes at a slow, regular rate, each followed by a T wave, with no P wave visible before any complex

E.q: After a first recurrence of pericarditis, colchicine is typically continued for how long?
opts: Two weeks is far shorter than any colchicine course in the treatment pathway. A first episode gets colchicine for 3 months, and a first recurrence for 6 months or more. Tell: colchicine durations in pericarditis are counted in months, not weeks.

About 3 months is the colchicine course for the initial occurrence of acute pericarditis. After a first recurrence it is lengthened to 6 months or more, alongside nonsteroidal drugs until pain resolves and markers normalize. Tell: first episode 3 months; first recurrence at least 6 months.

Correct. A first recurrence is treated with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs until chest pain resolves and inflammatory markers are normal, plus colchicine for 6 months or more. That is double the 3-month colchicine course used for the initial episode.

Colchicine is not given for life. After a first recurrence it continues for 6 months or more, and a second recurrence adds an interleukin-1 blocker or, with systemic autoimmune disease, prednisone. Tell: the pathway sets a minimum duration and then escalates; it does not prescribe endless colchicine.

E.q: A 74-year-old woman with known aortic atherosclerosis has sudden pain and tenderness of two toes, which have turned blue. Which pulse finding is expected on examination?
opts: A pulse with a double systolic peak

A double-peaked pulse is not a feature described for limb emboli. With atheroembolism, debris lodges in small vessels of muscle and skin and may not occlude large vessels, so distal pulses usually remain palpable. The expected finding is a preserved pulse despite blue toes.

Absent or diminished femoral pulses point to aortoiliac disease, as in Leriche syndrome with claudication and erectile dysfunction. Atheroemboli to the toes usually come with palpable distal pulses. Her problem is in the digits, not the groins.

Correct. Sudden painful blue toes with known aortic atherosclerosis point to atheroembolism. The debris of fibrin, platelets and cholesterol tends to lodge in small vessels of muscle and skin and may not occlude large vessels, so distal pulses usually remain palpable.
Pulses absent below the femoral artery

Absent pulses distal to an occlusion are the finding of acute limb ischemia, usually from a thromboembolus blocking a larger artery. Atheroemboli lodge in small vessels and usually leave distal pulses palpable. Blue toes with pulses means small-vessel debris.

E.q: A 72-year-old man has months of progressive breathlessness, abdominal swelling and bilateral pedal edema. He prefers to sit upright. Jugular venous pressure is raised and he has a Kussmaul sign (jugular venous pressure rises with inspiration), hepatomegaly and ascites. His electrocardiogram shows low voltage (small complexes) in all leads, and echocardiogram shows normal-sized ventricles, marked biatrial enlargement and a preserved ejection fraction. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. Right-sided congestion with normal-sized ventricles, marked biatrial enlargement and a preserved ejection fraction is restrictive cardiomyopathy: impaired diastolic filling with preserved chamber size, both atria enlarged and right heart failure often more prominent. Amyloidosis is the most common cause in the United States.

Dilated cardiomyopathy would show enlarged ventricles, but his are normal in size with a preserved ejection fraction. Restrictive cardiomyopathy keeps chamber size and systolic function reasonably preserved while both atria enlarge. Tell: big atria with normal-sized ventricles is restrictive.

Takotsubo does not fit months of progressive congestion. His normal-sized ventricles, biatrial enlargement and preserved ejection fraction show impaired diastolic filling with preserved chamber size, the restrictive pattern. Tell: a slowly building right-sided picture with big atria is restrictive.

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is not suggested: his ventricles are normal in size and the dominant picture is right-sided congestion with biatrial enlargement. In restrictive cardiomyopathy wall thickness is normal or only slightly increased, and right heart failure is often more prominent. Tell: right-sided failure plus big atria points to restriction.

E.q: A 26-year-old man with suspected viral myocarditis has an elevated troponin and normal coronary arteries. His cardiologist wants to see how much of the heart muscle is inflamed without an invasive procedure. Which test shows the extent of inflammation?
opts: Correct. For this man with suspected viral myocarditis, a raised troponin and normal coronary arteries, gadolinium-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging is the noninvasive test that shows the inflammation: gadolinium improves its visibility and shows its extent. Endomyocardial biopsy, the gold standard, is invasive.
Right heart catheterization with pressure tracings

Catheterization is invasive, which the cardiologist wants to avoid, and in myocarditis angiography is used to rule out coronary ischemia, already done here with normal coronaries. Gadolinium-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging shows the extent of inflammation noninvasively. Tell: noninvasive plus extent of inflammation means gadolinium imaging.

Exercise testing is not part of the myocarditis work-up, and an echo is not the test that shows how much muscle is inflamed. Gadolinium-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging improves visibility of inflammation and shows its extent. Tell: the clue is extent of inflammation, which is what gadolinium adds.
Ambulatory rhythm monitoring for forty-eight hours

Rhythm monitoring records the heart's electrical activity over time and cannot image heart muscle; in myocarditis the electrocardiogram may show sinus tachycardia or arrhythmias but not the extent of inflammation. Gadolinium-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging does. Tell: inflammation is seen on enhanced imaging, not on a rhythm strip.

E.q: A 63-year-old woman is diagnosed with constrictive pericarditis. She had mantle-field radiotherapy for Hodgkin lymphoma 25 years ago and is otherwise well. Which feature of her history most worsens her long-term prognosis?
opts: The lymphoma is cured and is not itself a named predictor; it is the radiation used to treat it that matters, since prior ionizing radiation carries the worst survival in constrictive pericarditis. Tell: look past the old disease to its treatment, because etiology is an important determinant of survival.

Sex is not named among the predictors of outcome. Older age, worse functional class and comorbidities such as renal dysfunction and pulmonary hypertension are, and etiology matters most, with prior ionizing radiation carrying the worst survival. Tell: her radiation history outranks demographics.

Being otherwise well helps her, since comorbidities such as renal dysfunction, pulmonary hypertension, ventricular dysfunction, coronary artery disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and hyponatremia predict a poor long-term outcome. Her prior radiation is what worsens it. Tell: absence of comorbidity is protective.

Correct. Etiology is an important determinant of survival in constrictive pericarditis, and prior ionizing radiation is associated with the worst survival rates. Her mantle-field radiotherapy 25 years ago is therefore the feature that most worsens her outlook.

E.q: A 45-year-old man who grew up in rural Bolivia has months of fatigue and exertional breathlessness. His heart rate is 38 and the electrocardiogram shows P waves completely dissociated from slow, wide QRS complexes. Which infection is a named cause of his conduction disease?
opts: Tuberculosis is not on the list of causes of complete block. Chagas disease is the named parasitic cause, and his upbringing in rural Bolivia points to it. Tell: only one listed infection is a parasite tied to Latin America.

Correct. A heart rate of 38 with P waves dissociated from slow, wide QRS complexes is complete block, and Chagas disease is a named cause. A Latin American parasitic infection, it fits a man raised in rural Bolivia with months of fatigue and exertional breathlessness. Definitive treatment is a permanent pacemaker.

Lyme carditis is a named cause of complete block, but nothing here suggests a tick exposure, while growing up in rural Bolivia points to Chagas disease. Tell: match the infection to the history; Chagas is the parasitic cause on the complete block list.

Malaria is not a named cause of complete heart block. His upbringing in rural Bolivia with complete block points to Chagas disease, the parasitic infection on the list. Tell: the infections on that list are Lyme carditis, Chagas disease and bacterial endocarditis with an abscess.
